  1. Sign-up needs an e-mail address, a name and accepted terms. The answer is the same for new and known addresses. Thus nobody can use it to find accounts. A policy hook that you can replace refuses disposable e-mail domains.
  2. E-mail verification uses a link that you can use one time (valid for 24 hours). It makes a tenant on the public tier with a default project. The new user is the admin of the project.
  3. Identity verification is necessary before any uploaded code. Tenants on the verified tier (allow-listed, M4) can upload code after verification. Public tenants can upload code only after cut line B (planned). Until then, VerificationStatus.uploaded_code_allowed is false for all public tenants.
  4. Deleting a tenant starts a grace period of 7 days. During this period, the tenant is suspended (read-only) and you can cancel the deletion. Then the platform purges each store: database rows, objects, queued work, logs and webhooks. It shows the progress for each store. The platform keeps the audit log (pseudonymised) and the cost ledger (amounts only, for tax law) for their legal retention period.
  5. A GDPR export puts all the data that the tenant stored into one archive. It gives a download link that expires after a short time. A suspended tenant can also ask for it.

docs.title: Labelled data
docs.text:
Each model on modeling-api reads one xr.Dataset. The dataset has variables with named dims, and dims with coordinate labels. Nothing depends on position. Thus the platform can safely reorder, subset and extend the data, and add labels. You can also score data that has its stores in a different sequence than at fit time.

A DataSchema describes such a dataset. It tells what each dim is and what can occur to it at score time. It also tells what each variable means to a model.

docs.title: A schema in one look
docs.text:
layout: dense                       # or: long (one row per observation + *_idx variables)
dims:
  market:  {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
  channel: {kind: categorical, policy: fixed}
  date:    {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: D}
vars:
  revenue: {dims: [market, date], dtype: float64, role: target, units: EUR}
  spend:   {dims: [market, channel, date], dtype: float64, role: spend, units: EUR,
            future_required: true}

docs.title: Dims and their policies
docs.text:
The policy is the most important part of the contract. It tells what a score request can do with a dim.

Policy For At score time Typical errors fixed channels, products, states Only labels from the fit (any subset, any sequence) UNSEEN_LEVELS extend time, observation index New labels after the fitted range, without gaps, up to max_extension NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION, COORD_NOT_ALLOWED, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT new_levels markets, stores, counties, households New labels are permitted. new_level_strategy controls them. UNSEEN_LEVELS when the strategy is error

new_level_strategy tells what a new level becomes:

Strategy Meaning Example hyperprior A new draw from the fitted population distribution, for each posterior draw A new market in a hierarchical MMM: the uncertainty is honest and wider pooled The population average (or an average of fitted levels, weighted by frequency) A new store in an xgboost demand model zero The level adds nothing A new category in a one-hot model error The platform refuses the level The default

Other DimSpec fields:

  • kind: categorical, time, integer, float or index.
  • freq: a pandas frequency for time dims (D, W-SUN, MS). With it, the platform can make forecast coordinates and do a check for gaps.
  • max_extension: the maximum number of periods that a forecast can go past the fit without a new fit.
  • ordered: tells if a categorical dim has a sequence that has a meaning.

Policies only tighten

The schema template of a model declares the least strict policy that the model can use. The schema of your data and the dim_policies of the spec can only make it stricter (fixed is the strictest). If you try to make it less strict, you get DIM_POLICY_LOOSENED.

docs.title: Variables and roles
docs.text:
Field Meaning dims, dtype The shape contract (float64, int64, bool, str, datetime64[ns], …) role What the variable means: target, covariate, media, spend, control, index, mask, constant, weight, exposure units A string in pint style (EUR, units, 1). Steps update it (fx_convert → EUR, scaling → 1), and outputs report it missing forbid (default), allow (NaN is permitted) or mask (a mask variable shows the valid cells) missing_sentinel A code, for example -99.99, that means "missing". core.replace_sentinel changes it to NaN future_required You must supply values over a forecast horizon (planned prices, promotions, budgets) index_of Long layout: this integer variable is the index of that dim (county_idx(obs) → county) bounds The permitted range of values. The platform does a check and reports in plain language

With roles, plugins and plot templates work across datasets. For example, "each spend variable" or "the target over time, one line for each geo".

docs.title: Two layouts for ragged data
docs.text:
Real panels are frequently ragged. For example, households have different numbers of trips, and animals have tracks of different lengths. A schema uses one of two canonical forms. The built-in steps core.to_long and core.to_padded change data from one form to the other.

LongPadded

One row for each observation along an obs dim, plus index variables:

layout: long
dims:
  obs:    {kind: integer, policy: extend}
  county: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
vars:
  log_radon:  {dims: [obs], dtype: float64, role: target}
  county_idx: {dims: [obs], dtype: int64, role: index, index_of: county}

A dense cube plus a mask variable:

dims:
  animal: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: pooled}
  step:   {kind: integer, policy: extend}
vars:
  y:    {dims: [animal, step], dtype: float64, role: target, missing: mask}
  mask: {dims: [animal, step], dtype: bool, role: mask}
ragged:
  - {group_dim: animal, within_dim: step, form: padded, mask_var: mask}

docs.title: Draft a schema from data
docs.text:
infer_schema gives you a schema to start with. Time dims become extend with a frequency that the function finds. Other dims become fixed. Variables become covariate, unless you give a different role.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from mapi_sdk import infer_schema, validate_dataset
from mapi_spec import DimPolicy

days = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=28, freq="D")
markets = ["DE", "FR", "UK"]
channels = ["tv", "search"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
media = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "revenue": (("market", "date"), rng.gamma(50.0, 20.0, (3, 28))),
        "spend": (("market", "channel", "date"), rng.gamma(5.0, 100.0, (3, 2, 28))),
    },
    coords={"market": markets, "channel": channels, "date": days},
)

schema = infer_schema(
    media,
    targets=["revenue"],
    policies={"market": "new_levels"},
    units={"revenue": "EUR", "spend": "EUR"},
)
print(schema.dims["date"].policy, schema.dims["date"].freq)  # extend D
print(schema.dims["channel"].policy)  # fixed
print(schema.vars["revenue"].role)  # target

docs.title: Data checks in plain language
docs.text:
validate_dataset does a check of a dataset against its schema. It describes each problem for a reader who is not an expert. The fit and the score do the same checks and stop if they find errors.

broken = media.copy(deep=True)
broken["revenue"].loc[{"market": ["FR", "UK"], "date": days[10:12]}] = np.nan

for issue in validate_dataset(schema, broken):
    print(issue.severity, issue.code, "-", issue.message)
# error SCHEMA_INVALID - 2 markets are missing 2 days of revenue in March 2026

docs.title: Binding: your names, the model's names
docs.text:
Steps and models use canonical names (geo, time, y, spend). The data.bind of a spec maps these names to the names of your dataset. The bundle stores the binding. The platform reverses the binding on each output. Thus the results use your names.

from mapi_sdk import BindingMap

binding = BindingMap({"dims": {"geo": "market", "time": "date"}, "vars": {"y": "revenue"}})
canonical = binding.apply(media)  # what steps and models see
print(sorted(canonical.dims))  # ['channel', 'geo', 'time']
print(sorted(binding.reverse(canonical).dims))  # ['channel', 'date', 'market'] - your names

data:
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, time: date}     # canonical: yours
    vars: {y: revenue, spend: spend}

docs.title: Side tables
docs.text:
Side tables are small constant datasets that steps read (FX rates, holiday calendars). The spec declares each side table with a policy for score time:

score_policy At score time pinned The exact version from the fit (holidays) latest The latest version of the table supplied The score request must name the table (request.side_tables), for example FX rates for the forecast period

If a step needs a table that does not have sufficient coverage, the step fails with SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE.

A side table that is a tree dataset reads one node, which node names (v0.8): fx: {ref: dataset://growth/reference@latest, node: /fx}.

docs.title: Tree datasets v0.8
docs.text:
A dataset version can also hold an xr.DataTree: a tree of nodes, each with its own variables. Node paths identify the nodes (/ is the root, /instrument/psf a group below /instrument). NetCDF-4 and HDF5 files with groups give trees, and so do versions made from several files. A node sees the coords of the nodes above it. Thus a dim that a node shares with a node above it has the same labels and the same DimSpec.

A TreeSchema describes a tree: one DataSchema for each node. A node without variables (a pure group) has an empty schema.

nodes:
  /:                                # the shared coords, no variables
    dims:
      market: {kind: categorical}
      date:   {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: W-SUN}
  /sales:                           # each node declares the dims that its variables use
    dims:
      market: {kind: categorical}
      date:   {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: W-SUN}
    vars:
      revenue: {dims: [market, date], dtype: float64, role: target, units: EUR}
  /media:
    dims:
      market:  {kind: categorical}
      channel: {kind: categorical}
      date:    {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: W-SUN}
    vars:
      spend: {dims: [market, channel, date], dtype: float64, role: spend, units: EUR}

A model still reads one flat xr.Dataset. The spec selects nodes in data.nodes, and the platform merges their variables into that dataset before the pipeline (TreeSchema.flat statically, mapi_sdk.tree.select_nodes on the arrays). A model that declares capabilities.input = "tree" also gets the whole tree. Refer to Tree datasets, HDF5 and multi-file versions.

docs.title: Wire formats
docs.text:
Format Use API XrJSON Small payloads, curl, TypeScript: the Dataset.to_dict() shape with explicit dtypes and limits mapi_sdk.wire.to_xrjson / from_xrjson zarr zip Datasets and trees as single objects (zarr v3, deterministic bytes, zstd/blosc only). A tree dataset version is a data.tree.zip write_zarr_zip, read_zarr_zip, write_datatree_zip, read_datatree_zip, mapi_sdk.tree.write_tree_zip / read_tree_zip (with the tree limits) Arrow IPC Tidy tables for UI views and plots mapi_sdk.wire.to_arrow_table pickle Never, across all boundaries –

Next: Pipelines and stages.

docs.title: Pipelines, stages and replay
docs.text:
A pipeline is a list of steps in sequence. Each step is a small transform with a version and typed settings. If a step learns something, it also has a fitted state. The promise of the platform is easy to say but difficult to keep:

When you score a model, the platform uses exactly the preprocessing that it learned at fit time. It never fits again.

This page tells about the parts that keep that promise. These parts are stages, the split stage, context tails, inverse transforms and the entry points for scenarios.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
A step has a fit function (it learns, on the training data only) and a transform function (it applies the step and never learns). When possible, a step also has an inverse function. This is a full step from the porting guide:

A scaling step, in full 
from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sdk import Step, StepContext, StepSettings, StepState
from mapi_spec import StepKind
from pydantic import Field, JsonValue


class ScaleSettings(StepSettings):
    vars: list[str]
    over: list[str] = Field(default=[])  # plain defaults: the exported JSON Schema keeps them
    unseen_levels: str = "error"  # error | pooled | fill: what a new level's scale becomes
    fill_value: float = 1.0  # the scale used by 'fill'


class ScaleStep(Step[ScaleSettings, StepState]):
    """Divide each variable by its mean absolute value over `over` (learned on train)."""

    id = "acme.scale"
    version = "1.0.0"
    kind = StepKind.VALUE
    Settings = ScaleSettings
    State = StepState  # stateful: fitted on the training data only
    invertible = True
    var_params = ("vars",)  # settings that name variables ...
    dim_params = ("over",)  # ... and dims, so the control plane can check them
    unseen_levels_param = "unseen_levels"
    effect_template: ClassVar[dict[str, JsonValue]] = {  # static: how the schema changes
        "template_params": ["vars"],
        "updates": {"{*vars as v}": {"units": "1"}},
    }
    summary = "Divide by the mean absolute value over the named dims"  # catalog and UI text
    summary_plain = "Puts each series on a comparable scale"

    def fit(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, ctx: StepContext) -> StepState:
        return StepState(arrays=xr.Dataset({f"scale__{v}": abs(ds[v]).mean(s.over) for v in s.vars}))

    def _scale(self, v: str, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, st: StepState, ctx: StepContext):
        state = st.array(f"scale__{v}")
        return ctx.align_state(state, ds, s.unseen_levels, fill_value=s.fill_value)

    def transform(self, ds, s, st, ctx):  # never learns; skips absent vars (the target at score)
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] / self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

    def inverse(self, ds, s, st, ctx):
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] * self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

Each step has a kind:

Kind Changes Inverted on the way out? Examples reshape Structure: dims, frequency, layout Never resample, to_long, stack, filter_coords value Values of variables that exist Yes, if invertible fx_convert, mean_scale, standardize, log1p feature Adds new variables Not necessary lag, fourier, calendar, one_hot, formula

Each step also has a static schema effect. This is a JSON template that tells how the step changes the schema. For example, it adds a lag dim, sets units to 1, or changes daily date into weekly time. The control plane uses the template to calculate the schema through the full pipeline. It does not run a step to do this.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
A stage is the dataset after a named step. raw is the bound input. Static validation calculates the schema at each stage. Thus you see problems before the platform reads data:

from mapi_plugin_mmm.examples import E33_SPEC_YAML, e33_dataset, e33_raw_schema
from mapi_sdk import default_registry
from mapi_spec import load_model_spec, validate_spec

catalog = default_registry().catalog()  # static JSON: settings schemas + schema effects
data, _ = e33_dataset(weeks=12)
raw_schema = e33_raw_schema(data)

check = validate_spec(load_model_spec(E33_SPEC_YAML), catalog, raw_schema)
rs = check.resolved
for stage, schema in rs.stages.items():
    y, time = schema.vars["y"], schema.dims["time"]
    print(f"{stage:7} time={time.freq:6} y in {y.units:4} vars={', '.join(schema.vars)}")
# raw     time=D      y in LCU  vars=y, spend
# to_eur  time=D      y in EUR  vars=y, spend
# weekly  time=W-SUN  y in EUR  vars=y, spend
# hols    time=W-SUN  y in EUR  vars=y, spend, holiday
print(rs.split_stage)  # weekly: the holdout is cut in whole weeks
print(rs.last_reshape_stage)  # weekly: outputs are reported in weekly EUR, not days

Specs use stages to refer to points in the pipeline:

  • data.split.after_step: the point of the train/holdout split
  • ScoreRequest.inputs_stage: the point where a scenario goes into the pipeline
  • the output space: the stage to which the platform inverts the outputs.

docs.title: Where the split happens
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["raw<br/>daily, LCU"] --> FX["to_eur<br/><i>stateless</i>"]
    FX --> W["weekly<br/><i>stateless reshape</i>"]
    W --> SPLIT{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
    SPLIT -->|train| SC["scale_spend, scale_y<br/><i>learn on train</i>"]
    SPLIT -.->|holdout| SC
    SC --> L["lags<br/><i>context tail</i>"]
    L --> M["model"]
    style SPLIT fill:#5eead4,stroke:#0f766e,color:#1e1b4b

Some dims exist only after preprocessing. For example, you cannot cut a holdout of "the last 8 weeks" from daily data before the data is resampled. Thus the split occurs at a stage. If you do not give after_step, the default is the end of the stateless prefix. The stateless prefix is the first steps that learn nothing (unit conversion, resampling).

If a step that learns runs before the split, it learns its state partly from the holdout. Then the evaluation is too optimistic. Validation reports this:

# standardise the holiday control, then cut the holdout only after that step
leaky = E33_SPEC_YAML.replace("after_step: weekly", "after_step: std_hol").replace(
    "\nmodel:\n",
    "\n  - {id: std_hol, use: core.standardize@^1, with: {vars: [holiday], over: [time]}}\n"
    "\nmodel:\n",
    1,
)
for issue in validate_spec(load_model_spec(leaky), catalog, raw_schema).errors:
    print(issue.code, issue.pointer)
    print("  ", issue.message)
# LEAKAGE_RISK /data/split/after_step
#    stateful step 'std_hol' (pipeline[3]) runs before the split at stage 'std_hol';
#    its state would be learned from holdout data

To change the error to a warning that you accept, set allow_leakage: true on the split.

docs.title: Evaluate the way you will forecast
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit (the default) does these steps:

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Data
    participant P as Pipeline + model
    participant B as Bundles
    D->>P: stateless prefix on all data, then split at the split stage
    P->>P: fit step states + model on TRAIN
    P->>P: score HOLDOUT through the score path<br/>(context tails from train)
    P->>B: evaluation bundle + metrics
    P->>P: refit states + model on ALL data
    P->>B: production bundle (links evaluation + metrics)

The platform never uses a separate code path to score the holdout. The holdout goes through score_bundle, with the context that it would have in production. Then the platform fits all parts again on all the data. Thus forecasts start from the latest context tails and terminal states. train_only stops after the evaluation and keeps the fit on the training data.

docs.title: Context tails: looking back across the fit boundary
docs.text:
Steps that look back in time (lags, carry-over) declare a context need, for example {along: time, n: 6, within: [geo]}. At fit time, the step stores the last n rows of its own input stage, for each group. At score time, the platform does these steps:

  1. It adds the stored rows before the new data, and then transforms the data.
  2. It makes sure that the new data continues the fitted range.
  3. It removes the stored rows from the output.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Fit
        T1["… w49 w50 w51 w52"] --> TAIL["stored tail per geo:<br/>w47–w52 (weekly, scaled)"]
    end
    subgraph Score
        TAIL --> CAT["w47–w52 ‖ w53 w54 w55 w56"]
        NEW["forecast payload<br/>w53–w56"] --> CAT
        CAT --> LAG["lag_tensor"] --> DROP["drop context rows"] --> OUT["w53–w56 with<br/>real carry-over"]
    end

The result is the same as when you transform the full series at one time. The contract kit does a check of this "context-window equivalence" for each step and model. A new market has no tail. Thus the step pads its lags as its settings tell (pad: first).

Sequential models (HMMs, Kalman filters) keep a terminal state in the model instead. Refer to Forecasting.

docs.title: Inverse transforms and the output space
docs.text:
On the way out, the platform reverses the invertible value steps in the opposite sequence. It stops at the last reshape step. A model that is fitted on weekly, scaled EUR returns weekly EUR. The platform can reverse the scaling, but it cannot reverse the weekly resample. Daily values are not available from weekly sums.

Each output records where it stopped:

Attribute Example Meaning output_space {"y_hat": "weekly"} The stage of the values units EUR The units after inversion retransform {"y_hat": "median"} For point models through a non-linear inverse. The inverse of a mean is not a mean. Thus the platform labels the value (or uses Duan smearing)

To skip inversion, ask for output: {units: model}. For example, use this to get contributions that add up exactly through a log1p.

docs.title: Scenarios enter at a stage
docs.text:
A planner must not have to make up daily spend in local currency to ask about a weekly EUR budget. With ScoreRequest.inputs_stage, data can go into the pipeline after a named step. The platform skips the steps before it, and the side tables that these steps need:

mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 8}
inputs_stage: weekly        # send weekly EUR spend; to_eur and the FX table are skipped

The E33 conformance fixture makes sure that this gives exactly the same forecast as the raw daily path for the same spend.

docs.title: Models that own their preprocessing
docs.text: Some models do their own scaling or carry-over (the mmm-framework MMMs do both). These models declare owns: [scaling, carryover, inverse_units] in their capabilities. Then the platform does not apply these steps. The outputs have a label that tells that they are already in the original units. Refer to the mmm-framework models.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
A lag of the target is a recursive feature. If a forecast has more periods than the smallest lag, it needs predictions as inputs. v1 forecasts are direct. Thus the platform refuses such specs with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED, unless the model declares owns: [recursion].

Next: Representations and summaries.

docs.title: Quotas and cost v0.3
docs.text:
Compute is the largest cost risk for a public modelling platform. Examples are an accidental 500-task sweep, a leaked token, or a person who mines on free fits. From v0.3, the platform does these steps for each run:

  1. It estimates the cost of the run before the run starts.
  2. It compares the run with quotas at three levels.
  3. It schedules the run fairly with the work of all other users.
  4. It meters the run into a cost ledger when the run ends.

The contracts are in mapi_spec.quotas, mapi_spec.cost and mapi_spec.admin.

docs.title: Quotas are vCPU-seconds
docs.text:
The platform limits compute in vCPU-seconds, not in runs. A two-minute fit on class S (2 vCPU) uses 240 vCPU-seconds. A five-minute fit on class M (4 vCPU) uses 1,200 vCPU-seconds. Each limit in the table is optional. If a limit is not set, there is no limit at this level.

Limit Kind Notes vcpu_seconds_per_day, vcpu_seconds_per_month Cumulative, UTC day and month The platform compares the limit with the estimate of the run at submit. concurrent_runs Live count Runs between queued and a terminal state max_fanout_tasks Per submission The maximum for one sweep, backtest or SBC (taskCount) max_resource_class Per submission For example, the free tier runs on class S only. The classes are in the sequence S < M < L < XL < GPU (v0.15), so a maximum below GPU refuses the GPU class. By default, only the internal and the self-hosted tiers allow it. storage_bytes Cumulative Dataset versions, uploads in progress and model bundles (the stored objects of all model versions) egress_bytes_per_month Cumulative, UTC month Downloads. This is the size of each object that the API gives a signed link for: dataset and model artifacts, ui/ views, and score and render outputs. It also includes public embed views. The platform charges the bytes when it mints the link. The platform never charges GDPR exports. requests_per_minute Rate API calls

docs.title: Three levels
docs.text:
The platform compares each request with a maximum of three policies. It starts with the most specific policy:

  1. Token: the rate limit and the vCPU-second budget of the token. The person who mints the token sets these values.
  2. Tenant: the policy of the tenant, or the defaults of its trust tier.
  3. Global: platform-wide limits that protect the cloud project. Cloud Run permits 1,000 running executions for each region. The global default stops at 700.

The first limit that a request goes above decides the answer:

Code HTTP When What the client does RATE_LIMITED 429 Too many requests per minute at one level Wait for Retry-After seconds. Then send the request again. QUOTA_EXCEEDED 429 All other limits Read detail to find the level and the limit. If the limit resets with the UTC day or month, the response sets Retry-After.

Cumulative limits stop only the requests that ask for more. A tenant that is above its storage quota can continue to read, download and delete.

from datetime import UTC, datetime

from mapi_spec.quotas import (
    QuotaDemand,
    QuotaLimits,
    QuotaPolicy,
    QuotaScope,
    QuotaUsage,
    evaluate_quota,
)
from mapi_spec.resources import ResourceClass

now = datetime(2026, 10, 15, 22, 0, tzinfo=UTC)
tenant = QuotaPolicy(
    scope=QuotaScope.TENANT,
    subject_id="acme",
    limits=QuotaLimits(vcpu_seconds_per_day=86_400, max_resource_class=ResourceClass.L),
)
used = QuotaUsage(vcpu_seconds_today=85_000)

fit = QuotaDemand(new_runs=1, vcpu_seconds=2_400, resource_class=ResourceClass.M)
decision = evaluate_quota([(tenant, used)], fit, now=now)
print(decision.allowed, decision.code, decision.limit_name)
# False QUOTA_EXCEEDED vcpu_seconds_per_day
print(decision.retry_after_seconds)  # 7200: the UTC day resets in two hours
print(decision.to_problem().status, decision.headers())  # 429 {'Retry-After': '7200'}

The table shows the default tenant limits for each trust tier. Operators can change them for one tenant with PUT /v1/admin/quotas.

Tier vCPU-s / day vCPU-s / month Concurrent runs Fan-out tasks Largest class Requests / min public 3,600 36,000 2 16 S 60 verified 86,400 1,000,000 20 256 L 600 internal — — 100 1,000 — 6,000 self-hosted-trusted — — — — — —

Returned draws. By default, a score request returns a summary and no draws. You can ask for draws with output.draws. Each tier has a maximum (mapi_spec.quotas.MAX_SCORE_DRAWS). The maximum is 300 on public and 500 on all other tiers. If you ask for more, the platform refuses the request with QUOTA_EXCEEDED at /output/draws. This occurs for POST /v1/models/…:score, for an endpoint, and for its …/validate. The score job also contains the maximum, and the runner applies it again.

docs.title: Interactive and batch work
docs.text:
Each run has a priority class:

  • interactive: score, render, derive, validate and describe runs. Usually, a person waits for these runs.
  • batch: fits, ingest, evaluation, optimisation and fan-out parents.

The dispatcher leases queued runs with weighted fair sharing. For each candidate run, it calculates (tenant's running tasks + the run's tasks) / (tenant weight × class weight). The class weight is 4 for interactive and 1 for batch. The dispatcher leases the smallest value first. It continues until it uses all the free capacity, or the Cloud Run jobs.run rate of 180 calls a minute. A tenant with 40 running tasks must wait for the score of an idle tenant. A 200-task SBC uses the remaining capacity and does not stop the work of other tenants:

from datetime import timedelta

from mapi_spec.quotas import LeaseCandidate, PriorityClass, plan_leases

t0 = datetime(2026, 10, 15, tzinfo=UTC)
queue = [
    LeaseCandidate(f"sbc_{i}", "acme", PriorityClass.BATCH, t0 + timedelta(seconds=i))
    for i in range(200)
] + [LeaseCandidate("score_1", "beta", PriorityClass.INTERACTIVE, t0 + timedelta(minutes=5))]

picked = plan_leases(queue, capacity=3, running_tasks={"acme": 40})
print([c.run_id for c in picked])  # ['score_1', 'sbc_0', 'sbc_1']

If the backend answers 429, the dispatcher waits for an exponentially longer time before each new attempt: 1, 2, 4 … 64 seconds. The time is never less than a Retry-After. The dispatcher submits the run one time only when the limit clears.

docs.title: Prices and the cost ledger
docs.text:
The platform calculates the cost of each run from its resource class and its wall time:

  • vCPU-seconds = vCPUs of the class × billed seconds × tasks
  • GiB-seconds = memory of the class × billed seconds × tasks
  • billed seconds = wall time, rounded up to 100 ms
  • accelerator-seconds (v0.15, class GPU only) = accelerators of the class × billed seconds × tasks

The prices come from a versioned price table. The default uses the list prices of Cloud Run: 0.000018 USD for each vCPU-second and 0.000002 USD for each GiB-second. From v0.15 the class GPU also costs 0.0001867 USD for each accelerator-second (the Cloud Run L4 list price; not verified against a GCP bill). A deployment can set its own prices. Unit prices are integer nanos. Amounts are integer micros (1 USD = 1,000,000 micros). Thus, each amount is exact, and you can calculate it again from its ledger row.

Each amount names the version of the price table that the platform used. New prices never change old costs.

from mapi_spec.cost import DEFAULT_PRICE_TABLE, estimate_cost, format_micros

est = estimate_cost(ResourceClass.M, wall_seconds=300)  # an E33-style fit, five minutes on M
print(est.vcpu_seconds, est.gib_seconds)  # 1200.0 4800.0
print(est.amount_micros, format_micros(est.amount_micros, est.currency))  # 31200 0.031200 USD
print(est.price_version == DEFAULT_PRICE_TABLE.version)  # True

sweep = estimate_cost(ResourceClass.S, wall_seconds=120, task_count=50)
print(format_micros(sweep.amount_micros, sweep.currency))  # 0.312000 USD

The cost ledger is append-only. Each finished attempt adds one actual entry. The entry contains the run, the attempt, the resource class, the task count and the wall time. It also contains the vCPU-seconds, the GiB-seconds, the price version and the amount. Operators can add adjustment entries, for example a refund after an infrastructure failure. The cost field of a run combines its entries:

Run.cost field Meaning estimated true until the platform meters the first attempt estimate_micros The estimate that the platform made at submit amount_micros, currency The total at this time, for all attempts vcpu_seconds, gib_seconds The metered usage price_version The price table that the platform used attempts_billed The number of metered attempts usd Kept from v0.2. The amount in dollars when the currency is USD.

GET /v1/usage gives the ledger totals of a project for a UTC day or month. It groups the totals by resource class, day, token or run. It also shows the usage of the project against each quota. Tenant admins see the full tenant at GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/usage. Operators see the cost of each tenant for the full platform at GET /v1/admin/usage. This is the Cost tab of the admin console.

The platform limits retries by cost and by count. After an infrastructure failure, the platform tries the run again automatically only if these two conditions are true:

  • The cost of the run stays below MAPI_AUTO_RETRY_COST_FACTOR (default 2) times its estimate. This cost includes the metered attempts and the attempt that failed.
  • The number of retries is not more than MAPI_MAX_INFRA_RETRIES.

A retry continues from the newest checkpoints that an earlier attempt wrote. If a run used more than 30 minutes, the platform tries it again only with the consent of the user.

docs.title: Kill switches
docs.text:
Operators have two platform-wide switches (PUT /v1/admin/kill-switches). The platform audits each change, and the operator must give a reason:

Switch Effect untrusted_execution_enabled When this switch is off, the platform does not accept or lease runs of plugin code that tenants uploaded. Built-in models continue to work. global_spend_cap_micros When the spend of the platform in the current UTC day (or month) gets to the cap, no new compute starts. Only internal tenants can start compute. The spend is the cost ledger plus the estimates of work that the platform did not meter yet. Admitted runs count at admission. Started runs count one by one at dispatch.

Both switches answer QUOTA_EXCEEDED at the global level. GET /v1/admin/usage returns the spend in the current window of the cap, next to the cap (spend_cap). The admin console shows this spend as a meter that gives a warning at 70% and at 90%. If you think that code escaped the sandbox, turn off untrusted execution. This is the first step of the incident runbook.

docs.title: Representations and summaries
docs.text:
Each model declares its representation. The platform uses the representation to decide which summaries and aggregations it will calculate. One output shape for all models is not correct. A conformal interval is not a distribution. You cannot add per-cell quantiles. A point prediction has no uncertainty to summarise.

Representation Shape Typical models Summaries Aggregate over cells draws (chain, draw, …) joint samples PyMC (MCMC, VI), bootstrap mean, sd, median, hdi_<p>, eti_<p>, q<p> any, per draw quantiles (quantile, …) per cell xgboost / sklearn quantile regression median, q<p>, eti_<p>, point (interpolated, never extrapolated) none interval (bound, …) + alpha split conformal interval, point none point (…) ridge, random forest, classifiers mean, point sum/mean, flagged moments (moment, …) mean and sd analytic Gaussian processes mean, sd, eti_<p>, point none

docs.title: Why aggregation depends on it
docs.text:
The representation controls which aggregations are correct. With joint draws, the total over 40 stores is easy and exact. Add the stores in each draw, then summarise. With quantiles, you cannot do this. The sum of 40 90% quantiles is not the 90% quantile of the sum. The sum is too large, frequently by a large quantity. Also, the quantiles do not tell how the stores change together.

Conformal intervals guarantee the coverage of each cell only. A "summed interval" would claim a coverage that nobody measured.

The rules are data in mapi_spec. The summariser and the API both use these rules:

from mapi_spec import Representation, can_aggregate, default_summary, summary_allowed

for rep in Representation:
    verdict = can_aggregate(rep, ["store"], how="sum")
    print(f"{rep.value:10} sum over stores: {verdict.allowed!s:5} default summary: {default_summary(rep)}")
# draws      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['mean', 'hdi_90']
# quantiles  sum over stores: False default summary: ['median', 'q5', 'q95']
# interval   sum over stores: False default summary: ['point', 'interval']
# point      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['point']
# moments    sum over stores: False default summary: ['mean', 'sd']

print(can_aggregate(Representation.POINT, ["store"]).flagged)  # True: allowed, but labelled
print(can_aggregate(Representation.QUANTILES, ["store"]).reason)
# Quantiles are marginal per cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.
print(summary_allowed(Representation.QUANTILES, "hdi_90"))  # False: no draws to find an HDI
print(summary_allowed(Representation.DRAWS, "q97_5"))  # True

If you ask for an output that the representation cannot supply, the request fails before the platform starts compute:

CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED - cannot aggregate 'quantiles' output: Quantiles are marginal per
cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.

docs.title: Asking for outputs
docs.text:
The output block of a score request is an OutputSelector:

output:
  kind: expected              # expected (the mean response) or predictive (with noise)
  summary: [mean, hdi_90]     # default depends on the representation
  draws: 200                  # also return 200 joint draws (draws representation only)
  aggregate: {over: [store]}  # reduce before summarising, if the representation allows
  units: original             # or: model (skip inverse transforms)
  names: dataset              # or: canonical (skip reverse binding)

The platform parses the summary names. It does not look them up in a list. Examples are hdi_90, eti_80, q5, q97_5, median and sd. If you do not set summary, you get the default of the representation. For draws, the default is mean, hdi_90. For quantiles, the default is median, q5, q95, adapted to the fitted quantile grid.

docs.title: Expected vs predictive
docs.text:
• expected returns the mean response of the model, without observation noise. For PyMC models, this is a Deterministic that the plugin names. Use it for the question "what is the effect of the plan?".
  • predictive returns draws of the observed variable, with noise. Use it for the question "what range of sales must we plan for?".

docs.title: Draws are thinned once, for the whole bundle
docs.text: When a request asks for draws, the draws come from a bundle-wide thinning index. This index uses the same (chain, draw) pairs for all outputs and all derived quantities. Contributions, response curves and predictions from the same draws stay jointly consistent. Thus, a Guided-mode slider that combines them keeps correct uncertainty bands.

docs.title: Counterfactuals share their noise
docs.text: In mode: counterfactual, the platform scores a baseline and a scenario. It returns the baseline/ and delta/ groups. Bayesian plugins use common random numbers. The predictive noise of the two runs is the same draw. Thus, the delta shows the effect of the intervention, not the difference between two independent noise samples.

docs.title: Circular outputs
docs.text:
An angle wraps at one turn. Thus a summary on a line is not correct for an angle. For draws at 350 and 10 degrees, the linear mean is 180 degrees, but the correct mean is 0 degrees. A model can declare an output as circular (OutputDecl.circular, see Capabilities). The model then sets a period attr on the scored array, for example 360 for degrees or 24 for hours.

For a circular output with draws, the summariser uses these rules:

  • mean is the circular mean of the draws.
  • sd is the circular standard deviation, sqrt(-2 ln R).
  • median, each quantile and each interval (hdi_<p>, eti_<p>) come from the deviations of the draws from the circular mean. Thus each interval is centred on the circular mean.
  • Each value is in [0, period). If lower is more than upper, the interval crosses the seam (for example from 350 to 10 degrees).
  • In mode: counterfactual, delta/ is wrapped to [-period/2, period/2).

The holdout metrics of a circular output use the same rules. Each table of summary.json (ScoreSummaryTable) for a circular output has the field period. Thus a reader knows that the statistics are on the circle.

The summary stays on a line if the scored array has no valid period attr, or if the request aggregates the output over a dim. A sum of angles is not an angle. The result then has a warning (CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED, severity warning).

Next: Bundles.

docs.title: Security model v0.4
docs.text:
modeling-api can run models and data from persons that it does not trust, from many organisations on one deployment. All controls that do not need a cloud are in the code, and we test them on a laptop. The cloud controls are also written: Terraform, the Cloud Run Jobs executor, Cloud KMS and authenticated Pub/Sub. We test them against fakes. A short list of cloud behaviours waits for a real project. This page tells what each control protects against, which controls each executor enforces, and the limits that apply today.

A local stack is not a security boundary

make dev and Docker Compose run the dev profile. Any person who can get access to the API can sign in as any seeded account through the built-in development identity provider. All ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not make a local stack available on a network that you do not trust. Do not run untrusted plugin code on a local stack. The local-process and plain docker executors give process isolation, not a multi-tenant boundary.

docs.title: What it protects
docs.text: Asset Threat Main controls The data of each tenant Another tenant, or a bug, reads or changes the data PostgreSQL row-level security, pinned for each transaction, that fails closed. The server makes the storage keys from ids. The server checks roles at each request. Operators never read tenant content. The control plane A hostile dataset, bundle or plot uses a parser in the API to attack it The API parses JSON and YAML only, with a strict loader: no anchors or tags, and limits on size and depth. Only the sandbox of a run opens arrays, zarr, netCDF, CSV and Parquet. Credentials and other runs Model code reads or steals the items that the run holds A new sandbox for each run. A supervisor/worker split. No secrets in the environment or the arguments. A one-time bootstrap object. Short-lived signed URLs for one object each. Results A run forges outputs, replaces an object later, or fakes progress The control plane compares the output claims with the checksums and generations of the store. Write-once bundles. Signed bundle manifests that the platform checks before each download link. HMAC-signed events. The bill A leaked token, a runaway sweep or abuse uses too much compute vCPU-second quotas for each token, tenant and platform. Fair-share scheduling. A global spend cap and a kill switch for uploaded code. The browser and the data of the user A malicious plot spec runs script in the app A server-side sanitizer. Then the plot renders only in a sandboxed iframe on a different origin, with strict CSPs on the two origins. Sessions in HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies with CSRF tokens. The terminal and the screen of the user Log lines or messages with escape codes, HTML or bidi tricks Untrusted text is in a separate field (untrusted_text). The platform removes ANSI, control and bidi characters from it and shows it as text only. Long-term trust in a model Pickle and other formats that execute code Bundles are zarr zips plus JSON. Native models are skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON. The platform refuses pickle on write and on read.

docs.title: Threats, in plain terms
docs.text:
This table gives the threat model of the plan as a user asks about it. Enforced means that the control is in the code and that tests cover it on each change. [verify M0] means that the control is built but depends on a cloud behaviour. We did not yet confirm this behaviour against a real Cloud Run Jobs execution (see the checklist).

If a person tries to… What stops them In v0.4 Break out of the sandbox into the machine A new microVM for each run. The model code runs as its own non-root user with no_new_privs, on a read-only root filesystem. Built for Cloud Run Jobs. The uid split there is [verify M0]. Local executors are not boundaries. Steal the credentials of the run No secret in the environment or the arguments. The run reads its instructions from a one-time object. The supervisor deletes the object before model code starts. The only credential can get and delete that object, and it can do nothing else. Enforced. Locally, the storage emulator enforces the same permissions. Send your data out over the network Deny-all egress, only the address of the Google restricted APIs, and a VPC Service Controls perimeter Terraform is written and tested offline. [verify M0] Send your data out over DNS A DNS response policy that answers nothing outside Google APIs [verify M0]. Until it passes, the platform does not put verified and public tenants on Cloud Run. Crash or take control of the API with a crafted file The API parses only JSON and YAML. A sandbox opens all other files. Enforced Make the sandbox read other files or load code with a crafted HDF5 file (v0.8) The HDF5 guard refuses links to other files, external storage, virtual datasets and filter plugins before a reader opens the file. Enforced Replace or replay the files of a model The control plane compares the outputs with the hashes and generations of the store. It copies them to a location where runs cannot write, and signs them. It checks the signature before each download link. Enforced. We tested Cloud KMS signing against a fake. Fake progress or results Only the supervisor writes events. It signs and numbers each event. The status from the executor decides if a run is alive. Enforced Read the work of another organisation Row-level security on all tables, which fails closed. The server checks ids against the tenant of the caller. A test uses the same pooled connections for two tenants. Enforced Use a leaked token Tokens have a scope and one project. They expire and can have rate limits and budgets. You can revoke them immediately. They never have operator powers. The platform audits failed uses. Enforced Use too much compute, or stop the work of all other users Quotas in vCPU-seconds for each token, tenant and platform. Interactive work goes before batch work. A global spend cap. A switch that stops all uploaded code. Enforced Run script in your browser through a plot A sanitizer, then a sandboxed iframe on a different origin with a strict CSP Enforced Take control of the runner with a malicious package The supervisor runs in its own environment (python -I -S). The platform checks package uploads for .pth and sitecustomize. Supervisor isolation is enforced. Uploaded packages come with the overlay pipeline, which is planned for a later release. Put a hostile item into the supply chain Hash-locked Python, digest-pinned images, a frozen JavaScript lockfile without install scripts, and keyless CI identities Enforced in the builds. Enforcement of signed images (Binary Authorization) comes with public code upload. Use a webhook to attack your network (SSRF) Static URL checks. One DNS resolution, with a check of each address. A connection pinned to the checked address. No redirects. Limits on time and size. The platform refuses private, loopback and link-local addresses and unusual ports. Enforced. Unit tests cover the delivery to public hosts. The multi-tenant profile refuses the development allow-list. Forge or replay a webhook delivery to your receiver An HMAC-SHA256 signature over a timestamp and the raw body. Each webhook has its own secret. The platform shows the secret one time and keeps it sealed. Receivers refuse old timestamps. Envelopes contain ids and states, never data, links or secrets. Enforced (mapi_client.webhooks.verify) Use an embed link to see more than one chart A tokenised link to one saved plot of a platform recipe, stored as a keyed hash. The public view reads no credential and contains only the data of that plot. It has rate limits for each link and each address. It stops on revocation or expiry. Enforced Sign up many workspaces to get free compute E-mail verification. The platform refuses disposable domains. Sign-up limits for each address, each domain and the platform. Operators review Sybil flags. public workspaces run only built-ins and declarative specs (cut line A). They run only on executors that enforce egress and DNS. Enforced. Vendor identity verification and a public run on such an executor wait for a deployment. Keep the data of a tenant after the tenant leaves After a grace period, tenant deletion purges all tables and object prefixes. It sends a notification by signed webhook. A GDPR export with the credentials redacted. Enforced. The platform keeps only the pseudonymised audit log and the cost ledger. Misuse the MCP server Curated tools with delimited untrusted text Not applicable yet. The MCP server is planned for a later release.

The security suite contains the probes that check these rows as hostile code, for each executor.

docs.title: What each executor enforces
docs.text:
Each executor declares its isolation level. It also declares if it enforces egress and DNS. Before each run, the dispatcher compares these values with the trust tier of the tenant. This check is in the code. No tenant setting can make the check less strict.

Executor Isolation Egress / DNS enforced Tenants it can run The security suite must show inproc NONE No Only your own notebook (never through the API) — local-process PROCESS No internal, self-hosted-trusted. It does not start under MAPI_PROFILE=multi-tenant. Platform probes BLOCKED. Sandbox probes can be ALLOWED. docker (runc) PROCESS Only with MAPI_DOCKER_NETWORK=none internal, self-hosted-trusted The same as above docker-gvisor GVISOR when the supervisor can move the worker to its own uid. If not, PROCESS. Only with MAPI_DOCKER_NETWORK=none. This needs an HTTPS bootstrap URL, thus not with the local shim. All tiers, when egress and DNS are enforced All probes BLOCKED cloudrun-jobs MICROVM Egress yes (MAPI_CLOUDRUN_EGRESS_ENFORCED). DNS only when MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED=true, after the M0 DNS check. internal, self-hosted-trusted. verified and public when DNS is enforced. All probes BLOCKED, run in an execution (not connected yet)

All executors share these items, for all isolation levels: the supervisor/worker protocol, the scrubbed worker environment, limits on logs and outputs, HMAC-signed events, and the verification of each output by the control plane. Only the stronger levels add a boundary between the model code and the machine that it runs on.

docs.title: Local development vs production
docs.text: Control make dev Docker Compose Google Cloud (v0.3) Authentication The development IdP: any seeded account, no password. 127.0.0.1 only. The same. Ports are published on 127.0.0.1 only. OIDC for persons (Google or a different provider). Scoped API tokens with budgets for programs. Tenancy Many tenants and row-level security, the same as in production The same The same, on Cloud SQL with a separate database login for each role Run isolation A separate worker process with a scrubbed environment, as your own user (DEV_MODE_ISOLATION) local-process: as above, in a hardened container. docker executor: one container for each run, read-only root, no-new-privileges. The supervisor has only the capabilities that the uid split needs. The worker runs as uid 10001 with no capabilities (MAPI_REQUIRE_ISOLATION). A new Cloud Run Jobs microVM for each run. The worker runs under its own uid with no_new_privs. Read-only root. Network egress from runs Not restricted docker executor: the network namespace of the GCS shim, or an internal network that contains only the shim Deny-all egress, DNS included, in a VPC Service Controls perimeter Object storage permissions The GCS shim enforces permissions for each principal. The credentials of runs can only get and delete their bootstrap object. The same Cloud Storage IAM, with the same layout and principals Bundle signatures EC P-256 with a local key in .local/keys/ EC P-256 with one key on the keys volume. migrate makes the key. It is mounted read-only into api and worker. Cloud KMS, with the same signed bytes Event integrity HMAC for each event, read from the stdout pipe of the supervisor The same HMAC for each event, through Cloud Logging and Pub/Sub push. The events service checks an OIDC token. Web app CSP The Vite dev server does not send the CSP of the app, because hot reload needs inline scripts. The CSP of the plot sandbox is enforced. nginx enforces it, with Trusted Types in report-only mode. Enforced Plot isolation Separate origin (port 5174), sandbox="allow-scripts" Separate origin (port 5174) Separate domain (plots.<domain>) Quotas and cost limits Tier defaults, quotas, the cost ledger and kill switches all apply. The same, plus limits on worker memory, CPU and /tmp The same, with the price table of the deployment

docs.title: The run sandbox
docs.text:
Each run is a pair of processes. An executor starts them and gives them only the run id and a 256-bit nonce. The trusted supervisor uses the nonce to get its instructions from a one-time bootstrap object. The instructions are signed URLs for its inputs and outputs, an event HMAC key, and limits. The supervisor deletes the object before any model code starts. Its storage credential can get and delete bootstrap objects only. It cannot list them.

The worker runs the SDK and the plugin. It gets an allow-listed environment with all MAPI_* variables removed, and its own session. If the supervisor starts as root, the worker also gets a separate uid with no_new_privs and no core dumps. The worker can talk only to the supervisor, in schema-checked frames.

On a laptop, the supervisor is not root. Thus, the worker runs as you, and the run reports DEV_MODE_ISOLATION. All other controls continue to apply: the split, the scrubbed environment, signed events, limits and output verification. But the boundary between your account and the model code is only as strong as the process separation of Python. Think of a local run as the same as a run of the plugin in a notebook.

docs.title: Uploads and the HDF5 guard v0.8
docs.text:
Only an ingest or inspect run in the sandbox opens an upload. The API never parses it. HDF5 (and NetCDF-4, which is HDF5) has features that can make a reader open other files, load code or do work without a limit. Thus, before xarray or h5py opens an HDF5 file, the runner walks the file with the low-level API of h5py. The walk never follows a link. It refuses the file with INGEST_UNSAFE_FILE when the file has:

  • external links, user-defined links, or soft links that do not resolve, make a loop, use .. or point to a group;
  • groups in a loop of hard links;
  • datasets with external raw storage, or virtual datasets (their bytes are in other files);
  • filters other than deflate, shuffle, fletcher32, scaleoffset, nbit and lzf (no szip, no plugins);
  • a user block larger than 64 KiB. The guard looks for the HDF5 superblock at each offset where libhdf5 looks for it. Thus a file that starts with other bytes is still checked. A file that starts with the NetCDF-3 magic is read only by scipy's NetCDF-3 reader, which never calls libhdf5;
  • too many objects or attributes, groups deeper than 32 levels, arrays with too many dims or attribute values that are too large;
  • arrays that declare more bytes than the budget of the run;
  • data types whose size has no limit (variable-length sequences, compound, array, reference and opaque types).

The supervisor also points HDF5_PLUGIN_PATH at an empty directory in the environment of the worker. The inspect run uses the same guard and reads only metadata. Refer to Tree datasets, HDF5 and multi-file versions.

docs.title: Outputs are claims
docs.text:
A run can write only under the prefix of its own attempt, through a POST policy with a size range. When the run finishes, the control plane does not read its outputs. It lists them. It compares the size, CRC32C, MD5 and generation that the store calculated with the signed manifest of the run. If an object is missing, changed or extra, the run fails with INTEGRITY_FAILURE, and the platform sends an alert.

The platform copies verified objects server-side into a write-once bundles bucket. The runs cannot get access to this bucket. The platform signs a bundle manifest that binds the tenant, the run, the hashes and the generation of each destination. The platform mints download links only after it verifies that signature. Each link is pinned to an object generation and expires after 15 minutes. Thus, if you delete the signing key (.local/keys/), you cannot download the existing model versions. This is intentional.

docs.title: Events and liveness
docs.text: Only the supervisor writes the real stdout. Each event line has a sequence number and an HMAC under the key of the run. The control plane verifies the HMAC in constant time. It removes duplicates on (run, attempt, seq). It drops forged lines and counts them as sandbox violations. Events never decide if a run is alive. The status from the executor decides this. Thus, a run cannot stay "running" because it sends messages, and it cannot cause its own stop because it becomes quiet.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
Plot specs come from recipes and plugins, and later from users. Vega and Plotly are large JavaScript libraries. Thus, the platform uses these controls:

  1. The server sanitizes each spec when a run finishes and again at each read. It uses pinned Vega-Lite and Plotly schemas. It permits no URL data, no href encodings, no external images, no tile maps and no prototype keys. It reduces Plotly HTML to b, i, br, sub and sup. It also has limits on size and depth.
  2. Each plot renders in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> (no allow-same-origin) from the origin of the plot sandbox. The CSP has default-src 'none' and scripts from its own origin only. connect-src is limited to its own topojson, and frame-ancestors is set to the app.
  3. Vega runs with the expression interpreter (no eval). It has a loader that refuses all URLs and a text-only tooltip. Plotly uses its strict bundle.
  4. The app and the sandbox use a small, validated postMessage protocol. The app accepts messages only from the window of that iframe, with an opaque origin.

One risk remains. A sandboxed frame can navigate itself and leak the data that the app sent into it. We accept this risk only for the own data of a viewer. Shared and embedded plots (v0.4) render only platform recipes.

docs.title: Untrusted text
docs.text: Log lines, tracebacks and plugin messages go in untrusted_text or LogLine.line, never in detail. The runner removes ANSI, control and bidi characters. The web app shows them as text (ESLint forbids dangerouslySetInnerHTML). The platform treats Monaco hovers as untrusted. The CLI removes escape sequences before it prints.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
• uv.lock locks the Python dependencies with hashes. The build makes container images from the lock with --frozen. Base images are pinned by digest (make docker-pin-check).
  • Build-time guards make an image fail if it contains prohibited items. The control-plane image must not contain numpy, xarray, PyMC, the SDK or a plugin. The import-linter contracts run against the installed packages in the server image build.
  • The web image installs JavaScript dependencies with --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts.
  • The OpenAPI explorer of this documentation site loads a vendored, hash-pinned Redoc bundle. It sends no request outside the site.

docs.title: Known gaps in v0.4
docs.text:
• Cloud behaviours that we did not verify yet. This is all items marked [verify M0] above. The most important item is that the DNS response policy applies to Cloud Run Jobs. Until we confirm it, the executor declares DNS as not enforced. The platform does not put shared tiers on it.
  • The nightly security suite does not run in the cloud yet. The probes run locally and against gVisor. The base images do not contain them, and Terraform defines no probe Job (Security suite).
  • The platform does not store executor conformance reports. Thus, the admin console shows all executors as conformance not passed. You can turn on an executor without a stored report (M2 verification). The platform enforces placement by trust tier in all cases.
  • The browser sign-in does not accept the tokens of Identity Platform yet. Use Google or a different OpenID provider (Authentication).
  • Public workspaces need an enforcing executor. Sign-up makes public workspaces. These run only on docker-gvisor, or on Cloud Run Jobs when we verify its DNS enforcement. A deployment with neither executor cannot run their work. Neither executor ran in the M3 verification (what remains).
  • Identity verification has no vendor integration yet. Operators verify tenants manually (audited), behind the IdentityVerifier protocol.
  • We tested webhook deliveries to the internet only through the development allow-list. Unit tests cover the SSRF policy for public hosts.
  • The built-in /docs and /redoc pages of the API (the FastAPI defaults) load Swagger UI and Redoc from a public CDN. Use the OpenAPI explorer or /openapi.json instead.
  • The Vite dev server does not enforce the CSP of the app (see the table).
  • With the local-process executor, run code runs as the uid of the orchestrator. Thus, it can read the control key of the shim and the bundle-signing key. The orchestrator is non-dumpable and logs a warning at start-up. Run only trusted plugin code in this mode. See Docker Compose.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Plugin upload for allow-listed teams is planned for a later release. It has no release number yet. The platform builds the plugins into hash-pinned overlays, and the contract kit checks them on upload. Public code upload lets all tenants upload their own plugins. It comes only after these items are available:

  • A dedicated overlay build pipeline with a curated package mirror
  • A separate execution project for public tenants
  • Binary Authorization on base images
  • Abuse controls (verification before any code runs)
  • A rehearsed kill-switch drill and an external penetration test
  • The security suite green in the cloud for two weeks

docs.title: Tenancy and authentication v0.3
docs.text:
From v0.3, one deployment serves many organisations. Each organisation is a tenant. In a tenant, the work is in projects. Persons and programs get roles in projects. For each request, the platform does three checks:

  • It authenticates the caller (who calls).
  • It finds the scope (in which project).
  • It authorizes the request (can the caller do this).

One pure function does these checks. The API, the web app and the tests share this function. The contracts are in mapi_spec.tenancy and mapi_spec.tokens. The endpoints are in HTTP API: Multi-tenant API.

Coming from v0.2

A v0.2 install had one tenant and one project, both with the name default, and no sign-in. Each row and storage key already contained the tenant and the project. Thus, v0.3 needs no data migration, and your work is in default/default. MAPI_PROFILE=single-tenant keeps the old behaviour without credentials. The Administration guide gives the practical side of this page: who does what, with screenshots and a tested walkthrough. Authentication tells how to sign in.

docs.title: Tenants and projects
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    T["Tenant <b>acme</b><br/>trust tier · status · data residency<br/><i>billing, isolation and quota boundary</i>"]
    T --> P1["Project <b>growth</b><br/>datasets · specs · runs · models"]
    T --> P2["Project <b>retail</b>"]
    U1(["Ana: runner in growth"]) -.-> P1
    U2(["IT: admin of acme (tenant-wide)"]) -.-> T
    K(["token mapi_7k2m…: bound to growth"]) -.-> P1

A tenant is the unit of billing, isolation and quotas. Postgres enforces the tenant with row-level security on tenant_id in all tables. Each storage key starts with t/{tenant}/. A tenant has these fields:

Field Values Effect Trust tier internal, verified, public, self-hosted-trusted The location where its runs can execute, and its default quotas Status active, suspended, deleting suspended tenants can read, but they cannot change or run items. You cannot get access to deleting tenants. Data residency A multi-region (eu, us, asia) or one region (europe-west1) Runs go only to executors that declare a matching region. Cloud Run Jobs declare their region. The self-hosted executors (local-process, docker, docker-gvisor) declare no region, and the platform does not check them. For these executors, the location of the install is the residency.

The trust tier decides the placement. The dispatcher enforces the placement. Tenant configuration never controls it.

Tier Who The executor must give internal The platform team Process isolation or better self-hosted-trusted One organisation that runs its own install Process isolation or better verified Known customers (identity or card verified) gVisor or a microVM, with egress and DNS enforced public All persons who signed up gVisor or a microVM, with egress and DNS enforced

Thus, the runs of a verified or public tenant never go to the local-process or plain docker executor. The executor must also pass the executor conformance suite and the security suite for its current configuration. An operator records these results (the shared-tier gate). Until an executor qualifies, the platform refuses the runs of those tenants at submission. By default, new tenants are verified.

A project is a workspace in a tenant and the unit of access control. Its id is a short slug that is unique in the tenant. The id is short because it shows in references such as dataset://growth/eu_media_daily.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
There are four project roles. Each role can do all the actions of the role before it:

Role Can viewer Read all items in the project: datasets, specs, runs, logs, models, plots and usage. Validate specs. Mint tokens for themselves. editor Also make and change datasets, specs, workflows and saved plots. runner Also spend compute. Submit, cancel, resume and retry runs. Run and cancel workflows. Score models and endpoints. Render plots. Submit models for governance validation. admin Also manage members, endpoints and their promotion, plugins, webhooks, governance policies and the tokens of other persons. Deprecate validated versions. Delete items.

The runner role is above the editor role intentionally. Compute costs money. Thus, you can let a team member edit a spec, but not start a 200-task sweep.

A membership gives one role, on one project or tenant-wide. It can also give capabilities in addition to the role (v0.5). With reviewer, an editor or a runner can approve or reject model validations that wait for a second person. They can never approve their own submissions, and they can never approve through a token. Project admins have all capabilities implicitly.

A tenant-wide grant applies to the tenant itself and to all projects in it. For the tenant, this includes its name, its member list, its audit log and its bill. In a project, the effective role of a member is the higher role of their tenant-wide grant and their project grant.

The full permission matrix is mapi_spec.tenancy.PERMISSIONS. A test checks each combination of role, action and resource against a table that a different person wrote. In summary:

Resource read create update delete Other tenant viewer (tenant-wide) operator admin (tenant-wide) operator manage (tier, status, residency): operator tenant members viewer (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) — project viewer admin (tenant-wide) admin admin (tenant-wide) — project members viewer admin admin admin — token viewer viewer — viewer (own) manage (tokens of other persons): admin catalog viewer — — — — dataset, spec viewer editor editor admin — run viewer runner runner (v0.11: name, note, tags, metric and param writes. v0.14: media writes, experiments and saved views) — cancel: runner model viewer — — admin run (score): runner endpoint viewer admin admin admin run: runner. promote: admin. plot viewer editor — — run (render): runner plugin viewer admin — admin — embed link viewer editor — editor — webhook admin admin admin admin — workflow (v0.5) viewer editor editor admin run, cancel: runner governance policy (v0.5) viewer admin admin admin tenant-wide policies: admin (tenant-wide) model validation (v0.5) viewer — admin (deprecate) — validate: runner. approve: editor or runner with reviewer, or admin. usage (project) viewer — — — — billing, audit (tenant) admin (tenant-wide) — — — — quotas, kill switches, executors operator — operator operator —

Operators run the platform. They manage tenants, quotas, kill switches and executors. They can read tenant metadata, usage and audit logs. They cannot read tenant content (datasets, specs, models and plots) through the API. No role or flag gives this access.

from mapi_spec.tenancy import Action, ProjectRole, ResourceKind, can

print(can(ProjectRole.EDITOR, Action.UPDATE, ResourceKind.SPEC))  # True
print(can(ProjectRole.EDITOR, Action.CREATE, ResourceKind.RUN))  # False: running costs money
print(can(ProjectRole.RUNNER, Action.CREATE, ResourceKind.RUN))  # True
print(can(ProjectRole.ADMIN, Action.UPDATE, ResourceKind.KILL_SWITCH))  # False: operators only

Experiments and saved views v0.14 have no permissions of their own. They use the permissions of runs: a viewer can read them, and a runner (or a token with runs:write) can make, change and delete them.

docs.title: Who can call
docs.text: Principal How it authenticates Identity User Signs in with OpenID Connect in the browser (issuer, subject) from the identity provider. At the first sign-in, the platform maps it to a platform id usr_…. Token Authorization: Bearer mapi_… The token id tok_…. The token acts as its owner: a user or a service account sa_… (a service token). Internal service Platform identity (for example, the signed OIDC token of Pub/Sub on /internal/events) svc_…. Only internal routes accept it.

docs.title: How a request is authorized
docs.text:
1. Authenticate. The caller uses a session cookie, a bearer token or a service identity. If the credential is missing or not valid, the answer is 401 UNAUTHENTICATED.
  2. Select the project. The project comes from the path, the X-Mapi-Project: <tenant>/<project> header, or the binding of the token (see below).
  3. Resolve roles. The platform gets the tenant-wide and project roles of the caller from the memberships now. For a token, it uses the memberships of the owner. Thus, if you remove a person from a project, their tokens stop working there immediately.
  4. Check the permission. AuthContext.allows(action, resource) applies these rules in this sequence: internal rules, operator rules, the status of the tenant, and the role at the level of the rule. For tokens, it then applies the scopes. If the caller cannot see a resource, the answer is 404. If the caller can see a resource but cannot change it, the answer is 403 FORBIDDEN.
  5. Check quotas. The platform checks quotas before each action that uses compute or storage (see Quotas and cost).
from mapi_spec.tenancy import AuthContext, TenantStatus, TokenPrincipal

token = TokenPrincipal(
    id="tok_01jaf3r1s2t3v4w5x6y7z8a9b0",
    prefix="7k2m9q4x",
    owner_id="usr_01jaf3a9b8c7d6e5f4g3h2j1k0",
    tenant_id="acme",
    project_id="growth",
    scopes=("score:geo-mmm-prod",),
)
ctx = AuthContext(
    principal=token,
    tenant_id="acme",
    project_id="growth",
    role=ProjectRole.ADMIN,  # the owner's role in the project, resolved now
    scopes=frozenset(token.scopes),
)
print(ctx.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # True
print(ctx.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="other"))  # False: not in the scopes
print(ctx.allows("read", "dataset"))  # False: scopes narrow even an admin's token

frozen = ctx.model_copy(update={"tenant_status": TenantStatus.SUSPENDED})
print(frozen.allows("read", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # True: reads still work
print(frozen.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # False

docs.title: Selecting the project
docs.text:
All resources of v0.2 (datasets, specs, runs, models and plots) are now in a project. Send X-Mapi-Project: acme/growth. If there is only one possible tenant, you can send only X-Mapi-Project: growth. Tokens have a binding to one project and do not need the header. If a token names a different project, the answer is 403 FORBIDDEN. A local single-tenant install uses default/default.

A token has a binding to one project. Thus, it cannot administer its tenant. These actions need a signed-in session: tenant members, the creation or deletion of projects, the tenant audit log and tenant usage. For a token, the answer is 403 FORBIDDEN. This is true for all scopes and all roles of the owner. A token can read its own tenant (GET /v1/tenants/{tenant}) and list its own project.

from mapi_spec.tenancy import resolve_project_scope

print(resolve_project_scope(header="acme/growth"))  # acme/growth
print(resolve_project_scope(header="growth", member_tenants=["acme"]))  # acme/growth
print(resolve_project_scope(token_binding=("acme", "growth")))  # acme/growth

docs.title: API tokens
docs.text:
Programs (the Python client, the CLI and BI exports) use API tokens:

mapi_7k2m9q4x_0123456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstvwxyz072gj7d
     prefix   secret (160 random bits)        checksum
  • Tokens use lowercase Crockford base32 (no i, l, o, u). Thus, you can read a token aloud or type it again without errors.
  • The prefix is public. Lists show the token as mapi_7k2m9q4x_….
  • The platform shows the secret one time, in the response to POST /v1/tokens. The server keeps only an HMAC-SHA256 of the full token under a server-side pepper. It compares tokens in constant time.
  • The checksum is a CRC-32 of the remaining characters. Clients and secret scanners use it to refuse typing errors and random strings, without a request to the server. The checksum finds all single-character typing errors. It also finds each swap of two adjacent characters.
from mapi_spec.errors import MapiError
from mapi_spec.tokens import generate_token, hash_token, parse_token, verify_token_hash

tok = generate_token()
text = str(tok)  # mapi_<8-char prefix>_<32-char secret><7-char checksum>
print(text.startswith("mapi_"), len(text))  # True 53
print(tok.display)  # mapi_<prefix>_…: the only form ever shown again

stored = hash_token(tok, pepper=b"server-side pepper")  # all the server keeps
print(verify_token_hash(text, stored, pepper=b"server-side pepper"))  # True

typo = text[:-1] + ("0" if text[-1] != "0" else "1")
try:
    parse_token(typo)
except MapiError as err:
    print(err.code.value)  # UNAUTHENTICATED: the checksum catches it without a lookup

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
The scopes of a token limit what the token can do. They never add to the role of its owner. The token of an admin with models:read can only read.

Scope Allows models:read Read datasets, specs, runs, models, endpoints, plots, usage and the catalog runs:create models:read, plus submit and cancel runs, score models and endpoints, and render plots score:{target} Score one model by its id, for example score:mdl_01jaf3r1s2t3v4w5x6y7z8a9b0 (POST /v1/models/{id}/versions/{v}:score). score:* covers all models in the project. When endpoints exist, an endpoint alias works in the same way, for example score:geo-mmm-prod. datasets:write Make datasets and add versions plugins:publish Publish and yank plugins (plugin upload is planned for a later release) endpoints:promote Make, promote, roll back and delete endpoints, and read models (CI pipelines). It never overrides a gate. webhooks:manage Manage the webhooks of the project and replay deliveries workflows:write (v0.5) Make workflows and save revisions (workflow-as-code from CI) workflows:run (v0.5) Run and cancel workflows, and manage their schedules and triggers models:validate (v0.5) Submit model versions for governance validation, and read policies. It never approves. policies:manage (v0.5) Make, edit and retire the governance policies of the project (policy-as-code) runs:write (v0.11) models:read, plus change the name, the note and the tags of runs, and log metrics and params to runs. From v0.14, also log images and tables to runs, and make, change and delete experiments and saved run views. Use it for a script that logs business KPIs after a deployment. runs:create does not give these writes. admin All actions that the role of the owner allows, except three: mint tokens, override a promotion gate and approve a validation

No scope lets a token mint tokens. A child token would escape the expiry, budget, rate limit and revocation of its parent. Mint tokens from a signed-in session (mapi login or the browser). To override a promotion gate or approve a model validation, a signed-in person is also necessary. These are human decisions, and the audit log names the person who made them. The generated permissions reference shows all scopes against all actions.

Each token also has an expiry. The default is 90 days, and the maximum is 365 days. A token can also have its own limit of requests per minute and a vCPU-second budget for each day or month. These limits apply in addition to the quotas of the tenant.

docs.title: Signing in from the browser
docs.text:
The web app never holds an OAuth token. The API acts as a backend-for-frontend:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant A as API (/auth)
    participant I as Identity provider
    B->>A: GET /auth/login?return_to=/runs
    A->>A: new state, nonce, PKCE verifier (kept server-side, 10 min)
    A-->>B: 302 to IdP (code_challenge S256, state, nonce) + __Host-mapi_login cookie
    B->>I: sign in
    I-->>B: 302 /auth/callback?code&state
    B->>A: GET /auth/callback (with the login cookie)
    A->>I: exchange code + PKCE verifier
    I-->>A: ID token
    A->>A: check issuer, audience, nonce, expiry; map (issuer, subject) to usr_…
    A-->>B: 302 /runs + __Host-mapi_session (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict)
    B->>A: fetch /v1/... (cookie sent same-site only)
  • The session cookie is HttpOnly, thus scripts cannot read it. It is Secure. It is SameSite=Strict, thus cross-site requests never send it. It is host-only (the __Host- prefix: no Domain, Path=/).
  • A session ends after 2 hours with no activity, or after 12 hours in total. POST /auth/logout ends a session immediately.
  • Requests that change state with the session cookie must also send the CSRF token of the session in X-CSRF-Token. The token comes from the readable __Host-mapi_csrf cookie or from GET /auth/session. If the token is missing, or if the request comes from a different origin, the platform refuses the request.
  • return_to accepts only a path on the same origin. Thus, an attacker cannot use the login flow as an open redirect.
  • GET /auth/session tells the web app if it is signed in. authenticated: false is a usual 200 answer.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
The platform writes actions that are important for security to an append-only audit log. These actions are:

  • Sign-ins
  • Token creation and revocation
  • Changes to memberships and projects
  • Changes to quotas and kill switches
  • Artifact links that the platform mints
  • Quota denials and refused run events
  • Changes to the name, the note or the tags of a run (run.update, v0.11). The entry names the changed fields and the number of tags. It never contains the text of the note.
  • Metrics and params that a person or a script logged through the API (run.log, v0.11). The entry gives the number of points or params. From v0.14, also images and tables (media and kind).
  • Changes to experiments (experiment.create, experiment.update and experiment.delete, v0.14). A bulk move of runs is an experiment.update with the number of runs added and removed.
  • Changes to saved run views (run_view.save and run_view.delete, v0.14).

Each entry records the platform id of the actor, the action, the resource, the result and a problem code. The platform keeps client IP addresses and user agents only as keyed HMACs. Thus, you can correlate entries, but you cannot get the original values back. Tenant admins read the log of their tenant at GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/audit. Operators read all entries at GET /v1/admin/audit.

docs.title: Workflows v0.5
docs.text:
