Where What HTTP API reference Conventions, errors, pagination, idempotency, SSE and all the endpoints with their DTOs OpenAPI explorer The OpenAPI 3.1 document, which you can browse, with all the schemas and examples GET /openapi.json on a running API The same document, from the API Error codes All the stable error codes and their HTTP status

First, start the stack and load the demo (see the quickstart):

  1. Run make dev.
  2. Run make seed.
  3. Run uv run python scripts/seed.py --export demo/.
  4. Run uv run mapi datasets upload demo/eu_media_future.zarr.zip --name eu_media_future.

From v0.3, make dev needs sign-in. Set MAPI_TOKEN to an API token. You get the token from the Tokens page of the web app, or from mapi tokens create. Set MAPI_PROJECT to the <tenant>/<project> for the token. The api function of the script then adds Authorization: Bearer … and X-Mapi-Project to each API call. It never sends them to signed storage URLs, because these URLs have their own authorization. See authentication.

docs.title: Health and the catalog
docs.text:
API=${MAPI_API_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:8000}
api() {  # curl the API; signed in when MAPI_TOKEN is set (every multi-tenant stack, v0.3)
  if [ -n "${MAPI_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
    curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" \
      -H "X-Mapi-Project: ${MAPI_PROJECT:-default/default}" "$@"
  else
    curl -s "$@"
  fi
}
curl -s "$API/readyz" | jq -c '{status, version, checks: .checks | map_values(.status)}'
api "$API/v1/catalog/models" \
  | jq -r '.items[].manifest | "\(.id)@\(.version)  \(.capabilities.representation)"'

{"status":"ok","version":"0.15.0","checks":{"postgres":"ok","object_store":"ok","catalog":"ok"}}
mmm.bayesian@1.0.0  draws
mmm.frequentist@1.0.0  draws
sklearn.tabular_bootstrap@1.0.0  draws
…
ts.hsgp_trend@1.0.0  draws

/healthz tells if the process is alive. /readyz checks PostgreSQL, the object store and the catalog. If one of them is not ready, it answers 503 with the same body. The catalog is what the runner image supplies. A sandboxed describe run exports it. The server validates specs against the catalog.

docs.title: Upload a CSV
docs.text:
Data never goes through the API. Do these steps:

  1. Make a dataset.
  2. Ask for an upload session.
  3. PUT the bytes to the signed URL that the session gives.
DS=$(api "$API/v1/datasets?limit=200" | jq -r '.items[] | select(.name == "weekly_sales") | .id')
if [ -z "$DS" ]; then
  DS=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/datasets" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name": "weekly_sales", "description": "a CSV upload from the HTTP guide"}' | jq -r .id)
fi
echo "dataset $DS"
printf 'week,sales\n2026-01-04,120\n2026-01-11,131\n2026-01-18,127\n2026-01-25,140\n' > sales.csv
SIZE=$(wc -c < sales.csv | tr -d ' ')
UP=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/datasets/$DS/uploads" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"filename\": \"sales.csv\", \"content_type\": \"text/csv\", \"size_bytes\": $SIZE}")
HEADERS=()  # the signed URL binds these headers: send them exactly
while IFS= read -r h; do HEADERS+=(-H "$h"); done \
  < <(jq -r '.upload.headers | to_entries[] | "\(.key): \(.value)"' <<<"$UP")
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'PUT %{http_code}\n' -X PUT "${HEADERS[@]}" \
  --data-binary @sales.csv "$(jq -r .upload.url <<<"$UP")"

dataset ds_01m4zy65cdbxtaa4vgsvpeb4rt
PUT 200

The URL is a V4-style signed URL for one object in the quarantine bucket. It is valid for one hour. Send the headers from upload.headers exactly, because they are part of the signature:

  • content-type must be the type that you declared.
  • x-goog-content-length-range limits the size to size_bytes.
  • x-goog-if-generation-match: 0 makes the object write-once. Thus the storage refuses a second PUT to the same URL.

Then change the upload into a dataset version. For CSV and Parquet, the mapping gives the column of each dim and variable. It also gives its kind, its score-time policy and its role:

MAPPING='{
  "format": "csv",
  "dims": {"week": {"column": "week", "spec": {"kind": "time", "policy": "extend", "freq": "W-SUN"}}},
  "vars": {"sales": {"column": "sales", "role": "target", "units": "units"}}
}'
DV=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/datasets/$DS/versions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -d "{\"upload_id\": $(jq .id <<<"$UP"), \"mapping\": $MAPPING}")
V=$(jq -r .version <<<"$DV")
STATUS=ingesting
while [ "$STATUS" = ingesting ]; do  # a sandboxed ingest run parses and checks the file
  sleep 1
  STATUS=$(api "$API/v1/datasets/$DS/versions/$V" | jq -r '.status // "ingesting"')
done
api "$API/v1/datasets/$DS/versions/$V" | jq '{ref, status, dims: .data_schema.dims | keys}'

{
  "ref": "dataset://default/weekly_sales@v1",
  "status": "ready",
  "dims": ["week"]
}

POST …/versions answers 202 with the version in status ingesting. The answer also has the id of the sandboxed ingest run that parses the file. The call accepts an Idempotency-Key. If you send the request again with the same key and body, you get the same version. The platform does not ingest the file two times.

docs.title: Validate and fit a spec
docs.text:
jq -Rs '{yaml: .}' demo/eu-geo-mmm.yaml \
  | api -X POST "$API/v1/specs:validate" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | jq '{valid, issues: [.issues[] | {code, pointer}], stages: [.stages[] | .name]}'

{
  "valid": true,
  "issues": [],
  "stages": ["raw", "to_eur", "weekly", "scale_spend", "scale_y", "lags", "season", "hols"]
}

POST /v1/specs:validate answers 200, also for a spec that is not valid. The result is in valid. Each problem is in issues with its code and JSON pointer. The server uses non-2xx statuses only for requests that it cannot validate. Examples are YAML that it cannot parse, or a request that is too large.

SPEC=$(api "$API/v1/specs?limit=200" | jq -c '.items[] | select(.name == "eu-geo-mmm")')
RUN=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/runs" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -d "{\"kind\": \"fit\", \"spec_id\": $(jq .id <<<"$SPEC"), \"revision\": $(jq .latest_revision <<<"$SPEC")}" \
  | jq -r .id)
echo "run $RUN"

POST /v1/runs answers 201 with the run in state created or queued. If you send the same Idempotency-Key with the same body, the answer is 200 with the same run. If you send it with a different body, the answer is 409 IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT. Make one key for each user intent. Use the same key again when you try again.

docs.title: Follow the run
docs.text:
# server-sent events: a snapshot, the persisted events, live progress, then `end`
api -N -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/events" | grep '^event:' | uniq -c
api "$API/v1/runs/$RUN" | jq '{state, output_model_version_id}'

   3 event: snapshot
   1 event: state
   1 event: warning
   2 event: state
   6 event: progress
   1 event: state
   5 event: diagnostic
   3 event: metric
   1 event: state
   1 event: complete
   1 event: state
   2 event: snapshot
   1 event: end
{
  "state": "succeeded",
  "output_model_version_id": "mv_01m4zy6yc82qy97jzjmv9phv1j"
}

With Accept: text/event-stream, the events endpoint is a live stream. It sends these items:

  1. A snapshot of the run.
  2. The persisted events. Each event has an id:.
  3. Live progress and log frames. These have no id, and the server never sends them again. From v0.11, live tracking frames tell that the metrics, the params or the tags of the run changed.
  4. A new snapshot at each change of state.
  5. end when the run is terminal. Then the server closes the stream.

To continue exactly after the last persisted event, connect again with Last-Event-ID: <id>. Without that Accept header, the same URL gives the persisted events as a JSON page. See Run events.

docs.title: Read the model version
docs.text:
MODEL=$(api "$API/v1/models?limit=200" | jq -c '.items[] | select(.name == "eu-geo-mmm")')
M=$(jq -r .id <<<"$MODEL")
MV=$(jq -r .latest_version <<<"$MODEL")
api "$API/v1/models/$M/versions/$MV" \
  | jq '{ref, scorecard: .scorecard.overall, metrics, signed: .manifest.signature.alg}'

{
  "ref": "model://default/eu-geo-mmm@v1",
  "scorecard": "warn",
  "metrics": {"mape": 7.59, "elpd_loo": 183.47, "coverage_90": 0.875},
  "signed": "KMS-EC-P256-SHA256"
}

GET …/artifacts/{name} gives a signed GET URL for a bundle object or a ui/ view. The server makes the link only after it verifies the signed manifest of the version. Each link is pinned to an object generation. It supports HTTP Range requests and expires after 15 minutes.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
RES=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/models/$M/versions/$MV:score" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Prefer: wait=60' -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -d '{"request": {
        "apiVersion": "mapi/v1", "kind": "ScoreRequest",
        "model": "model://default/eu-geo-mmm@latest",
        "mode": "forecast",
        "horizon": {"dim": "time", "periods": 8},
        "data": "dataset://default/eu_media_future@latest",
        "side_tables": {"fx": "dataset://default/fx_daily@latest"}}}')
jq '{done, state: .run.state, outputs: [.outputs[] | {name, size, crc32c}]}' <<<"$RES"
curl -s "$(jq -r '.outputs[] | select(.name == "result.json") | .url' <<<"$RES")" \
  | jq '{mode, representation, output_space}'

{
  "done": true,
  "state": "succeeded",
  "outputs": [
    {"name": "plots.json", "size": 4122, "crc32c": "d8PGZA=="},
    {"name": "result.json", "size": 406, "crc32c": "PonvmQ=="},
    {"name": "score.zarr.zip", "size": 9396, "crc32c": "Uwymhw=="},
    {"name": "ui/summary.arrow", "size": 27266, "crc32c": "hxiS8w=="}
  ]
}
{
  "mode": "forecast",
  "representation": "draws",
  "output_space": {"contributions": "weekly", "y_hat": "weekly"}
}

Prefer: wait=60 keeps the request open until the score run finishes, for a maximum of 60 seconds. Then it answers 200 with done: true and signed links to the outputs. If the run takes more time, the answer is 202 with done: false. In this case, do one of these steps:

  • To get the result of the same run, send the request again with the same Idempotency-Key.
  • Follow the run.

The response header Preference-Applied tells which wait the server used. Over HTTP, the ScoreRequest needs its apiVersion and kind. The Python client fills them in.

The request must give data to score: data, inline values, a scenario dataset or a horizon. If it gives none of them, the server refuses it before a run starts (SCHEMA_INVALID at /data, "the score request has no data").

ui/summary.arrow names its dim columns in the schema metadata mapi.dims (a JSON list). Use this list to find the keys of a row. A dim with numeric labels, for example a grid position in cm, has a numeric type, the same as a statistic. In summary.json, each table of a circular output (OutputDecl.circular) has the field period. Its statistics are then on the circle:

  • mean is the circular mean, and sd is the circular standard deviation.
  • Each interval and quantile is centred on the circular mean.
  • All values are in [0, period). An interval with lower more than upper crosses the seam.

Each table of summary.json also gives dims, the names of its coordinate columns (the columns before the statistics), and time_dim, the dim that is time when there is one. A server that predates these fields leaves them out.

docs.title: Track metrics, params and tags v0.11
docs.text:
A run keeps metrics, params, tags, a name and a note. The model logs most of them while it fits. You can add more, also after the run finished. The writes need the runner role. An API token needs the runs:write scope.

  1. Log a metric point. A point without step is a scalar:

    api -X POST "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/metrics" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"metrics": [{"key": "revenue_lift", "value": 0.042, "labels": {"region": "north"}}]}'

    {"accepted": 1, "duplicates": 0}

  2. Log params. A param does not change: a different value for a stored key gets 409 CONFLICT.

    api -X POST "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/params" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"params": {"analyst": "kim", "holdout_weeks": 8}}'

  3. Set the name, the note and the tags. A tag with the value null is deleted:

    api -X PATCH "$API/v1/runs/$RUN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "weekly sales, adstock 4", "tags": {"stage": "production"}}'

  4. Read the series and the points:

    api "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/metrics" | jq -c '.items[] | {key, labels, last, count}'
api "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/metrics/step_size?max_points=200&label=chain:0" \
  | jq '.series[0].values | length'

  5. Find runs by their metrics and params:

    api -G "$API/v1/runs" --data-urlencode 'filter=metric.rmse < 12' \
  --data-urlencode 'order_by=metric.rmse' --data-urlencode 'column=metric.rmse' \
  | jq -c '.items[] | {id, name, columns}'

In these examples, api is the helper function of http_tour.sh. For all the endpoints and the search grammar, see Run tracking. For the logging API inside a model, see Track metrics, params and tags.

docs.title: Media, experiments and comparison v0.14
docs.text:
1. Log an image to a run. data is the base64 of a PNG or a JPEG file (a maximum of 4 MiB):

    api -X POST "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/media" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"key\": \"holdout_map\", \"kind\": \"image\", \"content_type\": \"image/png\",
       \"data\": \"$(base64 < map.png | tr -d '\n')\"}"

  2. List the media of the run. Each item has a signed url:

    api "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/media-keys" | jq -c '.items[] | {key, labels, count, last_step}'
api "$API/v1/runs/$RUN/media?key=holdout_map" | jq -r '.items[0].url'

  3. Make an experiment and move two runs into it:

    EXP=$(api -X POST "$API/v1/experiments" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "adstock length study"}' | jq -r .id)
api -X POST "$API/v1/experiments/$EXP/runs" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"add\": [\"$RUN\", \"$RUN2\"]}"

    {"added": 2, "removed": 0, "missing": []}

  4. Compare the two runs:

    api -G "$API/v1/run-compare" --data-urlencode "run=$RUN" --data-urlencode "run=$RUN2" \
  | jq -c '.params[] | select(.differs) | {key, values}'

  5. Save a search of the runs table:

    api -X POST "$API/v1/run-views" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\": \"best fits\", \"experiment_id\": \"$EXP\",
       \"query\": {\"filters\": [\"metric.rmse < 12\"], \"order_by\": \"metric.rmse\"}}"

For all the endpoints, see Media, comparison, experiments and saved views.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
api -X POST "$API/v1/models/$M/versions/$MV:score" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"request": {"apiVersion": "mapi/v1", "kind": "ScoreRequest",
       "model": "model://default/eu-geo-mmm@latest", "mode": "filter",
       "data": "dataset://default/eu_media_future@latest"}}' | jq '{status, code, detail}'

{
  "status": 422,
  "code": "MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED",
  "detail": "validation failed with 2 errors; first at /mode: model 'mmm.bayesian@1.0.0' does not support mode 'filter'"
}

Each error is an RFC 7807 problem document (application/problem+json). It has a stable code, an HTTP status, and each individual problem in errors[] with a JSON pointer. Tracebacks and plugin messages show only in an untrusted_text field. Render them as text. The server refused the score request above statically. It did not make a run.

docs.title: Other clients
docs.text: The server makes the OpenAPI document itself. apps/web/scripts/gen_openapi.py writes apps/web/openapi.json, and CI fails if the file and the server do not agree. Thus all OpenAPI generators can make a typed client. The TypeScript client of the web app comes from this method (openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch). For Python, use mapi_client.

docs.title: Image data v0.14
docs.text:
You can upload a folder of small images, such as product photos, shapes or digits, as a dataset. The platform reads the images into one array of 8-bit pixels. Then you can look at the images in the Data Explorer, hold out a part of the images for a test, and classify the images with a model.

An image folder is for small images of the same size, for example a few thousand images of 64 × 64 pixels or smaller. Refer to Limits. For large image sets and images with different sizes, use a collection (v0.15).

See also Spec format: image folders and splits ImageFolderOptions, uint8 and the split kinds Explore a dataset The gallery and the colour images Model catalog tabular.image_logistic and sklearn.multiclass_classifier

docs.title: Prepare the zip
docs.text:
Put the images and a manifest table in one zip file:

shapes.zip
├── manifest.csv
└── images/
    ├── 0001.png
    ├── 0002.png
    └── ...

The manifest has one row for each image. It can be a CSV file, a TSV file or a Parquet file.

path,id,label,split
images/0001.png,0001,circle,train
images/0002.png,0002,square,test
images/0003.png,0003,cross,train
Column Necessary Meaning path Yes The path of the image in the zip, from the root of the zip An id column No A unique name for each image. If there is no id column, the images get the numbers of the rows. A label column No The class of each image, for example circle. The dataset gets a target variable label. A split column No The part of the data for each image, for example train or test Other columns No The ingest keeps them as coordinates of the images

The images can be PNG, JPEG or TIFF files (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .tif, .tiff). They must have 8 bits for each channel.

  • Gray images, palette images and images with transparency are accepted. The ingest removes the transparency (alpha) and changes palette colours to RGB.
  • CMYK and YCbCr images become RGB images.
  • A TIFF file with more than one page: the ingest reads only the first page.
  • The ingest does not turn images that have an EXIF rotation. It uses the pixels as they are in the file.

Caution

Do not upload images with 16 bits for each channel or with floating-point values. The ingest stops with an error. Convert the images to 8 bits first.

docs.title: Upload the zip
docs.text:
In the web app:

  1. Open Datasets and click Upload.
  2. Select the zip file.
  3. For Format, select image folder.
  4. Type the name of the manifest and the names of the columns.
  5. If the images do not have the same size, set Size (height and width) and Resize.
  6. Click Upload.

From Python:

from mapi_client import Client
from mapi_spec import ImageFolderOptions, IngestMapping

api = Client()
mapping = IngestMapping(
    format="image_folder",
    images=ImageFolderOptions(id_column="id", label_column="label", split_column="split"),
)
version = api.datasets.upload("shapes.zip", dataset="shapes", mapping=mapping)

From the command line, write the mapping in a YAML file:

format: image_folder
images:
  manifest: manifest.csv
  path_column: path
  id_column: id
  label_column: label
  split_column: split

mapi datasets upload shapes.zip --name shapes --mapping mapping.yaml

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning manifest manifest.csv The path of the manifest in the zip (.csv, .tsv or .parquet) path_column path The column with the image paths id_column none The column with a unique name for each image label_column none The column with the class of each image split_column none The column with the part of the data (train, test) columns all other columns The other columns to keep. A maximum of 64. var pixels The name of the pixel variable dim image The name of the image dimension. You cannot use sample, chain, draw, quantile, bound, moment, y, x or channel. mode auto gray, rgb or auto. With auto, the dataset is RGB when one or more images have colour. Else it is gray. size none The height and the width (1 to 4096 each) of all images after the ingest resize stretch How to change the size: stretch (change the aspect), crop (cut the centre to the aspect, then change the size) or pad (fit inside the size, then add black pixels). Use it only with size. max_images 20 000 The maximum number of rows of the manifest (1 to 100 000)

Without size, all images must have the same size. If they do not, the error gives the first five images with a different size.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
The ingest makes one dataset with these dimensions and variables:

Name Dimensions Type Contents pixels image, y, x, channel uint8 The pixels, 0 to 255. The role is covariate. label image text The class of each image (only with label_column). The role is target. An empty cell is an empty text. Numbers become text: 3, not 3.0. image coordinate The ids, or the row numbers with the same number of digits (000 to 199) y, x coordinate 0 to height − 1 and 0 to width − 1 channel coordinate gray, or r, g and b path, split and the other columns image coordinate The values of the manifest source_height, source_width image coordinate The size of each image before the resize (only with size)

uint8 is a numeric type of the schema. A model that needs numbers can use pixels directly. Values are whole numbers from 0 to 255.

Note

The name of the image dimension is image, not sample. The platform uses the name sample for draws of a posterior. A dimension with that name would show as draws in the plots and the metrics.

docs.title: Look at the images
docs.text:
The Data Explorer of an image dataset starts with two sections:

  • Gallery shows small pictures (thumbnails) of the images. Click a chip of a label or of a split to show only these images. Click a thumbnail to see a larger picture and the values of the image. When the dataset has more than 240 images, the gallery shows an even sample of each label and split. A note above the gallery tells you this.
  • Images and fields shows one image at a time in the field viewer. Colour images show in colour. The mean image of each class (for example, the mean of all circles) shows below the image.

See Explore a dataset.

docs.title: Hold out images for a test
docs.text:
Two split kinds are for images and other data that has no time order:

  • column uses a column of the data. With the split column of the manifest, the test uses the images with split = test:

    data:
  dataset: dataset://default/shapes@v1
  split:
    kind: column
    dim: image
    column: split
    holdout: [test]

    With train: [train], the fit uses only the train images. Images with other values are not used.

  • stratified holds out the same share of the images of each class, at random:

      split:
    kind: stratified
    dim: image
    by: label
    fraction: 0.25
    seed: 7

    A class with one image stays in the training part. Images with an empty label stay in the training part.

For the full description, see Spec format.

docs.title: Classify the images
docs.text:
tabular.image_logistic is a small Bayesian model for image classes. It changes the pixels to the main patterns of the images (PCA), then it fits a multinomial logistic regression. It gives the probability of each class for each image, with a range.

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: shapes, project: default}
data:
  dataset: dataset://default/shapes@v1
  split: {kind: column, dim: image, column: split, holdout: [test]}
model:
  use: tabular.image_logistic@1
  settings:
    n_components: 16
    downsample: 1
  fit: {engine: nutpie, draws: 500, tune: 500, chains: 2}
evaluate:
  metrics: [accuracy, accuracy_naive, brier, auc]

Name the metrics in evaluate.metrics. The default metrics (rmse, mae, mape) are for numbers, not for classes: without evaluate.metrics the fit gives no holdout metric. The metrics for classes are accuracy, accuracy_naive, accuracy_lift, log_score, brier and auc.

Setting Default Meaning pixels, target, image_dim pixels, label, image The names in the dataset features pca pca (the main patterns) or pixels (the pixels themselves) n_components 16 The number of patterns (2 to 64) downsample 1 Use the mean of blocks of this size before the features (1 to 16) max_features 256 With pixels: the maximum number of pixel values after downsample prior_sigma 1.0 The prior scale of the coefficients class_order sorted The sequence of the classes

The fit logs the parameters of the features and the explained variance. In the run, the Media tab shows two images: the first 8 patterns and the mean image of each class. The plots are the ROC and precision-recall curves for each class, the confusion matrix and the convergence of the chains.

For larger images or more classes, use sklearn.multiclass_classifier on features that you calculate first. See scikit-learn models. From v0.15, the step dl.embed calculates the features with a pretrained network, and the dl models train neural networks. See Deep learning.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Images in one dataset 20 000 by default (max_images), a maximum of 100 000 Pixels in one image 4096 × 4096, from the header of the file, before the ingest reads the image Bytes of one image file 32 MiB Values in pixels 268 435 456 (images × height × width × channels) Bits 8 for each channel Sizes One size for each dataset (use size to make the images the same size)

Before the ingest reads the images, it calculates the number of values. If the number is too large, the ingest stops with an error such as: "The images need 402,653,184 values. The maximum is 268,435,456 (about 21,845 images of this size). Make the images smaller (set size) or use fewer images." Use size to make the images smaller, or upload fewer images.

The ingest also stops with an error when:

  • the manifest is not in the zip, or the ingest cannot read it;
  • a column is not in the manifest (the error gives up to 20 columns of the manifest);
  • two images have the same id;
  • a path is absolute, contains .. or a backslash, or is not in the zip;
  • a file is not a PNG, JPEG or TIFF file, or the image library cannot open it.

An image_folder upload must be the only file of a dataset version. You cannot combine it with other files in one version.

docs.title: Large image sets: collections v0.15
docs.text:
An image collection keeps each image as a file. The platform does not read all images into one array. Use a collection when:

  • you have more images than an image folder can hold (more than 100 000 images, or more than 268 435 456 pixel values);
  • the images have different sizes;
  • you add images to the dataset again and again, and you do not want to upload all images each time;
  • you train a neural network on all images (see Deep learning).

A collection can hold up to 1 000 000 images. Each image is identified by the SHA-256 of its bytes.

docs.title: Prepare the folder
docs.text:
Put the images in a folder. Give the classes in one of two ways:

  • Labels from the folders: put the images of each class in a folder with the name of the class.

    photos/
├── bottle/
│   ├── 0001.jpg
│   └── ...
└── can/
    └── ...

  • A manifest table: a CSV, TSV or Parquet file with one row for each image. The path column gives the path of the image in the folder. The client adds the sha256 column.

    path,label,split
bottle/0001.jpg,bottle,train
can/0007.jpg,can,test

The images can be PNG, JPEG or TIFF files with 8 bits for each channel. The same rules as for an image folder apply (see Prepare the zip).

docs.title: Upload the collection
docs.text:
The client calculates the SHA-256 of each image. Then it asks the server which images the dataset does not have. It uploads only these images, in parts of 256 MB (zip files with no compression). Then it creates the version.

From the command line:

mapi datasets upload-images product_photos ./photos --label-from-folder --size 64x64 --wait
Option Meaning --manifest FILE A manifest table. Without it, the client uses all images in the folder. --label-from-folder The label of each image is the name of its first folder --id-column, --label-column, --split-column, --path-column The columns of the manifest --size HxW, --resize The size that samples and models use by default (stretch, crop or pad) --mode auto, gray or rgb --base-version N, --no-base The version to compare with (default: the latest ready collection version) --part-size The size of each part (default 256MB) --state FILE The file that records the uploaded parts (to continue later) --wait Wait until the version is ready

To see the number of new images before you upload, use mapi datasets missing-images product_photos ./photos.

From Python:

from pathlib import Path

from mapi_client import Client
from mapi_spec import CollectionOptions

api = Client()
version = api.datasets.upload_collection(
    "product_photos",
    Path("photos"),
    label_from_folder=True,
    options=CollectionOptions(size=(64, 64)),
    wait=True,
)

In the web app:

  1. Open the dataset and click Upload.
  2. Select Folder of images.
  3. Select the folder. If you have a manifest, select it too.
  4. Select how to get the labels: from the folders or from a column.
  5. If necessary, set the size, the mode and the base version.
  6. Click Upload. The app shows the progress of each stage. It calculates the SHA-256 values, finds the missing images, uploads the parts and creates the version.

docs.title: Continue an upload
docs.text:
The upload of a large collection can stop, for example when the network fails. Start the same command again with the same folder:

  • The command line and the Python client read the state file. They skip the parts that the server has. They sign the upload URL again for a part whose URL is expired.
  • In the web app, select the same folder again. The app skips the parts that the server has.

The parts are the same bytes each time that the client builds them. Thus a part that arrived does not need an upload again.

docs.title: Add images to a collection
docs.text:
A new version compares its images with a base version of the same dataset. By default, this is the latest ready collection version. The client uploads only the images that the base version does not have. The new version uses the stored images of the base version for the other images.

  • --base-version 3 compares with version 3.
  • --no-base uploads all images.

The comparison is only with the versions of the same dataset. Images that are in another dataset are uploaded again.

docs.title: What a version holds
docs.text:
A collection version has the layout collection. The version page shows the number of images (new and reused), the classes (the first 10), the splits, the packs, the total size, the range of image sizes and the base version.

Object Contents manifest.parquet One row for each image: the id, the SHA-256, where the bytes are, the size, the format, the label, the split, the path and the other columns collection.json A summary (CollectionInfo): counts, classes, splits, sizes, formats and the packs members.bin The SHA-256 of each image (the server uses it to find missing images) schema.json The schema: pixels(image, y, x, channel) (a virtual variable) and label(image) Packs Zip files with the images. The tenant keeps each pack one time. All versions that use it share it.

The size of a collection version is the size of all the packs that it uses, or the size of its images if that is larger. The storage quota uses this size. A part keeps all its images, also the images that the manifest does not use. Thus put only the images of the manifest in the parts.

The ingest run makes sure that each image in a part has the SHA-256 of its name. It also reads the header of each image and checks the size. Each time a run reads an image, it makes sure that the SHA-256 is correct.

docs.title: Explore a collection
docs.text:
The Data Explorer shows a sample of up to 2000 images (a stratified sample of the labels). The gallery and the field viewer work as for an image folder. The sample has the size of the collection, or the most frequent size with a maximum of 64 × 64.

Other runs that read a collection as a dataset (Data Explorer sections, priors, checks and workflows) read a sample of 5000 images. The sample has the size of the collection, or 64 × 64 if the images do not have one size. The views of a fit read 500 images in the same way. If a sample needs more than 268,435,456 values, the run makes the images smaller and keeps their aspect.

docs.title: Use a collection in a spec
docs.text:
There are two kinds of models:

  • Models that train on batches (dl.cnn_classifier and dl.finetune_classifier) read all images. The loader reads the images from the packs while the model trains.

  • All other models read a sample of the collection as pixels(image, y, x, channel). Set the sample in data.collection:

    data:
  dataset: dataset://default/product_photos@v5
  collection:
    max_samples: 5000     # 1 to 100 000
    size: [32, 32]        # default: the size of the collection
    resize: stretch       # stretch, crop or pad
    mode: auto            # auto, gray or rgb
    stratify: label       # keep the share of each label (null: a uniform sample)
    seed: 7               # default: the fit seed
  split: {kind: column, dim: image, column: split, holdout: [test]}
model:
  use: tabular.image_logistic@1

Validation shows a note with the sample size. A collection has these rules:

  • A collection takes row splits only: column, stratified or leave_group_out.
  • With a model that trains on batches, the spec takes no pipeline steps. Put augmentation in the model settings.
  • Side tables and the inputs of workflows must be datasets, not collections.

docs.title: Limits of collections
docs.text:
Limit Value Images in one version 1 000 000 (max_images: 100 000 by default) Parts in one version 64 new parts Bytes of one part 2 GB − 64 MB (256 MB by default) Images in one part 60 000 Packs that one version reads 128 (new parts and packs of the base version) Size of the manifest upload 256 MB SHA-256 values in one missing-images request 5000 (the client sends more in groups) Classes in collection.json 1000 are listed. The count of the others is other_classes. Sample of data.collection 100 000 images

If a version needs more than 128 packs, upload all images again without a base version (--no-base). The new version then has new, larger packs.

Note

The tenant keeps the packs until the tenant is deleted. A deleted dataset version does not delete its packs, because other versions can use them.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
The known gaps of image collections in v0.15:

  • The client compares images only with a base version of the same dataset.
  • The platform keeps packs until the tenant is deleted.
  • There are no thumbnails for each image. The gallery shows the sample of the ingest.
  • A collection takes no pipeline steps with a model that trains on batches, and no time splits.
  • Workflows and side tables do not take collections.

docs.title: The Integrations hub v0.4
docs.text:
Integrations in the sidebar of the web app (G then I) is where a fitted model goes out of the platform. For example, a spreadsheet scores the model, a dashboard embeds its chart, or your pipeline gets a message when a fit is ready. Each action on these pages is one or two calls of the HTTP API. Integrations tells the concepts: the promotion gate, signed webhooks, and embed links only for platform recipes. Endpoints and webhooks does the same tasks with curl.

The hub has four tabs:

  • Overview: The Guided cards and the entry points for developers.
  • Endpoints.
  • Webhooks.
  • Plots and links.

The last step of Guided mode, Share, goes to the hub. If you make an endpoint or a chart link in that step, the hub lists it immediately. Its Code for this endpoint button opens the snippets of the endpoint. In a project that is locked to Guided mode, the hub stays in the navigation.

docs.title: Overview: connect in a few steps
docs.text:
Three cards cover the usual cases. You do not need to read API documentation:

Card What you get You need Google Sheets The Apps Script that scores an endpoint from a sheet, with the steps to install it. The script reads the rows of a sheet with the name Input, or it uses the example call. The Input sheet has a header row with the dims and inputs of the endpoint, and one row for each coordinate. For a forecast, it has your actuals and the dates to forecast, with the target empty. The card shows a preview. The script writes the summary of the answer (mean and 90% interval for each coordinate) to a sheet with the name Result. Above the summary, it writes a note that tells the conditions of the forecast An endpoint. A token from Create a token. This token can only score that endpoint BI dashboard A read-only embed link that expires, for Looker Studio, Power BI or Notion. Slack shows a link as a card without the chart. For Slack, post the PNG A saved plot of a platform recipe Webhook A signed call to your URL when a model is ready or a run fails The project admin role

Below the cards, For developers has links to these items:

  • The endpoints.
  • Scoped tokens.
  • The interactive API documentation of the server (/docs).
  • The OpenAPI 3.1 document of the server (/openapi.json).

docs.title: Endpoints and aliases
docs.text: The Endpoints tab lists the endpoints of the project. For each endpoint, it shows the alias, the model version that it serves and its revision. It also shows the gate that it passed and the date of the promotion. To open the page of an endpoint, click it.

docs.title: Promoting through the gate
docs.text:
Only project admins can promote.

  1. Click Promote a model.
  2. Type the name of the endpoint, and select a model and a version. The dialog shows the sanity scorecard of the version and the expected gate.
  3. Click Promote. The server decides:

The gate says The dialog What to do Passes The endpoint page opens on the new revision - Needs an override (409 OVERRIDE_REQUIRED) The reasons, each with its check (holdout.mape), and an Override reason field A project admin who is signed in to the app writes the reason and clicks Override and promote. The audit log records the override as endpoint.promote_override. An API token cannot override Blocked (409 PROMOTION_BLOCKED) The reasons. No override The cause is a scorecard that fails, a fit that stopped, a train_only fit or an input change that breaks callers. Repair the cause and promote a new version

The server also checks two things that the app cannot see:

  • The version was fitted again on all the data after its holdout evaluation.
  • Its input contract still agrees with what callers send.

Thus an expected Passes can still come back blocked. Description and evaluation policy sets the EvaluationPolicy of the endpoint. With it, you can accept exploration fits. You can also block, warn about or allow changes to the input contract. If a different person promoted the endpoint while the dialog was open, the server refuses the old revision. The dialog tells you this.

docs.title: An endpoint's page
docs.text:
• Version and history: This shows these items:

    • The version that serves now, with a link to its model page.
    • The person who promoted it, and how.
    • The reasons of the gate.
    • Each promotion and rollback with its reason.

    Roll back goes back to the version of the previous revision. Roll back here goes back to an earlier revision. The two buttons ask for a reason, and the audit log records it. A rollback does not run the gate again, because that version passed it before. Delete endpoint needs you to type the alias. Integrations that call a deleted endpoint get 404.

  • Schema and Try it: This shows the input contract from the time of the promotion. The contract has the score modes, the dim that a forecast extends, and the dimensions and variables. It also shows the example call. To try your own call, edit the call first.

    • Validate runs the static checks of the server (POST …/validate).
    • Score does a real score run (POST …/score with Prefer: wait=30). It needs the runner role.

    A forecasting endpoint also has Your latest actuals and the dates to forecast. This is its input table: the time column, the target and the drivers. The periods after the fit are rows. To use it, do these steps:

    1. Fill the target where you have actuals.
    2. Leave the target empty on the dates to forecast. Use Add a period or Paste from a spreadsheet.
    3. Click Use in the call.

    After Score, a note above the first summary tables tells the conditions of the forecast. Examples are Conditioned on 3 actuals through 1961-03-01 and From the end of the fitted history (Forecasts with actuals).

  • Snippets: Code that is ready to run for Python, TypeScript, curl, R, Apps Script and Notebook. Notebook is a Jupyter or marimo cell that returns an xarray.Dataset. The server makes the code with the example call. The app shows and copies the code exactly as the server wrote it. Each snippet tells what to install first. Snippets never contain a secret. They read the token from MAPI_TOKEN.

Token for this endpoint opens the New token dialog of the Tokens page. Create a score:… token on the Snippets tab opens the same dialog. The dialog is filled for a score:<alias> token. This token can read and score that endpoint and nothing more. Its initial limit is 120 requests each minute.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
The Webhooks tab is for project admins. Other users see why the tab is empty. The tab lists each webhook with its events, its status and its last delivery. New webhook asks for an https URL, a description and the events to send. The platform refuses URLs on private or internal addresses (WEBHOOK_URL_BLOCKED). It tells you this below the URL field.

The app shows the signing secret one time, immediately after you make the webhook. Copy the secret into the configuration of your receiver. The Done button of the dialog stays disabled until you copy the secret, or tick that you stored it. The dialog also shows the lines of code that verify the Mapi-Signature of a delivery.

The page of a webhook has these items:

  • Settings: Enable or disable the webhook, and change its events. Rotate secret makes a new secret. The app shows the new secret one time. The old secret continues to sign for 24 hours.

  • Delivery log: Each try, newest first. For each try, the log shows the event and its status (Delivered, Retrying, Failed, Blocked, Pending). It also shows the try number, the response code of your receiver and the duration.

    • Details shows the error, the next retry and the first KiB of the answer of your receiver, as untrusted text.
    • Replay sends a delivery again.
    • Resend newest sends the newest delivery again. Thus you can check a receiver that you repaired.

    There is no synthetic test event. A new webhook gets its first delivery from the next subscribed event in the project. Examples are a fit or a score that finishes, a version that is ready, or a promotion.

  • A webhook that continues to fail is disabled automatically. This occurs after 20 failed events in a sequence, or after a 410 Gone. The page tells the reason. To enable the webhook again:

    1. Repair the receiver.
    2. Switch the webhook on again on this page, or with mapi webhooks update WEBHOOK_ID --enable. This sets the failure count to zero.

docs.title: Plots and links
docs.text:
The Plots and links tab keeps the plots that you use in reports:

  • Save a model plot selects a model, a version and one of its plots. The Share button in the plot gallery of a model version opens the same dialog, already filled. A saved plot continues to point at that version. Thus a link to it never changes when you fit the model again.
  • Download renders PNG, SVG or PDF in the sandbox. This is a render run, and it needs the runner role. The app monitors slow formats until they finish. It checks the checksum of the file before it saves the file. Plotly figures need kaleido and a Chrome in the runner image. If the server answers MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED, the app disables the Plotly download buttons and shows the reason of the server.
  • Create link makes a read-only link with a token. The link expires after 7 to 365 days, and the default is 30 days. Optionally, you can limit the link to the sites that can frame it (https origins). You can share only plots of the recipes of the platform. For other plots, the app tells why the button is disabled. The app shows the link and its <iframe> code one time. The table below each plot lists its links with their status, expiry and view count. Revoke stops a link immediately. Then viewers see "This link has expired".

See Sharing plots for what the embed page loads and does not load.

docs.title: Sign-up and e-mail verification
docs.text:
If the server allows self-service sign-up, the sign-in screen has a link to Create a workspace (/signup). This page works without a session:

  1. Type a work e-mail and your name. Optionally, type the organisation. The organisation gives the workspace its name.
  2. Accept the terms. The terms of service and the acceptable-use policy open in a new tab. These are /terms and /acceptable-use, or the documents of the installation that VITE_TERMS_URL and VITE_ACCEPTABLE_USE_URL set. The e-mail field refuses disposable e-mail addresses. If sign-up is closed on the server, the page tells you this.
  3. Look at your e-mail (Check your inbox). The answer is the same if the address already has an account or not. The link works one time, for 24 hours. Send the link again replaces the link. On a development server, the page links directly to the mail in the outbox (make outbox).
  4. Open the link. It opens /verify-email, which removes the token from the address bar.
  5. Click Confirm and create my workspace. The app makes a public-tier workspace with a default project, and makes you its admin.
  6. Click Sign in. The usual identity-provider flow starts and opens the new workspace in Guided mode.

If the link expired or you used it before, the page tells you how to get a new link.

docs.title: Settings > Data
docs.text:
Organisation admins find a Data section at the bottom of Settings:

  • Export your data puts all the data that the organisation stored into one archive. You select the items: workspace records (with credentials removed), datasets, model manifests, the audit log and the cost ledger. The page monitors the export and shows Download archive. The link is valid for 15 minutes. For a new link, reload the page. Exports work while the organisation is suspended.
  • Delete the organisation needs you to type the organisation id. The platform suspends the organisation (read-only) immediately and cancels its runs. For 7 days, a banner on each page tells when the purge starts. Cancel the deletion restores the organisation. Then the platform purges each store, and shows the progress for each store. The platform keeps the audit log (pseudonymised) and the cost ledger (amounts only) for their legal retention. See Deleting and exporting data.

docs.title: Admin console additions
docs.text:
Platform operators get these items in Admin:

  • Sign-ups: The review queue of sign-ups that a Sybil heuristic flagged. The heuristic looks for the same network address, the same browser, a repeated address, or a burst from one domain. The queue gives the reasons in plain words. Approve removes the flag. Reject suspends the workspace that the sign-up made. The two buttons need a reason, and the audit log records it.

  • Trust on each tenant row: This shows the e-mail and identity verification of the tenant, and if uploaded code is allowed. Mark identity verified sets the verification, with the method and a reason. You can also withdraw it. The row also shows the status of the deletion for each store. After a failure, use Retry the purge.

  • Promotions: The endpoint promotions that needed attention, across tenants and newest first. These are admin overrides of the scorecard gate, with the reason and the checks that failed. They are also refused promotions: blocked, or with a need for an override. Nothing waits in a queue, because the gate decides each promotion immediately. The rows come from the audit log (endpoint.promote_override, and endpoint.promote with the outcome denied).

docs.title: Marketing-mix models
docs.text:
mapi-plugin-mmm contains the marketing-mix models (MMMs) of the platform. The four models use mmm-framework:

Plugin What it is Use it when mmm.bayesian The Bayesian MMM of mmm-framework, national or hierarchical over geos and products You want the contribution and the return of each channel with honest ranges. You also want business priors and lift tests, what-if answers and budget plans mmm.frequentist The ridge estimator of mmm-framework with bootstrap intervals You need a first result in seconds, or you want to compare many set-ups quickly mmm.nested v0.12 The nested (mediated) model of mmm-framework, national Your channels act through an intermediate measure, such as visits or awareness, and you want to know how much of each effect goes through it mmm.multivariate v0.12 The multivariate-outcome model of mmm-framework, national One budget acts on two or more results, such as the sales of related products

The plugins register through the mapi.models entry point. Thus a spec only gives their names: use: mmm.bayesian@^1. This guide shows a complete analysis. The model reference gives all the settings, and how each setting maps onto mmm-framework.

docs.title: From daily spend in local currency to weekly EUR decisions
docs.text:
A typical European media dataset is daily, for each market and channel, in the currency of each market. mmm-framework does the scaling, the carry-over and the seasonality. Thus the pipeline of the platform only does these steps:

  • It changes the currencies.
  • It aggregates the data to weeks.
  • It adds a holiday control.

The pipeline keeps each learned step. Thus a score does exactly the same work again:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: eu-geo-mmm, project: growth}
data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/eu_media_daily@latest
  side_tables:
    fx:       {ref: dataset://growth/fx_daily@latest, score_policy: supplied}
    holidays: {ref: dataset://shared/holidays_eu@v3, score_policy: pinned}
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, channel: channel, time: date}
    vars: {y: revenue_local, spend: spend_local}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 8, after_step: weekly}   # weeks exist after `weekly`
pipeline:
  - id: to_eur
    use: core.fx_convert@^1
    with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, table_along: date, currency_dim: geo,
           currencies: {UK: GBP}, default_currency: EUR}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1, with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}
  - {id: hols,   use: core.holidays@^1, with: {table: holidays, table_along: date, along: time}}
model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1
  settings:
    hierarchy: {pool_over: [geo]}       # one baseline per market, partially pooled
    new_levels: hyperprior              # a new market is drawn from the fitted spread
    adstock: {kind: geometric, l_max: 6}
    saturation: {kind: logistic}
    seasonality: {yearly_order: 3}
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, engine: nutpie, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, seed: 7}
outputs:
  derived: [contributions, response_curves, marginal_cost]
  plots: [core.ppc_fan, core.convergence, mmm.decomposition, mmm.response_curves]
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo, coverage_90, mape]}

The platform does these things with this spec. You do not write model code:

  • Binding. Your names (market, revenue_local) become the canonical names of the model (geo, y). The platform changes them back on each output.
  • Split at the right stage. The holdout is the last 8 weeks. The platform cuts the holdout after the resample. Thus no partial week goes into the training data.
  • Evaluate, then refit. The platform fits the model on the training weeks. It scores the holdout through the score path, which is the same code that a forecast uses. Then it fits the model again on all the weeks. Thus forecasts start from the latest data.
  • Owned scaling and carry-over. mmm-framework scales the data itself. It carries spend over with its own adstock kernel. The platform puts a score window on top of the stored fit history. Thus carry-over from the TV burst of last month gets to the sales of next month. Validation refuses a scaling or lag step on y or spend (CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED).
  • Weekly EUR. Predictions and contributions come back in the units of the model stage. Here, these are weekly EUR. The outputs tell this in their output_space (model-owned) and units.

mapi_plugin_mmm.examples.E33_SPEC_YAML is a smaller version of this spec that you can run. It comes with a simulator (e33_dataset) with known true contributions.

docs.title: Settings at a glance
docs.text:
Setting Level Default Meaning hierarchy.pool_over basic [] Panel dims of the data (geo, product). Each level gets its own baseline, partially pooled adstock.kind / l_max basic geometric, 8 Carry-over shape (geometric, delayed, weibull, none) and length saturation.kind basic logistic Diminishing returns (logistic, hill, michaelis_menten, tanh, root, none) trend.kind basic linear none, linear, piecewise, spline or gp seasonality.yearly_order basic 2 Yearly Fourier pairs channels.<c> advanced - Adstock/saturation overrides for each channel hierarchy.media_by_geo advanced false Channel effects for each geo, partially pooled media_prior advanced roi Channel effects given as returns on spend priors advanced - roi.<c>: {mu, sigma}, roi_default, intercept likelihood advanced normal student_t for heavy-tailed outliers; poisson, negative_binomial for counts; beta for shares media_effect_sigma advanced 0.5 The prior scale of the channel effects of a count or share likelihood time_varying advanced none channels, innovation_sigma (0.15) and forecast (random_walk) of time-varying channel effects new_levels advanced pooled How the model scores unseen geos/products controls advanced auto Control variables (default: all other numeric variables over time) grid advanced 0-2.5x in 26 steps The spend-multiplier grid of the response curves

Guided mode shows only the basic settings. Each field has x-ui-level in the JSON Schema of the manifest. The models catalog lists all the settings with their defaults.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Score requests for MMMs work as for all other models. MMM users need these requests most.

ForecastA new marketA weekly EUR planWhat if 
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://growth/eu-geo-mmm-prod
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 8}
side_tables: {fx: dataset://growth/fx_daily@latest}    # fx is `supplied` at score time
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 200}

Send daily spend in local currency for the next 8 weeks. You get weekly EUR revenue.

Add a market that the model did not see (FR). With new_levels: hyperprior, the model draws the baseline of the market from the fitted spread for each posterior draw. Thus its forecast is honest about what the model does not know. The forecast is wider than the forecast of a fitted market. The response has an UNSEEN_LEVELS notice.

mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 8}
inputs_stage: weekly          # enter after fx conversion and resampling

Planners send weekly EUR budgets. They do not need to invent daily spend in local currency. You do not need an FX table, because the platform skips the steps that use it. The forecast is the same as the forecast from the raw data for the same spend.

mode: counterfactual
interventions: [{var: spend_local, sel: {channel: tv}, multiply: 1.2}]
output: {kind: predictive, draws: 200}

The scenario and the baseline share their noise (common random numbers). Thus the delta group shows the effect of the change, not sampling noise. Only the contribution of the changed channel moves.

Each score gives y_hat and contributions(component, geo, time). There is one component for each channel, baseline, trend, seasonality, and one component for each control. The components add up to y_hat.

docs.title: What a Guided report reads
docs.text:
The fit calculates contributions, response_curves and marginal_cost (in outputs.derived) one time. It uses the first outputs.ui_draws posterior draws. These items read the values:

  • mmm.decomposition, mmm.response_curves and mmm.marginal_cost plot them.
  • The what-if sliders of Guided mode interpolate the response curves for each draw. The answer is instant, with joint uncertainty bands.
  • The plausibility checks of the scorecard read them: negative or absurd ROI, the share of a channel, and the baseline share.

Business priors (ROI or share ranges) and lift tests calibrate the model through the calibration block of the spec. See Guided modelling and the model reference.

docs.title: Calibrate with a geo-lift test v0.13
docs.text:
A geo-lift test changes the spend of one channel in some markets for some weeks. The result of the test is a good lift test for the model, because the test measures the effect directly.

  1. Fit causal.synthetic_control on the KPI of all markets around the test. The geo_lift Guided template does this for you.
  2. Get the lift test from the fit: the lift-test card of the Guided report, or the workflow node model.lift_test.
  3. Add the lift test to calibration.lift_tests of the MMM spec.
  4. Fit the MMM again.
  5. Look at the mmm.lift_tests chart. The estimate of the model must be near the test.
calibration:
  lift_tests:
    - id: tv-geo-lift-2024-03
      channel: tv
      geo: geo_03            # one test market; null for two or more markets
      start: 2024-03-04
      end: 2024-04-14
      spend_delta: 50000
      kpi_delta: 4100        # the mean of the total effect
      se: 1100               # the sd of the total effect

The workflow template geo_lift_mmm does all the steps in one run. See Measure the effect of a change.

docs.title: Effects that change over time v0.12
docs.text:
Use this when the effect of a channel changes during the data, for example when an advertisement gets old.

  1. Put the channel in time_varying.channels. Remove its ROI prior, if it has one.
  2. Select the forecast policy after the fit window.
  3. Add effectiveness to outputs.derived and mmm.effectiveness to outputs.plots.
model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1
  settings:
    adstock: {kind: geometric, l_max: 8}
    saturation: {kind: hill}
    time_varying: {channels: [tv], innovation_sigma: 0.15, forecast: hold_last}
outputs:
  derived: [contributions, response_curves, marginal_cost, adstock, effectiveness]
  plots: [core.ppc_fan, mmm.decomposition, mmm.effectiveness, mmm.roi]

The chart shows the effect of one unit of spend in each period, with a range. A forecast with random_walk has a range that becomes wider with the horizon. Use hold_last if you think that the last effect continues. Response curves and budget plans use the average effect over the fit window. Refer to Effects that change over time.

docs.title: Counts and shares v0.12
docs.text:
Use a count likelihood when the KPI is a number of items, such as orders, sign-ups or visits. Use beta when the KPI is a share between 0 and 1.

  1. Set likelihood to poisson, negative_binomial or beta.
  2. Remove priors.roi and priors.roi_default. These likelihoods use coefficient priors.
  3. Remove the calibration block. Business priors and lift tests need a normal or Student-t likelihood.
model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1
  settings:
    likelihood: negative_binomial   # use poisson only when the variance is near the mean
    media_effect_sigma: 0.5
    adstock: {kind: geometric, l_max: 8}
    saturation: {kind: hill}

The contributions still add up to y_hat, in KPI units. The baseline then includes the trend, the seasonality and the controls. A predictive score gives whole numbers for a count and values between 0 and 1 for a share. Refer to Counts and shares.

docs.title: Effects through an intermediate measure v0.12
docs.text:
Use mmm.nested when you measure a step between the spend and the KPI, for example site visits or brand awareness from a monthly survey. The Guided template Marketing mix with an intermediate measure (mediated_mmm) makes this spec from your columns.

  1. Put the measures in one variable along a mediator dim. Leave the periods without a value empty.
  2. Bind the dims channel, mediator and time, and bind the measures to mediators.
  3. Optionally, give each mediator its channels and signs in mediators.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: online-mmm, project: growth}
data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/online_weekly@latest
  bind:
    dims: {channel: channel, mediator: mediator, time: week}
    vars: {y: online_sales, spend: spend, mediators: measures}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 8}
model:
  use: mmm.nested@^1
  settings:
    trend: {kind: linear}
    seasonality: {yearly_order: 2}
    mediators:
      - {name: awareness, channels: [tv, social], observation_sigma: 0.2}
      - {name: visits, outcome_sign: positive}
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, engine: nutpie, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, seed: 7}
outputs:
  derived: [contributions, response_curves, marginal_cost, adstock, mediation]
  plots: [core.ppc_fan, core.convergence, mmm.decomposition, mmm.mediation, mmm.roi]

mmm.mediation shows the direct and the indirect effect of each channel. Lift tests calibrate the total effect of a channel, as for mmm.bayesian.

Note

The nested model uses national data only and takes no control variables. If price or promotions change your sales much, mmm.bayesian with controls is a better start.

docs.title: Several results v0.12
docs.text:
Use mmm.multivariate when one budget acts on two or more results, for example the sales of a premium range and a basic range. The Guided template Marketing mix for related products (multi_kpi_mmm) makes a start of this spec from your columns, without weights and without cross-effects. Add them in the spec editor.

  1. Put the results in y along an outcome dim.
  2. Give each outcome a weight: the value of one unit of it in a budget plan.
  3. Add the cross-effects that you expect, with their kind.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: range-mmm, project: growth}
data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/ranges_weekly@latest
  bind:
    dims: {channel: channel, outcome: outcome, time: week}
    vars: {y: sales, spend: spend}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 8}
model:
  use: mmm.multivariate@^1
  settings:
    trend: {kind: linear}
    seasonality: {yearly_order: 2}
    outcomes: [{name: premium, weight: 3.0}, {name: basic, weight: 1.0}]
    cross_effects: [{source: premium, target: basic, kind: halo}]
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, engine: nutpie, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, seed: 7}
outputs:
  derived: [contributions, response_curves, marginal_cost, adstock, cross_effects]
  plots: [core.ppc_fan, core.convergence, mmm.decomposition, mmm.cross_effects, mmm.roi]

Response curves, the ROI and budget plans use the weighted total of the outcomes. The decomposition and the waterfall show the primary outcome. This is also true for a score that gives the dataset's names, where the outcome dim has the name that you bound (for example, product). Set outcome on mmm.decomposition or mmm.waterfall to show a different one.

Read cross-effects as associations

Do not use a cross-effect as proof that one product takes sales from a different product. The model cannot separate it from the correlation of the noise. Use a test to measure a cause.

docs.title: Charts for a marketing team v0.12
docs.text:
Add these recipes to outputs.plots. Each chart has a caption in plain words.

Question Recipe Needs in outputs.derived Which channel returns the most for each unit of spend? mmm.roi response_curves (and marginal_cost for the marginal return) How long does the effect of spend continue? mmm.adstock adstock What adds up to the total result? mmm.waterfall contributions Does each channel get spend in proportion to its effect? mmm.spend_effect response_curves Do the lift tests agree with the model? mmm.lift_tests none (the fit keeps the lift_tests group) Does the effect of a channel change over time? mmm.effectiveness effectiveness Did the sampler explore the posterior well? core.energy none How much did the data change each prior? core.prior_posterior none

docs.title: Optimising budgets
docs.text:
The platform optimises budgets with the planning module of mmm-framework. You do not need an external optimiser:

import httpx

with httpx.Client(base_url=API, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
                                         "X-Mapi-Project": "growth"}) as http:
    r = http.post(
        f"/v1/models/{model_id}/versions/3:optimize",
        json={"budget_change_pct": 10, "objective": "mean", "frontier": {"n_points": 8}},
        headers={"Prefer": "wait=60"},
    )
    plan = r.json()["result"]          # None while the run is still going (202)
for a in plan["allocation"]:
    print(a["channel"], round(a["current_spend"]), "->", round(a["optimal_spend"]))
print("uplift", plan["uplift"]["mean"], "chance it helps", plan["prob_positive_uplift"])

See Optimise a budget for a walk-through. See the model reference for all the options. In Python, you can also use the decision objective of a fitted bundle directly. MMMBayesian().objective(bundle.model, budget, ScoreContext()) gives the value of a budget for each period, spend(channel) or spend(geo, channel). It gives this value at steady state, for each posterior draw.

docs.title: Live progress and cancel v0.11
docs.text:
mmm.bayesian reports its progress while it samples. Before v0.11, the progress went from 10% to 90% in one step.

  • The progress bar moves with the draws of the slowest chain.
  • The run page shows one lane for each chain, with its draws, divergences and step size.
  • The fit logs the step metrics step_size, num_steps and divergences for each chain (label chain). With nuts_sampler: pymc, it also logs tree_depth. The Metrics tab shows them. See Live chains and step metrics.
  • If you cancel the run while it samples, the sampler stops. The run becomes cancelled and makes no model version.

This applies to nuts_sampler: nutpie and nuts_sampler: pymc. The approximate methods (ADVI, Pathfinder) of mmm-framework do not send progress while they fit. From v0.12, mmm.nested and mmm.multivariate send the same progress and step metrics. Each MMM fit also logs summary metrics, such as the ROI of each channel (see What an MMM fit logs).

docs.title: The fast frequentist model
docs.text:
mmm.frequentist takes the same data and settings, and answers in seconds:

  • It searches the transforms out of sample.
  • It solves the model with ridge regression, with non-negative channel effects.
  • The ranges are bootstrap confidence intervals.

Use it for a first look. Then fit mmm.bayesian before you make decisions.

docs.title: Trust, but verify
docs.text:
The four plugins pass the SDK contract kit (mapi_sdk.testing.check_model). The kit tests these items:

  • Bundle round trips.
  • Shuffled and subset markets.
  • New levels.
  • Typed errors.
  • The holdout scored through the same path as a forecast.
  • Additive contributions.

The conformance corpus runs the plugins through the full spec -> fit -> score path (e33, guided_mmm, mmm_frequentist). The tests of the plugin check the forward pass against the forecaster and the graph of mmm-framework.

docs.title: Explore a model v0.5
docs.text:
The Model Explorer shows what a fitted model learned and how well it works. It does this for all model families:

  • Bayesian: posterior means with highest-density intervals, and R-hat.
  • Frequentist: estimates with confidence intervals and p-values, and information criteria.
  • Machine learning: coefficients or importances.

The sandbox calculates the views from the bundle and the data that the fit used. The views come with Vega-Lite plots. The web app shows each section with governance evidence and lineage. It also compares versions and optimises budgets. The rest of this guide uses the HTTP API that the web app calls.

docs.title: In the web app
docs.text:
The page of a model version has Explore and Compare. For marketing-mix models, it also has Optimise budget. The Model Explorer (/models/<model>/versions/<n>/explore) puts its sections into groups by the question that they answer:

Group Sections Overview At a glance: the plain readings of the diagnostics and the fit, the holdout metrics and the About card of the model What it learned Parameters (a table that you can sort and filter, with intervals, p-values, R-hat and ESS, and a forest plot for each parameter), contributions, response curves, impulse responses, variance decomposition and fields (the outputs of the model on a 2-D grid) Can you trust it? Diagnostics (convergence, fit statistics for each series, the tests of the model), fit vs actual (with the coverage of the band in plain words), residuals (over time, ACF, histogram, QQ plot, Ljung-Box, Jarque-Bera, Breusch-Pagan and ARCH-LM), backtest Looking ahead Forecast (a fan for each series) Trust and origin Governance (the status badge of the latest validation, each check with its evidence, the status history) and lineage (dataset, spec revision, fit run and workflow run, and also plugin, image, seed and libraries)

The explorer lists the sections that do not apply to the model last, with the reason. For example, an MMM has no impulse responses. The explorer calculates forecasts and backtests only when you ask:

  • Click Compute forecast and backtest.
  • Or click Explore with options. Then set the horizon, the interval and the backtest plan. The plan has these items: expanding window or rolling origin, horizons, folds, minimum training periods and gap.

As in the Data Explorer, Guided mode shows the plain reading first. Expert mode shows all the numbers.

The header shows the validation status of the version. It has a link to the validations of the version, where you can request a new validation. Under Governance evidence, these links show:

  • Open this validation goes to the latest validation: its status path, the decisions of the reviewers and the evidence pack.
  • Policies goes to the governance policies. See Validate models with governance policies.

If a workflow fitted the version, Lineage has a link to the monitor of the workflow run.

Compare (/models/compare) shows two to eleven versions side by side. To use it:

  1. Select each model and version. The tests use the first version as the reference.
  2. Click Compare.

The page shows these items:

  • The holdout metrics, with a mark on the best value of each metric.
  • The Diebold-Mariano tests in plain words. For example, "about equally accurate", or an advantage that is more than chance.
  • The ranking for each metric.
  • The fit statistics of each version.
  • Which version predicts new data best? (v0.10): the core.model_comparison plot. It shows the expected log predictive density (elpd) of each version and its difference to the best version. The card shows only when two or more versions have elpd_loo (or elpd_waic) on the same number of observations. The description of the card tells you which of the two estimates the plot shows.

Time-series forecasters (statsmodels and the other ts models) forecast the full held-out period from one origin. Thus their errors make a single path, and no test of equal accuracy is valid on it. For these models, the page shows the metrics and rankings. It tells you to compare their backtests. You can also run a compare.diebold_mariano workflow node on rolling-origin backtest errors.

Optimise budget (/models/<model>/versions/<n>/optimize) is only for marketing-mix models. It asks for these items:

  • How much to spend: the current total, a new total, a change in percent, or the total that the model would select. The last option is only in Expert mode.
  • How careful to be: the expected result, the 25th or 10th percentile, or the average of the worst 10%.
  • Limits for each channel: multiples of the current spend, an amount of money, or no change.
  • Portfolio groups and the frontier.

If the page cannot meet a bound, it tells you why before anything runs. The plan reads like this: "Move money from tv (−7,491) to search (+7,491). That adds about +3,063 to revenue (90% likely between +674 and +6,030)…". The plan also shows these items:

  • The allocation for each channel (and market).
  • The expected result now and with the plan.
  • The probability that the plan is better than the current allocation.
  • The return of the next unit for each channel.
  • The efficient frontier.

The expected results show the number of digits that is necessary to make the two ends of each range different. For example, "1.305M – 1.312M", not "1.3M – 1.3M". In Guided mode, the What if… step goes to this page with Optimise my budget. The page gives the goal and the notes of the optimiser in plain words, for example "Goal: the most likely revenue". The text of the optimiser itself is under For experts: how the plan was found. The request and the result are the request and result of POST …:optimize.

docs.title: From Python and the command line
docs.text:
model_id, version = "mdl_01jaf3c1d2e3f4g5h6j7k8m9n0", 3
explored = api.models.explore(
    model_id, version, sections=["params", "residuals", "forecast"], horizon=13
)
residuals = api.explorations.view(explored, "residuals")

compared = api.models.compare(
    ["model://growth/arimax@v3", "model://growth/ets@v1", "model://growth/theta@v2"], horizon=4
)
table = api.explorations.view(compared, "comparison")  # metrics, ranking, Diebold-Mariano

mapi explore model model://growth/sales-arimax@v2 -s params -s residuals -s irf --horizon 12
mapi explore compare model://growth/sales-arimax@v2 model://growth/sales-ets@v1 --horizon 4

docs.title: Views written at fit
docs.text:
Each fit writes params, diagnostics, fit, residuals, decomposition, response_curves, irf, fevd and fields. The fit lists the sections that do not apply to the model as skipped, with the reason. Read the index and the views through the UI route of the model version:

api "$API/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/versions/3/artifacts/ui/explore/index.json"
api "$API/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/versions/3/artifacts/ui/explore/residuals.json"

docs.title: Forecasts, backtests and more, on demand
docs.text:
api -X POST "$API/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/versions/3/explore" -d '{
  "sections": ["forecast", "backtest"],
  "horizon": 12,
  "backtest": {"kind": "expanding_window", "horizons": [1, 4, 12], "n_folds": 5,
               "min_train": 104}
}'

The answer (202) is an Exploration. Poll GET /v1/explorations/{run_id} to get the index and the signed view links. If you send the same request again, the answer is 200 from the last run.

docs.title: Error by horizon v0.11
docs.text:
The backtest view has the error metrics for each horizon, pooled over all the folds (BacktestView.by_horizon, for example by_horizon["4"]["mae"]). Each fold also keeps its own by_horizon. If the plan has no horizons, the backtest uses the horizons 1 to the length of the first test window (a maximum of 32).

The backtest section has a second chart, "Backtest error by horizon". It shows the pooled MAE for each number of periods ahead, and a light line for each fold. The chart shows only when two or more horizons have a pooled MAE. The error usually increases with the horizon. A fast increase tells you that the model is good only for short forecasts.

docs.title: Compare model versions
docs.text:
api -X POST "$API/v1/models:compare" -d '{
  "models": ["model://growth/sales-arimax@v3", "model://growth/sales-ets@v1",
             "model://growth/sales-mmm@v2"]
}'

This call explores the first version with the other versions as compare_with. It writes the comparison view, which has these items:

  • The holdout metrics of each version, side by side.
  • A ranking for each error metric. A lower value is better.
  • Pairwise Diebold-Mariano tests on the held-out periods of the first version. The tests use the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold small-sample correction and a Newey-West number of autocovariances. They answer the question "is the difference in accuracy more than chance?".
  • The core.model_comparison plot (v0.10), in ui/explore/plots/comparison.json after the metric bars. The view adds it when two or more versions have elpd_loo estimates on the same number of observations (else elpd_waic). The difference to the best version has a standard error when the two versions keep their pointwise values. To get elpd_loo, fit each version with keep: {log_likelihood: true} and evaluate.metrics: [elpd_loo].

If a version forecasts the held-out periods from one origin (time-series forecasters), the view does not include the tests. It gives a warning. For more sections, add "sections": ["comparison", "params"].

docs.title: The sections
docs.text:
Section What you see Families params One row for each parameter cell: mean, sd, interval (hdi_90 for Bayesian, ci_90 for other models), p-value, R-hat, bulk ESS all with parameters diagnostics R-hat max, ESS min, divergences, optimiser status, AIC/BIC, holdout metrics, the diagnostics of the plugin, warnings in plain words all fit Actual against fitted with a 90% band, and the split line at the first held-out period models over time residuals Residuals over time, their ACF, Ljung-Box, Jarque-Bera, Breusch-Pagan and ARCH-LM tests, a histogram and a normal QQ plot models over time decomposition The contributions of the model over time (added over markets) and the share of each part models with a component output (MMMs, linear models) response_curves Mean contribution for each channel at each spend level, with a 90% band MMMs with a response grid irf Impulse responses (response × shock × horizon) with bands VAR, VARMAX, VECM fevd Forecast-error variance decomposition VAR, VARMAX, VECM fields Each output on a 2-D grid as an image: the mean, the sd, the mean÷sd, the 5% and 95% quantiles and some posterior draws for each frame, with arrows for a vector field. Play the draws to see some possible fields that agree with the data models with an output that has a grid (maps, images, space-time fields) forecast A forecast fan over horizon periods after the history. The drivers stay at their last values models that forecast backtest New fits on a rolling-origin or expanding-window plan: metrics for each fold and horizon, against "same as last period" and "same as last season" models over time comparison More than one version side by side (above) all

The science models have many outputs on a grid. Some examples:

  • sci.heat_plate: field, the temperature of each cell for each run.
  • sci.turing_pattern: pattern, settled and turing_space.
  • sci.storm_localisation: render, patch_fit and frames_hat.
  • sci.ibp_features: ink_hat and features.
  • sci.graphical_model: pcor and edge_prob.
  • sci.network_latent_space: tie_prob and tie.
  • sci.circular_regression: density and overlap.

The fields section calculates its statistics on a line. It does not use the circular rules of an output that is an angle (OutputDecl.circular), as the score summaries do. At this time, no circular output of a bundled model has a grid. The section does not show an output that is not numeric, or an output that does not have the dims of its grid.

docs.title: For plugin authors: what the explorer reads
docs.text:
The explorer does not depend on the model. Plugins get these views if they follow some conventions:

  • Predictions come from the score path (predict, expected values). Thus each plugin gets fit and residuals automatically.

  • Parameters: The explorer reads them from these sources, in this sequence:

    1. The posterior group (chain, draw).
