    2. A params or coefficients group. This group is a table (variables estimate, and optionally std_err, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper along one parameter dim). Or it has one variable for each parameter.
    3. learned["params"] as {name: number} or {name: {estimate, std_err, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper}}.

    Confidence intervals without explicit bounds are estimate ± z · std_err.

  • Convergence: Diagnostics with the code RHAT/ESS_BULK, sample_stats.diverging, learned["converged"] (a bool) or a NOT_CONVERGED diagnostic, and learned["aic"|"bic"|"llf"].

  • Decomposition: An output with a component dim (contributions).
  • Impulse responses: A group or derived quantity irf with the variable irf over (response, shock, horizon) (optional lower/upper), and fevd over (variable, horizon, shock).
  • Response curves: The response_curves derived quantity that the what-if sliders use.

The governance checks use the same reads (see Validate models with governance policies).

docs.title: Can you trust this model? v0.5
docs.text:
A flexible model will find something in all data. Give a marketing-mix model ten channels and two years of weekly sales. It will tell you what each channel returned, also if the sales were random. The fit statistics will look good. The charts will look convincing. There is only one way to know if the model learned something real. Show it data that has nothing to learn, and make sure that the model sees this.

The null tests of the platform do this. Thus a governance policy can make them necessary before a person uses a model. The first half of this page tells about the tests without formulas. The second half gives the statistics. Validate models with governance policies tells how to use policies, validations, approvals and evidence packs.

docs.title: Shuffled results: does the model beat luck?
docs.text:
The test does these steps:

  1. Take the drivers that the model uses, for example weekly spend and prices.
  2. Shuffle the drivers in time. The spend of each week goes to a different week, but the sales stay exactly the same.
  3. Fit the same model to the shuffled data.
  4. Measure how well the shuffled fit predicts weeks that it was not fitted on.
  5. Do steps 2 to 4 twenty or forty times.

The shuffle removes the relation between spend and sales, by design. But it does not change the trend and the season of the sales.

A model without drivers is a forecast from the past of the series. For this model, the test uses the series itself. It shuffles the changes from week to week and adds them up again. This keeps the quantity of wander, but removes all that is predictable.

Possibly the model really learned how sales depend on the drivers. Then it predicts the real held-out weeks much better than the shuffled versions predict their weeks. If one shuffled fit in twenty does as well as the real fit, the skill of the model is like the skill of noise. The check gives this as a p-value. This is the share of shuffled fits that did as well or better. A small correction makes sure that it is never exactly zero.

What you see What it means "lower than all 39 fits on shuffled results (p = 0.025)" It is very improbable that the skill of the model is luck. "1 of 20 fits on shuffled results did as well (p = 0.095)" Borderline: a real signal, but weak, or too few shuffles to know. "9 of 20 did as well (p = 0.48)" The model fits noise. Do not use it to make decisions.

The test shuffles the drivers in blocks. A block is a sequence of weeks that moves together. Thus the flighting patterns of the drivers stay. The test breaks only the link between the drivers and the result. The test does not shuffle the sales. Thus, if a model wins only because of a trend or a season, it does equally well on the shuffled copies. Then it fails the check.

Persistence does not trick this test. Some series wander (a random walk). On such a series, a model that differences the series gets much of its skill from "next week is like this week". But the shuffled fits also keep that persistence, because the test does not shuffle the result. Also, the test measures skill against the null forecast. Thus only the contribution of the drivers counts. The ARIMAX of the cookbook on such a series has a price driver that is really important. It forecasts better than all 20 shuffled fits (p = 0.048, the output).

docs.title: Fake drivers: does the model credit anything it is given?
docs.text:
The test adds three drivers that are pure noise, and fits the model again. The fake drivers are copies of a real spend column that are mixed in time. Or they are random numbers with the same average and spread. A trustworthy model gives them almost nothing. This is a few hundredths of a percent of sales, with a range that easily includes zero.

If a channel of random numbers gets 8% of sales, the model gives credit too easily. Thus the credit that it gave your real channels is also suspect. The usual causes are these:

  • Too many drivers for the quantity of history.
  • Priors that are too wide.
  • Drivers that move together.

docs.title: Shifted drivers: is it the timing, or just the season?
docs.text: The test moves each driver six months away from its real time, and fits the model again. Real advertising effects must go away, because spend in March cannot cause sales in September. If the model still finds most of the effect, it finds the season or the trend. Then it calls this effect advertising.

docs.title: The other checks, briefly
docs.text:
• Beats naive: On weeks that it did not see, the model must be better than two benchmarks: "same as last week" and "same as this week last year". If a forecast cannot do this, it is not worth its complexity.
  • Nothing left in the errors: The errors of the model must look like noise. A pattern in the errors shows that the model did not find something predictable.
  • Stable over time: If you fit the model again on different parts of the history, the key numbers must not change very much.
  • Signs make sense: Spend must not decrease sales. Prices must not increase demand, unless you tell this.
  • Assumptions do not decide the answer (Bayesian models): If you make the priors wider and narrower, the answer must almost not move.
  • Finds known values: The check simulates data from the fitted model and fits it again. It makes sure that the ranges contain the truth about 90% of the time.
  • The fit is complete and stable, the error on unseen data is below your limit, and the data is good enough. The last check means no long gaps, no constant drivers and no negative spend.

docs.title: What the platform does with the results
docs.text:
A policy lists these items:

  • The checks that a type of model must pass.
  • How strict each check is. blocking stops validation. warning shows to the reviewer. info is only evidence.
  • If a second person must approve.

When you validate a model version, the checks run in the sandbox. The platform stores each result with its evidence. The version becomes validated, awaiting_approval or checks_failed. You can set endpoints to serve only validated versions. All the results are in the evidence pack. An auditor can read the evidence pack without access to the platform.

mapi validate model model://growth/geo-mmm@v7     # runs the checks, shows every result
mapi approve "$VALIDATION" --comment "Null tests convincing"   # a second person
mapi validations pack "$VALIDATION" --out evidence.html

docs.title: For statisticians
docs.text:
Notation:

  • y is the target over n periods.
  • ŷ is the predictions of the model.
  • H is the held-out periods of the data split of the model.
  • L is the loss of the check (RMSE by default).

Each refit uses the spec and pipeline of the model through the SDK harness. This is the same code path as a fit. Each refit has a refit budget (RefitBudget): a maximum of max_refits refits. Bayesian refits have a maximum of 200 draws and 200 tuning steps on 2 chains.

docs.title: null.permutation_target - a permutation test with a matching null
docs.text:
The statistic has no scale. It is the held-out skill of a refit against the null forecast on the same dataset, T = 1 − L(model) / L(null forecast). For an integrated series (a random walk), the null forecast is the last training value. For other series, it is the training mean. You cannot compare raw held-out errors across shuffles of the result. Their spread comes from the levels that a shuffle puts in the test periods, not from the model. In simulation, a level-shuffling test with raw RMSE rejected 35% of random walks and 33% of real AR alternatives. Thus it had no size and no power.

The null depends on what the model must learn:

  • Models with drivers (ARIMAX, marketing mix, regressions on time): The test does not change y. It block-permutes the drivers together. Each block has ℓ = max(1, n // 20) periods. The block parameter changes this. H0: the drivers have no information about y in addition to the trend, season, controls and dynamics of the model. If the refit of a model ignores the drivers, the test uses the method for a model without drivers. A refit ignores the drivers when the first shuffled fit gets exactly the same score.
  • Models without drivers (ARIMA, ETS, Theta, UC): The test permutes the d-th differences of y i.i.d. It integrates them again from the original first values. d comes from the ARIMA order of the model. If there is no ARIMA order, d is 1 when ADF keeps a unit root or KPSS rejects stationarity. This method keeps the integration order and the distribution of the increments. But it removes predictable dynamics. In simulation (ARIMA(1,1,0), 12 held-out periods, B = 19), it keeps its size on random walks. It rejects AR dynamics much more frequently.
  • Data without a time order: The classic row permutation of y, on the held-out loss.

T_b is the statistic of the b-th shuffled refit, b = 1..B. The Monte-Carlo p-value is:

p = (1 + #{b : T_b >= T0}) / (B + 1)

Under exchangeability, this p-value is exact. It is valid at each B. The smallest possible p is 1 / (B + 1). With the default B = 20, it is 0.048. Thus a 5% test is possible, but only at the limit. For a 2.5% resolution, use B >= 39. The policy parameter is n_permutations.

The thresholds are on p: pass ≤ 0.05, warn ≤ 0.10, fail above.

docs.title: null.noise_regressors - placebo regressors measured by ablation
docs.text:
The test adds K placebo drivers (n_noise, default 3). Each placebo is one of these:

  • A real driver, block-permuted in time (kind: shuffled_driver). This keeps its distribution and its short-run autocorrelation.
  • Gaussian noise with the mean and variance of the real driver.

The placebos are new channels of a marketing-mix model, or new variables of other models. Placebos get the default prior of the model. The test never copies the prior or the calibration of a real channel to them. This calibration can be a business-prior or lift-test ROI. If the test copied it, a well-calibrated model would fail because of its prior. The test copies the carry-over and saturation shapes.

After the refit, the test measures the effect share of each placebo through the score path. It does not read the share from a coefficient. The share is a share of the total effect of the real drivers:

s_k = Σ_t |ŷ_t(full) - ŷ_t(placebo k off)|  /  Σ_t |ŷ_t(full) - ŷ_t(real drivers off)|

If the test cannot measure the effect of the drivers, it uses Σ_t |ŷ_t(full)| as the denominator. Thus the method works equally for non-linear models (saturation, adstock, trees). It does not depend on the size of the baseline. The check gives max_k s_k (pass ≤ 2%, warn ≤ 5%).

For Bayesian models, the check flags a placebo when its share is above the warn limit with a minimum of 90% posterior probability. This is P(s_k > 2%) ≥ 0.9 for each draw. A rule of "90% interval excludes zero" cannot work for a marketing mix model, because its channel effects are positive in all draws. For frequentist models, the check uses Holm's correction for the K placebos on the placebo p-values. Without the correction, the check flags a good model about one time in seven runs with K = 3.

A flag changes a nominal pass into a warning. If the share is above the fail limit, the flag changes it into a failure. Some models have in-sample predictions that follow the stored history (the statsmodels plugins). These models use |β_k| · Σ_t |z_k,t − z_k,t(off)|.

docs.title: null.placebo_time_shift
docs.text: The test shifts each driver circularly by each δ in shifts (default ±26 periods). Then it fits the model again. The statistic is the placebo effect as a share of the real effect, max_δ Σ|Δ_δ ŷ| / Σ|Δ ŷ| (pass ≤ 0.25, warn ≤ 0.5). The test looks for confounding by seasonality and trend. A shift of half a year puts annual seasons out of alignment on purpose. Thus, if an effect stays after the shift, the driver did not cause it.

docs.title: baseline.beats_naive - out-of-sample skill
docs.text:
On H, with the training-only fit, the check calculates skill = 1 − MAE(model) / min_j MAE(benchmark_j). The benchmarks are forecasts from the training history:

  • Naive (last value).
  • Seasonal naive (same period last season).
  • Mean.
  • Drift.

The check also gives MASE as evidence. Pass ≥ 0.05, warn ≥ 0. For a formal test of the difference on backtest folds, use the compare.diebold_mariano workflow node:

d_t  = L(e1_t) - L(e2_t)                       (squared or absolute loss)
DM   = mean(d) / sqrt(lrv(d) / n)              lrv: autocovariances up to lag h - 1
HLN  = DM * sqrt((n + 1 - 2h + h(h - 1)/n) / n)
p    = 2 * P(T_{n-1} > |HLN|)

There is one h-step error for each backtest fold, and the folds are step periods apart. Thus only ceil(h / step) − 1 neighbouring folds share test periods. The node uses that number of autocovariances in lrv. In the correction, it replaces h with that number plus one. The node reads the spacing from the folds. It needs more paired errors than that number. If there are too few folds, the node tells this. It does not give a number.

docs.title: residuals.whiteness
docs.text:
The check calculates Ljung-Box Q = n(n + 2) Σ_{k=1..m} ρ̂_k² / (n − k) on the in-sample residuals of each series. It removes the start-up residuals of a diffuse-initialised fit. These are the burn-in of the fit itself, for example for differencing or unobserved components. Only the ARMA terms decrease the degrees of freedom (m − p − q − P − Q). The constant, the drivers and the variance never decrease them. The smallest p-value across the series counts (pass ≥ 0.05, warn ≥ 0.01).

Think about multiplicity. With many series, some rejections are expected. Thus a policy for a full panel can use severity: warning.

docs.title: stability.rolling_params
docs.text: The check fits the model again on rolling windows of history (window, by default about half the sample). For each key estimate, it gives the coefficient of variation across the windows. If the estimate is near zero, the check scales this value by the standard error of the estimate. If it did not, a coefficient that moves a small quantity around zero would look unstable by design. Pass ≤ 25%, warn ≤ 50%.

docs.title: sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated
docs.text:
Prior sensitivity does these steps:

  1. It writes out each prior that the model uses. These are its settings with the defaults of the plugin, and the business priors that the platform translates at fit time. For mmm.bayesian, the defaults are the default ROI prior LogNormal(0, 1), seasonality.prior_sigma and trend.growth_prior_sigma.
  2. It multiplies each prior width by each value of scales. Widths are sigma, scale, sd and tau under a prior… key, and keys named …prior_sigma or …_sigma. It never changes Beta or Gamma beta/b parameters.
  3. It gives the largest relative change of a key posterior mean (pass ≤ 20%).

If the check finds no prior width in the settings, the result is skipped with the reason. For example, the check does not find the widths of sci.areal_bym2 (intercept_sd, slope_sd and sigma_scale), because these names do not agree with the rules of step 2.

Recovery is a small version of simulation-based calibration with S refits. It gives the coverage of the 90% intervals for the known values (target 90%, pass within 10 points). The check makes the simulated data in one of two ways:

  • A Bayesian model that gives predictive draws: each dataset is one draw of the posterior predictive. It comes from one posterior draw and the noise of the model, so counts stay whole numbers and ties stay 0 or 1. The known values are the values of that posterior draw. The draws come from the predict score mode with predictive draws. Thus the model must have the predict mode.
  • Other models: y* = E[y] + ε* with block-bootstrapped residuals. The known values are the fitted values. The platform skips this check when the target holds whole numbers (counts or yes/no values), because E[y] + ε* is not a whole number. The result is skipped with the reason. The platform also skips this check for autoregressive models that are not Bayesian, because resampled residuals do not make the same dynamics as the model.

If the model cannot fit one simulated dataset, the check continues with the next dataset. The evidence gives the number of these datasets (failed_simulations), and the message tells how many fits failed. If no refit gives parameter intervals, the result is error.

docs.title: Interpreting a set of results
docs.text:
A policy is a multiple-testing procedure. With twelve checks at their own thresholds, a good model will sometimes warn on something. Severities exist for this reason. Make the checks that protect the decision blocking:

  • For a marketing-mix model, these are the null tests and the signs.
  • For a forecast, these are the naive benchmark and the holdout accuracy.

Set the diagnostics to warning or info for the reviewer. Each CheckResult has these items:

  • value and threshold.
  • message_plain and an expert message.
  • A suggested_action.
  • The evidence: the real score next to each shuffled score, and the share and interval of each placebo.

Thus the reviewer can see how close a decision was.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
CLIPythonPolicy file 
mapi governance checks                        # what a policy can require
mapi governance checks --about null.permutation_target --expert
mapi governance policies ls                   # in force here: tenant-wide first
mapi governance policies create forecast-policy.yaml
mapi validate model model://growth/wf-weekly-readiness-fit@v1   # runs the checks, waits
mapi validations ls --queue                   # reviewers: what waits for a decision
mapi approve "$VALIDATION" --comment "Null tests convincing; beats naive by 25%"
mapi validations pack "$VALIDATION" --out evidence.html          # for the auditor

import yaml

with open("forecast-policy.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    policy = api.governance.create_policy(yaml.safe_load(fh))
print(policy.id, policy.version, [c.check for c in policy.checks])

# edit and save the next version (refused with 409 if someone saved one meanwhile)
stricter = api.governance.update_policy(
    policy.id, policy.model_copy(update={"approvals_required": 2}), expected_version=1
)
for p in api.governance.policies():  # in force in the project: tenant-wide first
    print(p.scope, p.name, f"v{p.version}")

validation = api.models.validate(model_id, version, note="Q4 refresh", wait=True)
print(validation.status.value)  # validated, awaiting_approval or checks_failed
for r in validation.results:
    print(r.check, r.status.value, r.message_plain, r.suggested_action or "")
if validation.status.value == "checks_failed":
    validation = api.validations.resubmit(validation.id, note="refitted on clean data")

# A project policy for the forecasts this team publishes (validated by a docs test).
# `mapi governance policies create forecast-policy.yaml`, or
# `api.governance.create_policy(yaml.safe_load(open("forecast-policy.yaml")))`.
name: Forecasts we publish
description: Every forecast must beat naive, survive the null tests and be signed off.
applies_to: {families: [ts]}
checks:
  - check: baseline.beats_naive                  # better than "same as last period"
  - check: null.permutation_target               # better than on shuffled results
    params: {n_permutations: 39}                 # smallest possible p = 1/40 = 0.025
  - check: null.noise_regressors                 # fake drivers made of noise get ~0 credit
    params: {n_noise: 3}
  - check: residuals.whiteness                   # no pattern left in the errors
    severity: warning
  - check: holdout.accuracy                      # MAPE on unseen weeks
    thresholds: {warn: 0.10, fail: 0.20}
  - check: stability.rolling_params
    severity: info
require_approval: true                           # a second person signs off
approvals_required: 1
require_validated_for_promotion: true            # endpoints refuse unvalidated versions

A workflow can run the same checks as a node (governance.policy with submit: true). It can also record the validation itself. See the cookbook.

docs.title: Plots: recipes, templates and safe sharing
docs.text:
Each model that you fit gets a set of standard plots at no cost. The set includes a data overview, convergence, posterior predictive checks, a fan of the fit and forecast, decomposition, scenario comparisons and more. Plots are Vega-Lite (or Plotly for 3D, maps and animation). A small envelope, the PlotSpec, contains each plot. The data goes next to the spec as named Arrow tables, never as a URL. Each plot goes through a sanitizer before a person sees it.

uv add "mapi-plots[recipes]"   # recipes + Altair/Plotly helpers (runner images, notebooks)
uv add mapi-plots              # sanitizer and templates only (JSON in, JSON out)

`core.ppc_fan`: the model estimate, the 50% and 90% bands, the actual values and the end of the training data. The plot shows one panel for each market.

docs.title: Render a recipe in a notebook
docs.text:
A recipe is a function. It changes a fitted bundle or a score output into a PlotSpec:

from mapi_plots.examples import example_inputs
from mapi_plots.recipes import get_recipe

inputs = example_inputs()  # synthetic bundle/score trees for every recipe (xarray only)
data, options = inputs["core.ppc_fan"]
plot = get_recipe("core.ppc_fan").render(data, **options)

print(plot.kind, plot.persona)  # vega-lite both
print(sorted(plot.datasets))  # named Arrow tables travel next to the spec, never as URLs
print(plot.caption_plain[:60], "...")

A recipe accepts different inputs:

  • An xr.DataTree (a bundle or a score output)
  • An xr.Dataset
  • A plain {"group": Dataset} mapping

A recipe finds its groups at the root, under model/ (for bundles) or at other positions in the tree. The recipe does a check of its options. If an option is unknown or a group is missing, the recipe raises a typed RecipeDataError (SCHEMA_INVALID). The error tells what the recipe expected.

Each plot contains these items:

  • persona: guided (analysts), expert (data scientists) or both.
  • caption_plain: a description of the chart in plain language, with the actual numbers. For example: "The scenario changes total revenue by 184 (90% interval 139 to 251) compared with the baseline. Probability of an increase: 100%."
  • provenance: the recipe and its version, the bundle id and a timestamp.

Try each recipe without a model

mapi_plots.examples.example_inputs() returns synthetic bundle trees and score trees for each recipe. It makes them with xarray only:

for recipe_id, (data, options) in example_inputs().items():
    rendered = get_recipe(recipe_id).render(data, **options)
    print(f"{recipe_id:28} {rendered.kind:10} {rendered.persona}")

docs.title: The standard catalog
docs.text:
Recipe What it shows Reads core.data_overview Each variable over time for each group, a heatmap of missing values, the group sizes raw data / observed_data core.prior_predictive The datasets that the model makes before it sees data, compared with your data. Also a prior fan. prior_predictive, observed_data core.convergence R-hat and ESS for each parameter, a table of the worst parameters, trace plots and rank plots, divergences posterior, sample_stats core.posterior_forest The median, the 50% HDI and the 94% HDI for each parameter. One panel for each variable. posterior core.ppc Predictive densities compared with observed values, a PIT histogram, interval coverage posterior_predictive, observed_data core.ppc_fan A fan of the fit and the forecast, with the line between the training data and the forecast draws or summary, observed core.fit_vs_actual Predicted values against actual values, with R² and MAPE predictions + observed core.residuals_over_time Actual values minus predicted values over time predictions + observed core.decomposition Stacked contributions over time, and the total share of each component. A part that the model marks as not additive (a trend slope) is not in the stack. contributions, decomposition or components core.model_comparison The elpd of each model and the difference to the best model (PSIS-LOO table or WAIC) comparison, or one child for each model with log_likelihood core.counterfactual The scenario compared with the baseline over time, and the distribution of the total change draws/summary, baseline/…, delta/… core.decision_distribution The distribution of a decision objective for each option, and P(best) decision/objective core.pair A grid of the draws of each pair of parameters, a histogram of each parameter, divergent transitions in red posterior, sample_stats core.ridge One density curve for each level of a dim (such as each group), sorted by the mean, with HDI bars draws in posterior, predictions or posterior_predictive core.rank_matrix The probability of each rank for each item, and the probability that one item is above another draws in posterior, predictions or posterior_predictive core.calibration The PIT-ECDF difference with a simultaneous band, or a reliability diagram for 0/1 targets. For 0/1 targets, one predicted probability for each row is sufficient. draws or point probabilities, observed_data core.state_sequence The observed series above the stacked probability of each hidden state over time hidden_states, regimes, a score summary, state draws; observed_data core.roc_pr The ROC curve and the precision-recall curve of a binary or multiclass target, with the AUC and the average precision (multiclass: one curve for each class and the macro AUC) draws or point probabilities, observed_data core.confusion The table of actual and predicted classes, for a binary or multiclass target: 2 × 2 at one threshold, or K × K of the most probable class, with accuracy and F1 draws or point probabilities, observed_data core.loss_curve The loss of each step of a fit (for example ADVI), raw and smoothed fit_history or metrics_history core.loo_pit The LOO-PIT check of calibration and the Pareto k of each observation log_likelihood, posterior_predictive, observed_data core.energy v0.12 The marginal energy and the energy transitions of the sampler, and the BFMI of each chain against a threshold sample_stats with energy core.prior_posterior v0.12 The prior and the posterior of each parameter, ranked by how much the data moved it, with their overlap prior, posterior

The marketing-mix pack (mmm.*) adds these plots:

  • Response curves that mark the current spend
  • The marginal cost (or the marginal ROI) for each channel
  • A comparison of budget plans
  • A channel decomposition
  • Your beliefs and the priors (mmm.prior_beliefs): the range that you gave for each channel, next to the values that the model allows before it sees your sales

From v0.12, the pack also has these plots:

Recipe What it shows Reads mmm.roi The return on spend of each channel with a range, and the marginal return (mROAS), against a break-even line response_curves, optional marginal_cost mmm.adstock The part of the effect of spend that comes in each later period, with a range and the mean delay adstock mmm.waterfall The contribution of each component (baseline, trend, channels) to the total result contributions mmm.spend_effect The share of spend against the share of the effect of each channel response_curves mmm.lift_tests The result of each lift test with its error bar, next to the estimate of the model lift_tests mmm.effectiveness The effect of one unit of spend over time, for time-varying channels effectiveness mmm.mediation The direct and the indirect effect of each channel (mmm.nested) mediation mmm.cross_effects The effects between the results (mmm.multivariate) cross_effects

mmm.decomposition and mmm.waterfall show one outcome of a model with an outcome dim: the primary outcome, or the outcome that you set in outcome.

The causal pack (causal.*, v0.13) draws the results of the causal models:

Recipe What it shows Reads causal.impact The actual values and the values without the change (with a range), the effect in each period and the cumulative effect impact causal.pre_fit The fit of the model before the change, with its error impact causal.donor_weights The weight of each market in the synthetic control, with a range donor_weights causal.event_study The effect for each period before and after the change, with a range event_study

The tabular pack (ml.*) adds ml.feature_importance. This plot shows ranked tree importances, or signed coefficients for linear estimators. It reads them from the groups that the scikit-learn plugin and the xgboost plugin keep in their bundles. From v0.15, the pack also has three plots for neural networks (see Deep learning).

The science pack (sci.*) draws gridded fields and images (sci.field_map, sci.image_residuals, sci.ppc_image_grid, sci.power_spectrum), areas on a map (sci.area_map), trees (sci.phylogeny), angles (sci.rose), colours (sci.swatches), points with error ellipses (sci.point_pattern) and profiles and ensembles of curves. The network pack (net.*) adds net.graph, a node-link drawing and an adjacency matrix of an edge variable. The plot reference lists the settings of each recipe.

docs.title: Plots for classifiers, training and states
docs.text:
These plots read the outputs of more model types:

  • 0/1 targets. core.calibration, core.roc_pr and core.confusion accept draws or one probability for each row. Thus they apply to a Bayesian model and to a scikit-learn classifier. The larger of the two target values is the positive class. To change it, set positive.
  • Three or more classes v0.14. core.roc_pr and core.confusion also accept a prediction with a class dim (the probability of each class, for example from sklearn.multiclass_classifier or tabular.image_logistic), or an actual target with more than two values. core.roc_pr then draws one curve for each class against all other classes (the 12 most frequent classes, or the classes in classes). Its title gives the macro AUC. core.confusion shows a K × K matrix of the most probable class (a maximum of 30 classes) with the accuracy and the macro F1. threshold and positive are not used. The caption tells you this.
  • Fits in steps. An ADVI fit keeps its loss in the fit_history group. The fit run adds core.loss_curve to the plots of that fit. If the loss still goes down at the end, the caption tells you to use more steps.
  • Hidden states. core.state_sequence reads the hidden_states group of the HMM and the regimes group of the Markov switching model. If the data has more than one series (for example one series for each animal), the plot shows the first series. The caption names it. To show a different series, set select.
  • Pareto k. core.loo_pit shows which observations make the LOO estimate unreliable. It is not a default plot. Add it in the plot builder or in the plots list of a model.

docs.title: Deep learning v0.15
docs.text:
The dl models of mapi-jax keep their training history in the bundle. The fit adds these plots to the run:

Recipe What it shows Reads Settings ml.training_curves One panel for each metric (loss, accuracy or error, up to 4), one line for each split (train and val, val with points). The caption gives the best validation value. It also tells you when the validation loss goes up while the training loss goes down: "The validation loss goes up while the training loss goes down: the model starts to overfit." metrics_history with the label split, else training keys, label (split), x (step or epoch), smooth, log_y, max_points (2000) ml.confusion_epochs The confusion matrix of the validation data at up to 6 epochs: the first, some epochs between, the best and the last. The caption gives the validation accuracy at the first, the best and the last epoch. training.confusion epochs, normalize (true or none), max_classes (20; the others are "(other)") ml.misclassified A grid of the validation images that the network classifies incorrectly, with "true → predicted (p=0.83)" above each image. The caption: "{n} of {N} validation images are wrong at epoch {e}." misclassified max_items (24), columns (6)

The fit adds a recipe only when the bundle has the group that the recipe reads. The labels of the images are untrusted text: the plots show them as text only. ml.misclassified draws the pixels as Plotly image traces, with no image URLs.

Recipes obey the representation of each output. If a dim must go, a recipe adds the joint draws. A recipe never adds quantiles or intervals. If a summary has an extra dim, the recipe tells you to request an aggregated output. The recipe shows summed means without a band. Predicted-vs-actual plots and residual plots never need a total. Thus they compare these summaries cell by cell (one dot or line for each store × sku, with the color of the facet dim).

docs.title: Find a recipe in the web app
docs.text:
The Plots tab of the Catalog shows a card for each recipe, with an example plot made from synthetic data. The buttons above the cards filter the recipes by pack:

  • All plots
  • All models (core.*)
  • Marketing mix (mmm.*)
  • Machine learning (ml.*)
  • Science (sci.*)
  • Networks (net.*)

A pack shows only when the catalog has a recipe of that pack. Type words in the search field to find a recipe by its id, title or About card. Click a card to see the About card and a larger example.

docs.title: Plots in a workflow
docs.text:
A workflow can draw a recipe with the node plot.render. Set recipe to the id (for example sci.field_map) and, if necessary, settings and source (auto, data, model or predictions, default auto). model.forecast and evaluate.residuals also give plot outputs. A report.summary can show the plots in its plots input. The server puts each plot through the sanitizer. A plot that is not safe fails its node with PLOT_UNSAFE. See Score a model and draw plots.

The plot sandbox applies the theme to polar plots (barpolar and scatterpolar), for example sci.rose.

docs.title: Bring your own chart
docs.text:
Make the chart with Altair or Plotly as usual. Then put it in an envelope:

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
from mapi_plots import from_altair

frame = pd.DataFrame({"week": pd.date_range("2026-01-04", periods=6, freq="W-SUN"),
                      "revenue": [10.0, 12.5, 11.0, 14.2, 15.1, 13.8]})
chart = alt.Chart(frame).mark_line().encode(x="week:T", y="revenue:Q")
mine = from_altair(chart, id="acme.revenue", caption_plain="Weekly revenue.")
print(list(mine.datasets))  # the inline data became a named dataset

import plotly.express as px
from mapi_plots import from_plotly

fig = px.scatter(frame, x="week", y="revenue")
theirs = from_plotly(fig, id="acme.scatter")  # typed arrays -> named Arrow datasets
print(list(theirs.datasets))  # one dataset per trace, referenced as {"$ref": "trace0.y"}
  • from_altair moves the inline data of Altair (and all data.values) into named Arrow datasets. It also writes the references again. The function fills named data (alt.Data(name="pts")) from datasets={"pts": frame}.
  • from_plotly decodes plotly.py 6 typed arrays ({"dtype": "f8", "bdata": ...}) into Arrow datasets, one for each trace. It binds them with {"$ref": "trace0.y"}. The function removes the default plotly.py template, because the renderer applies the theme to plots. To keep the template, set keep_template=True.

Both functions run the sanitizer. If the chart breaks a rule, they raise a SanitizeError. from_plotly also removes HTML from the strings that it moves into datasets (see below).

Colors and dark mode. An explicit mark color has priority over all themes. Thus the platform recipes use only colors from mapi_plots.palette (for example OBSERVED, ESTIMATE, BAND, ALERT). In dark mode, the plot sandbox replaces each palette color with its dark variant. Each stroke, dot and text color keeps a contrast of 3:1 or more on the two card backgrounds. To get the same behavior in your own charts, use the palette. The plot shows all other colors as written, in the two themes.

docs.title: Role- and dim-bound templates
docs.text:
A template binds channels to roles and dims, not to the variable names of one model. Thus a plot of "the target over time, one line for each geo" applies to all models of a family:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from mapi_plots.recipes import builtin_templates, render_template

weekly = xr.Dataset(
    {"revenue": (("geo", "time"), np.random.default_rng(0).gamma(20.0, 50.0, (3, 12)),
                 {"role": "target", "units": "EUR"})},
    coords={"geo": ["DE", "FR", "UK"], "time": pd.date_range("2026-01-04", periods=12, freq="W-SUN")},
)
tmpl = builtin_templates()["tmpl.target_over_time"]
print(tmpl.bindings)  # x="dim:time", y="role:target", color="dim:geo" - no variable names
chart = render_template(tmpl, weekly)  # the schema is inferred; roles come from attrs
one_market = render_template(tmpl, weekly.sel(geo="DE", drop=True), optional=["color"])

In a template spec, {"$bind": "y"} becomes a Vega-Lite field definition. The bound name replaces "{{y}}" (also {{y.field}}, {{y.type}}, {{y.title}}). The kinds of binding are dim:, role:, var:, coord: and stat: (a summary statistic, for example stat:hdi_90_lower). The API runs the half that uses only JSON, mapi_plots.templates.apply_template. It does a check that a saved template applies to a model before the app renders a plot.

docs.title: What the sanitizer allows
docs.text:
Plots run in an isolated iframe on a different origin. But the server does a check of each plot first:

Rejected Why url data (in all positions, also lookups and topojson) Data must have a name as its reference. The plot cannot fetch data. href encodings and mark properties The plot cannot go to other pages. image marks, url channels, layout.images / image traces with sources that are not data: The plot cannot fetch external data (only base64 PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP). Tile-map traces and subplots (scattermap, choroplethmap, densitymap, layout.map) The tiles come from third-party servers. Use scattergeo/choropleth. __proto__, constructor, prototype keys or field paths Prototype pollution javascript:, data:text/html, SVG data URIs, CSS url() in a string Vectors for scripts and fetches Vega expressions that are not in a small allow-list of functions, method calls, window/document/fetch, computed member names Escapes from the expression sandbox Custom format types, Plotly network options (topojsonURL, showLink, ...) Hooks for code and the network All items that do not agree with the pinned Vega-Lite v6.4.1 / plotly.js 4.1.1 schemas Unknown keys are where exploits hide.

Plotly text keeps only <b>, <i>, <br>, <sub> and <sup> (and <extra> in hover templates). The sanitizer removes all other tags and reports each removal as a change. The server never decodes Arrow. Thus the sandbox removes tags from the text that from_plotly moves into a dataset (text, hovertext, category labels), and scans it, during conversion. The plot iframe must also treat dataset strings as not trusted. It must remove the tags again before it gives the strings to plotly.js.

Vega shows dataset strings as text, and the tooltip handler of the iframe escapes them. The sanitizer does a check of the method args of Plotly buttons and sliders. It checks the {attr: value} form and the positional [attr, value] form. It rejects usermeta.embedOptions in Vega-Lite specs. Specs have limits on size, depth, node count and string length. For the full list of rules and error codes, see the plots reference.

from mapi_plots import check_plot, sanitize_plot
from mapi_plots.sanitize import SanitizeError

hostile = {
    "id": "evil.chart",
    "title": "Totally normal chart",
    "kind": "vega-lite",
    "spec": {
        "data": {"url": "https://attacker.example/steal.json"},  # fetches are not allowed
        "mark": "point",
        "encoding": {"href": {"field": "link"}},  # neither is navigation
    },
}
try:
    sanitize_plot(hostile)
except SanitizeError as err:
    print(err.code, sorted(rule.value for rule in err.rules))  # PLOT_UNSAFE ['href', 'url_data']

for issue in check_plot(hostile):  # editor-friendly: every problem, never raises
    print(issue.pointer, "-", issue.message)
# /spec/data/url - data must be referenced by dataset name, never by URL
# /spec/encoding/href - href links are not allowed in plots
# /spec/$schema - added $schema

docs.title: Write a step or a model plugin
docs.text: A plugin author writes very little code. A step implements fit/transform (and inverse if it can). A model implements fit/score. The platform owns all other work: binding, splits, context tails, coordinates, inverse transforms, summaries and bundles. The contract kit tells you if you obeyed the rules. It tells you before other persons run your code.

docs.title: A preprocessing step
docs.text:
from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sdk import Step, StepContext, StepSettings, StepState
from mapi_spec import StepKind
from pydantic import Field, JsonValue


class ScaleSettings(StepSettings):
    vars: list[str]
    over: list[str] = Field(default=[])  # plain defaults: the exported JSON Schema keeps them
    unseen_levels: str = "error"  # error | pooled | fill: what a new level's scale becomes
    fill_value: float = 1.0  # the scale used by 'fill'


class ScaleStep(Step[ScaleSettings, StepState]):
    """Divide each variable by its mean absolute value over `over` (learned on train)."""

    id = "acme.scale"
    version = "1.0.0"
    kind = StepKind.VALUE
    Settings = ScaleSettings
    State = StepState  # stateful: fitted on the training data only
    invertible = True
    var_params = ("vars",)  # settings that name variables ...
    dim_params = ("over",)  # ... and dims, so the control plane can check them
    unseen_levels_param = "unseen_levels"
    effect_template: ClassVar[dict[str, JsonValue]] = {  # static: how the schema changes
        "template_params": ["vars"],
        "updates": {"{*vars as v}": {"units": "1"}},
    }
    summary = "Divide by the mean absolute value over the named dims"  # catalog and UI text
    summary_plain = "Puts each series on a comparable scale"

    def fit(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, ctx: StepContext) -> StepState:
        return StepState(arrays=xr.Dataset({f"scale__{v}": abs(ds[v]).mean(s.over) for v in s.vars}))

    def _scale(self, v: str, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, st: StepState, ctx: StepContext):
        state = st.array(f"scale__{v}")
        return ctx.align_state(state, ds, s.unseen_levels, fill_value=s.fill_value)

    def transform(self, ds, s, st, ctx):  # never learns; skips absent vars (the target at score)
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] / self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

    def inverse(self, ds, s, st, ctx):
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] * self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

The rules:

  • transform never learns. transform(train, fit(train)) must be equal to the output at fit time. A subset of the data must transform to the same subset of the output.
  • A reduction names the dims that it reduces over. The rest of the dims stay as the labels of the state.
  • Steps that look back (lags, rolling windows) declare context_template ({"along": "{along}", "n": "{max:lags}", "within": "{within}"}). The platform keeps the last n rows for each group at the input of the step. At score time, it puts them before the data.
  • Unseen levels go through ctx.align_state(state, ds, policy).
  • effect_template must describe the real schema of the output. The control plane uses it to validate specs. The control plane never imports your code.

docs.title: A model
docs.text:
from mapi_sdk import PREDICTIONS, CustomModel, FitOutput, ModelSettings, new_level_mask
from mapi_spec import Capabilities, DataSchema, Representation


class BaselineSettings(ModelSettings):
    ridge: float = 1e-6


class GeoBaseline(CustomModel[BaselineSettings]):
    """y = intercept[geo] + beta * spend, by least squares (point predictions)."""

    id = "acme.geo_baseline"
    version = "1.0.0"
    Settings = BaselineSettings
    capabilities = Capabilities(
        inference="point",
        representation=Representation.POINT,
        score_modes=frozenset({"predict", "forecast", "evaluate"}),
    )
    # the data contract the model needs, in canonical names (a DataSchema, or a
    # DataSchemaTemplate whose names come from settings)
    schema_template = DataSchema.model_validate(
        {
            "dims": {
                "geo": {"kind": "categorical", "policy": "new_levels", "new_level_strategy": "pooled"},
                "time": {"kind": "time", "policy": "extend"},
            },
            "vars": {
                "y": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "dtype": "float64", "role": "target"},
                "spend": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "dtype": "float64", "role": "covariate"},
            },
        }
    )
    outputs: ClassVar[dict] = {"y_hat": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "units_of": "y"}}
    pad_extend = False  # time is not indexed by position

    def fit(self, ds, s, cfg, ctx):
        g, t = ds.sizes["geo"], ds.sizes["time"]
        x = np.concatenate(
            [np.repeat(np.eye(g), t, axis=0), ds["spend"].values.reshape(-1, 1)], axis=1
        )
        coef = np.linalg.solve(x.T @ x + s.ridge * np.eye(g + 1), x.T @ ds["y"].values.ravel())
        params = xr.Dataset(
            {"intercept": ("geo", coef[:g]), "beta": coef[g]}, coords={"geo": ds["geo"].values}
        )
        return FitOutput(groups={"params": params})

    def score(self, fitted, ds, req, ctx):
        # `ds` arrives canonicalised: fit order, unseen geos appended and flagged
        p = fitted.group("params")
        new = new_level_mask(ds, "geo")
        known = p["intercept"].reindex(geo=ds["geo"].values)
        pooled = 0.0 if ctx.strategy("geo") == "zero" else float(p["intercept"].mean())
        intercept = xr.where(new, pooled, known.fillna(pooled))
        y_hat = (intercept + p["beta"] * ds["spend"]).transpose("geo", "time")
        return xr.DataTree.from_dict({PREDICTIONS: xr.Dataset({"y_hat": y_hat})})

outputs lists each variable that score returns, with its dims. You can omit representation dims, for example chain/draw or quantile. If the data dims change with the settings, add "dims_of": "y". The output then also gets each dim of that input variable in the resolved schema (for example settings.rows of the sklearn models).

If the NaN of an input are part of the design of the data, list its canonical name in the class attribute structural_missing. An example is a grid of cells where only some cells have a sensor. The scorecard check data.missing then does not count these NaN. Do not use it for gaps in observed series: the check must show them.

FitOutput.native is only for safe native formats (skops, xgboost JSON, safetensors). The platform rejects pickle when it writes a bundle and when it reads a bundle.

docs.title: Settings rules that need no data
docs.text: Put the rules that join two or more settings in a pydantic model_validator of your ModelSettings class. An example is "set offset_adu and scale_adu together" in sci.storm_localisation. The SDK parses the settings before it transforms, splits or fits the data. Thus a bad value stops the fit at the start with SETTINGS_INVALID (/model/settings). Do not put such rules in fit: there, they fail only after the data steps. Note: spec validation does a check of the JSON Schema only. It does not run the validator.

docs.title: Outputs that are images or maps
docs.text:
If an output is a 2-D field (an image, a map or a vector field), give it a grid (OutputDecl.grid):

outputs = {
    "sky": {
        "dims": ["row", "col"],
        "units": "uK",
        "grid": {"y": "row", "x": "col", "origin": "lower", "colormap": "diverging"},
    },
}
Field What it holds y, x The dims of the rows and of the columns of the raster frame Optional. A third dim, with one raster for each level (for example years) component Optional. A dim of length two with the (x, y) parts of a vector field origin upper (default: row 0 at the top) or lower colormap viridis (default), magma, cividis, gray or diverging log true draws log10 of the value (for counts and intensities). The default is false.

The dims in grid must be different from each other. The Model Explorer shows the output in its Fields section. The sci.* image recipes (sci.field_map, sci.image_residuals, sci.ppc_image_grid) find the grid in the manifest, or in a grid attribute of the scored variable. When the binding of a spec renames dims, the platform also renames them in the grid attribute.

docs.title: Outputs that are angles
docs.text:
If an output is an angle (a direction or a time of day), set circular: true in its declaration. Then, in score, set the attribute period on the array. The period is one full turn in the units of the output, for example 360 (degrees), 2π (radians) or 24 (hours):

outputs = {"direction_hat": {"dims": ["obs"], "units_of": "direction", "circular": True}}
# in score(): the angles in [0, 360)
pred["direction_hat"] = xr.DataArray(
    theta, dims=("chain", "draw", "obs"), attrs={"kind": "predictive", "period": 360.0}
)

The platform then calculates on the circle:

  • The holdout metrics use the circular mean of the draws and errors that wrap at half a turn (359 against 1 is an error of -2). crps uses the arc distance. The intervals are centred on the circular mean. The metrics mape, smape, wape and r2 are skipped.
  • The score summaries of draws use the circular mean and the circular standard deviation. Each value is in [0, period). An interval with lower more than upper crosses the seam. The summary table (summary.json) has the field period.
  • The difference between a scenario and its baseline wraps to [-period/2, period/2).

The circular metrics need the draws representation. An output without a valid period attribute, or an output aggregated over a dim, keeps the summary on a line, and the result has a warning.

docs.title: Score modes
docs.text:
Declare in capabilities.score_modes only the modes that score can do. The SDK refuses each other mode with MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED before it builds a forecast horizon or a payload. Thus score never gets a mode that you did not declare. Read the mode in ctx.mode and the output kind in ctx.kind (expected or predictive).

In simulate mode, return new data that the model makes from its posterior: new latent values and the noise of the model. For example, sci.cmb_field draws a new patch of sky from the spectrum of each posterior draw, and then adds noise. In predict mode with kind: predictive, keep the latent values of each posterior draw and add only the noise. Set the attribute kind: predictive on such draws. The governance check recovery.simulated makes its simulated datasets from these draws.

docs.title: Models that give elpd_loo
docs.text:
The fit calculates elpd_loo and elpd_waic from a log_likelihood group, if the spec lists the metric in evaluate.metrics. Put the group in FitOutput.groups, next to posterior, with the same chain and draw dims. Usually, keep it when cfg.keep.log_likelihood is true. A model for comparisons can always keep it, as sci.areal_bym2 does. For data of up to 10,000 points, the fit also keeps the pointwise values (MetricsReport.elpd), and the workflow node compare.stacking uses them.

If pointwise LOO is not correct for your model, declare loo_valid=False and a loo_invalid_reason in Capabilities. An example is a model where all pixels depend on one latent field. The fit then skips the metric with that reason.

docs.title: A model with its own sampler
docs.text:
A CustomModel can run its own MCMC sampler, for example a Gibbs sampler. sci.cmb_field does this. Follow these rules:

  • Declare inference="mcmc" and representation=Representation.DRAWS.
  • Read cfg.tune, cfg.draws, cfg.chains and cfg.seed (use ctx.seed when cfg.seed is None). If the spec names an engine that your sampler does not use, tell the user with ctx.info.
  • Call ctx.check_cancelled() and ctx.progress(fraction, message) in the loop of the sampler.
  • Return posterior and sample_stats with the dims chain and draw, and also observed_data.
  • Override the diagnostics(fitted, ds) hook. Call mapi_pymc.convergence_diagnostics(posterior, sample_stats, var_names=[...]) for R-hat and ESS, and add the diagnostics of your sampler. sci.cmb_field adds CG_NOT_CONVERGED.
  • Give each draw of a score its own generator, seeded from the seed of the score, the chain and the draw. Then declare deterministic_given_seed=True.
  • From v0.11, report the progress of each chain with ctx.chains([...]) (a list of mapi_spec.run.ChainProgress). Log the step metrics of your sampler with the label chain, for example ctx.log_metrics({"step_size": eps}, step=i, labels={"chain": str(c)}). Do this only when ctx.tracking is true.

docs.title: Log metrics, params and tags v0.11
docs.text:
FitContext and ScoreContext have logging methods. The run page shows the values, and the fit keeps the stepped metrics in the bundle group metrics_history. Thus core.loss_curve can draw them.

def fit(self, data, ctx):
    ctx.log_params({"solver": "lbfgs", "max_iter": 200})
    for i in range(1, n_iter + 1):
        loss = step()
        if i % 10 == 0:
            ctx.log_metric("loss", loss, step=i)
    ctx.log_metric("rmse", rmse, labels={"split": "train"})   # a scalar: no step
    ctx.set_tag("converged", "yes" if ok else "no")
    if not ok:
        ctx.log_line("the solver did not converge", level="warning", fields={"iterations": n_iter})

Follow these rules:

  • Metric keys match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$. Put qualifiers in labels: write loss with labels={"split": "val"}, not val/loss.
  • A bad key, a bad label or a negative step raises ValueError at the call, also without a run. The SDK ignores NaN and infinity.
  • A param does not change. A second, different value for the same key raises ValueError.
  • The methods are thread-safe. You can call them from the callback of a sampler.
  • Use ctx.tracking to skip metrics that take a long time to calculate.
  • The fit already logs the params of the spec (model, fit.*, settings.*). Do not log them again.

To see the values in a test, give the fit a recorder: fit_spec(spec, data, hooks=FitHooks(tracker=MetricRecorder())). The recorder keeps the points, the params, the tags and the log lines (mapi_sdk.MetricRecorder). See Track metrics, params and tags for the full API.

docs.title: Data for a case study (mapi-plugin-science)
docs.text:
If you add a model to mapi-plugin-science, add an export case so that users can upload its data. mapi_plugin_science.export.EXPORTS maps a case id to an ExportCase. The case id is e and the notebook number (e18), with a letter for a second dataset of the same notebook (e81b). Add one _register(ExportCase(...)) entry at the end of export.py:

_register(
    ExportCase(
        case="e18",
        title="Disease mapping of lip cancer in Scotland",
        notebook="E18_areal_models_icar_bym2.py",
        model="sci.areal_bym2",
        files=(areal_data.CHALLENGES_FILE,),
        loader=lambda d: areal_data.from_challenges(d / areal_data.CHALLENGES_FILE),
        synthetic=lambda: areal_data.areal_dataset(),
        schema=areal_data.AREAL_SCHEMA,
        project="epidemiology",
        dataset="scotland_lip_cancer",
        spec=areal_data.SCOTLAND_SPEC_YAML,
    )
)
  • files lists the files that the loader reads from the data/ directory of pymc-challenges. Use an empty tuple when the notebook simulates its data (E51, E61).
  • synthetic returns the simulated data of the model, in the same layout.
  • schema is the raw DataSchema of the model (a TreeSchema for a tree dataset).
  • spec is the suggested spec as YAML, or a function of the exported data that returns it. Its data.dataset must be dataset://<project>/<dataset>@latest.

The tests make sure that each suggested spec validates against the schema of its exported file. A slow test fits each spec on the simulated data. Then python -m mapi_plugin_science.export --list shows the case.

docs.title: Train on batches: fit_batches v0.15
docs.text:
A model that trains on many images can read them in batches from an image collection. It does not need all images in memory. Declare input="collection" in the capabilities, and add two methods to the model:

from mapi_sdk import CustomModel, ImageLoader


class NearestMean(CustomModel[Settings]):
    id = "demo.nearest_mean"
    capabilities = Capabilities(..., input="collection")

    def fit(self, ds, s, cfg, ctx):
        # plain image datasets (image folders, inline payloads)
        return self.fit_batches(ArrayImageLoader(ds, target=s.target), s, cfg, ctx)

    def fit_batches(self, loader: ImageLoader, s, cfg, ctx):
        sums = {}
        for epoch in range(s.epochs):
            ctx.check_cancelled()
            for batch in loader.batches(64, epoch=epoch, shuffle=True, seed=cfg.seed or 0):
                ...  # one training step
        return FitOutput(...)

    def score_batches(self, fitted, loader: ImageLoader, req, ctx):
        ...  # predictions for loader.ids, in loader order

Follow these rules:

  • fit_batches(loader, s, cfg, ctx) gets a loader of the training rows of the split. score_batches(fitted, loader, req, ctx) gets a loader of the requested images. The harness puts the predictions in the order of the request.
  • Implement fit and score too. Image folder versions and inline payloads come as plain datasets. ArrayImageLoader(ds) gives the same loader interface for them.
  • A spec on a collection takes no pipeline steps. Put random changes in the settings (mapi_sdk.Augment) and apply them in batches(augment=...).
  • Use ctx.fit_key (32 hex characters, stable for the spec, the data and the role) as the base of checkpoint keys.
  • For checkpoints, use ctx.checkpoint_sink when it is a FileCheckpointSink. Save files with save_files(key, {"weights": ..., "opt": ...}, meta, progress=epochs_done), and load them with load_files(key) at the start.
  • In score, use requested_positions(ds, dim) to score only the rows that the request asked for.

The contract kit runs the batch path one time when you give it a collection: check_model(MyModel, collection=local_collection(tmp_path)).

docs.title: Read a side table in a model v0.15
docs.text:
A model can read a side table, for example pretrained weights. Name the settings that hold side table names in side_table_params:

class Finetune(CustomModel[Settings]):
    id = "demo.finetune"
    side_table_params = ("pretrained",)

    def fit(self, ds, s, cfg, ctx):
        weights = ctx.side_tables[s.pretrained]          # an xr.Dataset
        tensors, doc = tensors_from_dataset(weights)
        ...

build_manifest writes side_table_params into the manifest. Static validation makes sure that each named table is in data.side_tables (REF_UNRESOLVED at /model/settings/<param>). The model gets the tables in FitContext.side_tables, by their names in the spec. A score request never needs a table that only the model reads: keep what the model learned from it in the fitted state.

docs.title: Run the contract kit
docs.text:
mapi-sdk installs a pytest plugin. Thus the fixtures are available in all test suites:

import pytest
from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, toy  # toy: small reference steps and models


@pytest.mark.mapi_contract
def test_step_follows_the_contract(mapi_check_step, mapi_panel):
    data, _fx = mapi_panel  # a daily market x channel panel and its FX side table
    report = mapi_check_step(
        toy.ScaleStep, data, {"vars": ["spend_local"], "over": ["date"], "unseen_levels": "pooled"}
    )
    assert report.ok, report.summary()


SPEC = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: toy, project: demo}
data:
  dataset: dataset://demo/panel@latest
  bind: {dims: {geo: market, time: date}, vars: {y: revenue_local, spend: spend_local}}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 14}
model: {use: toy.linear@^1, fit: {seed: 1}}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse]}
"""


@pytest.mark.mapi_contract
def test_model_follows_the_contract(mapi_check_model, mapi_panel, mapi_toy_registry):
    data, _fx = mapi_panel
    fixture = ModelFixture(spec=SPEC, data=data, registry=mapi_toy_registry)
    report = mapi_check_model(toy.LinearModel, fixture)  # raises ContractViolation on failure
    assert report.ok

check_step does a check of these items:

  • The exported catalog entry
  • A deterministic fit
  • A pure and deterministic transform
  • That transform never learns
  • The bundle round trip of the state
  • That the declared schema effect agrees with the real output
  • That the step accepts a missing target
  • The inverse round trip
  • The equivalence of the context window
  • Each policy for unseen levels

check_model fits the fixture and does a check of these items:

  • The bundle round trip, and that the bundle has no pickle
  • Scores with shuffled data and with a subset of the data
  • The policies for new levels
  • The typed errors of each dim policy:
    • Gaps and coordinates out of range on datetime and integer extend dims
    • HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT after max_extension
    • MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE for a forecast without a variable that the future needs
    • RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED for a horizon that is longer than a target lag
  • Modes that the model does not support
  • The equivalence of the context window
  • That the score path makes the same evaluation metrics again
  • The output units (also outputs that get the units of the target)
  • That outputs declares each returned prediction with the same dims
  • Legal aggregation
  • Additive contributions
  • Seed determinism
  • That the plots of the manifest render and pass the sanitizer
  • If the manifest declares fast_score: that fast scores agree with exact scores within MCSE

The last check calls the check_fast_score(fitted, ds, *, seed) hook of the plugin. PyMCModel gives this hook.

If a check fails, it raises ContractViolation with a report that is easy to read:

contract kit: step acme.scale@1.0.0
  [PASS] catalog_entry: exported acme.scale@1.0.0
  [FAIL] transform_never_learns: AssertionError: ...

mapi_sdk.testing.toy contains small, real reference implementations that you can copy. It has the scale, log1p, lag, resample, Fourier and FX steps, and the point, draws and quantile models.

docs.title: Port a model in 15 minutes
docs.text:
You have a model that works in a notebook. This guide changes it into a plugin. The platform can fit the plugin, score it on new data, forecast with it, keep its versions and plot it. The contract kit proves that the plugin works. You write the statistics. The platform writes all the other code.

flowchart LR
    A["0–3 min<br/><b>Pick a base class</b>"] --> B["3–6 min<br/><b>Declare the data contract</b>"]
    B --> C["6–11 min<br/><b>Write build / estimator / fit+score</b>"]
    C --> D["11–13 min<br/><b>Write a tiny spec</b>"]
    D --> E["13–15 min<br/><b>Run the contract kit</b>"]

docs.title: What you write, what you get
docs.text:
You write The platform does PyMCModel build(ds, settings, ctx) -> pm.Model Engines (nutpie, PyMC with segments that can continue, MAP, ADVI), convergence diagnostics, scores that build the model again and predict, new levels from the hyperprior, counterfactuals with common random numbers, fast scores SklearnModel estimator(settings) It stacks labelled dims into rows and features. Also coordinate features, safe persistence (skops / xgboost JSON), quantile / bootstrap / conformal uncertainty, pooled new levels, contributions CustomModel fit(...) and score(...) Binding, preprocessing, splits, context tails, the canonical form of coordinates, inverse transforms, summaries, bundles

The three base classes get these items at no cost:

  • Validated settings with JSON Schemas
  • Static validation of the spec
  • An evaluation, then a new fit
  • CoordPlan checks
  • Summaries that obey the representation
  • Plots and bundles

docs.title: 1. Pick a base class (0–3 min)
docs.text:
• If your model is a PyMC model, use mapi_pymc.PyMCModel.
  • If your model is an sklearn or xgboost estimator on a design matrix, use mapi_sklearn.SklearnModel (or the quantile, bootstrap, conformal or classifier variants).
  • For all other models (statsmodels, JAX, a Kalman filter, closed-form mathematics), use mapi_sdk.CustomModel.

docs.title: 2. Declare the data contract (3–6 min)
docs.text:
Write the dims and the variables that your model needs, in canonical names. For each dim, write what can occur to it at score time. This is the schema_template of the model. In the spec, users bind the names of their own dataset to it.

Three questions for each dim

Can a score request bring a new level (a new county, store or market)? If yes, the dim is new_levels, with a strategy. Does the dim grow at forecast time (time, observations)? If yes, the dim is extend. If not, the dim is fixed.

docs.title: 3. Write the model (6–11 min)
docs.text:
PyMCscikit-learn / xgboostCustom 
from typing import Any, ClassVar

import pymc as pm
import xarray as xr
from mapi_pymc import BuildContext, PyMCModel
from mapi_pymc.examples import RADON_SCHEMA  # dims obs (extend) + county (new_levels)
from mapi_sdk import ModelSettings
from mapi_spec import Capabilities, Representation
from pydantic import Field


class RadonSettings(ModelSettings):
    beta_sigma: float = Field(1.0, gt=0)


class Radon(PyMCModel[RadonSettings]):
    """log radon ~ Normal(a[county] + b * floor, sigma), with partially pooled a."""

    id = "acme.radon"
    version = "1.0.0"
    Settings = RadonSettings
    capabilities = Capabilities(
        inference="mcmc",
        representation=Representation.DRAWS,
        score_modes=frozenset({"predict", "counterfactual", "evaluate"}),
    )
    schema_template = RADON_SCHEMA
    outputs: ClassVar[dict[str, Any]] = {"y": {"dims": ["obs"], "units_of": "y"}}
    expected: ClassVar[dict[str, str]] = {"y": "mu"}  # output -> Deterministic for E[y]
    pad_extend = False  # long layout: no positional time axis

    def build(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: RadonSettings, ctx: BuildContext) -> pm.Model:
        with pm.Model(coords=ctx.coords()) as model:
            floor = ctx.data("floor")
            county = ctx.data("county_idx")
            a = ctx.hier_effect("a", "county")  # new counties come from the hyperprior
            b = pm.Normal("b", 0.0, s.beta_sigma)
            mu = pm.Deterministic("mu", a[county] + b * floor, dims="obs")
            sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", 1.0)
            pm.Normal("y", mu, sigma, observed=ctx.observed("y"), dims="obs")
        return model

The ctx helpers make the scores work. You do not have to think about them:

Helper Why you use it ctx.coords() The coords of the model. At score time, it includes new levels. ctx.data(name) A pm.Data over the training values at fit time and over the score values at score time (the platform builds the model again) ctx.observed(name) The target at fit time. A placeholder at score time (never imputed). ctx.hier_effect(name, dim) A partially pooled effect. Its new levels come from the hyperprior, for each posterior draw. ctx.position(dim) 0, 1, 2, … along an extend dim. The count continues into the forecast horizon.

expected names the Deterministic that is the expected value of each output. Thus output.kind: expected returns it without observation noise.

from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sklearn import PointSettings, SklearnModel, capabilities_for
from mapi_spec import Capabilities
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge


class LinearDemand(SklearnModel[PointSettings]):
    id = "t.acme.linear_demand"
    version = "1.0.0"
    capabilities: ClassVar[Capabilities] = capabilities_for("none").model_copy(
        update={"contribution_scale": "additive"}  # a linear model decomposes exactly
    )

    def estimator(self, s: PointSettings) -> Ridge:
        return Ridge(alpha=0.5)  # must be exactly an allow-listed class

estimator() returns an estimator instance from the allow-list (or a {kind, params} mapping). The platform rejects subclasses and parameters that are not in the params model of the estimator. Thus the platform can always load the bundle safely. Rows, columns and coordinate features are settings, not code. See Tabular models.

from mapi_sdk import PREDICTIONS, CustomModel, FitOutput, ModelSettings, new_level_mask
from mapi_spec import Capabilities, DataSchema, Representation


class BaselineSettings(ModelSettings):
    ridge: float = 1e-6


class GeoBaseline(CustomModel[BaselineSettings]):
    """y = intercept[geo] + beta * spend, by least squares (point predictions)."""

    id = "acme.geo_baseline"
    version = "1.0.0"
    Settings = BaselineSettings
    capabilities = Capabilities(
        inference="point",
        representation=Representation.POINT,
        score_modes=frozenset({"predict", "forecast", "evaluate"}),
    )
    # the data contract the model needs, in canonical names (a DataSchema, or a
    # DataSchemaTemplate whose names come from settings)
    schema_template = DataSchema.model_validate(
        {
            "dims": {
                "geo": {"kind": "categorical", "policy": "new_levels", "new_level_strategy": "pooled"},
                "time": {"kind": "time", "policy": "extend"},
            },
            "vars": {
                "y": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "dtype": "float64", "role": "target"},
                "spend": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "dtype": "float64", "role": "covariate"},
            },
        }
    )
    outputs: ClassVar[dict] = {"y_hat": {"dims": ["geo", "time"], "units_of": "y"}}
    pad_extend = False  # time is not indexed by position

    def fit(self, ds, s, cfg, ctx):
        g, t = ds.sizes["geo"], ds.sizes["time"]
        x = np.concatenate(
            [np.repeat(np.eye(g), t, axis=0), ds["spend"].values.reshape(-1, 1)], axis=1
        )
        coef = np.linalg.solve(x.T @ x + s.ridge * np.eye(g + 1), x.T @ ds["y"].values.ravel())
        params = xr.Dataset(
            {"intercept": ("geo", coef[:g]), "beta": coef[g]}, coords={"geo": ds["geo"].values}
        )
        return FitOutput(groups={"params": params})

    def score(self, fitted, ds, req, ctx):
        # `ds` arrives canonicalised: fit order, unseen geos appended and flagged
        p = fitted.group("params")
        new = new_level_mask(ds, "geo")
        known = p["intercept"].reindex(geo=ds["geo"].values)
        pooled = 0.0 if ctx.strategy("geo") == "zero" else float(p["intercept"].mean())
        intercept = xr.where(new, pooled, known.fillna(pooled))
        y_hat = (intercept + p["beta"] * ds["spend"]).transpose("geo", "time")
        return xr.DataTree.from_dict({PREDICTIONS: xr.Dataset({"y_hat": y_hat})})

The rules for score:

  • The dataset comes in the canonical form. It has the fit order. New levels come at the end, with the flag <dim>__is_new (new_level_mask(ds, dim)). Thus parameters that use the position as an index stay aligned.
  • Return an xr.DataTree with a predictions group in the representation that you declared.
  • Never look at the targets in the payload. The evaluate mode sends them for the metrics, not for you.

FitOutput.groups uses the ArviZ group names (posterior, sample_stats, …). learned contains small JSON. native contains bytes in a safe format only (skops, xgboost JSON, safetensors). The platform rejects pickle.

docs.title: What the notebook models of science needed
docs.text:
The 15 sci.* models came from notebooks in the same way. Some of them needed more than the three steps above. If your model is similar, see these sections:

Your model What to use See Its rules join two or more settings A pydantic model_validator on the settings. The SDK refuses bad settings before it uses the data. Settings rules that need no data An output is an image, a map or a vector field grid in the output declaration Outputs that are images or maps An output is a direction or a time of day circular: true, and a period attribute on the scored array Outputs that are angles It makes new data from the posterior The simulate mode, and real predictive draws for kind: predictive Score modes You compare variants by elpd_loo A log_likelihood group, or loo_valid=False with a reason Models that give elpd_loo NUTS gets stuck at the default start EnginePlan.initvals and jitter=False Start every chain at one point It has its own sampler (for example Gibbs) A CustomModel with inference="mcmc" and a diagnostics hook A model with its own sampler Some NaN of an input are part of the design structural_missing A model Users must upload the data of a case study An export case in mapi_plugin_science.export.EXPORTS Data for a case study

docs.title: 4. Write a tiny spec (11–13 min)
docs.text:
The contract kit fits this spec. Keep it small and fast: use few draws and few trees.

PyMCCustom (with a step) 
from mapi_pymc.examples import radon_dataset
from mapi_sdk import Registry
from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, check_model

SPEC = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: radon, project: demo}
data: {dataset: dataset://demo/radon@latest}
model:
  use: acme.radon@^1
  fit: {mode: train_only, engine: pymc, tune: 100, draws: 100, chains: 2, seed: 3}
"""
report = check_model(
    Radon, ModelFixture(spec=SPEC, data=radon_dataset(), raw_schema=RADON_SCHEMA, registry=Registry())
)
print(report.summary())

from mapi_sdk import default_registry
from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, check_model

registry = default_registry().copy()
registry.register(ScaleStep)  # the model is registered by check_model itself

SPEC = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: acme-baseline, project: demo}
data:
  dataset: dataset://demo/sales@latest
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 6}
pipeline:
  - {id: scale, use: acme.scale@^1, with: {vars: [spend], over: [time], unseen_levels: pooled}}
model:
  use: acme.geo_baseline@^1
  fit: {seed: 1}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mape]}
"""
raw_schema = infer_schema(data, targets=["y"], policies={"geo": "new_levels"})
report = check_model(
    GeoBaseline,
    ModelFixture(spec=SPEC, data=data, raw_schema=raw_schema, registry=registry),
)
print(report.summary())
# contract kit: model acme.geo_baseline@1.0.0
#   [PASS] fit: ...
#   [PASS] bundle_roundtrip_no_pickle: ...
#   [PASS] shuffled_scoring: ...
#   ...

docs.title: 5. Run the contract kit (13–15 min)
docs.text:
check_model fits your fixture. Then it tries to break your plugin in the same ways that real users will:

contract kit: model acme.geo_baseline@1.0.0
  [PASS] manifest: acme.geo_baseline@1.0.0 (point)
  [PASS] fit: bundle ef4100375dbb, metrics ['mape', 'rmse']
  [PASS] bundle_roundtrip_no_pickle: scores match after write/read
  [PASS] shuffled_scoring: shuffled ['geo']
  [PASS] subset_scoring: subset of 'geo'
  [PASS] new_level_policies: geo: new level scored (pooled)
  [PASS] extend_typed_errors: raised NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION; raised COORD_NOT_ALLOWED
  [PASS] unsupported_mode: raised MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED
  [PASS] context_window_equivalence: holdout via stored context == in-sample full series
  [PASS] evaluate_path_equals_score_path: metrics ['rmse', 'mape'] reproduced through the score path
  [PASS] output_space_and_units: y_hat in raw (None)
  [PASS] representation_aggregation: point aggregation over 'geo' allowed
  [SKIP] additive_contributions: contribution_scale is not additive
  [PASS] seed_determinism: same seed, same fit and scores
Check What it proves bundle_roundtrip_no_pickle The scores are the same after the kit writes and reads the bundle. The bundle contains no pickle. shuffled_scoring, subset_scoring Labels in a different sequence and subsets give the same answers for the same cells. new_level_policies Each strategy that your dims declare works (or raises UNSEEN_LEVELS when it must). extend_typed_errors Gaps and time labels out of range raise typed errors. unsupported_mode The model refuses modes that it does not declare. context_window_equivalence A forecast score of the last training periods is equal to the in-sample result. evaluate_path_equals_score_path The normal score path makes the same holdout metrics again. output_space_and_units The outputs are inverted. They have labels for the units and the output space. representation_aggregation The representation controls which aggregations the model allows or refuses. additive_contributions The sum of the contributions that are declared additive is equal to the prediction. seed_determinism If the plugin claims it, the same seed gives the same fit and scores.

If a check fails, the kit raises ContractViolation with the report. To get the report as a return value, pass raise_on_failure=False.

from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, toy  # toy: small reference steps and models
