mapi-sklearn changes each scikit-learn, xgboost, LightGBM or CatBoost estimator on the allow-list into a full modeling-api plugin. You tell which dims are samples and which variables are features. The platform does the rest:

  • It stacks your labelled xr.Dataset into a design matrix.
  • It fits the estimator and keeps it safely.
  • At score time, it builds exactly the same columns again.
  • It accepts new stores and forecast horizons.
  • It unstacks the predictions back into labelled arrays, with correct uncertainty.

docs.title: The plugins
docs.text:
The kind of uncertainty sets the representation of the output. The representation then sets which summaries and aggregations are valid. Each kind is a different plugin:

Plugin Representation What y_hat contains Aggregate over cells? sklearn.tabular_regressor point A point prediction (+ contributions) Linear only, with a flag sklearn.tabular_quantiles quantiles Conditional quantiles (quantile, ...) No sklearn.tabular_bootstrap draws One joint draw for each bootstrap replicate (chain, draw, ...) Yes, all sklearn.tabular_conformal interval (bound=[lower, upper, point], ...), attr alpha No sklearn.tabular_classifier point The probability of the positive class Linear only, with a flag sklearn.multiclass_classifier (v0.14) point The probability of each class: y_hat(..., class) No

Why conformal is an interval, not draws

A split-conformal interval guarantees the coverage for each cell (P(y in interval) >= 1 - alpha). It is not a distribution. A sum of intervals across stores or weeks claims a coverage that nobody measured. Thus the platform rejects these aggregations with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. For totals, use sklearn.tabular_bootstrap, because its draws are joint.

docs.title: A store-demand forecast
docs.text:
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: store-demand-xgb, project: retail}
data:
  dataset: dataset://retail/store_sku_weekly@latest
  bind:
    dims: {store: store_id, sku: sku, time: week}
    vars: {y: units_sold, price: price, promo: promo_flag}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 12}
pipeline:
  - {id: imp,   use: core.impute@^1,   with: {vars: [price], method: ffill, along: time, within: [store, sku]}}
  - {id: plags, use: core.lag@^1,      with: {vars: [promo], along: time, within: [store, sku], lags: [1, 2]}}
  - {id: cal,   use: core.calendar@^1, with: {along: time, features: [week_of_year, month]}}
  - {id: logy,  use: core.log1p@^1,    with: {vars: [y]}}
model:
  use: sklearn.tabular_quantiles@^1
  settings:
    estimator: {kind: xgboost.XGBRegressor, params: {n_estimators: 600, max_depth: 6, learning_rate: 0.05}}
    rows: [store, sku, time]                  # dims stacked into samples
    columns: {roles: [covariate]}             # which variables become features
    coord_features: {store: category, sku: category}
    uncertainty: {kind: quantile, quantiles: [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]}
    forecast_strategy: direct
  fit: {seed: 7, mode: evaluate_then_refit}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mape, coverage_80]}
execution: {resource_class: S, timeout: 10m}

What occurs:

  1. The platform scores the holdout (the last 12 weeks) through the score path. It uses context tails from the training weeks. It calculates rmse, mape and coverage_80 in units sold. The platform inverts the log1p. Quantiles map exactly through monotone transforms.
  2. The platform fits the model again on all weeks. The bundle keeps the xgboost model as JSON.
  3. A forecast request gives the future prices and promotions. The platform builds the lags again from the stored tail. It also does a check that the weeks continue the fitted range without gaps.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://retail/store-demand-xgb
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
data: dataset://retail/plan_next_4_weeks
output: {summary: [median, q10, q90]}

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning estimator — {kind, params} from the allow-list below (necessary for the built-in plugins) target y The canonical name of the target variable rows — The dims that the platform stacks into samples. Each row dim of the target. time_dim / time_kind time / time The row dim that extends at forecast time, and its kind (time, integer, index). Use none if no row dim extends. columns {roles: [covariate, media, spend, control, exposure]} The feature variables by role, or an explicit vars list. exclude removes names. coord_features {} Encode the labels of row dims as features: category, onehot, ordinal, numeric new_levels pooled What an unseen level of a row dim becomes: pooled, zero or error pooled_max_levels 256 Pool over a maximum of this number of fitted levels (the most frequent) weight, mask — A variable for the sample weight. A boolean mask of the cells that you can use. forecast_strategy direct In v1, the platform rejects recursive with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED. retransform median Point predictions through a non-linear inverse (log1p): median or Duan smearing contributions auto For the point and bootstrap plugins: auto, exact, zeroing, none n_jobs 1 The threads of the estimator. The default is 1, so that fits are the same bit for bit.

A variable with dims that are not in rows becomes one column for each label. For example, spend(store, channel, time) with the rows [store, time] gives spend[tv], spend[search]. The platform broadcasts a variable that does not have a row dim (calendar features over time only). The platform does not use some rows for the training:

  • Rows with a missing target
  • Rows with a weight that is zero or less
  • Rows where mask is false
  • Rows with a missing feature, for estimators that cannot accept missing values natively

A ROWS_DROPPED diagnostic reports these rows.

docs.title: Coordinate features
docs.text:
• category: integer codes. The platform declares them natively to xgboost and to HistGradientBoostingRegressor (a maximum of 254 levels). For all other estimators, it uses one-hot columns.
  • onehot: one 0/1 column for each fitted level.
  • ordinal: the position of the level as a number (for ordered dims).
  • numeric: the label. Numbers stay as they are. Datetimes become the days since the first fitted label.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text:
Kind Task Quantiles Missing values Categories Stored as sklearn.LinearRegression regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.Ridge, sklearn.Lasso, sklearn.ElasticNet regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.QuantileRegressor regression one model for each level — one-hot skops sklearn.RandomForestRegressor regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.GradientBoostingRegressor regression one model for each level — one-hot skops sklearn.HistGradientBoostingRegressor regression one model for each level native native skops xgboost.XGBRegressor regression one native multi-quantile model native native xgboost JSON sklearn.LogisticRegression, sklearn.RandomForestClassifier, xgboost.XGBClassifier binary and multiclass classification — xgboost only xgboost only skops / JSON sklearn.HistGradientBoostingClassifier (v0.14) binary and multiclass classification — native native skops lightgbm.LGBMClassifier (v0.14) binary and multiclass classification — native one-hot LightGBM text model catboost.CatBoostClassifier (v0.14) binary and multiclass classification — native one-hot CatBoost JSON model

LightGBM and CatBoost are in the extra mapi-sklearn[gbm]. The base-ml runner image has this extra. The other runner images do not have LightGBM or CatBoost. If the extra is not installed, a fit with these estimators stops with SETTINGS_INVALID. The message tells you to install mapi-sklearn[gbm]. The platform sets their output to quiet and their threads from n_jobs. CatBoost writes no files outside the run.

Each kind has a bounded Pydantic params model (extra="forbid"). You cannot set the parameters that the platform owns: seeds, threads, categorical declarations, and the loss or objective that a kind of uncertainty needs. For example, sklearn.tabular_quantiles sets the xgboost objective: reg:quantileerror. It rejects an objective that does not agree. The params models are a discriminated union. Thus the control plane validates them statically. For example, it rejects max_depth: -1 with a JSON pointer before a run starts.

docs.title: Hyperparameters as run params v0.11
docs.text: A fit logs the hyperparameters of the fitted estimator as run params with the prefix estimator., for example estimator.max_depth = 6. The fit logs only booleans, numbers and text (a maximum of 100 params). It does not log nested estimators, arrays or None. The Params tab of the run page shows them, and you can search runs by them (--filter 'param.estimator.max_depth >= 6'). See Track metrics, params and tags.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
Quantiles. xgboost fits all levels at the same time. The sklearn estimators that can do quantiles fit one model for each level. The platform sorts quantiles that cross (monotone rearrangement, which never increases the pinball loss). It reports the fraction of rows that cross as QUANTILE_CROSSING. If you do not set output.summary, the default (median, q5, q95) changes to agree with your grid. For example, with [0.1, 0.5, 0.9] you get median, q10, q90. If you request a level outside the grid, you get an error. The platform interpolates quantiles. It never extrapolates them.

Bootstrap. n replicates fit the estimator again on resampled rows. With by: store, they fit it on resampled whole stores. This is a cluster bootstrap that keeps the dependence in each store. expected outputs are the predictions of the replicates. predictive outputs add an out-of-bag residual for each cell. The draws are joint. Thus totals over stores, counterfactual deltas and all summaries are valid.

Split conformal. The platform keeps a calibration fraction out of the fit. By default, this fraction is the most recent weeks (calibration_by: last), as in a forecast. random selects rows at random. The radius is the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))-th smallest absolute calibration residual. The calibration set can be too small for the requested alpha. Then you get a SETTINGS_INVALID error, not an infinite interval. refit: true fits the point model again on all rows after the calibration. The interval is then narrower, but the finite-sample guarantee is only approximate (not exact).

docs.title: New stores, skus and markets
docs.text:
Score data can contain a label of a row dim that the fit did not see. Then the effective policy of the dim decides. This policy is the stricter of the policy of the data and the new_levels of the plugin:

  • pooled: the prediction is an average of the predictions that the row gets under each fitted level. The training frequency of each level is the weight. For a linear model with one-hot features, this is equal to a prediction with the average encoding. The platform calculates the average of quantiles and interval bounds (Vincentisation). It calculates the average of bootstrap draws for each draw, so that they stay joint.
  • zero: the level adds nothing. All one-hot columns are 0. The category codes are missing (for estimators that accept missing values natively).
  • error (or a fixed dim): UNSEEN_LEVELS before the run starts.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The point plugins and the bootstrap plugins can return contributions(component, ...) next to y_hat:

  • exact (linear estimators. This is the default with contributions: auto): intercept plus coef × x for each column. The platform adds the one-hot columns of a coordinate feature into one component. The sum of the components is exactly equal to the prediction.
  • zeroing (all estimators): counterfactual zeroing. baseline is the prediction with all features at zero. The contribution of each feature is the decrease when only that feature is zero. interaction contains the remainder, so that the sum of the components stays correct. These contributions have the label counterfactual_zeroing. They are not Shapley values. SHAP is not in the scope of v1.

Contributions are additive in model space (output: {units: model}). Through a non-linear inverse, for example log1p, the inverse of each component is not a decomposition. If you want a sum of the parts that is correct, request model units.

docs.title: Default plots and metrics v0.10
docs.text:
Each sklearn plugin now declares its standard plots. The fit run draws only the plots that the spec lists in outputs.plots. Thus, add the plots that you want to outputs.plots. In the spec editor, the Insert panel shows the plots of the model first.

outputs:
  plots: [core.calibration, core.roc_pr, core.confusion, ml.feature_importance]

An evaluate run from the Score page does not need this list. It draws the plots for the shape of each output: a classifier gets core.calibration, core.roc_pr and core.confusion.

Plugins Plots Regressor, quantiles, bootstrap, conformal core.fit_vs_actual, core.residuals_over_time, ml.feature_importance Classifier core.calibration, core.roc_pr, core.confusion, ml.feature_importance

The three classifier plots read the probability in y_hat and the 0/1 target. They do not need draws. core.calibration shows a reliability diagram: do the predicted probabilities agree with how often the positive class occurs? core.roc_pr shows how well the model puts the positive rows before the negative rows. core.confusion counts the errors at the threshold 0.5. Refer to the plot guide.

Classifier metrics. The fit pairs the probability in y_hat with the target. Thus evaluate.metrics can include auc, brier and accuracy:

evaluate: {metrics: [auc, brier, accuracy]}

Before v0.10, the fit calculated no metric for a classifier. metrics.json was empty. The point metrics (rmse, mae and the other point metrics) use the probability too. Thus rmse is the root of the Brier score. Refer to Metrics in evaluate for the definitions.

A known limit

Validation refuses log_score for the classifier, because the plugin gives point predictions. Use brier. A regression target that has only the values 0 and 1 also gets the classifier plots on the Score page.

docs.title: Multiclass classification v0.14
docs.text:
sklearn.multiclass_classifier puts each row into one of 3 or more classes. The target can be text ("cat") or whole numbers (3).

model:
  use: sklearn.multiclass_classifier@1
  settings:
    target: topic                       # text or whole-number labels
    rows: [ticket]
    time_kind: none                     # the rows have no time order
    columns: {roles: [covariate]}
    estimator: {kind: lightgbm.LGBMClassifier, params: {n_estimators: 300, num_leaves: 31}}
    max_classes: 50
outputs:
  plots: [core.roc_pr, core.confusion, ml.feature_importance]
evaluate: {metrics: [accuracy, brier, auc]}
Setting Default Meaning estimator A classification estimator of the table above class_order none The classes in a fixed sequence. It must contain all the classes of the training data. Without it, the classes are in sorted sequence. A maximum of 200. max_classes 50 The fit stops when the target has more classes (2 to 200) target_dtype str The dtype of the target in the schema template: str or int64

The fit changes the labels to text. Whole numbers become 3, not 3.0. Rows with no label are not used. The output y_hat has a class dim with the class labels as coordinates. Each row of y_hat has the probabilities of the classes, and they add up to 1. y_hat has the attribute meaning: class_probability.

Plots and metrics. core.roc_pr draws one ROC curve and one precision-recall curve for each class against the other classes, and gives the macro AUC. core.confusion shows a K × K matrix of the most probable class. The metrics accuracy, brier and auc (the mean one-vs-rest AUC of the classes) use the class probabilities. As for the binary classifier, validation refuses log_score, because the plugin gives point predictions.

sklearn.tabular_classifier (binary) also accepts the new estimators.

docs.title: Persistence and safety
docs.text:
The bundle keeps the fitted estimators in its /native group. It never uses pickle:

  • scikit-learn estimators with skops. Before the platform loads the file, it lists the types in the file. It refuses all types that are not on the allow-list of that estimator. For example, a random forest can contain sklearn.tree._tree.Tree. A ridge regression can contain no extra types. The loaded object must be exactly the expected class.
  • xgboost models as the JSON document of the booster.
  • LightGBM models as the text model of the booster (v0.14). The text must start with tree. The platform loads it into a LightGBM booster, not into a pickled object.
  • CatBoost models as the JSON model (v0.14). The JSON must be an object with oblivious_trees.

The bundle manifest records the size, CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256 of each file. The contract kit does a check that the bundle contains no entry that looks like pickle.

docs.title: Write your own sklearn plugin
docs.text:
Implement estimator(). Then select a base class for the representation that you want:

from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sklearn import PointSettings, SklearnModel, capabilities_for
from mapi_spec import Capabilities
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge


class LinearDemand(SklearnModel[PointSettings]):
    id = "t.acme.linear_demand"
    version = "1.0.0"
    capabilities: ClassVar[Capabilities] = capabilities_for("none").model_copy(
        update={"contribution_scale": "additive"}  # a linear model decomposes exactly
    )

    def estimator(self, s: PointSettings) -> Ridge:
        return Ridge(alpha=0.5)  # must be exactly an allow-listed class

estimator() can return an instance from the allow-list, a {kind, params} mapping or a choice model. The platform rejects subclasses of estimators and parameters that are not in the params model. The base classes are SklearnModel (point), SklearnQuantileModel, SklearnBootstrapModel, SklearnConformalModel and SklearnClassifier.

Before you publish, run the contract kit on synthetic data:

from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, check_model
from mapi_sklearn.testing import demand_dataset, demand_registry, demand_schema, demand_spec

data = demand_dataset()  # a store x sku x week demand panel
report = check_model(
    LinearDemand,
    ModelFixture(
        spec=demand_spec("t.acme.linear_demand@^1", {"estimator": None}),
        data=data,
        raw_schema=demand_schema(data),
        registry=demand_registry(),
    ),
)
print(report.summary())
# ... [PASS] additive_contributions: contributions sum to 'y_hat' ...

docs.title: Limits in v1
docs.text:
• Forecasts are direct only. You must give the future features, or the pipeline must calculate them.
  • sklearn.tabular_classifier is binary. The positive class is the larger target value. For three or more classes, use sklearn.multiclass_classifier.
  • The multiclass classifier has no calibration plot.
  • The platform declares all row dims other than time_dim as categorical. Thus groups with integer labels (numeric store ids) need string labels.
  • Contributions are not available for the quantile plugins or the conformal plugins.

docs.title: Forecasting and sequential models
docs.text:
Time causes many problems that most modelling platforms do not show. A forecast can silently go past the range that the model can represent. A state-space model can start again from zero at each score. A platform can score a holdout without the history that the holdout needs. modeling-api makes each of these items explicit. It does a check of them before it uses compute.

Classical models

ARIMA/ARIMAX, exponential smoothing, theta, ARDL and error correction, VAR, VECM, VARMAX, dynamic factors and Markov switching come from statsmodels. See statsmodels time-series models.

docs.title: Horizons are part of the contract
docs.text:
A time dim declares its policy extend and, optionally, a max_extension. The max_extension is the distance after the fitted range that a forecast can go without a new fit. The control plane does a check of each score request against it. It uses only the metadata:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://climate/mauna-loa-co2
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: t, periods: 30}

{"code": "HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT", "status": 409,
 "detail": "horizon of 30 exceeds the 24 periods this fit supports along 't'; a refit is required"}

Models that need a bounded domain get it from the same place. ts.hsgp_trend sets the size of its Hilbert-space GP from ctx.anticipated_coords (the fitted labels and max_extension future labels). Thus the basis that it calculates at a forecast month is exactly the basis of the fit:

dom = HSGPDomain.from_positions(positions_of(ctx.anticipated_coords["t"]), s.c)
phi = hsgp_basis(dom.scale(ctx.position("t")), s.m, dom.L)   # same at fit and at score

Score payloads must also continue the fitted range without gaps (NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION). They cannot start before the fitted range (COORD_NOT_ALLOWED).

The runner does a check of the mode before it builds a forecast payload:

  • If the model does not declare the mode in capabilities.score_modes, the runner refuses the request with MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED. The error lists the modes that the model supports.
  • The labels of the horizon dim must be numbers or dates. A horizon along text labels (for example the names of images or areas) gives COORD_NOT_ALLOWED.
  • A request without data, without a scenario dataset and without a horizon gives SCHEMA_INVALID ("the score request has no data"). Thus a model that has no forecast mode always needs data to score. The Score page of the web app shows No new data only for Forecast, or when a scenario dataset gives the values.

docs.title: Evaluate the way you will forecast
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit is the default for models that you can promote. In this mode, the platform does these steps:

  1. It fits on the training window.
  2. It scores the holdout through the score path, with the context and the state from the training only.
  3. It records the metrics.
  4. It fits again on all the data, so that forecasts start from the latest data.

The production bundle links the evaluation bundle and its metrics.

MASE. Add mase to evaluate.metrics to compare the holdout error with a seasonal naive forecast. The fit divides the holdout mae by the mean absolute error of the naive forecast on the training data. The season length comes from the frequency of the time dim (for example 52 for weekly data). If the training data is shorter than one season, the naive forecast uses the value of the period before. The naive error has the same units as the holdout error. For a pipeline that aggregates the data, or for a model that sets its own output units (for example an MMM model), these are the units of the model outputs. The fit calculates mase only when it has the training data. Thus an evaluate run from the Score page skips mase and gives the reason in skipped. A value less than 1 shows that the model is better than the naive forecast.

docs.title: Sequential models keep a terminal state
docs.text:
Hidden Markov models, Kalman filters and particle filters keep a summary of the past in a state. They keep the state in a terminal_state group that the plugin owns. At score time, they read this group. They do not process the history again. ts.gaussian_hmm keeps the filtered state distribution at the last fitted step, alpha_T(chain, draw, animal, state):

  • forecast propagates it: P(z_{T+h}) = alpha_T · A^h, for each posterior draw.
  • filter continues the forward filter over new observations. It returns an updated terminal_state group. Thus, if you filter six new steps at the same time or in two batches of three, you get the same state.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://ecology/animal-tracks-hmm
mode: filter
data: dataset://ecology/tracks_live@v1

The result has predictions (the one-step-ahead y_hat and the filtered state_prob). It also has a terminal_state group. Its attrs.step is the last filtered step.

docs.title: A Bayesian structural time series v0.13
docs.text:
ts.bsts is a Kalman filter model: a level, a trend, seasonal patterns and drivers. It keeps the state at the end of the fit in its terminal_state group, as ts.gaussian_hmm does. The group has the mean and the covariance of the state for each kept draw (a maximum of 250 draws), and the matrices of the model.

  • In the fitted range, predict gives the one-step-ahead prediction. This is the value that the model expected before it saw the period.
  • forecast starts from the terminal state. The model propagates the state and adds the noise of each period. A forecast thus has a range that becomes wider with the horizon. The drivers need their future values.
  • filter continues the Kalman filter over new periods. It returns the one-step-ahead predictions and an updated terminal_state. Then a forecast starts from the latest period without a new fit.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://retail/monthly-sales-bsts
mode: filter
data: dataset://retail/sales_last_3_months@v1

The model accepts periods without a value. The filter does not update the state in these periods, and the prediction continues over them. The core.decomposition chart shows the level, the seasonal parts and the effect of the drivers from the components group. See Causal models and Bayesian structural time series. causal.impact uses the same model to measure the effect of a change.

docs.title: Plots of hidden states v0.10
docs.text:
ts.gaussian_hmm and the statsmodels Markov switching model now include core.state_sequence in their standard plots. The plot shows the observed series above the probability of each state over time.

  • For the HMM, the plot reads state_prob in the hidden_states group. The data has one series for each animal. The plot shows the first animal, and the caption names it. To show a different animal, set select in the plot builder, for example {"animal": "a2"}.
  • For the Markov switching model, the plot reads smoothed_prob in the regimes group. The state dim is regime.
  • A score run with a state output (for example state_prob of a filter score) also draws the plot from the score summary. A state output has a dim with the name state or regime, and its values are probabilities over that dim. A panel dim such as the state of a country is not a state output.

Decomposition. The unobserved components model, exponential smoothing (ETS) and ts.hsgp_trend now include core.decomposition (ts.bsts too, from v0.13). The plot stacks the level, the seasonal part and the other parts over time. The slope of a trend is a rate, not a part of the level. Thus the plot does not stack it. An ETS model has a components group only when its error, trend and season are additive.

docs.title: Missing values and sentinels
docs.text:
Raw series often use numbers for gaps (-99.99). Declare the code in the schema (missing_sentinel). Then change it into NaN with core.replace_sentinel. Some models can accept gaps (for example ts.hsgp_trend). These models do not use those periods in the likelihood, but they predict them.

For all settings, see Built-in models. For the fixtures (c08, e24) that keep this behavior tested, see the Conformance corpus.

docs.title: Track metrics, params and tags v0.11
docs.text:
Each run keeps a log of what happened in it. Model code, workflow nodes and you (from a notebook, a script or the command line) can add to this log. The log has these parts:

  • Metrics. A metric is a series of points, for example the loss at each step of an optimiser. A point without a step is a scalar, for example a business KPI.
  • Params. A param is a value that does not change, for example the number of draws.
  • Tags. A tag is a text value that you can change at any time, for example stage=candidate.
  • The name and the note. A display name and a free-text note for the run.
  • Structured log lines. Log lines with a level (debug, info, warning or error) and fields.
  • Images and tables v0.14. Images (PNG or JPEG), matplotlib figures and small tables, for example a sample of predictions at each step.

The run page in the web app shows all of them (the Metrics, Params, Media, Logs and Notes tabs). You can search for runs by their metrics, params and tags. To compare runs and to group them into experiments, see Compare runs and use experiments.

See also HTTP API: Run tracking The endpoints, the DTOs and the search grammar Run protocol: Tracking events The metrics, params and tags events and the budgets Python SDK FitContext.log_metric and the other methods Compare runs and use experiments The runs table, saved views, the compare page and experiments

docs.title: What the platform tracks for you
docs.text:
You do not have to write code for these items.

Params of the spec. Each fit logs these params:

Param Value model The model and its version, for example mmm.bayesian@1.2.0 fit.engine, fit.draws, fit.tune, fit.chains, fit.target_accept, fit.seed, fit.mode Only the fields that the spec sets data.split The kind of split, when the spec has a split settings.<path> One param for each value of the model settings, for example settings.adstock.l_max. A list or a dict becomes compact JSON (a maximum of 500 characters). A maximum of 200 settings params.

Live chains. PyMC models (with nutpie or the PyMC NUTS sampler) and the MMMs (mmm.bayesian, mmm.nested and mmm.multivariate) send the progress of each chain while they sample. The run page shows the draws, the divergences and the step size of each chain.

Step metrics of samplers and optimisers.

Source Keys Labels Step nutpie (PyMC models, mmm.bayesian, mmm.nested, mmm.multivariate) step_size, num_steps (leapfrog steps of the latest draw), divergences (cumulative) chain The draws that the chain finished, with tuning (starts at 1) PyMC NUTS sampler (PyMC models, the MMMs with nuts_sampler: pymc) step_size, tree_depth, num_steps, divergences (cumulative) chain The draw index, with tuning (starts at 1). For a long chain, each k-th draw and the last draw, k = ceil(n / 5000). ADVI loss (negative ELBO) none The optimisation step (starts at 1). For a long fit, each k-th step, k = ceil(n / 5000). The evaluation fit of evaluate_then_refit All of the above also fit=evaluation As above. The params of the evaluation fit get the prefix evaluation., for example evaluation.n_obs.

End-of-run metrics. The holdout metrics of a fit (for example rmse and elpd_loo) become scalar series.

scikit-learn. A fit of a sklearn.* model logs the hyperparameters of the estimator as estimator.<name> params (only numbers, booleans and text).

Marketing-mix models. Each MMM fit logs a summary of its result. See What an MMM fit logs.

Causal models and ts.bsts. Each fit logs the effect of the change and the fit before the change. See What a causal fit logs.

Workflows. The search.grid node logs each grid point and its scores. The model.backtest node logs the metrics of each fold. See Workflow nodes.

docs.title: What an MMM fit logs v0.12
docs.text:
At the end of a fit, each marketing-mix model (mmm.bayesian, mmm.frequentist, mmm.nested and mmm.multivariate) logs params and scalar metrics (no step). The metrics come from 200 thinned draws of the posterior (or of the bootstrap). Thus, you can sort and filter runs by the return of a channel.

Params.

Param Models Value mmm.framework_version all The version of mmm-framework mmm.n_channels all The number of channels mmm.n_periods all The number of periods of the fit window mmm.n_cells all The number of panel cells (geo and product combinations; 1 for national data) mmm.link all identity, log (poisson, negative_binomial) or logit (beta) mmm.time_varying mmm.bayesian The time-varying channels, separated by commas (empty when there are none) mmm.mediators mmm.nested The mediators, separated by commas mmm.outcomes mmm.multivariate The outcomes, separated by commas mmm.cross_effects mmm.multivariate The number of cross-effects

A param value has a maximum of 6000 characters. If a list of names is longer, the model cuts it and adds ... at the end. The fit does not stop because of this.

Metrics.

Metric Labels Value roi channel The posterior mean of the return on spend: the contribution of the channel over the fit window divided by its spend roi_p05, roi_p95 channel The 5th and the 95th percentile of the return on spend mroi channel The marginal return: the extra KPI for each extra unit of spend at the current spend (a central difference at 1 ± 1%) contribution_share channel The part of the total KPI that the channel gives baseline_share none The part of the total KPI with no media

A channel with no spend gets no roi. The label value is the channel name with characters other than letters, digits, _, . and - changed to _ (TV spend becomes TV_spend). For mmm.multivariate, the metrics use the weighted total of the outcomes. It also logs a roi for each outcome, with the labels channel and outcome.

Find the runs where TV returns more than 2:

mapi runs ls --filter "metric.roi{channel=tv} > 2" --column "metric.roi{channel=tv}"

docs.title: What a causal fit logs v0.13
docs.text:
At the end of a fit, ts.bsts and the causal models (causal.impact, causal.synthetic_control and causal.did) log params and scalar metrics (no step). Their samplers also send live chains and step metrics, as the other PyMC models do. The causal metrics come from the impact group of the bundle (a maximum of 500 draws), in the units of the target.

Params of ts.bsts and causal.impact.

Param Value bsts.trend level, local_linear or smooth bsts.seasonality The seasonal periods, separated by commas. x3 gives the harmonics, for example 12,52.18x3. bsts.regressors The drivers (the control series of causal.impact), separated by commas bsts.n_states The number of states of the model bsts.n_periods, bsts.missing_periods The number of periods of the fit, and the number of periods without a value

Metrics of ts.bsts.

Metric Value sigma_obs, sigma_level The posterior means of the observation noise and of the level innovations, in the units of the target one_step_rmse The error of the one-step-ahead predictions in the fitted range one_step_coverage_90 The part of the observed values in the 90% interval of the one-step-ahead predictions

Params of the causal models.

Param Models Value causal.intervention_start, causal.intervention_end all The dates (or period numbers) of the change. The end is empty when the change did not stop. causal.n_pre, causal.n_post all The number of periods before the start and in the effect window causal.n_treated all The number of treated units (1 for causal.impact) causal.n_donors, causal.weights causal.synthetic_control The number of donor markets, and simplex or horseshoe causal.design, causal.staggered, causal.leads, causal.lags causal.did The design, if the units got the change at different times, and the event window

Metrics of the causal models.

Metric Labels Value effect_total none (unit with two or more treated units) The mean of the total effect over the effect window effect_total_sd, effect_total_p05, effect_total_p95 none The sd, the 5th and the 95th percentile of the total effect effect_average none The mean effect in one period effect_relative none (unit with two or more treated units) The total effect divided by the total of the values without the change p_effect_positive none (unit with two or more treated units) The probability that the total effect is more than zero pre_rmse, pre_mape none The error of the model before the change donor_weight unit, donor causal.synthetic_control: the posterior mean of the weight, for the 10 largest donors of each treated unit att, att_p05, att_p95 none causal.did: the average effect after the change, with its interval event_coef event_time causal.did: the posterior mean of the coefficient for each period relative to the change

Find the geo-lift tests with an effect that is more than zero with a probability of 95% or more:

mapi runs ls --filter "metric.p_effect_positive >= 0.95" --column metric.effect_total

docs.title: What a network fit logs v0.15
docs.text:
The dl models of mapi-jax log the training while it runs:

  • loss and accuracy (classification) or rmse and mae (regression), with the label split=train (batch values) and split=val (at the end of each evaluation);
  • lr, grad_norm and epoch;
  • one log line for each epoch, with the fields epoch, train_loss, val_loss and images_per_second;
  • the params dl.arch.*, dl.train.*, dl.backend, dl.device and dl.parameters;
  • the media val_predictions and confusion (label split=val) at a maximum of 20 evaluations.

See Deep learning.

docs.title: Keys, labels and values
docs.text:
Metric keys match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$. Write qualifiers as labels, not in the key:

Do not write Write train/loss key loss, labels {"split": "train"} rmse_fold_3 key rmse, labels {"fold": "3"} chain0.step_size key step_size, labels {"chain": "0"}

These rules apply:

  • A series is one key and one set of labels. loss and loss with {"split": "val"} are two series.
  • A series has a maximum of 8 labels. A label key matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$. A label value matches ^[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]{1,63}$.
  • A metric value must be a finite number. The SDK ignores NaN and infinity.
  • A param key and a tag key can have letters, digits, _, ., - and / (for example settings.adstock.l_max). A param value is a boolean, a number or a text of a maximum of 6000 characters.
  • A param does not change. If you log a param again with the same value, nothing occurs. A different value is an error.
  • A tag value is a text of a maximum of 1000 characters. The last value is kept. Tag keys that start with mapi. are for the platform only.
  • A step is an integer, 0 or more. For a stepped series, the first value of a step is kept. For a scalar series (no step), the newest value is kept.

docs.title: Log from a model plugin
docs.text:
FitContext and ScoreContext have the logging methods. The SDK does a check of each key and each label when you call the method, also in a notebook without a run. Thus a bad key fails at the line that has the error.

class MyModel(CustomModel):
    def fit(self, data, ctx):
        ctx.log_param("solver", "lbfgs")
        ctx.set_tag("family", "gaussian")
        for step in range(1, n_steps + 1):
            loss = self._update()
            ctx.log_metric("loss", loss, step=step)
        ctx.log_metrics({"rmse": rmse, "mae": mae}, labels={"split": "train"})
        ctx.log_line("refit done", level="info", fields={"iterations": n_steps})
        ...
Method What it does log_metric(key, value, step=None, labels=None) Log one point log_metrics(values, step=None, labels=None) Log some metrics with the same step and labels log_param(key, value), log_params(params) Log params set_tag(key, value), set_tags(tags) Set tags log_line(message, level="info", fields=None) Write a structured log line (a maximum of 16 fields) chains(chains) Report the progress of each chain (mapi_spec.run.ChainProgress) tracking True when the platform records the values. Use it to skip metrics that take a long time to calculate.

The methods are thread-safe. A sampler callback on a different thread can call them.

Inside a run, the values go to the platform each second. The fit also writes them into the bundle: the model group metrics_history keeps the stepped series, the scalars, the params and the tags. The core.loss_curve plot reads this group. For the layout, see Bundles.

docs.title: Log images, figures and tables v0.14
docs.text:
A run can log images, matplotlib figures and small tables. Each item has a key, and can have a step, labels and a caption, as a metric point has. Use the same key for the same picture at different steps, for example the predictions on a sample at each epoch.

class MyModel(CustomModel):
    def fit(self, data, ctx):
        for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
            ...
            if ctx.tracking_media:  # skip the work when nothing records the images
                ctx.log_image("samples", grid, step=epoch, labels={"split": "val"},
                              caption=f"Predictions after epoch {epoch}")
        fig = plot_residuals(...)
        ctx.log_figure("residuals", fig)
        ctx.log_table("confusion_counts", counts_df, caption="Holdout counts per class")
Method Accepts log_image(key, image, step=None, labels=None, caption=None) A numpy array: (height, width) gray, (height, width, 1), (height, width, 3) RGB or (height, width, 4) RGBA. uint8 values as they are, booleans as 0 and 255, other integers from 0 to 255, floats from 0 to 1 (NaN becomes 0). Also PNG or JPEG bytes, a Pillow image or an xarray.DataArray with the dims (y, x) or (y, x, channel). log_figure(key, figure, step=None, labels=None, caption=None) A matplotlib figure. The SDK saves it as a PNG file (100 dpi). log_table(key, table, step=None, labels=None, caption=None) A pandas DataFrame, a dict of columns or a list of records. Numbers, booleans, text and empty values. NaN and infinity become empty values. Dates become ISO text. tracking_media True when the platform records images. A figure takes time to draw: use this property to skip it.

The SDK does a check of the key, the labels, the step and the caption at each call, also without a run. A bad key fails at the line that has the error. Media keys follow the rules of metric keys. When nothing records the media (a notebook without a run, or a run that has no media upload), the call does not encode the image.

Limits:

Limit Value Size of one image 8 MiB, a maximum of 4096 pixels on each side Size of one table 1 MiB, a maximum of 10 000 rows, 64 columns and 200 000 cells. A cell has a maximum of 1000 characters. Caption 500 characters Items in the run 1000 Bytes in the run 256 MiB

The limits count the items of all attempts of the run and the items logged through the API. If a run logs more, the platform does not keep the extra items and each attempt gets one MEDIA_BUDGET warning. The run does not fail. An item that replaces another item (the same key, labels and step) frees the bytes of the old item.

What the platform does with an image. The worker writes the file in its scratch directory. The supervisor reads the file, calculates its SHA-256 and does a check of the format and the size. Then it uploads the file. The server downloads the file again, does the same checks, and keeps a copy in the bundles bucket. The platform accepts only PNG and JPEG images (no SVG, no GIF). For the details, see Run protocol: Media.

Where you see the media.

  • Web app. The Media tab of the run shows each key. A slider selects the step. A select shows one value of a label. A table shows its first 200 rows. The compare page shows the images of several runs side by side.
  • Python. api.runs.media(run_id) lists the items. api.runs.download_media(run_id, item) gets the bytes and does a check of the size, the CRC32C and the SHA-256.
  • Command line. mapi runs media RUN lists the items. --download DIR writes the files.

Log media from a notebook. You can add an image or a table to a run that already exists, also after it finished. One request has a maximum of 4 MiB.

api.runs.log_image(run_id, "holdout_map", "map.png", caption="Holdout error by region")
api.runs.log_table(run_id, "lift_by_region", {"region": ["north", "south"], "lift": [0.04, 0.02]})

mapi runs log-image run_01… holdout_map map.png --step 3 --label split=val --caption "Holdout error"

docs.title: Log from a workflow node
docs.text:
The NodeContext of a workflow node has the same methods. The values go to the run of the node.

search.grid logs these items in its search run. The search run is the first item in the child_runs of the node. The run_id of the node is the refit of the winner, which does not have these items.

  • The params grid.metric, grid.direction, grid.points and grid.nested.
  • One param for each value of each grid point: trial.<i>.<pointer>, for example trial.3.adstock/l_max = 4.
  • The scores of grid point i as metrics with step i (mae, rmse, mape, smape, mase, coverage_90, when they are present). A nested search adds the labels {"stage": "inner", "fold": "<j>"} to the inner scores. The outer scores have the label {"stage": "outer"} and step j.
  • The scalar best_<metric> (for example best_rmse) and the tag grid.best_point.
  • A warning log line for each grid point that failed.

model.backtest logs the metrics of each fold as scalars with the label {"fold": "<j>"}. The inner fits of a backtest do not log step metrics.

docs.title: Log from a notebook or a script
docs.text:
You can add metrics, params and tags to a run that already exists, also after it finished. For example, log the revenue lift that you measured after you deployed the model. You need the runner role. An API token needs the runs:write scope.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()  # MAPI_URL, MAPI_TOKEN and MAPI_PROJECT, or a profile
run_id = "run_01jaf3q2x8m9v7k5h4g3f2e1d0"

api.runs.log_metric(run_id, "revenue_lift", 0.042, labels={"region": "north"})
api.runs.log_params(run_id, {"analyst": "kim", "holdout_weeks": 8})
api.runs.set_tags(run_id, {"stage": "production", "old_tag": None})  # None deletes a tag
api.runs.update(run_id, name="weekly sales, adstock 4", note="Holiday weeks removed.")

with api.runs.track(run_id) as t:      # sends the points in batches
    for week, value in weekly_kpi:
        t.log_metric("weekly_lift", value, step=week)

runs.log_metrics sends a maximum of 1000 points in each request. It divides a larger list. runs.track keeps the points and sends them when 500 wait and when the with block ends.

The same with the command line:

mapi runs log-metric run_01… revenue_lift 0.042 --label region=north
mapi runs log-param run_01… analyst kim
mapi runs tag run_01… stage=production --delete old_tag
mapi runs rename run_01… "weekly sales, adstock 4"
mapi runs note run_01… "Holiday weeks removed."

The same with HTTP: POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/metrics, POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/params and PATCH /v1/runs/{run_id} (see HTTP API).

docs.title: Read the tracking data
docs.text:
• Web app. Open the run. The Metrics tab shows a chart for each key. Use Colour by to give each chain (or each other label) a colour. The Params tab shows the params and the tags. The Logs tab has a level filter. The Notes tab changes the name, the tags and the note.
  • Python. api.runs.metrics(run_id) lists the series with their summaries (last, min, max, count). api.runs.metric_history(run_id, "step_size", max_points=500) gets the points. api.runs.params(run_id) lists the params.
  • Command line. mapi runs metrics RUN, mapi runs metrics RUN --key loss and mapi runs params RUN.
  • Several runs. The compare page shows the curves of 2 to 10 runs on one chart.

The server downsamples a long series to max_points (the default is 1000). It keeps the shape of the curve, the first point and the last point.

docs.title: Search runs
docs.text:
GET /v1/runs, api.runs.list(...) and mapi runs ls can filter, sort and show runs by their tracking data:

mapi runs ls --filter 'metric.rmse < 12' --filter 'param.fit.engine = nutpie' \
  --order-by metric.rmse --column metric.rmse --column param.settings.adstock.l_max

runs = api.runs.list(
    filters=["metric.loss{split=val}.min < 0.3", "tag.stage = candidate"],
    order_by="-metric.elpd_loo",
    columns=["metric.elpd_loo", "param.fit.draws"],
)

A metric filter compares the summary of one exact series. Add .min, .max or .count to compare a value different from the last value. A run that does not have the series does not match. For the full grammar, see Search runs.

In the web app, the runs table shows tracked columns and has a filter bar. You can save a search as a view. See Compare runs and use experiments.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
Each run has budgets for its tracking data. The defaults are:

Budget Default Points in one series 10 000 Points in the run 500 000 Series in the run 1000 Params 5000 Tags 100 Structured log lines 10 000 lines, 2 MiB Images and tables v0.14 1000 items, 256 MiB

If a run logs more, the platform does not keep the extra points and the run gets one TRACKING_BUDGET warning. The run does not fail. A worker that sends more than 64 MiB of tracking data fails with SANDBOX_VIOLATION. An API write that is more than the budget gets 429 QUOTA_EXCEEDED.

Note

Log curves with a step that grows slowly, for example each 10th step. The chart shows a maximum of 1000 points for each series.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
An operator can set MAPI_TRACKING_RETENTION_DAYS. Then the server deletes the metric points and the structured log lines of runs that finished more days ago than the setting. The server keeps the summaries, the params, the tags, the name and the note. It also keeps the value of each metric without a step. Thus search continues to work for old runs. If you log more points to a series after this, the server adds them to the summary that it kept (count, minimum, maximum and the last value). See Configuration.

The retention setting does not delete images and tables. The server keeps them until you delete the tenant v0.14.

docs.title: Tree datasets, HDF5 and multi-file versions v0.8
docs.text:
Some data does not fit in one table of variables. A telescope file has an image and, in a second group, the point-spread function (PSF) of the instrument. A sales study has one file for each market, and a separate file for the media plan. From v0.8, a dataset version can hold this data as a tree: an xr.DataTree with one node for each group.

This guide tells you how to:

  • upload NetCDF-4 and HDF5 files that have groups (tree datasets);
  • map a raw HDF5 file, which has no dim names, after an inspection;
  • make one version from several files: one file for each node, files stacked along a dim, or files merged on shared coords;
  • read nodes of a tree in a spec with data.nodes;
  • write a model that reads the whole tree;
  • use a tree dataset in a workflow (v0.9).

All existing datasets, specs and plugins continue to work without changes. A file without groups still gives a plain dataset version, as before.

The examples on this page are in docs/snippets/tree_data.py. The docs tests run this script. The script ingests the example files with the code of the ingest run, and it checks each JSON body, spec, client call and CLI command on this page.

docs.title: What a tree dataset is
docs.text:
A tree dataset has nodes. A node path identifies each node: / is the root, /instrument is a group below the root and /instrument/psf is a group below /instrument. Each node holds variables over its own dims. A node also sees the coords of the nodes above it (xarray inherits them). Thus a dim that a node shares with a node above it must have the same labels.

A node without variables is a pure group. The ingest keeps it as an empty node. It never drops a group without a warning.

Layout Stored as Schema When dataset (the default) data.zarr.zip schema.json (DataSchema) A file with no groups, or a version whose sources are all in the root tree data.tree.zip tree_schema.json (TreeSchema: one DataSchema for each node) A file with groups, or a version with sources below the root

A DatasetVersion gives the layout in layout. A tree version also has tree_schema, and its data_schema is the schema of the root node. Thus an older reader sees the root node and fails softly. sources lists the uploads of the version.

docs.title: NetCDF-4 and HDF5 files with groups
docs.text:
NetCDF-4 files are HDF5 files. xarray writes one HDF5 group for each node of a tree:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rows = np.round(np.arange(-1.6, 1.6, 0.05), 2)  # 64 labels, in arcsec
cols = np.round(np.arange(-1.6, 1.6, 0.05), 2)
image = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "image": (("row", "col"), rng.poisson(20.0, (64, 64)).astype("float32")),
        "noise": (("row", "col"), np.full((64, 64), 4.5, "float32")),
    },
    coords={"row": rows, "col": cols},
)
psf = xr.Dataset({"psf": (("prow", "pcol"), np.full((9, 9), 1 / 81))})

lens = xr.DataTree.from_dict({"/": image, "/instrument/psf": psf})
lens.to_netcdf("lens.nc", engine="h5netcdf")  # NetCDF-4: one HDF5 group for each node

Upload lens.nc with format netcdf, as for any NetCDF file. The ingest opens the file as a tree. The groups become nodes: /, /instrument (a pure group) and /instrument/psf. The dims and vars of a NetCDF mapping rename and select variables in each node, by name, as for a plain file.

  • A NetCDF file that has only a root group gives a dataset version, as before v0.8.
  • NetCDF-3 files have no groups. The ingest reads them with SciPy.
  • A .zarr.zip with nested groups also gives a tree. The Python client writes an xr.DataTree in this format (data.tree.zip).

You can make and check a tree schema in Python:

from mapi_sdk.tree import infer_tree_schema, read_tree_zip, write_tree_zip

schema = infer_tree_schema(lens)
print(list(schema.nodes))  # ['/', '/instrument', '/instrument/psf']
print(schema.default_node())  # '/' (the root has variables)
write_tree_zip(lens, "lens.tree.zip")  # the 'data.tree.zip' wire format
assert read_tree_zip("lens.tree.zip").groups == lens.groups

docs.title: Node names
docs.text: A node name starts with a letter or _. The other characters are letters, digits, _, . and -, to a maximum of 64 characters. A tree has a maximum of 8 levels below the root. If a file has a group with a name that is not valid, the ingest refuses the file. The error names the group.

docs.title: Raw HDF5: inspect, then map
docs.text:
A raw HDF5 file (.h5, .hdf5 or .he5, written with h5py or by an instrument) has arrays but no dim names and no coords. For example:

import h5py

with h5py.File("lens_raw.h5", "w") as f:  # no dim names, no coords: raw HDF5
    obs = f.create_group("observations")
    obs.create_dataset("image", data=image["image"].values, compression="gzip")
    obs.create_dataset("noise", data=image["noise"].values, compression="gzip")
    f.create_dataset("psf/kernel", data=psf["psf"].values)
    f.create_dataset("axes/col_arcsec", data=cols)
    f.create_dataset("meta/exposure_s", data=np.array([1200.0]))

To ingest a raw HDF5 file, use format hdf5 and a mapping (mapping.hdf5). The mapping tells which arrays become which variables, in which nodes, with which dims and coords. If the file is self-describing (written by xarray or netCDF4), use format netcdf instead. It does not need a mapping.

docs.title: Step 1: inspect the upload
docs.text:
You do not have to know what is in the file. An inspection lists the groups and arrays of an upload from its metadata. It does not read array data, and it does not make a dataset version.

  1. Make an upload session and PUT the file, as for any upload (HTTP API guide).
  2. Start the inspection: POST /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}/uploads/{upload_id}/inspect. The server answers 202 with an inspect run.
  3. Get the result: GET /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}/uploads/{upload_id}/inspection. While the run is not complete, the server answers 409 NOT_READY. Try again after some seconds.

The result is an UploadInspection (shortened here to two of its five arrays):

{
  "format": "hdf5",
  "size_bytes": 18042,
  "groups": ["/", "/axes", "/meta", "/observations", "/psf"],
  "arrays": [
    {"path": "/observations/image", "shape": [64, 64], "dtype": "float32",
     "chunks": [32, 64], "filters": ["deflate"], "dims_hint": null, "attrs": {}},
    {"path": "/psf/kernel", "shape": [9, 9], "dtype": "float64",
     "chunks": null, "filters": [], "dims_hint": null, "attrs": {}}
  ],
  "truncated": false,
  "warnings": []
}

The inspection runs the same HDF5 safety checks as an ingest. dims_hint gives dim names when the file has them (HDF5 dimension scales, zarr _ARRAY_DIMENSIONS or NetCDF dims). The inspection of an upload occurs one time: a second request gets the same run, or the finished result. If the run failed, a new request starts a new run.

docs.title: Step 2: write the mapping
docs.text:
This is the full body of POST /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}/versions for the file above. It ingests the staged upload with an hdf5 mapping:

{
  "upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p0",
  "message": "lens observation of 2026-10-01, mapped from raw HDF5",
  "mapping": {
    "format": "hdf5",
    "hdf5": {
      "vars": [
        {"path": "/observations/image", "name": "image", "dims": ["row", "col"],
         "role": "target", "units": "counts"},
        {"path": "/observations/noise", "name": "noise", "dims": ["row", "col"],
         "units": "counts"},
        {"path": "/psf/kernel", "node": "/psf", "name": "psf", "dims": ["prow", "pcol"]}
      ],
      "coords": [
        {"dim": "row", "start": -1.6, "step": 0.05,
         "spec": {"kind": "float", "ordered": true}},
        {"dim": "col", "path": "/axes/col_arcsec",
         "spec": {"kind": "float", "ordered": true}},
        {"dim": "prow", "node": "/psf"},
        {"dim": "pcol", "node": "/psf"}
      ]
    }
  }
}

Each entry of vars is an Hdf5Var:

Field Meaning path The HDF5 path of the array in the file node The node of the variable (default /) name The name of the variable in the node dims One dim name for each axis of the array, in sequence. The ingest makes sure that the number of names is the same as the number of axes role, units, missing, description As for a column mapping (default role covariate, missing forbid)

Each entry of coords is an Hdf5Coord. It gives the labels of one dim in one node, from one of these sources:

Source Fields Example A 1-D array of the file path {"dim": "col", "path": "/axes/col_arcsec"} A range of numbers start and step {"dim": "row", "start": -1.6, "step": 0.05} A range of dates start (a date) and step (a pandas frequency) {"dim": "date", "start": "2024-01-01", "step": "W-MON"} An integer index 0 … n-1 neither path nor start {"dim": "prow", "node": "/psf"}

spec sets the DimSpec of the dim (kind, policy, frequency). Without it, the ingest infers the spec from the labels. A dim without an Hdf5Coord has no coord. A coord in a node also applies to the nodes below it. A date range must start on its frequency: 2024-01-02 with W-MON is an error, because 2 January 2024 is not a Monday.

The result of the example is a tree with two nodes: / has image and noise over row and col, and /psf has psf over prow and pcol. The ingest does not read the arrays that the mapping does not name. One warning of the run lists them (here /meta/exposure_s).

If all the variables of the mapping are in the root, the version is a plain dataset version.

docs.title: Versions made from several files
docs.text:
One dataset version can come from as many as 64 uploads. Each upload is a source. Send an assembly in POST /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}/versions instead of upload_id and mapping. Each source of assembly.sources (an AssemblySource) gives:

Field Meaning upload_id A complete upload of this dataset. Each upload can be in one source only mapping The IngestMapping of this file ({"format": "netcdf"} for a self-describing file) node Where the file goes (default /) combine How the file joins the other sources of the same node: node, concat or merge concat_dim, concat_label For concat: the new dim, and the label of this file along it join How the coords align for concat and merge: exact (default), inner or outer

The three rules are:

combine Sources in the node What the ingest does node (the default) One Puts the file at the node. A file that is a tree puts its groups below the node: group /psf of a file at node /instrument becomes /instrument/psf concat One or more (the CLI asks for two or more) Stacks the files along a new dim concat_dim. Each file gives one label, for example one file for each market or each year. The files must have the same variables over the same dims merge One or more (the CLI asks for two or more) Merges the variables of the files on their shared coords. A variable that is in two files must have the same values where the files overlap

All sources of one node use the same rule. Sources of a concat use the same concat_dim and different labels (all numbers, or all text). Sources of a concat or a merge use the same join.

The server checks every upload before it uses any. If one source is not correct, the server refuses the version and all the uploads stay available. One ingest run reads all the sources (inputs upload.0, upload.1, …). The sum of the upload sizes sets the resource class of the run.

docs.title: Example: one node from several files, and a second node
docs.text:
These files are one sales file for each market and one media file:

weeks = pd.date_range("2024-01-07", periods=40, freq="W-SUN")
channels = ["tv", "search"]


def market_sales(level: float) -> xr.Dataset:
    revenue = level + rng.normal(0.0, 5.0, 40)
    return xr.Dataset({"revenue": (("date",), revenue, {"units": "EUR"})}, coords={"date": weeks})


market_sales(300.0).to_netcdf("sales_nl.nc", engine="h5netcdf")  # one file for each market
market_sales(250.0).to_netcdf("sales_de.nc", engine="h5netcdf")
media = xr.Dataset(
    {"spend": (("market", "channel", "date"), rng.gamma(2.0, 50.0, (2, 2, 40)))},
    coords={"market": ["NL", "DE"], "channel": channels, "date": weeks},
)
media.to_netcdf("media.nc", engine="h5netcdf")

This body stacks the two sales files along a new market dim in node /sales. It puts the media file in node /media:

{
  "message": "sales of each market (one file each) and the media plan",
  "assembly": {
    "sources": [
      {"upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p1", "mapping": {"format": "netcdf"},
       "node": "/sales", "combine": "concat", "concat_dim": "market", "concat_label": "NL"},
      {"upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p2", "mapping": {"format": "netcdf"},
       "node": "/sales", "combine": "concat", "concat_dim": "market", "concat_label": "DE"},
      {"upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p3", "mapping": {"format": "netcdf"},
       "node": "/media"}
    ]
  }
}

The version is a tree with the nodes /, /sales and /media. /sales has revenue(market, date) with the labels NL and DE.

docs.title: Example: merge two files
docs.text:
This body merges a sales file and a weather file in the root. join: inner keeps only the weeks that both files have:

{
  "message": "sales and weather on the same markets and weeks",
  "assembly": {
    "sources": [
      {"upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p4", "mapping": {"format": "netcdf"},
       "combine": "merge", "join": "inner"},
      {"upload_id": "upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p5", "mapping": {"format": "netcdf"},
       "combine": "merge", "join": "inner"}
    ]
  }
}

All sources are in the root. Thus the result is a plain dataset version.

docs.title: With the Python client
docs.text:
client.datasets.upload_files checks the full assembly before it uploads a byte. Then it uploads each file, creates the version and waits for the ingest.

Stack files along a new dim (one label for each file):

version = api.datasets.upload_files(
    ["sales_nl.nc", "sales_de.nc"],
    dataset="sales",
    concat="market",
    labels=["NL", "DE"],  # one label for each file, in file order
)

Merge files on shared coords:

version = api.datasets.upload_files(
    ["sales.nc", "weather.nc"], dataset="sales_weather", merge=True, join="inner"
)

Give each file its own node and rule with AssemblyFile:

version = api.datasets.upload_files(
    [
        AssemblyFile("sales_nl.nc", node="/sales", concat_dim="market", concat_label="NL"),
        AssemblyFile("sales_de.nc", node="/sales", concat_dim="market", concat_label="DE"),
        AssemblyFile("media.nc", node="/media"),
    ],
    dataset="sales_tree",
)
print(version.layout, list(version.tree_schema.nodes) if version.tree_schema else None)

client.datasets.upload also accepts an xr.DataTree (it uploads a data.tree.zip) and a raw HDF5 file with an IngestMapping(format="hdf5", hdf5=...). Without a mapping, the client refuses a raw HDF5 file before it uploads anything. For a raw HDF5 file, inspect first, then ingest the staged upload:

staged = api.datasets.inspect_file("lens_raw.h5", dataset="lens")  # upload, no ingest
for array in staged.inspection.arrays:
    print(array.path, array.shape, array.dtype, array.dims_hint)

mapping = IngestMapping.model_validate_json(Path("mapping.json").read_text())  # format hdf5
version = api.datasets.create_version(
    staged.dataset_id, upload_id=staged.upload_id, mapping=mapping
)
version = api.datasets.wait_version(staged.dataset_id, version.version)

inspect_file uploads the file without an ingest (stage_upload) and waits for the inspection (inspect). The async client has the same methods.

docs.title: With the CLI
docs.text:
mapi datasets upload takes one or more files. Several files, or one of the options --node, --concat or --merge, make one version from all of the files:

# Two files, one for each market, stacked along a new 'market' dim
mapi datasets upload sales_nl.nc sales_de.nc --name sales --concat market=NL,DE

# Two files on the same markets and weeks: merge their variables, keep the shared labels
mapi datasets upload sales.nc weather.nc --name sales_weather --merge --join inner

# One file for each node: the image at the root, the PSF file under /instrument
mapi datasets upload image.nc psf.nc --name lens --node / --node /instrument
  • --node PATH: give it one time (for all the files) or one time for each file, in file order.
  • --concat DIM=LABEL: one label for each file of the node, in file order. Repeat the option or give the labels as a list (market=NL,DE). Labels that look like numbers are numbers.
  • --merge: merge the files of the same node.
  • --join exact|inner|outer: only with --concat or --merge.
  • --mapping FILE: one time (for all the files that it can read) or one time for each file.

For a raw HDF5 file:

# 1. Upload the raw HDF5 file without an ingest, and show its groups and arrays
mapi datasets inspect lens lens_raw.h5
# 2. Write a mapping for the arrays (mapping.json), then ingest the staged upload
mapi datasets ingest lens upl_01jaf3d1e2f3g4h5j6k7m8n9p0 --mapping mapping.json
# Or do the two steps in one: upload and ingest with the mapping
mapi datasets upload lens_raw.h5 --name lens --mapping mapping.json

mapi datasets inspect shows a table of the arrays (path, shape, dtype, dims hint, chunks, filters). With the global --json option (mapi --json datasets inspect …), the command prints the upload id and the full UploadInspection.

docs.title: Read a tree in a spec: data.nodes
docs.text:
A pipeline step and most models read one flat xr.Dataset. For a tree dataset, data.nodes selects the nodes. The platform merges their variables into one flat dataset before the pipeline:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: sales-tree, project: growth}
data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/sales_tree@latest
  nodes:                                  # these nodes make the flat input of the pipeline
    sales: {path: /sales}                 # all the variables of /sales
    media: {path: /media, vars: [spend]}  # only 'spend' from /media
    plan: {path: /plan, prefix: plan_}    # /plan 'spend' becomes 'plan_spend'
  join: exact                             # the default: the labels must be equal
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, time: date}
    vars: {y: revenue}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 4}
pipeline: []
model:
  use: toy.tree_linear@^1                 # test-only reference model (mapi_sdk.testing.toy)
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, seed: 3}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse]}

The model of this example

toy.tree_linear is a reference model of the SDK test kit (mapi_sdk.testing.toy). The documentation tests use it to check and fit this spec. The platform and the CLI catalog do not have it, so mapi check reports REF_UNRESOLVED for it. Put a model of your platform in model.use (mapi catalog lists them).

Each entry of data.nodes is a NodeSelect:

Field Meaning path The node to read vars The variables to read from the node (default: all) prefix Text to put before each variable name of the node, for example plan_. Use it when two nodes have variables with the same name

The rules of the merge are:

  • Dims keep their names. A dim that two selected nodes use must have the same DimSpec.
  • A variable name can come from one node only. If two nodes give the same name, validation tells you to add a prefix.
  • data.join aligns the labels of the shared dims: exact (the default) refuses labels that are not equal, inner keeps the shared labels, and outer keeps all labels and adds missing values.
  • data.bind applies to the merged names (for example plan_spend).

Static validation (mapi check --remote, POST /v1/specs:validate) uses the tree_schema of the version. A local mapi check spec.yaml --data lens.tree.zip reads the tree schema of the local tree dataset in the same way. It finds an unknown node or variable, a name clash and dims that are not the same before a run starts. These rules also apply:

  • If a spec reads a tree dataset without data.nodes, the platform reads the root node. If the root has no variables, validation reports SCHEMA_INVALID: "this dataset is a tree: pick nodes in data.nodes".
  • data.nodes on a plain dataset is an error.
  • A data.join other than exact without data.nodes is an error. (exact is the default and has no effect without nodes.)

The same merge is available in Python:

from mapi_sdk.testing import toy
from mapi_sdk.tree import select_nodes

tree = toy.tree_dataset()  # '/sales' revenue, '/media' spend, '/adjust' offset
tree["plan"] = xr.DataTree(tree["media"].to_dataset(inherit=False) * 1.1)  # a 2nd 'spend'

flat = select_nodes(
    tree,
    {
        "sales": {"path": "/sales"},
        "media": {"path": "/media", "vars": ["spend"]},
        "plan": {"path": "/plan", "prefix": "plan_"},
    },
    join="exact",
)
print(sorted(flat.data_vars))  # ['plan_spend', 'revenue', 'spend']

docs.title: Side tables that are trees
docs.text:
A side table can be a tree dataset too. It reads one node, which node names:

data:
  side_tables:
    fx: {ref: dataset://growth/reference@latest, node: /fx}

The server checks that the node exists in the version. A side table that is a plain dataset does not need node.

docs.title: The Data Explorer
docs.text:
The Data Explorer shows one node at a time. A DataExploreRequest takes an optional node. The default is the root, or the first node that has variables. The ingest writes the views of each node.

The explorer finds the shapes of each node separately. For example, the E80 lens tree has two images of 81 × 81 pixels (image and weight) in the node /image, and an image of 31 × 31 pixels (psf) in the node /psf. Thus each node has its own sections and its own sequence of sections. Do not confuse a tree dataset with the section Tree. That section shows a tree that is in the data of one node, for example the parent variable of a phylogeny. Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: Models that read the whole tree
docs.text:
Some models need more than the flat merge, for example the PSF of an instrument next to the image. A model declares capabilities.input = "tree" in its manifest. It then gets the whole tree in ctx.tree (FitContext and ScoreContext), with the binding renames applied in each node. ds is still the flat merge of data.nodes. Thus the steps of the pipeline work as before. Models that do not declare it (input = "dataset", the default) see only the flat dataset.

toy.tree_linear in mapi_sdk.testing.toy is a reference model. This minimal plugin follows it and passes the contract kit for tree-input models (check_tree_model):

from mapi_sdk.models import FitContext, FitOutput
from mapi_sdk.testing import TreeModelFixture, check_tree_model
from mapi_sdk.testing.toy import LinearModel, PanelSettings
from mapi_spec.spec import FitConfig


class NodeCountModel(LinearModel):
    """toy.linear that also reads the whole tree (capabilities.input = "tree")."""

    id = "demo.node_count"
    version = "1.0.0"
    capabilities = LinearModel.capabilities.model_copy(update={"input": "tree"})

    def fit(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: PanelSettings, cfg: FitConfig, ctx: FitContext) -> FitOutput:
        out = super().fit(ds, s, cfg, ctx)  # ds: the flat merge of data.nodes, as always
        if ctx.tree is not None:  # the bound tree: binding renames applied in each node
            out.learned["nodes"] = sorted(str(node.path) for node in ctx.tree.subtree)
        return out


registry.register_model(NodeCountModel)
report = check_tree_model(
    NodeCountModel,
    TreeModelFixture(spec=toy.tree_spec("demo.node_count@^1"), tree=toy.tree_dataset(),
                     registry=registry),
)  # fmt: skip
print(report.ok)  # True

check_tree_model fits the model from a tree through the harness. It makes sure that fit and score get the bound tree, that a tree payload scores the same as its flat merge plus the tree, and that a bundle round trip keeps the scores. It also makes sure that a flat payload without a tree scores, or the model refuses it with a typed error.

The platform gives the tree to tree-input models in fit, score, evaluate, the Model Explorer, governance checks and workflow scoring. With a data.split, the evaluation fit and the holdout score see only their part of the tree.

sci.strong_lens is a built-in tree-input model. When the tree has a /psf node with psf over psf_row and psf_col, the fit uses that PSF. Otherwise it uses the flat psf, as before. With the setting psf_source: tree, a spec can select only the image node in data.nodes. Refer to the model's section in the model reference.

docs.title: Tree datasets in a workflow v0.9
docs.text:
A workflow input can be a tree dataset. In the local runner, it can be an xr.DataTree. model.fit and model.backtest take the parameters nodes and join. They are the same as data.nodes and data.join of a spec. If you do not give nodes, the node reads the root node. join is exact (the default), inner or outer.

- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: toy.tree_linear@^1
    nodes: {sales: {path: /sales}, media: {path: /media}}
    join: inner

model.score, model.forecast and plot.render (source: predictions) send a tree on their data input as a whole tree. They select the same nodes as the fit. A tree-input model gets the tree of that input, not the tree of its fit. With source: data, plot.render keeps all the groups of a tree input. For example, sci.area_map reads the group geometry, and sci.phylogeny reads the group tree.

These limits apply:

  • A backtest of a tree dataset gives the full tree to each fold. A tree-input model that reads its target from the tree can see the test window. The node shows a warning.
  • search.grid has no nodes parameter.

Refer to Tree datasets in the workflows guide.
