docs.title: Run it with the Python client
docs.text:
Do these steps:

  1. Validate the file on the server. The server saves nothing.
  2. Make the workflow, or save a new revision.
  3. Run the workflow.
  4. Follow the live events.
from pathlib import Path

check = api.workflows.validate(Path("weekly-readiness.yaml"))  # on the server; saves nothing
for issue in check.issues:  # every problem with a JSON pointer into the document
    print(issue.severity.value, issue.pointer, issue.message)
print(" -> ".join(check.order))  # the order the nodes will run in

from mapi_client import WorkflowEnd, WorkflowEventFrame, WorkflowSnapshot

# create the workflow, or save the file as its next revision when it changed
workflow, revision = api.workflows.upsert(Path("weekly-readiness.yaml"))
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},  # pinned to a version at start
    params={"drivers": ["price"], "window": 80, "max_p": 2, "max_q": 2},
)
for item in api.workflows.stream_events(run.run_id):  # server-sent events, resumable
    match item:
        case WorkflowSnapshot(run=now):
            print(f"{len(now.nodes)} nodes, {now.status.value}")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.type.value == "workflow.branch.decided":
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: took the {e.data['arm']} arm")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.node_id is not None:
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: {e.type.value.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}")
        case WorkflowEnd(status=status):
            print("run", status.value if status else "ended")

Read the results. They include the verdict of each test, each branch with the values that it read, the selected orders and the Diebold-Mariano verdict. They also tell why the workflow selected the model or did not select it:

run = api.workflows.wait(run.run_id)  # raises the run's error if it failed
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["adf"].result["verdict_plain"])  # e.g. "The series wanders: consider differencing it."
for d in run.decisions:
    print(d.node_id, d.arm, d.inputs)  # every branch with the values its condition read
order, d = nodes["order"].result, 1 if nodes["wanders"].result["value"] else 0
print(f"ARIMA({order['best_p']}, {d}, {order['best_q']})")  # chosen by information criterion
print(nodes["dm"].result["verdict_plain"])  # is ARIMAX's edge over naive more than luck?
print(nodes["select"].result["reason_plain"])  # kept only if it beats the benchmarks
model_ref = run.outputs["model"].ref  # model://growth/wf-weekly-readiness-fit@v1
report = run.outputs["report"].inline  # mapi.report/v1: every test, decision and table

The governance node measured the selected model against the policy that applies. Because submit: true is set, it recorded a validation of that model version:

gov = nodes["governance"].result  # the policy in force, measured on the selected model
print("passed" if gov["passed"] else f"failed: {gov['failed_checks']}")
validation = api.validations.get(gov["validation_id"])  # recorded because submit: true
print(validation.status.value)  # validated, or awaiting_approval when a reviewer must sign
for r in validation.results:
    print(f"{r.check:28} {r.status.value:7} {r.message_plain}")
api.validations.download_evidence_pack(validation.id, "evidence.html")  # for the auditor

This is the output on a live local stack, from the first run of the walkthrough on this data:

passed
validated
data.quality                 pass    No data problems found (156 periods of history).
convergence                  pass    The fit reported no convergence problems.
baseline.beats_naive         pass    On the 13 held-out periods the model's error is 25% lower than 'same as last period' (the strongest simple benchmark).
holdout.accuracy             pass    On data it was not fitted on, the model's average percentage error is 1.8% (limit 15%).
residuals.whiteness          pass    No pattern is left in the errors (Ljung-Box p = 0.39 at 10 lags).
null.permutation_target      pass    The model did better on held-out data (skill 0.236) than all 20 fits with the drivers price shuffled in blocks of 7 (the result untouched) (p = 0.048).
stability.rolling_params     fail    ar.L1 changes a lot across windows of history (variation 1205%): the relationship may not be stable over time.

Read the output as a reviewer does. On unseen weeks, the model is 25% better than naive. Its errors have no pattern. It forecasts better than each fit with the price driver shuffled in time. But the AR coefficient is not stable across windows.

That check failed, but the version is still validated. The status of a check and its severity are different things. The default forecast policy sets stability to information, so the check does not block. The reviewer can see it in the record and in the evidence pack. A stricter policy (see governance) makes the check block. Then this model needs more history or a simpler specification. This is the purpose: the evidence is written, and the decision is explicit.

What the shuffle test measures on a random walk

The model has a driver. Thus the test shuffles the driver in blocks and does not change the result. It scores each fit by its skill against the null forecast on the held-out weeks. Persistence ("next week is like this week") helps the shuffled fits exactly as much as it helps the real fit. Thus the test measures what the driver adds to persistence. For a model without drivers, the test uses shuffled changes of the series (null tests explained).

Then keep the workflow up to date:

weekly = api.workflows.schedule(
    workflow.id,
    "0 6 * * 1",  # Mondays at 06:00
    timezone="Europe/Berlin",
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},
    params={"drivers": ["price"]},
)
on_upload = api.workflows.trigger(
    workflow.id, "dataset://growth/weekly_sales", "data", debounce_seconds=600
)
print(weekly.next_run_at, on_upload.id)

docs.title: VAR/VECM cointegration
docs.text:
In plain words. Some series wander but stay together. Examples are the prices of close substitutes, sales and distribution, and income and consumption. If they have a relation, a model that knows the relation (an error-correction model) forecasts better. It also tells you how fast a gap closes. If they do not have a relation, model their changes. In the two cases, find out if one series helps to predict a different series.

For the statistician. The Johansen trace test (at 5%) on the levels decides the branch. If the series have a relation, search.coint_rank selects the rank. Then the workflow fits a VECM with k_ar_diff: 1 on the levels. If the series do not have a relation, the workflow differences them. Then AIC selects the VAR lag order up to maxlags, and the workflow fits a VAR on the changes. If the workflow took the changes (the first alternative), it tests Granger causality on them. If not, it tests on the levels. The forecast node uses the model that exists, with the related data.

# Workflow cookbook: do these series move together for good? VECM if they are tied in the
# long run, a VAR on the levels if they are already stable, else a VAR on the changes;
# Granger tests either way; a forecast of the winner.
# (validated by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: macro-system, project: growth}
params:
  target: {type: string, required: true, description: "The main result (one of the series)"}
  driver: {type: string, required: true, description: "A series that may help predict it"}
  maxlags: {type: integer, default: 8, minimum: 1, maximum: 52}
  horizon: {type: integer, default: 8, minimum: 1, maximum: 104}
inputs:
  # one value per series and period: value(series, quarter), the layout of ts.var/ts.vecm
  data: {type: dataset, description: "The series along one dimension"}
nodes:
# 1. Is there a long-run relationship? (Johansen trace test, every series of the dimension)
- {id: johansen, use: test.johansen, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: "0.05"}}
# rank 0: no tie; rank = number of series: every series is stable (no unit root)
- id: tied
  use: branch.if
  with: {condition: "nodes.johansen.rank > 0 and nodes.johansen.rank < len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats)"}
# 2a. Tied: choose the cointegration rank and fit an error-correction model on the levels.
- {id: rank, use: search.coint_rank, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: tied.then}
- id: vecm
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  when: tied.then
  with:
    model: ts.vecm@^1
    settings:
      coint_rank: {$expr: "min(max(nodes.rank.rank, 1), len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats) - 1)"}
      k_ar_diff: 1
# 2b. Not tied: a VAR on the levels when every series is stable, else on the changes.
- id: stationary
  use: branch.if
  when: tied.else
  with: {condition: "nodes.johansen.rank >= len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats)"}
- {id: diff, use: transform.difference, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: stationary.else}
- {id: lags, use: search.var_lag_order, inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]},
   when: tied.else, with: {maxlags: {$param: maxlags}, criterion: aic}}
- id: var
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  when: tied.else
  with:
    model: ts.var@^1
    settings: {lags: {$expr: nodes.lags.best_lag}}
# 3. Does the driver help predict the target? (on the changes when they were taken)
- id: granger
  use: test.granger
  inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  with: {y: {$param: target}, x: {$param: driver}, maxlag: {$param: maxlags}}
# 4. Forecast with whichever system was fitted (the first alternative that ran).
- id: forecast
  use: model.forecast
  inputs: {model: [vecm.model, var.model], data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  with: {horizon: {$param: horizon}}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [johansen.result, granger.result]
    items: [rank.table, lags.table]
    model: [vecm.model, var.model]
  with: {title: Series that move together}
outputs: {report: report.report, forecast: forecast.forecast}

The data keeps the series along one dimension, with one value for each series and period (value(series, quarter)). This is the layout of ts.var and ts.vecm. To ingest a wide sheet, use the wide mapping. Run the workflow as the first recipe, with the two parameters that it needs:

mapi workflows apply macro-system.yaml
mapi workflows run macro-system -i data=dataset://growth/us_macro@latest \
  -p target=realcons -p driver=realgdp --watch

run = api.workflows.run(
    wf.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/us_macro@latest"},
    params={"target": "realcons", "driver": "realgdp", "maxlags": 4},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["johansen"].result["verdict_plain"])  # "The series share at least one long-run relationship."
print(nodes["granger"].result["verdict_plain"])   # "Past values of the driver help predict the result."
print([n.node_id for n in run.nodes if n.status.value == "skipped"])  # the branch not taken

A run on a laptop used three simulated weekly series. Two of the series have the same stochastic trend (target=a, driver=b). The run printed the two verdicts above and ['diff', 'lags', 'var']. The Johansen trace statistic (69.1) set the rank to 1, and the VECM branch ran. Granger found that b helps to predict a (p = 0.0015). See Macro and VAR analysis.

The Model Explorer shows the impulse responses, the variance decomposition, the Granger table and the Johansen table of the fitted model (mapi explore model … -s irf -s fevd).

docs.title: Forecast bake-off
docs.text:
In plain words. If you do not know which forecast method is correct for your data, let the methods compete fairly. They use the same history, the same cut-off points, the same horizons and the same naive benchmarks. Keep the winner only if it is clearly better than a simple method.

For the statistician. The plan is an expanding window with n_folds origins, one each 4 periods. The workflow scores each horizon. SARIMAX(1,1,1)(0,1,0)₅₂, ARIMA(0,1,1), damped-trend ETS and Theta compete against naive, seasonal-naive and drift. MASE puts them in sequence. MASE has no scale, so you can compare series of different sizes. Two Diebold-Mariano tests (absolute loss, horizon 1) compare the leaders with the benchmark. select.best needs a 5% MASE improvement over each benchmark. Only then does the branch fit the winner again.

# Workflow cookbook: a forecast bake-off. Four models and the naive benchmarks compete on the
# same expanding-window folds; Diebold-Mariano tests say whether the winner's edge is more
# than luck; the winner is refitted on all the data only if it beats naive.
# (validated by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: forecast-bakeoff, project: growth}
params:
  horizons: {type: array, default: [1, 4, 8]}
  season: {type: integer, default: 52, minimum: 2, maximum: 400}
  n_folds: {type: integer, default: 6, minimum: 2, maximum: 50}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset}
nodes:
- id: folds
  use: split.expanding_window
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {horizons: {$param: horizons}, n_folds: {$param: n_folds}, step: 4, gap: 0}
# the candidates, each backtested on the same plan
- {id: sarimax, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.sarimax@^1, settings: {order: [1, 1, 1], seasonal_order: [0, 1, 0, 52]}}}
- {id: arima, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.arima@^1, settings: {order: [0, 1, 1]}}}
- {id: ets, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.ets@^1, settings: {trend: add, damped_trend: true}}}
- {id: theta, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.theta@^1}}
- {id: naive, use: evaluate.baseline, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {methods: [naive, seasonal_naive, drift], season: {$param: season}}}
# the league table, then two head-to-head tests against the benchmark
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs: {candidates: [sarimax.metrics, arima.metrics, ets.metrics, theta.metrics, naive.metrics]}
  with: {metric: mase}
- {id: dm_ets, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: ets.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: absolute, horizon: 1}}
- {id: dm_sarimax, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: sarimax.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: absolute, horizon: 1}}
# the winner, if it beats naive by at least 5%, refitted on everything
- {id: best, use: select.best, inputs: {table: compare.table},
   with: {metric: mase, must_beat: [naive], margin: 0.05}}
- {id: winner, use: branch.if, with: {condition: nodes.best.beats_baselines}}
- id: refit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  when: winner.then
  with: {model: {$expr: nodes.best.selected_model}}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [dm_ets.result, dm_sarimax.result]
    items: [compare.table]
    model: [refit.model]
  with: {title: Forecast bake-off}
outputs: {model: refit.model, comparison: compare.table, report: report.report}

mapi workflows apply forecast-bakeoff.yaml
mapi workflows run forecast-bakeoff -i data=dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest \
  -p 'horizons=[1,4]' -p n_folds=6 --watch
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare      # the league table
mapi workflows node "$RUN" best         # who won, and whether they beat naive by 5%

On a short series with much noise, the usual result is the honest result: "ets is the best model (0.0456) but does not beat naive.drift by the required 5%: no model is selected." The workflow skips the refit node, and the report tells why. Thus nobody ships a model that only looks clever.

docs.title: Disease map: which spatial model?
docs.text:
In plain words. A disease map shows the risk in each area, for example in each district. Small areas have few cases, so their raw rates have much noise. A model can let adjacent areas share their risk. This makes the estimates of small areas more stable. But is this correct for your data? And does it change your answer about a cause, for example the percentage of people who work outdoors?

This workflow fits three models, from independent areas to areas that share their risk. Then it keeps the model that predicts best. It tells you if the effect of the covariate is clear, and if the effect stays clear with different priors.

For the statistician. Each rung is sci.areal_bym2, Poisson(E exp(b0 + b1 x + u)), on all the data. The area effects u are iid, icar or bym2. Each fit keeps the pointwise PSIS-LOO values (evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}), so the rungs are scored on the same areas. compare.models ranks them by elpd_loo. compare.stacking gives the stacking weights (Yao et al. 2018). select.best keeps the rung with the largest elpd_loo. model.summary gives the HDI of b1 (hdi_prob). governance.check (convergence) reads R-hat of the winner. If the check does not fail and the HDI excludes zero, the workflow fits the winner again with the prior widths of b0, b1 and sigma multiplied and divided by prior_scale.

flowchart LR
  D["dataset"] --> I["iid"] & C["icar"] & B["bym2"]
  I & C & B --> R["compare.models<br/>(elpd_loo)"] & W["compare.stacking"]
  R --> S["select.best"]
  S --> E["model.summary<br/>(b1)"] & G["convergence"]
  E & G --> Q{"chains agree and<br/>b1 clear?"}
  Q -- then --> P["refit: wider and<br/>narrower priors"]
  S --> M["sci.area_map"]
  M & E & P --> Rep["report"]

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: which spatial model for a disease map? Fit iid, ICAR and BYM2 area
# effects on the same areas, compare them by PSIS-LOO (ranking and stacking weights), keep the
# best one, read its covariate effect, check convergence, refit it with wider and narrower
# priors when the chains agree and the effect is clear, and draw the relative-risk map.
# This is the sci_spatial_ladder template of the gallery (a test keeps the two the same).
# (validated and run by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: disease-map-ladder, project: epidemiology}
params:
  # the names of the area dims and of the covariate in your dataset (the e18 export)
  bind:
    type: object
    default: {dims: {area: district, area_: district_}, vars: {covariate: aff}}
    description: The names in your dataset of the area dims and of the covariate (the default
      fits the e18 export)
  islands:
    type: string
    default: link_nearest
    enum: [link_nearest, isolate, error]
    description: What to do with areas that have no neighbours. link_nearest links each one to
      the area with the closest border
  hdi_prob: {type: number, default: 0.94, minimum: 0.5, maximum: 0.999,
             description: The probability inside the range of each parameter}
  prior_scale:
    type: number
    default: 2.0
    minimum: 1.1
    maximum: 10
    description: When the effect is clear, the workflow fits the best model again with the
      prior widths multiplied and divided by this value
  # one MCMC configuration for every rung, so the rungs are comparable
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 50, maximum: 20000,
          description: The posterior draws to keep in each chain}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 50, maximum: 20000,
         description: The warm-up steps of each chain (the sampler discards them)}
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 2, maximum: 16,
           description: 'The number of chains (two or more, for R-hat)'}
  target_accept: {type: number, default: 0.9, minimum: 0.6, maximum: 0.99,
                  description: The target acceptance rate of the sampler. A higher value gives
                    smaller steps and fewer divergences}
  engine: {type: string, default: pymc, enum: [pymc, nutpie],
           description: The sampler (nutpie is faster on large data)}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 18, minimum: 0, maximum: 2147483647,
         description: The random seed of each fit}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: 'Counts, expected counts, a covariate, the adjacency matrix
      and the outlines of the areas'}
nodes:
# 1. Three rungs on all the data. PSIS-LOO scores each area as if the fit had not seen it.
- id: iid
  use: model.fit
  label: Independent areas
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.areal_bym2@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: {kind: iid, islands: {$param: islands}}
    fit: &fit
      mode: train_only
      draws: {$param: draws}
      tune: {$param: tune}
      chains: {$param: chains}
      target_accept: {$param: target_accept}
      engine: {$param: engine}
      seed: {$param: seed}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: icar
  use: model.fit
  label: Neighbours share risk (ICAR)
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.areal_bym2@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: {kind: icar, islands: {$param: islands}}
    fit: *fit
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: bym2
  use: model.fit
  label: Neighbours and noise (BYM2)
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.areal_bym2@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: {kind: bym2, islands: {$param: islands}}
    fit: *fit
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
# 2. Rank the rungs, weigh them by stacking and keep the best one.
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs: {candidates: [iid.metrics, icar.metrics, bym2.metrics]}
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
- id: weights
  use: compare.stacking
  label: Stacking weights
  inputs: {candidates: [iid.metrics, icar.metrics, bym2.metrics]}
- id: best
  use: select.best
  inputs: {table: compare.table, models: [iid.model, icar.model, bym2.model]}
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
# 3. Is the covariate effect clear in the best rung?
- id: effect
  use: model.summary
  label: Covariate effect
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with: {vars: [b0, b1, sigma], hdi_prob: {$param: hdi_prob}}
- id: converged
  use: governance.check
  label: Did the chains agree?
  inputs: {model: best.model, data: inputs.data}
  with: {check: convergence}
# an effect is clear only when the chains of the best model agree
- id: clear
  use: branch.if
  label: Is the effect clear?
  with:
    condition: >-
      coalesce(nodes.converged.status, 'error') not in ['fail', 'error'] and
      (nodes.effect.params.b1.hdi_low > 0 or nodes.effect.params.b1.hdi_high < 0)
    explain_then: The chains of the best model agree, and the range of the covariate effect
      does not include zero. The covariate has a clear effect on the risk. The workflow fits
      the best model again with wider and narrower priors.
    explain_else: The chains of the best model do not agree, or the range of the covariate
      effect includes zero. Look at the convergence evidence first. When the chains agree,
      the data does not show a clear effect of the covariate when the areas share their
      risk.
# 4. A clear effect must come from the data, not from the priors: refit the best rung
#    (kind = the id of the winner) with the prior widths x prior_scale and / prior_scale.
- id: wide
  use: model.fit
  label: Wider priors
  when: clear.then
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.areal_bym2@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings:
      kind: {$expr: nodes.best.selected}
      islands: {$param: islands}
      intercept_sd: {$expr: params.prior_scale}
      slope_sd: {$expr: params.prior_scale}
      sigma_scale: {$expr: params.prior_scale}
    fit: *fit
- id: narrow
  use: model.fit
  label: Narrower priors
  when: clear.then
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.areal_bym2@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings:
      kind: {$expr: nodes.best.selected}
      islands: {$param: islands}
      intercept_sd: {$expr: 1 / params.prior_scale}
      slope_sd: {$expr: 1 / params.prior_scale}
      sigma_scale: {$expr: 1 / params.prior_scale}
    fit: *fit
- id: effect_wide
  use: model.summary
  label: 'Wider priors: effect'
  inputs: {model: wide.model}
  when: clear.then
  with: {vars: [b1], hdi_prob: {$param: hdi_prob}}
- id: effect_narrow
  use: model.summary
  label: 'Narrower priors: effect'
  inputs: {model: narrow.model}
  when: clear.then
  with: {vars: [b1], hdi_prob: {$param: hdi_prob}}
# 5. The map and the report (skipped nodes leave their tables out of the report).
- id: map
  use: plot.render
  label: Relative risk map
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with:
    recipe: sci.area_map
    source: model
    settings: {var: rr, stats: [mean, sd, exceedance], threshold: 1.0}
    title: Relative risk of each area (best model)
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    items: [compare.table, weights.table, effect.table, effect_wide.table, effect_narrow.table]
    metrics: [iid.metrics, icar.metrics, bym2.metrics]
    model: best.model
    plots: [map.plot]
  with: {title: 'Disease map: which spatial model?'}
outputs:
  model: best.model
  comparison: compare.table
  weights: weights.table
  effect: effect.table
  map: map.plot
  convergence: converged.evidence
  report: report.report

The document is the sci_spatial_ladder template of the gallery. A test makes sure that the two stay the same. Copy these three details into your own workflows:

  • The winner sets the next fit. kind: {$expr: nodes.best.selected} gives the id of the winner (iid, icar or bym2) to the refits. The id of each rung is also its kind.
  • One fit configuration for all rungs. The YAML anchor &fit gives the same draws, chains and seed to each rung. Thus the rungs differ only in their area effects.
  • The workflow writes the priors out. governance.check with sensitivity.prior finds only prior widths with names such as prior_sigma. The prior widths of sci.areal_bym2 are intercept_sd, slope_sd and sigma_scale. Thus the workflow fits the model again with these widths, and model.summary shows the effect for each fit.

docs.title: Get the data
docs.text:
The workflow needs counts, expected counts, one covariate, an adjacency matrix and the outline of each area. The e18 export makes this dataset from the Scottish lip cancer data of pymc-challenges. See Export the data of a case study.

python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 --challenges ~/pymc-challenges/data --out scotland.nc
mapi datasets upload scotland.nc --name scotland_lip_cancer

If your names are different, give them in the bind parameter. For example, -p 'bind={"dims": {"area": "county", "area_": "county_"}, "vars": {"covariate": "smokers"}}'.

docs.title: Run it with the CLI
docs.text:
mapi workflows init sci_spatial_ladder --name disease-map-ladder   # writes disease-map-ladder.yaml
mapi workflows apply disease-map-ladder.yaml
mapi workflows run disease-map-ladder \
  -i data=dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest -p engine=nutpie --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs disease-map-ladder -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare    # the rungs, best first
mapi workflows node "$RUN" weights    # the stacking weights
mapi workflows node "$RUN" clear      # is the covariate effect clear?

The defaults fit 4 chains of 1000 draws after 1000 warm-up steps. To get a fast first look, use -p draws=300 -p tune=300. Then do the full run before you use the results.

docs.title: Run it with the Python client
docs.text:
from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()
workflow = api.workflows.create(template="sci_spatial_ladder")
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest"},
    params={"engine": "nutpie"},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["compare"].result["ranking"])  # for example ['bym2', 'icar', 'iid']
print(nodes["weights"].result["weights"])  # the stacking weight of each rung
print(nodes["clear"].result["arm"])        # then: the effect is clear
for fit in ("effect", "effect_wide", "effect_narrow"):  # skipped when the effect is not clear
    if nodes[fit].result:
        print(fit, nodes[fit].result["params"]["b1"])

On a laptop, LocalRunner runs the same document in-process. Use the science registry, so that the runner knows the sci.* models:

from mapi_plugin_science.areal_data import areal_dataset
from mapi_spec.workflow_templates import instantiate_template
from mapi_workflows.runtime.local import LocalRunner
from mapi_workflows.testing import science_registry

spec = instantiate_template("sci_spatial_ladder", name="disease-map", project="epidemiology")
res = LocalRunner(registry=science_registry()).run(
    spec, inputs={"data": areal_dataset()}, params={"draws": 500, "tune": 500}
)
print(res.node("best").result["reason_plain"])

docs.title: Read the outputs
docs.text:
Output Node What it tells you comparison compare The rungs from the best elpd_loo to the worst. A difference of less than about two standard errors is not clear. weights weights The stacking weights. A weight near 1 shows that one rung predicts best on almost all areas. Weights that are spread show that a mix of rungs predicts better than one rung. effect effect The mean, the HDI, R-hat and the bulk ESS of b0, b1 and sigma in the best rung. b1 is the change in the log risk for one covariate_scale (10 units) of the covariate. (decision) clear then if the convergence check does not fail and the HDI of b1 excludes zero. The report gives the reason in plain words. (tables) effect_wide, effect_narrow b1 with wider and narrower priors. If the two HDIs also exclude zero, the effect comes from the data, not from the priors. convergence converged The largest R-hat of the best rung. A fail sends clear to the else arm. Then fit with more draws or more warm-up steps. map map The mean and the sd of the relative risk of each area, and the probability that it is above 1. report report All the tables, the decision and the map, with a summary in plain words.

On the Scottish data, the E18 notebook gets b1 = 0.67 with independent areas, 0.37 with ICAR and 0.40 with BYM2. Thus, when the neighbours share their risk, the effect of outdoor work becomes smaller, but it stays clear.

docs.title: Network ties: which model?
docs.text:
In plain words. In a network, some pairs of nodes have a tie, for example two lawyers who work together. Shared traits can explain the ties: two lawyers in the same office work together more often. But some lawyers work with many colleagues, and groups form for other reasons.

This workflow fits three models of the ties. The first model uses only the shared traits. The second model adds the activity of each node. The third model adds a hidden map of the group. The workflow keeps the model that predicts best. Then it simulates new networks from that model. The workflow does not calculate the statistics of the real network. To compare, calculate them from your data yourself (the E21 tutorial shows a table of them).

For the statistician. Each rung is sci.network_latent_space, a Bernoulli-logit model of the pairs i < j. covariates uses alpha + x β. sociality adds s_i + s_j. latent_space also subtracts the distance ‖z_i − z_j‖ between Procrustes-aligned positions. The log-likelihood is over the observed pairs, in the same order for each rung. Thus elpd_loo is leave-one-pair-out, and compare.stacking can weigh the rungs. model.score in simulate mode draws whole graphs from the best rung. It gives graph_stat(statistic) for each graph: density, sd and maximum of the degree, isolates, triangles, transitivity, ties without shared partners (esp0), mean geodesic and the share of unreachable pairs.

flowchart LR
  D["dataset"] --> C["covariates"] & S["sociality"] & L["latent_space"]
  C & S & L --> R["compare.models<br/>(elpd_loo)"] & W["compare.stacking"]
  R --> B["select.best"]
  B --> E["model.summary<br/>(alpha, beta)"] & G["net.graph"] & X["model.score<br/>simulate"]
  X --> P["core.ridge<br/>(graph_stat)"]
  E & G & P --> Rep["report"]

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: which model explains the ties of a network? Fit pair covariates only,
# + a sociality effect per node, + a latent space on the same pairs, compare them by PSIS-LOO
# (ranking and stacking weights), keep the best one, read its pair effects, draw the network
# and simulate whole graphs from it for a posterior predictive check of graph statistics.
# This is the sci_network_ladder template of the gallery (a test keeps the two the same).
# (validated and run by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: coworker-ladder, project: sociology}
params:
  # the names of the node dims, the tie table, the pair values and the group code in your
  # dataset (the e21 export)
  bind:
    type: object
    default:
      dims: {node: lawyer, node_: lawyer_, cov: covariate}
      vars: {tie: cowork, dyad_cov: homophily, node_group: office}
    description: The names in your dataset of the node dims, the tie table, the pair values and
      the group code (the default fits the e21 export)
  node_groups:
    type: boolean
    default: true
    description: The dataset has a group code for each node (set false and remove node_group
      from bind when it has not)
  latent_dims: {type: integer, default: 2, minimum: 1, maximum: 3,
                description: The dimensions of the hidden map}
  n_sims: {type: integer, default: 500, minimum: 10, maximum: 4000,
           description: The number of networks to simulate from the best model}
  hdi_prob: {type: number, default: 0.94, minimum: 0.5, maximum: 0.999,
             description: The probability inside the range of each parameter}
  # one MCMC configuration for every rung, so the rungs are comparable
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 50, maximum: 20000,
          description: The posterior draws to keep in each chain}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 50, maximum: 20000,
         description: The warm-up steps of each chain (the sampler discards them)}
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 2, maximum: 16,
           description: 'The number of chains (two or more, for R-hat)'}
  target_accept: {type: number, default: 0.9, minimum: 0.6, maximum: 0.99,
                  description: The target acceptance rate of the sampler. A higher value gives
                    smaller steps and fewer divergences}
  engine: {type: string, default: pymc, enum: [pymc, nutpie],
           description: The sampler (nutpie is faster on large data)}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 21, minimum: 0, maximum: 2147483647,
         description: The random seed of each fit}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: 'A symmetric table of ties, the pair values and (optional) a
      group code for each node'}
nodes:
# 1. Three rungs on the same observed pairs. PSIS-LOO leaves out one pair at a time.
- id: covariates
  use: model.fit
  label: Pair covariates only
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.network_latent_space@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: &rung
      kind: covariates
      node_groups: {$param: node_groups}
      latent_dims: {$param: latent_dims}
    fit: &fit
      mode: train_only
      draws: {$param: draws}
      tune: {$param: tune}
      chains: {$param: chains}
      target_accept: {$param: target_accept}
      engine: {$param: engine}
      seed: {$param: seed}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: sociality
  use: model.fit
  label: Covariates and activity
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.network_latent_space@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: {<<: *rung, kind: sociality}
    fit: *fit
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: latent_space
  use: model.fit
  label: Covariates, activity and a hidden map
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.network_latent_space@^1
    bind: {$param: bind}
    settings: {<<: *rung, kind: latent_space}
    fit: *fit
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
# 2. Rank the rungs, weigh them by stacking and keep the best one.
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs: {candidates: [covariates.metrics, sociality.metrics, latent_space.metrics]}
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
- id: weights
  use: compare.stacking
  label: Stacking weights
  inputs: {candidates: [covariates.metrics, sociality.metrics, latent_space.metrics]}
- id: best
  use: select.best
  inputs:
    table: compare.table
    models: [covariates.model, sociality.model, latent_space.model]
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
# 3. The pair effects (beta[same_office], ...) and the network of the best rung.
- id: effects
  use: model.summary
  label: Pair effects
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with: {vars: [alpha, beta], hdi_prob: {$param: hdi_prob}}
- id: graph
  use: plot.render
  label: Network of the best model
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with:
    recipe: net.graph
    source: predictions
    settings: {var: tie_prob, panels: both}
    title: Tie probabilities of the best model
# 4. Graph posterior predictive check: simulate whole networks from the best rung and
#    plot the spread of their statistics (graph_stat has nine of them).
- id: simulate
  use: model.score
  label: Simulate networks
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with:
    mode: simulate
    group: draws    # n_sims draws, thinned evenly from the posterior
    request:
      output: {vars: [graph_stat], draws: {$param: n_sims}}
      seed: {$param: seed}
- id: ppc
  use: plot.render
  label: Statistics of simulated networks
  inputs: {data: simulate.scores}
  with:
    recipe: core.ridge
    source: data
    settings:
      var: graph_stat
      dim: statistic
      select: {statistic: [density, transitivity]}
    title: Density and transitivity of the simulated networks
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    items: [compare.table, weights.table, effects.table]
    metrics: [covariates.metrics, sociality.metrics, latent_space.metrics]
    model: best.model
    plots: [graph.plot, ppc.plot]
  with: {title: 'Network ties: which model?'}
outputs:
  model: best.model
  comparison: compare.table
  weights: weights.table
  effects: effects.table
  graph: graph.plot
  simulations: simulate.scores
  ppc: ppc.plot
  report: report.report

The document is the sci_network_ladder template of the gallery. Two details are important:

  • The YAML merge key keeps the rungs the same. settings: {<<: *rung, kind: sociality} changes only kind. The rungs use the same node_groups and latent_dims.
  • group: draws keeps n_sims graphs. The score request asks for n_sims draws (output.draws). The node outputs these draws, not all the posterior draws.

docs.title: Get the data
docs.text:
The workflow needs a symmetric table of ties, the pair values and (optional) a group code for each node. The e21 export makes this dataset from the law firm data of pymc-challenges (71 lawyers).

python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e21 --challenges ~/pymc-challenges/data --out lazega.nc
mapi datasets upload lazega.nc --name lazega_coworkers

If your dataset has no group code, use -p node_groups=false and remove node_group from the bind parameter.

RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs coworker-ladder -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare    # the rungs, best first

docs.title: Read the outputs
docs.text:
Output Node What it tells you comparison compare The rungs from the best elpd_loo to the worst weights weights The stacking weights of the rungs effects effects alpha and each pair effect beta[<pair value>] of the best rung, with the HDI. A positive effect makes a tie more probable. graph graph The network with the tie probabilities of the best rung (a graph and a matrix) simulations simulate graph_stat(statistic) of each simulated network ppc ppc The spread of the density and the transitivity of the simulated networks report report All the tables and the two plots, with a summary in plain words

Compare the spread in the ppc plot with the statistics of your network. If the value of your network is far from the spread, the model does not make networks like yours. On the law firm data, the E21 notebook gets elpd_loo −894.2 with covariates only, −763.4 with sociality and −761.6 with the latent space.

docs.title: Trait regression across species
docs.text:
In plain words. Close relatives are similar because they share most of their history. If you use each species as an independent data point, an effect can look clear only because related species are near each other. This recipe fits the same regression four times. The first fit ignores the tree. The other three fits let relatives share part of their residual.

The workflow keeps the fit that predicts best. Then it tells you if the effect that you ask about is clear of zero in that fit. It reports a clear effect only with a check that the fit agrees with the data.

For the statistician. sci.phylo_regression regresses the log of the trait on the log of each predictor (standardised). The four fits differ only in the residual kind:

  • iid: no tree, K = σ²I.
  • brownian: Brownian motion on the tree, K = σ²R. R is the shared branch length of two tips divided by the depth of the tree.
  • lambda: Pagel's lambda, K = σ²(λR + (1 − λ)I).
  • ou: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck on the patristic distance.

Each fit stores the leave-one-out density of each species given the other species. Thus elpd_loo compares the four kinds correctly. compare.models ranks them by elpd_loo, compare.stacking gives the stacking weights and select.best keeps the highest elpd_loo. model.summary with focus reads the slope of one predictor of the winner. The branch tests if the HDI of that slope excludes zero. Only then does evaluate.ppc compare the predictions of the winner with the observed traits.

flowchart LR
  D["traits and<br/>the tree"] --> F["four fits: iid, brownian,<br/>lambda, ou (elpd_loo)"]
  F --> C["compare +<br/>stacking weights"]
  C --> S["select the best<br/>elpd_loo"]
  S --> M["slopes of the winner<br/>(focus: group_size)"]
  M --> B{"range of the slope<br/>excludes zero?"}
  B -- then --> P["predictive check"]
  S --> T["trait on the tree<br/>(sci.phylogeny)"]
  B --> R["report"]
  P --> R
  T --> R

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: does an effect across species hold when the tree is in the model?
# Four fits of sci.phylo_regression differ only in the residual correlation (no tree,
# Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck). PSIS-LOO ranks them, stacking
# weighs them, and the winner's slope of `focus` decides the branch.
# (the gallery template sci_phylo_signal; validated and run by
# conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: primate-brains, project: biology}
params:
  predictors: {type: array, default: [body, group_size],
               description: The predictor variables on the species dim}
  focus: {type: string, default: group_size,
          description: "The predictor whose slope the decision tests. It must be one of the
            predictors: another name fails the run after the four fits"}
  hdi_prob: {type: number, default: 0.94, minimum: 0.5, maximum: 0.999,
             description: The probability inside the range of the slope}
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 20000,
          description: The posterior draws that each chain keeps}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 20000,
         description: The tuning steps of each chain (the sampler drops them)}
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 1, maximum: 16,
           description: The number of chains (two or more give R-hat)}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 2017, minimum: 0, maximum: 2147483647,
         description: The random seed of the sampler}
  bind:
    type: object
    default: {}
    description: >-
      The names of the model (dims and vars) mapped to the names in your dataset, when they
      are different. The workflow finds the target itself when your dataset has one target.
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset,
         description: "Species traits and the tree (parent, branch_length, is_tip and tip_label on the node dim)"}
nodes:
# 1. the same regression four times; only the residual correlation changes
- id: iid
  use: model.fit
  label: No tree (independent species)
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.phylo_regression@^1
    settings: {kind: iid, predictors: {$param: predictors}}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains}, seed: {$param: seed}}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: brownian
  use: model.fit
  label: Brownian motion on the tree
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.phylo_regression@^1
    settings: {kind: brownian, predictors: {$param: predictors}}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains}, seed: {$param: seed}}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: lambda
  use: model.fit
  label: Pagel's lambda
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.phylo_regression@^1
    settings: {kind: lambda, predictors: {$param: predictors}}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains}, seed: {$param: seed}}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
- id: ou
  use: model.fit
  label: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: sci.phylo_regression@^1
    settings: {kind: ou, predictors: {$param: predictors}}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains}, seed: {$param: seed}}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
# 2. rank by elpd_loo, give the stacking weights and keep the winner
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs: {candidates: [iid.metrics, brownian.metrics, lambda.metrics, ou.metrics]}
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
- id: weights
  use: compare.stacking
  inputs: {candidates: [iid.metrics, brownian.metrics, lambda.metrics, ou.metrics]}
- id: best
  use: select.best
  inputs: {table: compare.table, models: [iid.model, brownian.model, lambda.model, ou.model]}
  with: {metric: elpd_loo, direction: max}
# 3. the slopes of the winner; `focus` puts one slope in the result field `focus`
- id: slope
  use: model.summary
  label: Slopes of the winner
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with: {vars: [slope], focus: {$param: focus}, hdi_prob: {$param: hdi_prob}}
- id: clear
  use: branch.if
  label: Is the effect clear of zero?
  with:
    condition: nodes.slope.focus.excludes_zero
    explain_then: >-
      The range of the slope does not include zero. The data show an effect of the predictor
      when the model includes the tree.
    explain_else: >-
      The range of the slope includes zero. The data do not show a clear effect of the
      predictor when the model includes the tree.
# a clear effect is reported only with a check that the winner agrees with the data
- id: ppc
  use: evaluate.ppc
  label: Does the winner agree with the data?
  when: clear.then
  inputs: {model: best.model}
# 4. the trait on the tree, and the report
- id: tree
  use: plot.render
  label: Trait on the tree
  inputs: {model: best.model}
  with: {recipe: sci.phylogeny}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    items: [compare.table, weights.table, slope.table]
    metrics: [ppc.metrics]
    model: best.model
    plots: [tree.plot]
  with: {title: Trait regression across species}
outputs: {model: best.model, comparison: compare.table, weights: weights.table,
          slopes: slope.table, tree: tree.plot, report: report.report}

The recipe reads one dataset. The traits are on a species dim. The tree is on a node dim: parent, branch_length, is_tip and tip_label. The tip labels are the labels of species. The workflow binds the target of the dataset (for example brain) to the trait of the model. The predictors are names of variables in your dataset. The focus is one of them.

To try the recipe, export the E23 case study and upload it as primates301 in the project biology:

python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e23 --challenges ~/pymc-challenges/data --out primates301.nc
# or the simulated data of the model (you do not need pymc-challenges)
python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e23 --synthetic --out primates301.nc
mapi datasets upload primates301.nc --name primates301

docs.text:

mapi workflows apply primate-brains.yaml

  -p 'predictors=["body","group_size"]' -p focus=group_size --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs primate-brains -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare   # the four fits, the best elpd_loo first
mapi workflows node "$RUN" slope     # the slopes of the winner and the focus value

print(nodes["weights"].result["weights"])  # the stacking weight of each fit

docs.title: Read the outputs
docs.text:
A local run (LocalRunner) of the recipe with its default settings (4 chains of 1000 draws) on the 186 primates of the primates301 dataset (E23) took 3.3 minutes on a laptop. It gave these results:

Node Result iid, brownian, lambda, ou elpd_loo 15.0, 90.5, 129.9 and 91.2. The notebook gives 130 for lambda. weights lambda 1.00. The other fits get no weight. best "Pagel's lambda has the best elpd_loo (130) of 4 candidate(s)." slope slope[body] 0.766 (94% range 0.710 to 0.823), as the notebook. slope[group_size] 0.027 (94% range −0.010 to 0.066), p_positive 0.91. max_rhat 1.001, no divergences. clear The else arm: the range of the slope includes zero. ppc is skipped.

Read the results in this sequence:

  1. The ranking. A large gap between iid and the other fits shows that relatives are similar. Here the tree adds 115 to elpd_loo.
  2. The weights. If one fit gets all the weight, the winner is clear. If the weight is divided, more than one correlation agrees with the data. Then the slope of the winner is only one of some possible answers.
  3. The decision. The focus value gives the slope, its range and p_positive. In E23 the effect of group size is positive in 91% of the draws, but the 94% range includes zero. Thus the data do not show a clear effect of group size on brain size when the model includes the tree.
  4. The plot. The tree output (sci.phylogeny) shows the tree with the observed and the predicted trait of each species. Look for clades where the predictions are far from the observations.

The report output has the decision, the three tables, the plot and the predictive check (when it ran).

docs.title: Calibrate, then design
docs.text:
In plain words. A heated plate conducts heat in its plane and loses heat through its faces and its edges. Some calibration runs with a known heater and some thermocouples tell how much heat the plate conducts and loses. The calibrated model can then predict the temperature of each point of the plate for a heater layout that you did not build.

Before you trust such a prediction, test the calibration on a run that it did not see. This recipe holds out one calibration run, fits the other runs and predicts the run held out. It predicts the new layout only if that error is small and the sampler converged.

For the statistician. sci.heat_plate solves the 2-D steady heat equation A(θ) u = η q on the finite-volume grid of the data. θ is the conductivity k, the face and edge loss coefficients h and h_edge, and the heater efficiency η. split.holdout holds out one random run (leave_group_out, n: 1). model.fit with mode: evaluate_then_refit fits the other runs and scores the run held out (rmse, mae, coverage_90). Then it fits all the runs again. model.summary gives the parameters and max_rhat. The branch needs rmse ≤ max_error and max_rhat ≤ max_rhat. The field is linear in the heater power, so model.score (predict) gives the posterior draws of the expected field of each new run. These draws have no sensor noise. plot.render draws them with sci.field_map, one frame for each run.

flowchart LR
  D["calibration runs"] --> H["hold out<br/>one run"]
  H --> F["fit, score the run held out,<br/>fit all runs again"]
  F --> S["plate parameters<br/>and R-hat"]
  F --> RES["calibration residuals<br/>(sci.image_residuals)"]
  S --> B{"error ≤ max_error<br/>and R-hat ≤ max_rhat?"}
  F --> B
  L["new layout"] --> P
  B -- then --> P["predict the field<br/>of the layout"]
  P --> M["field map<br/>(sci.field_map)"]
  B --> R["report"]
  RES --> R
  M --> R

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: calibrate a heated plate, then predict a new heater layout.
# sci.heat_plate is fitted on the calibration runs with one run held out. The design step
# runs only if the calibration predicts that run within `max_error` and the sampler
# converged. The split and the plot read the bound dim names (`bind`), else the model's.
# (the gallery template sci_calibrate_then_design; validated and run by
# conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: heat-plate-design, project: engineering}
params:
  thickness_mm: {type: number, default: 5.0, minimum: 0.01, maximum: 1000,
                 description: The thickness of the plate in mm}
  room_temperature: {type: number, default: 20.0, minimum: -100, maximum: 1000,
                     description: The temperature of the room in degC}
  max_error: {type: number, default: 0.5, minimum: 0,
              description: The largest RMSE in degC on the run held out that the design step accepts}
  max_rhat: {type: number, default: 1.01, minimum: 1, maximum: 2,
             description: The largest R-hat that the design step accepts}
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 20000,
          description: The posterior draws that each chain keeps}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 20000,
         description: The tuning steps of each chain (the sampler drops them)}
  # the gate reads R-hat, and one chain gives no R-hat
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 2, maximum: 16,
           description: The number of chains (two or more give R-hat)}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 51, minimum: 0, maximum: 2147483647,
         description: The random seed of the sampler}
  bind:
    type: object
    default: {}
    description: >-
      The names of the model (dims and vars) mapped to the names in your dataset, when they
      are different. The workflow finds the target itself when your dataset has one target.
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset,
         description: "The calibration runs: heater power and the thermocouple readings on the grid"}
  layout: {type: dataset, required: false,
           description: The new heater layouts to predict (the heater power of each new run on the same grid)}
nodes:
# 1. calibrate: hold out one random run, fit the others, score it, then fit all the runs
- id: holdout
  use: split.holdout
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    split: {kind: leave_group_out, dim: {$expr: "coalesce(params.bind.dims.run, 'run')"},
            n: 1, seed: {$param: seed}}
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  label: Calibrate
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: holdout.plan}
  with:
    model: sci.heat_plate@^1
    settings: {thickness_mm: {$param: thickness_mm}, room_temperature: {$param: room_temperature}}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains},
          seed: {$param: seed}, mode: evaluate_then_refit, target_accept: 0.9}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mae, coverage_90]}
- id: plate
  use: model.summary
  label: Plate parameters
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  with: {vars: [k, h, h_edge, eta, sigma, spread_length]}
- id: residuals
  use: plot.render
  label: Calibration residuals
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  with: {recipe: sci.image_residuals}
# 2. the gate: the error on the run held out, and convergence
- id: good
  use: branch.if
  label: Is the calibration good enough?
  with:
    condition: >-
      coalesce(nodes.fit.metrics.rmse, 1e9) <= params.max_error and
      coalesce(nodes.plate.max_rhat, 99) <= params.max_rhat
    explain_then: >-
      The calibration predicted the run that it did not see within the error limit, and the
      sampler converged. The workflow predicted the new layout.
    explain_else: >-
      The calibration did not predict the run that it did not see within the error limit, or
      the sampler did not converge. The workflow did not predict the new layout. Add
      calibration runs or thermocouples.
# 3. design: the expected field of the new layout (else of the calibration runs), as a map
- id: design
  use: model.score
  label: Predict the layout
  when: good.then
  inputs: {model: fit.model, data: [inputs.layout, inputs.data]}
  with: {mode: predict}
- id: field
  use: plot.render
  label: Field of the layout
  when: good.then
  inputs: {data: design.scores}
  with:
    recipe: sci.field_map
    source: data
    settings:
      var: field
      y: {$expr: "coalesce(params.bind.dims.y, 'y')"}
      x: {$expr: "coalesce(params.bind.dims.x, 'x')"}
      frame: {$expr: "coalesce(params.bind.dims.run, 'run')"}
      origin: lower
      colormap: magma
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    items: [plate.table]
    metrics: [fit.metrics]
    model: fit.model
    plots: [residuals.plot, field.plot]
  with: {title: "Calibrate a heated plate, then test a heater layout"}
outputs: {model: fit.model, parameters: plate.table, residuals: residuals.plot,
          design: design.scores, field: field.plot, report: report.report}

The recipe reads two datasets:

  • data: the calibration runs. heater_power(run, y, x) in W and temperature(run, y, x) in degC on a regular grid in cm. temperature has no value where there is no thermocouple. The run dim needs the policy new_levels, because the fit does not see the run held out. Use three runs or more.
  • layout (optional): the new heater layouts. heater_power(run, y, x) on the same grid, with new run labels. If you do not give a layout, the workflow predicts the calibration runs.

If the names in your datasets are different, give bind. The split and the map read the names of the run, y and x dims from bind. To try the recipe, export the E51 case study and make a layout with two 5 W heaters:

python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e51 --out heat_plate_e51.nc
mapi datasets upload heat_plate_e51.nc --name heat_plate_e51

import xarray as xr

cal = xr.load_dataset("heat_plate_e51.nc")  # heater_w(run, y_cm, x_cm), 3 runs, 24 x 12 grid
power = xr.zeros_like(cal["heater_w"].isel(run=[0])).assign_coords(run=["two_heaters"])
power[0, 3, 5] = power[0, 8, 18] = 5.0  # two 5 W heaters (row, column)
xr.Dataset({"heater_w": power}).to_netcdf("heat_plate_layout.nc")

Then upload heat_plate_layout.nc with mapi datasets upload heat_plate_layout.nc --name heat_plate_layout.

docs.title: Run it with the CLI
docs.text:
mapi workflows init sci_calibrate_then_design --name heat-plate-design
mapi workflows apply heat-plate-design.yaml
mapi workflows run heat-plate-design \
  -i data=dataset://engineering/heat_plate_e51@latest \
  -i layout=dataset://engineering/heat_plate_layout@latest \
  -p 'bind={"dims": {"y": "y_cm", "x": "x_cm"}, "vars": {"heater_power": "heater_w", "temperature": "reading_c"}}' \
  --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs heat-plate-design -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" fit     # the error on the run held out
mapi workflows node "$RUN" plate   # k, h, h_edge, eta, sigma and the spread length

from mapi_client import Client

workflow, revision = api.workflows.upsert(Path("heat-plate-design.yaml"))
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,

        "data": "dataset://engineering/heat_plate_e51@latest",

    },
    params={
        "bind": {
            "dims": {"y": "y_cm", "x": "x_cm"},
            "vars": {"heater_power": "heater_w", "temperature": "reading_c"},
        }

print(nodes["fit"].result["metrics"])  # rmse, mae and coverage_90 on the run held out

docs.title: Read the outputs
docs.text:
A local run (LocalRunner) of the recipe with its default settings (4 chains of 1000 draws, the pymc engine) on the E51 calibration and the layout above took 14 minutes on a busy laptop. It gave these results:

Node Result holdout The fit did not see the run cal1. fit On cal1: rmse 0.12 degC, mae 0.09 degC, coverage_90 1.0. The thermocouples have a noise of 0.2 degC. plate k 59.2 W/m/K (94% range 53.7 to 63.9), h 9.05, eta 0.91, sigma 0.19 degC and spread_length 12.8 cm. The notebook gives 59.3, 9.07, 0.91, 0.19 and 12.9 cm. max_rhat 1.002, 8 divergences. good The then arm: the error and R-hat are in their limits. design, field The expected field of two_heaters. The hottest point is 33.3 degC, at x = 30.8 cm and y = 14.2 cm.

Read the results in this sequence:

  1. The error on the run held out. This is the error of a prediction for a heater layout that the fit did not see. That is the same task as the design. An rmse near the noise of the thermocouples shows that the calibration predicts new layouts well.
  2. The parameters. k, h and eta are strongly correlated, because a stronger heater and a stronger loss can give the same readings. The range of spread_length is narrower (1% of its value, against 5% for k). The data fix how far the heat spreads, and that controls the field.
  3. Convergence. The branch reads only max_rhat. n_divergent in the plate result shows the divergent transitions (8 here, 2 in the notebook). If there are many, set a higher target_accept in the fit node.
  4. The maps. The residuals plot shows the calibration readings against the fit. The field plot shows the mean and the sd of the predicted field, one frame for each new run. A large sd far from the thermocouples shows where more sensors help.

If the branch takes the else arm, the workflow skips design and field. The report tells you to add calibration runs or thermocouples.

docs.title: Bayesian workflow audit
docs.text:
In plain words. A Bayesian model gives ranges, not only numbers. Before you use the ranges, do the checks of a careful Bayesian workflow:

  • Can the model make data like your data before it sees the data (the priors)?
  • Do the chains of the sampler agree (R-hat and the effective sample size)?
  • Can the fitted model make data like your data (the posterior predictive check)?
  • Do the results change much when the priors are wider or narrower?
  • Does the model find known values in data that it simulated?

This workflow does all five checks on one model and writes one report with the plots. It works with each model that gives posterior draws. You give the model, its settings and the binding as parameters, the same as in a model spec.

For the statistician. The fit keeps prior_predictive.draws prior predictive draws (500 by default) for core.prior_predictive. model.summary gives the rank-normalised split R-hat and the bulk ESS of all the posterior values. The branch converged needs R-hat under rhat_max (1.01) and the ESS at or over min_ess (400, that is 100 for each of 4 chains). Only then do the other checks run:

  • evaluate.ppc: the coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges, the PIT distance and the p-value of statistic (sd by default).
  • governance.check with sensitivity.prior: refits with the prior widths times each of prior_scales.
  • governance.check with recovery.simulated: n_sims refits on targets that the fit simulated.

The branch trusted needs ppc.ok and no fail or error from the two refit checks. A check that does not apply to the model (skipped) does not block. The plots use on_failure: continue. If a recipe cannot read the model, the report tells why, and the audit continues. The defaults are for real use: 4 chains of 1000 draws after 1000 tuning steps. The recovery check fits the model n_sims more times, at the refit budget of the governance run.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: the checks of a careful Bayesian workflow for any model with draws.
# Prior predictive draws -> convergence gate -> posterior predictive check, prior
# sensitivity and simulated recovery -> plots -> one report.
# (the gallery template bayes_workflow_audit; validated and run by
# conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: bayes-workflow-audit, project: templates}
params:
  model:
    type: string
    required: true
    description: The model to audit, for example tabular.hierarchical_glm@^1 or sci.heat_plate@^1
  settings: {type: object, default: {}, description: The settings of the model (see its About card)}
  bind:
    type: object
    default: {}
    description: The binding of the dataset names to the names of the model (dims and vars), as in data.bind of a model spec
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 100000, description: The posterior draws for each chain}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 0, maximum: 100000, description: The tuning steps for each chain (the sampler drops them)}
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 2, maximum: 16, description: "The number of chains (two or more, so that R-hat is available)"}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 1, minimum: 0, description: The random seed of the fit}
  prior_predictive:
    type: object
    default: {draws: 500}
    description: "The prior predictive draws of the fit, as {draws: N}. Type {} for a model that cannot sample its priors (the workflow then does not draw the prior plot)"
  vars: {type: array, default: [], description: "The parameters of the pair plot and the estimate plot (empty: the plots select them)"}
  rhat_max: {type: number, default: 1.01, minimum: 1.0, maximum: 1.5, description: The largest R-hat that passes}
  min_ess: {type: number, default: 400, minimum: 0, description: The smallest bulk effective sample size that passes (100 for each of 4 chains)}
  statistic: {type: string, default: sd, enum: [mean, sd, max, min], description: The statistic of the predictive p-value}
  prior_scales: {type: array, default: [0.5, 2.0], description: "The prior widths that the sensitivity check tries, as multiples of the model priors"}
  n_sims: {type: integer, default: 20, minimum: 5, maximum: 100, description: The simulated datasets of the recovery check (each one is a fit)}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: The dataset that the model fits}
nodes:
# 1. Fit the model and keep draws from the priors (unless prior_predictive is {}).
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  label: Fit with prior draws
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: {$param: model}
    settings: {$param: settings}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    fit:
      draws: {$param: draws}
      tune: {$param: tune}
      chains: {$param: chains}
      seed: {$param: seed}
      prior_predictive: {$expr: "if(len(params.prior_predictive) > 0, params.prior_predictive, null)"}
- id: has_prior
  use: branch.if
  label: Prior draws?
  with:
    condition: len(params.prior_predictive) > 0
    explain_then: The run asked for draws from the priors, so the workflow compared them with the data.
    explain_else: The run did not ask for draws from the priors, so the workflow did not draw the prior plot.
# 2. Can the priors make data like the observed data? (A plot that fails does not stop the audit.)
- id: prior_plot
  use: plot.render
  label: Prior predictive check
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  when: has_prior.then
  on_failure: continue
  with: {recipe: core.prior_predictive, source: model}
# 3. The parameters, R-hat, the bulk ESS and the divergences; a pair plot of a few parameters.
- {id: summary, use: model.summary, label: Parameters and convergence, inputs: {model: fit.model}}
- id: pair_plot
  use: plot.render
  label: Pair plot
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  on_failure: continue
  with:
    recipe: core.pair
    source: model
    settings:
      var_names: {$expr: "if(len(params.vars) > 0, params.vars, null)"}
# 4. The gate: the other checks only mean something when the chains agree.
- id: converged
  use: branch.if
  label: Did the sampler converge?
  with:
    condition: coalesce(nodes.summary.max_rhat, 99) < params.rhat_max and coalesce(nodes.summary.min_ess, 0) >= params.min_ess
    explain_then: R-hat and the effective sample size are in their limits, so the chains agree. The workflow did the checks of the predictions and the priors.
    explain_else: R-hat is too large or the effective sample size is too small, so the chains do not agree. The workflow stopped the audit. Fit with more draws and tuning steps, or change the model.
# 5. Posterior predictive check (coverage, PIT, a p-value) and its plot.
- id: ppc
  use: evaluate.ppc
  label: Predictions against the data
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  when: converged.then
  on_failure: continue
  with: {statistic: {$param: statistic}}
- id: ppc_plot
  use: plot.render
  label: Posterior predictive check
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  when: converged.then
  on_failure: continue
  with: {recipe: core.ppc, source: predictions}
# 6. Refits: wider and narrower priors, and data simulated from the fit.
- id: sensitivity
  use: governance.check
  label: Prior sensitivity
  inputs: {model: fit.model, data: inputs.data}
  when: converged.then
  with:
    check: sensitivity.prior
    params: {scales: {$param: prior_scales}}
- id: recovery
  use: governance.check
  label: Recovery of known values
  inputs: {model: fit.model, data: inputs.data}
  when: converged.then
  with:
    check: recovery.simulated
    params: {n_sims: {$param: n_sims}}
# 7. The verdict; a skipped check (one that does not apply to the model) does not block.
- id: trusted
  use: branch.if
  label: Can you trust the model?
  when: converged.then
  with:
    condition: coalesce(nodes.ppc.ok, false) and nodes.sensitivity.status not in ['fail', 'error'] and nodes.recovery.status not in ['fail', 'error']
    explain_then: No check failed. The model makes data like the observed data, and the prior and recovery checks did not fail. Read their warnings, then use the estimates.
    explain_else: One or more checks failed. Look at the predictive check, the prior sensitivity and the recovery evidence before you use the estimates.
- id: estimates
  use: plot.render
  label: Estimates
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  when: trusted.then
  on_failure: continue
  with:
    recipe: core.posterior_forest
    source: model
    settings:
      var_names: {$expr: "if(len(params.vars) > 0, params.vars, null)"}
# 8. One report: the decisions, the table, the predictive scores and the plots that ran.
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    items: [summary.table]
    metrics: [ppc.metrics]
    plots: [prior_plot.plot, pair_plot.plot, ppc_plot.plot, estimates.plot]
    model: fit.model
  with: {title: Bayesian workflow audit}
outputs:
  model: fit.model
  report: report.report
  summary: summary.table
  ppc: ppc.metrics
  sensitivity: sensitivity.evidence
  recovery: recovery.evidence

Note

A model that cannot sample its priors (for example sci.areal_bym2, because of its ICAR prior) fails the fit when the run asks for prior draws. For such a model, set prior_predictive to {}. The branch has_prior then skips the prior plot.

docs.title: Get the data
docs.text:
The examples audit a hierarchical model of radon in homes. The test data of the tabular plugin has a simulated version: 64 homes in 8 counties, with log_radon, floor and county_idx for each home and log_uranium for each county. Write it to a file and upload it in the project environment:

python -c "from mapi_plugin_tabular.datasets import RADON_SCHEMA, radon_dataset; \
ds = radon_dataset(); ds.attrs['mapi_schema'] = RADON_SCHEMA.model_dump_json(exclude_none=True); \
ds.to_netcdf('radon_homes.nc')"
mapi datasets upload radon_homes.nc --name radon_homes

docs.title: Run it with the CLI
docs.text:
mapi workflows init bayes_workflow_audit --name radon-audit   # writes radon-audit.yaml
mapi workflows apply radon-audit.yaml -m "audit of the radon model"
mapi workflows run radon-audit \
  --input data=dataset://environment/radon_homes@latest \
  --param model=tabular.hierarchical_glm@^1 \
  --param 'settings={"group_dim": "county", "covariates": ["floor"], "group_covariates": ["log_uranium"]}' \
  --param 'bind={"dims": {"obs": "home"}, "vars": {"y": "log_radon"}}' \
  --param 'vars=["intercept", "beta", "sigma"]' \
  --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs radon-audit -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows status "$RUN"                  # each decision and what each check found
mapi workflows node "$RUN" summary            # R-hat, ESS and the range of each parameter
mapi workflows node "$RUN" recovery           # the recovery check and its evidence

docs.title: Run it with the Python client
docs.text:
from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()
workflow = api.workflows.create(template="bayes_workflow_audit")
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://environment/radon_homes@latest"},
    params={
        "model": "tabular.hierarchical_glm@^1",
        "settings": {"group_dim": "county", "covariates": ["floor"],
                     "group_covariates": ["log_uranium"]},
        "bind": {"dims": {"obs": "home"}, "vars": {"y": "log_radon"}},
        "vars": ["intercept", "beta", "sigma"],
    },
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["converged"].result["arm"])        # "then": the chains agree
print(nodes["ppc"].result["verdict_plain"])    # the posterior predictive check in words
print(nodes["sensitivity"].result["message_plain"])
print(nodes["recovery"].result["message_plain"])
print(nodes["trusted"].result["arm"])          # "then": no check failed
report = run.outputs["report"].inline          # mapi.report/v1 with the plots in it

docs.title: Read the outputs
docs.text:
Output What it tells you has_prior, converged, trusted The three decisions, with the values that each condition read. The report starts with their plain words. summary (table) The mean, sd, 94% HDI, R-hat and bulk ESS of each parameter (the first 200 values). The result also has max_rhat, min_ess and n_divergent. prior_plot The data that the priors can make (grey) and your data (black). If your data is far from the grey curves, the priors are on the wrong scale. pair_plot The draws of two parameters at a time. Red points are divergent transitions. Look at funnels and strong correlations. ppc, ppc_plot The share of the observations in the 50% and 90% ranges, the PIT distance, and the p-value of the statistic. ok is true when all of them pass. sensitivity The largest relative change of a key estimate when the priors change. Above 0.2 is warn, above 0.5 is fail. skipped if the settings do not set the priors. recovery How often the 90% ranges contained the known values in the simulated data (target 90%). estimates The posterior forest of the parameters. It shows only when no check failed.

If the chains do not agree, the workflow skips the checks and the report tells you to fit with more draws and tuning steps, or to change the model. A run on a laptop audited the radon model (8 counties, 64 homes, 2 chains of 100 draws for the test). R-hat was below 1.07 and 91% of the homes were in the 90% ranges. The sensitivity check gave warn (the uranium effect moved by 41% with priors two times narrower), recovery gave pass and the branch trusted took the then arm.

docs.title: Image model check
docs.text:
In plain words. When a model predicts a full image, a table of numbers does not show where the model is wrong. This workflow fits the model and puts its predicted images next to the observed image. It shows the residuals as maps, so that you can see the areas where the model does not agree with the data. Use it for a sky map (sci.cmb_field), a lensed galaxy (sci.strong_lens), a Turing pattern (sci.turing_pattern) or a different model that predicts an image.

For the statistician. The plots read the in-sample predictions of the model (source: predictions) with the observed image as observed_data:

  • sci.image_residuals shows the observed image, the posterior predictive mean, the residual and the normalised residual (obs − mean) / √(sd² + σ²), with a histogram against N(0, 1).
  • sci.ppc_image_grid shows the observed image next to n_draws predicted images on one colour scale. With shuffle: true the observed image has a random position, and the caption gives the answer.
  • evaluate.ppc pools all the pixels: the coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges, the PIT distance and a p-value. It needs 10 or more predictive draws. If it fails, the report tells why and the plots stay.

The parameters var and frame select the image variable and the dim of the slider when the recipes cannot find them.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: does an image model make images like the observed image?
# Fit -> parameter summary -> residual maps and a grid of predicted images -> posterior
# predictive check -> one report.
# (the gallery template sci_image_model_check; validated and run by
# conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: sci-image-model-check, project: templates}
params:
  model: {type: string, required: true, description: "The image model, for example sci.cmb_field@^1"}
  settings: {type: object, default: {}, description: The settings of the model (see its About card)}
  bind:
    type: object
    default: {}
    description: The binding of the dataset names to the names of the model (dims and vars), as in data.bind of a model spec
  draws: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 10, maximum: 100000, description: The posterior draws for each chain}
  tune: {type: integer, default: 1000, minimum: 0, maximum: 100000, description: The tuning steps for each chain (the sampler drops them)}
  chains: {type: integer, default: 4, minimum: 2, maximum: 16, description: "The number of chains (two or more, so that R-hat is available)"}
  seed: {type: integer, default: 1, minimum: 0, description: The random seed of the fit}
  var: {type: string, default: "", description: "The predicted image variable (empty: the plots find it)"}
  frame: {type: string, default: "", description: "The dim with one image for each level, for example run or t (empty: the plots find it)"}
  n_draws: {type: integer, default: 5, minimum: 1, maximum: 11, description: The predicted images next to the observed image}
  shuffle: {type: boolean, default: false, description: Hide which panel is the observed image (the caption gives the answer)}
  statistic: {type: string, default: sd, enum: [mean, sd, max, min], description: The statistic of the predictive p-value}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: The observed image (or images) and the inputs of the model}
nodes:
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: {$param: model}
    settings: {$param: settings}
    bind: {$param: bind}
    fit: {draws: {$param: draws}, tune: {$param: tune}, chains: {$param: chains}, seed: {$param: seed}}
- {id: summary, use: model.summary, label: Parameters and convergence, inputs: {model: fit.model}}
# Both plots read the in-sample predictions with the observed image (source: predictions).
# An empty var or frame becomes null, and the recipe finds the image and the slider dim.
- id: residuals
  use: plot.render
  label: Residual maps
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  with:
    recipe: sci.image_residuals
    source: predictions
    settings:
      var: {$expr: "if(params.var == '', null, params.var)"}
      frame: {$expr: "if(params.frame == '', null, params.frame)"}
- id: grid
  use: plot.render
  label: Observed and predicted images
  inputs: {model: fit.model}
  with:
    recipe: sci.ppc_image_grid
    source: predictions
    settings:
      var: {$expr: "if(params.var == '', null, params.var)"}
      frame: {$expr: "if(params.frame == '', null, params.frame)"}
      n_draws: {$param: n_draws}
      shuffle: {$param: shuffle}
