print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("oklahoma-quakes-lgcp.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "oklahoma-quakes-lgcp")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://geoscience/oklahoma-quakes-lgcp@latest",
        "mode": "forecast",
        "horizon": {"dim": "period", "periods": 8},
        "output": {"kind": "predictive", "summary": ["mean", "q5", "q50", "q95"]},
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["total"].sel(stat="q50").values)

To run the audit recipe:

workflow = api.workflows.create(template="bayes_workflow_audit")
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://geoscience/oklahoma_quakes_grid@latest"},
    params={
        "model": "sci.lgcp_grid@^1",
        "settings": {"max_extension": 8, "era_periods": 4, "m_row": 10,
                     "m_col": 14, "cell_km": 25.0},
        "bind": {"dims": {"period": "quarter"}, "vars": {"count": "quakes"}},
    },
    wait=True,
)

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the binned grid of notebook section 2 and the model of rung 4. It leaves out these parts:

  • Rung 1 (time only). The model always has a map. The other rungs are settings of the same model: field: static with likelihood: poisson is rung 2, and likelihood: poisson alone is rung 3.
  • The prior predictive check of section 4. The model has the "how many" and "where" parametrisation from the start, so the priors do not explode.
  • The LOO comparison of section 9. The spec of this tutorial does not ask for it. Add elpd_loo to evaluate.metrics in a spec for each rung. Many Pareto k values are high for this model, as in the notebook, so use the order of the models and not the exact numbers.
  • The centre of activity (section 8). The web app has no plot for it. Calculate it from the draws of rate (step 6.3).
  • The yearly maps with the epicentres. Fields shows quarters, not years, and it does not show the epicentres. The notebook shows the sum of each year.
  • The magnitudes. The dataset keeps only the counts. The notebook does not use them in the model either.

Next steps:

  • Fit the rungs of the ladder with field and likelihood, and compare them with elpd_loo and the hold-out metrics.
  • Add the magnitudes as marks, or a term for aftershocks (notebook "Try it yourself", items 1 and 2). These need a new model.
  • Add injection volumes as a cause. This is the only way to answer the policy question. The model does not accept columns for causes.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the audit recipe.

docs.title: E18 Scottish lip cancer disease map (ICAR/BYM2)
docs.text:
This tutorial does the main analysis of the pymc-challenges notebook E18_areal_models_icar_bym2.py in the web app. You use the model sci.areal_bym2@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project epidemiology. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads the file data/scotland_lip.geojson.
  • About 15 minutes. One fit takes less than one minute of sandbox time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Between 1975 and 1980, 536 men in Scotland got lip cancer. For each of the 56 districts, you know the observed count and an expected count. The expected count is the count of the district if each age group had the national rate. The ratio of the two is the standardised morbidity ratio (SMR). The SMR is a raw estimate of the relative risk of the district.

The notebook asks two questions:

  1. Where is the risk really high, when you include the noise of small counts?
  2. Does outdoor work explain the risk? AFF is the percentage of the workers in agriculture, fishing and forestry. Lip cancer has a relation to sunlight.

Small districts have few cases, so their SMRs have much noise. The notebook lets each district share its risk with its neighbours on the map. It puts graph priors on the district effects: the intrinsic CAR (ICAR), the proper CAR and BYM2. BYM2 is a scaled ICAR plus independent effects. Its parameter rho is the share of the variation that follows the map.

The decision at the end of the notebook is this:

  • Do not publish the raw SMR map. Publish the BYM2 smoothed relative risk and the probability that the relative risk is more than 1. In 19 districts this probability is more than 0.95. These are the districts where the risk is "high and certain".
  • Use BYM2 as the default model. The graph models predict equally well, and all three predict better than independent districts. BYM2 has a rho that you can read, and its priors mean the same thing on each map.
  • Report the AFF effect as an association. Its 90% interval excludes 0 in each model. But its size changes from a relative risk of 1.96 for each 10 points (independent districts) to 1.50 (BYM2). The size depends on what you assume about risk factors that you did not measure. This is spatial confounding.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The graph of the districts, with the island links (Plots, net.graph) Section 2 (the queen graph) and section 3 (the island links) The posterior of b0, b1, sigma and rho (Parameters) Section 4, the BYM2 row of the diagnostics table, and section 6 The smoothed relative risk rr and p_exceed, the probability that rr is more than 1 (Plots, sci.area_map) Section 7, the three maps elpd_loo and the Pareto k warning (Diagnostics) Section 8, the LOO table The error on 7 districts that the fit did not see (Diagnostics) Section 8, a smaller version of the 8-fold cross-validation The ladder of kind values, compared by elpd_loo (the recipe sci_spatial_ladder) Section 4 (the five models) and section 9 (b1 in each model) New maps of risk and counts (Score, Simulate) Section 3, the prior predictive draws "by hand"

Some parts of the notebook are not in the port, for example the unscaled BYM and the Moran's I checks of the residual effects. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads the GeoJSON file of pymc-challenges and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. Run it from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out scotland_lip.nc --spec scotland_lip.yaml

The command writes:

wrote scotland_lip.nc (variables cases, expected, aff, adjacency, ring_x, ring_y on district=56, district_=56, vertex=51)
upload it as dataset epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer and fit sci.areal_bym2
wrote the suggested spec to scotland_lip.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning district 56 categorical, fixed The district names, as in the GeoJSON file (Orkney has the name Okney) district_ 56 categorical, fixed The same districts again: the second axis of adjacency vertex 51 integer, fixed The points of the outline of each district cases district float64, target The observed cases, 1975 to 1980 (CANCER) expected district float64, exposure The expected cases (CEXP), from 1.07 to 88.66 aff district float64, covariate The percentage of workers in agriculture, fishing and forestry (AFF) adjacency district, district_ int64, constant 1 when two districts touch (queen contiguity), else 0 ring_x, ring_y district, vertex float64, constant The outline of each district in British National Grid metres. NaN fills the unused points

The export makes the graph as the notebook does. Two districts are neighbours when their outlines share at least one point. The graph has 117 edges. Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles have no neighbours. The model links them when it fits (step 6.1).

The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

Simulated data

--synthetic writes a map of 43 square districts (one of them is an island) with counts from the model itself. The true values are b0 = 0.1, b1 = 0.4, sigma = 0.5 and rho = 0.8. You do not need pymc-challenges for it.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 --synthetic --out disease_map_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type scotland_lip_cancer in Name. Type a description, for example "Male lip cancer in 56 districts of Scotland, 1975 to 1980, with district outlines".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select scotland_lip.nc.
  6. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows cases, expected and aff on district, and adjacency on district and district_.
  7. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  8. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, cases has the role target, expected has the role exposure and aff has the role covariate. Missingness shows missing values only in ring_x and ring_y. These are the unused points of the shorter outlines.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Map.

  3. The map shows the 56 districts. Select cases, expected, aff or the ratio cases / expected (the standardised morbidity ratio) to set the colours. The lines join the neighbour districts.

  4. The list of areas with no neighbour shows the labels of the data: Okney (Orkney), Shetland and WesternIsles (the Western Isles). The model links them when it fits (step 6.1).
  5. The table of Moran's I tells if neighbour districts have similar values. A positive value with a small p-value is a reason for a spatial model.
  6. ring_x, ring_y and adjacency are geometry. They are not in Distributions, Unusual values or Data quality.
  7. The time sections are in Not for this data. The data has no time dim.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select scotland_lip_cancer. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type areal in the search field. Under Models, select Disease risk on a map of areas (sci.areal_bym2@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name scotland-lip-cancer-bym2 from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: scotland-lip-cancer-bym2
  project: epidemiology
data:
  dataset: dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest
  bind:
    dims:
      area: district
      area_: district_
    vars:
      covariate: aff
  split:
    kind: mask_block
    dims: [area]
    fraction: 0.125
    seed: 1987
model:
  use: sci.areal_bym2@^1
  settings:
    kind: bym2
    islands: link_nearest
    covariate_scale: 10.0
    center_covariate: true
    intercept_sd: 1.0
    slope_sd: 1.0
    sigma_scale: 1.0
    rho_alpha: 1.0
    rho_beta: 1.0
    exceed_threshold: 1.0
  fit:
    mode: evaluate_then_refit
    seed: 1987
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    target_accept: 0.9
    engine: nutpie
evaluate:
  metrics: [rmse, mae, coverage_90, elpd_loo]
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - sci.area_map
    - net.graph

The settings are the defaults of the model. They are also the choices of the notebook. The --spec file of the export has the short form of the same spec. This table tells what each setting means for the question:

Setting Value Meaning for this question kind bym2 The prior of the district effects. bym2 is the model that the notebook recommends. Use poisson, iid, icar or car to fit the other models of the notebook (step 6.5) islands link_nearest Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles have no neighbours. The model links each one to the district with the closest outline, as the notebook does. Without a link, the BYM2 scaling factor is not defined covariate_scale 10 b1 is the effect of 10 percentage points of AFF on the log relative risk, as in the notebook center_covariate true The model subtracts the mean AFF (8.66%). Thus b0 is the log relative risk of a district with a mean AFF intercept_sd, slope_sd 1, 1 The priors b0 ~ Normal(0, 1) and b1 ~ Normal(0, 1) of the notebook sigma_scale 1 The prior sigma ~ HalfNormal(1) of the total sd of the district effects rho_alpha, rho_beta 1, 1 The prior rho ~ Beta(1, 1): all shares are equally probable before the data exceed_threshold 1 p_exceed is the probability that rr is more than 1, that is, more than the national rate
  • bind gives the dataset names to the names of the model. The model calls the districts area and the covariate covariate. The outputs come back with your names.
  • split holds out 12.5% of the districts (7 districts). The model keeps these districts in the graph, but it does not use their counts. It predicts them from their neighbours. This is the question "what is the risk in a district without data?" of notebook section 8.
  • fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit first fits without the held-out districts and calculates the metrics on them. Then it fits again on all 56 districts. The parameters and the maps come from the second fit.
  • engine: nutpie is the sampler of the notebook. engine: pymc gives the same result, but it is slower.
  • The model always keeps the log-likelihood of each district, so you do not need a keep block for elpd_loo.

The plots

The model declares core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.area_map, net.graph and core.ridge. The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. core.ridge needs the setting dim, and a spec cannot give settings to a plot. Without dim, the fit skips the plot with the issue SCHEMA_INVALID. Thus the spec does not name core.ridge.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The run fits two times: first without the 7 held-out districts, then on all 56 districts. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://epidemiology/scotland-lip-cancer-bym2@v1. Click it.

The two fits took 21 s in our test. Each fit samples b0, b1, sigma, rho and two effects for each district (phi for the ICAR part and theta for the independent part).

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text:
On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

The outputs of this model are on the districts, not on a grid. Thus the Fields section is under "Does not apply". Fit vs actual and Residuals also show there, because they need a time dimension. The maps are in the Plots tab of the model version page.

Open Overview to see the scorecard. The check "Few missing values" passes. It counts only the variables that contain observations. Thus it does not count the padding of the outlines ring_x and ring_y (and adjacency), because they have the role constant. The expert message names these variables.

docs.title: 6.1 The graph that the model used
docs.text:
The model links the three islands before it fits. The bundle of the version keeps the result in learned:

Value Result Notebook n_components_input 4 (the mainland and three islands) 4 connected components islands_input Okney, Shetland, WesternIsles the same links Okney to Caithness (28 km), Shetland to Okney (192 km), WesternIsles to Ross-Cromarty (41 km) the same links and distances n_edges 120 120 scaling_factor 0.632 0.632

The link from Shetland is 192 km long, because the GeoJSON file draws only the north part of Shetland. The rule still selects Orkney, as in the notebook.

On the model version page, open Plots and select the plot with the title "Network of adjacency" (net.graph). It draws the 120 links at the centres of the districts, next to the full adjacency matrix. Look for the three long links to the islands in the north and the north-west.

docs.title: 6.2 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

  • The largest R-hat is 1.006 (phi), the smallest bulk ESS is 588 (rho) and there are 0 divergences. The sampler has no problems.
  • TREE_DEPTH shows that 1 of 4000 draws hit the largest tree depth. This is information only. The results are correct.
  • PARETO_K_HIGH is a warning: 17 of 56 districts have a Pareto k above 0.7. This is expected. Each district has its own effect, so when PSIS-LOO removes the count of a district, the posterior changes too much. The notebook found 24 such districts. Do not quote elpd_loo as a precise value.

The diagnostics also show the metrics of the 7 held-out districts (Wigtown, Badenoch, Inverness, Kyle-Carrick, Dumbarton, Edinburgh and East Kilbride). The model predicted their counts from their neighbours only:

Metric Value Meaning rmse 7.64 cases The error of the predicted counts. Edinburgh has 50.7 expected cases, so a large error in cases is possible mae 4.81 cases The mean absolute error coverage_90 1.00 All 7 observed counts are in their 90% intervals elpd_loo −153.0 PSIS-LOO of the fit on all 56 districts (notebook: −152.7)

docs.title: 6.3 What the model learned
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The table shows the posterior mean and the 90% highest-density interval:

Parameter Mean 90% interval Meaning b0 0.102 0.003 to 0.206 The log relative risk of a district with a mean AFF. Scotland has 11% more cases than the expected counts give b1 0.406 0.201 to 0.625 The effect of 10 points of AFF on the log risk. exp(0.41) = 1.50 for each 10 points sigma 0.518 0.382 to 0.656 The total sd of the district effects on the log scale rho 0.802 0.569 to 1.000 The share of the district variation that follows the map

The table also has 56 rows each for rr, effect, phi and theta.

The answer to "how much of the risk follows the map?" (notebook section 6) is rho. Its median is 0.84 and its 90% interval is wide. Most of the variation after AFF is spatial. A district's risk is better predicted by its neighbours than by an independent quirk of the district. Thus there are possibly more risk factors that change smoothly over Scotland, and that AFF does not include.

docs.title: 6.4 The maps
docs.text:
On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for Sampler convergence (core.convergence) The text says "All 228 parameters look converged." Posterior forest (core.posterior_forest) The intervals of step 6.3 and of each district. b1 is clearly above 0 Area map (sci.area_map) The title is "Area map of rr". This is the map of notebook section 7. See below Network (net.graph) The title is "Network of adjacency". The graph of step 6.1

The area map has four panels for the relative risk rr:

  • Observed smr: the raw SMR (observed ÷ expected). The extreme colours are on the smallest districts. Skye-Lochalsh has 9 cases where 1.4 were expected.
  • Mean: the smoothed relative risk. The contrast between the north-west and the central belt stays, but the extremes are smaller. The two districts with zero cases (Annandale and Tweeddale) are not the "healthiest" districts of Scotland on this map.
  • SD: the uncertainty. It is large on small districts.
  • P(rr > 1): the probability that rr is more than 1. A cross marks each district where this probability is more than 95%. There are 19 crosses (notebook: 19).

The districts with the highest smoothed risk are Skye-Lochalsh (median rr 4.56), Banff-Buchan (4.27), Orkney (3.79), Ross-Cromarty (3.22) and Sutherland (3.17). In 14 districts, the probability that rr is more than 1 is less than 0.05 (notebook: 14).

docs.title: 6.5 The decision and the numbers
docs.text:
Make the notebook's decision with these outputs:

  1. Where is the risk high? Use the P(rr > 1) panel of the area map, not the Observed smr panel. Report the 19 districts with a cross. Report the smoothed map (Mean) for all districts.
  2. Which graph prior? Fit the same spec with kind: iid, kind: icar and kind: car (change the setting, then save and fit each spec). Then select the versions in Models and click Compare. Or run the recipe of step 8, which does these fits for you. The three graph models are within about 1 elpd of each other. All three are about 11 elpd better than iid. Thus use BYM2, because its rho has the same meaning on each map.
  3. Does AFF explain the risk? Look at b1 in each kind. With iid, b1 is 0.67. With the graph models, it is about 0.4. AFF has a map like the risk, so the district effects take part of its effect. Report that AFF has a clear association with the risk. Do not report one size of the effect as "the" effect.

We fitted the spec above on the exported data (seed 1987, 4 chains of 1000 draws, nutpie). The table compares the platform with the notebook:

Quantity Notebook Platform b0 (BYM2) 0.101 0.102 b1 (BYM2), 5% to 95% 0.19 to 0.62 (median 0.41) 0.19 to 0.62 (median 0.41) Relative risk for each 10 points of AFF (BYM2) 1.50 1.51 sigma (BYM2) 0.515 0.518 rho (BYM2), median and 5% to 95% 0.86, 0.52 to 0.99 0.84, 0.48 to 0.99 Districts with P(RR > 1) > 0.95 19 19 Districts with P(RR > 1) < 0.05 14 14 elpd_loo (BYM2) −152.7 −153.0 Districts with Pareto k > 0.7 (BYM2) 24 17 Scaling factor of the linked graph 0.632 0.632 b1 with iid and with icar 0.670 and 0.374 0.673 and 0.378 alpha with car 0.958 0.956 Sampler (BYM2) 0 divergences, R-hat up to 1.003 0 divergences, R-hat up to 1.006

Your numbers can be a little different if your sandbox has a different version of PyMC or nutpie.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
A score needs the district labels. The model takes expected and aff from the fit when the dataset does not give them. A dataset can change them, for example to ask a "what if" question about AFF. A district that was not in the fit stops the score with UNSEEN_LEVELS.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model has no time dimension and cannot forecast, so the server refuses a request without a dataset ("the score request has no data"). A note under Values to score gives this reason.

Predict the risk of each district:

  1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. In Dataset, select dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest.
  4. Open Advanced. Type rr, p_exceed in Variables (optional). Set Seed (optional) to 1987.
  5. Click Predict.

The Results region shows rr and p_exceed for each district, with the statistics mean, hdi_90_lower and hdi_90_upper. For Skye-Lochalsh, the mean of rr is 4.74, from 2.35 to 6.82. The mean of p_exceed is the probability of step 6.4. It is more than 0.95 in 19 districts.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://epidemiology/scotland-lip-cancer-bym2@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 0,
    "units": "original",
    "names": "dataset",
    "vars": ["rr", "p_exceed"]
  },
  "seed": 1987
}

Simulate a new map:

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset and the same dataset.
  3. In Advanced, type cases, rr in Variables (optional).
  4. Click Simulate.

For each posterior draw, the model draws a new map of district effects from the fitted sigma and rho, and then new counts. pm.ICAR cannot draw values, so the model uses its own ICAR sampler. This is the "prior predictive, by hand" of notebook section 3, but with the posterior values of sigma and rho. The new maps do not follow the observed map. The spread of rr is largest in districts with few neighbours, for example Orkney and Shetland. The sum of the mean counts is about 636. The request is the same as above, with "mode": "simulate" and "vars": ["cases", "rr"].

What if no worker worked outdoors?

Make a copy of the dataset with aff set to 0 in each district, and upload it as scotland_lip_cancer_aff0:

import xarray as xr
from mapi_plugin_science.areal_data import AREAL_SCHEMA
from mapi_plugin_science.export import write_export

ds = xr.load_dataset("scotland_lip.nc")
ds["aff"] = ds["aff"] * 0.0
write_export(ds, "scotland_lip_cancer_aff0.nc", schema=AREAL_SCHEMA)

Predict cases and rr on this dataset. The sum of the expected cases falls from 537 to 386. The rr of Skye-Lochalsh (AFF 16%) falls from 4.74 to 2.52 (1.19 to 3.90). This is the BYM2 estimate of the association. Spatial confounding (step 6.5) also applies to this answer.

forecast and counterfactual give MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED. "kind": "predictive" gives Poisson draws of cases in place of the expected counts.

Try it on an endpoint

If you promote the version to an endpoint, open Integrations, then the endpoint, then the Schema and Try it tab. Paste the same request there, without the model field, and click Score.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_spatial_ladder (Disease map: which spatial model?) does notebook sections 4, 8 and 9 in one run:

  • It fits three rungs on all the data: iid ("Independent areas"), icar ("Neighbours share risk (ICAR)") and bym2 ("Neighbours and noise (BYM2)").
  • It ranks them by elpd_loo and calculates the stacking weights. It keeps the best rung.
  • It shows the range of b1 in the best rung. If the range does not include zero, it fits the best rung again with wider and narrower priors.

  • It does a convergence check, draws the relative risk map (sci.area_map) and writes a report.

  • Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.

  • Find the card Disease map: which spatial model? and click Run on my data.
  • In 1. Your data, select scotland_lip_cancer in Dataset.
  • Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set Engine to nutpie. The default Bind fits the names of the export, so do not change it.
  • Click Run this recipe.

The recipe has no parameters that you must set, so the page does not show "2. What the recipe needs to know".

The app opens the monitor of the run. It has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. The recipe took 46 s in our test.

The Outputs tab shows the report of the run. It has the comparison table, the stacking weights, the effect of b1 with each prior width, the elpd_loo of each rung and the map of the best rung. The map of the recipe has no Observed smr panel.

We ran the recipe on the exported data with engine: nutpie and the other defaults:

Node Result compare The ranking is icar, bym2, iid. The best elpd_loo is −151.8 weights The stacking weight of icar is 1.00. The pseudo-BMA weights are 0.67 (icar) and 0.33 (bym2) best "Neighbours share risk (ICAR) has the best elpd_loo (-152) of 3 candidate(s)." effect b1 0.379, 94% interval 0.148 to 0.625 clear then: the chains agree and the range of b1 does not include zero effect_wide, effect_narrow b1 0.379 (0.139 to 0.627) and 0.366 (0.133 to 0.585) converged pass, R-hat 1.004

The recipe selects icar, not bym2. The notebook also found that the ICAR has the best elpd_loo (−151.9) and that the difference to BYM2 (0.8) is less than one standard error. The stacking weights put all the weight on one rung when the rungs are almost equal. Thus do not read the selection as "BYM2 is wrong". The notebook's decision to use BYM2 comes from its meaning, not from a difference in elpd. The b1 interval excludes zero with each prior width, so the association with AFF comes from the data, not from the priors.

Note

The default bind is {dims: {area: district, area_: district_}, vars: {covariate: aff}}. If your dataset has other names, change Bind in Fine-tune. For example, {"dims": {"area": "county", "area_": "county_"}, "vars": {"covariate": "smokers"}}.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) also applies to this model. Type sci.areal_bym2@^1 in Model. In Fine-tune, type the bind above in Bind and {} in Prior predictive: the ICAR prior cannot give prior draws, and with prior draws the fit stops. The audit adds a posterior predictive check, a prior sensitivity check and a recovery check on simulated data. Its prior sensitivity check changes only prior widths with names such as prior_sigma. The prior widths of sci.areal_bym2 have other names (intercept_sd, slope_sd and sigma_scale), so this check is skipped. Thus the ladder recipe above fits the model again with these widths itself. The recovery check simulates the counts from the posterior predictive of the model, so each simulated dataset has whole counts.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
# get the data and the suggested spec
uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out scotland_lip.nc --spec scotland_lip.yaml

# upload, check and fit on the platform (scotland-lip-cancer-bym2.yaml is the spec of step 4)
mapi use <tenant>/epidemiology
mapi datasets upload scotland_lip.nc --name scotland_lip_cancer
mapi check scotland-lip-cancer-bym2.yaml --remote @
mapi fit scotland-lip-cancer-bym2.yaml --remote @
mapi explore model scotland-lip-cancer-bym2 -s params -s diagnostics

# the risk of each district (step 7)
cat > lip-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://epidemiology/scotland-lip-cancer-bym2@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [rr, p_exceed]}
seed: 1987
EOF
mapi score lip-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o lip.zarr.zip

# the recipe (step 8)
mapi workflows init sci_spatial_ladder --name disease-map-ladder
mapi workflows apply disease-map-ladder.yaml
mapi workflows run disease-map-ladder \
    -i data=dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest \
    -p engine=nutpie --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs disease-map-ladder -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare    # the rungs, best first
mapi workflows node "$RUN" weights    # the stacking weights
mapi workflows node "$RUN" clear      # is the effect of AFF clear?

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()  # MAPI_URL, the `mapi login` sign-in (or MAPI_TOKEN) and MAPI_PROJECT

version = api.datasets.upload("scotland_lip.nc", dataset="scotland_lip_cancer")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("scotland-lip-cancer-bym2.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])

revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "scotland-lip-cancer-bym2")
mv = api.models.version(model.id, model.latest_version)
print(mv.ref, mv.metrics)

result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    mv.version,
    {
        "model": mv.ref,
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "expected",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "vars": ["rr", "p_exceed"],
        },
        "seed": 1987,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
p = summary["p_exceed"].sel(stat="mean")
print(int((p > 0.95).sum()), "districts with P(RR > 1) > 0.95")
print(summary["rr"].sel(stat="mean").to_series().nlargest(5))

workflow = api.workflows.create(template="sci_spatial_ladder")
wf_run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://epidemiology/scotland_lip_cancer@latest"},
    params={"engine": "nutpie"},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in wf_run.nodes}
print(nodes["compare"].result["ranking"])  # ['icar', 'bym2', 'iid']
print(nodes["effect"].result["params"]["b1"])

To compare with the notebook, load its printed posterior means with mapi_plugin_science.areal_data.challenges_reference().

The CLI and the client send the same spec and the same score request as the web app.

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the likelihood, the five priors of the district effects, the scaling factor, the island links and the maps of notebook sections 3 to 7. It leaves out these parts:

  • Other graphs (section 2). The export makes the queen graph only. In Python, areal_data.from_challenges(path, graph="rook") makes the rook graph, and graph="published" reads the hand-edited WinBUGS list. Write the result with write_export and upload it as a new dataset. This is "Try it yourself" item 2 of the notebook.
  • Moran's I checks (sections 2 and 4). The fit keeps Moran's I of the log SMR on the linked graph (learned["morans_i_log_smr"], 0.53). The notebook uses the mainland graph and gets 0.50. The platform does not calculate Moran's I of the residual effects.
  • The prior correlation against distance (section 3). Not in the platform.
  • The isolated islands (failure 1). islands: isolate with kind: icar gives the "quiet" failure of the notebook: the islands get no information from other districts. kind: bym2 with islands: error gives the "loud" failure as SCHEMA_INVALID, and islands: isolate gives SETTINGS_INVALID.
  • The unscaled BYM (failure 3). The platform has BYM2 only. It does not have separate priors on sigma_phi and sigma_theta.
  • The shrinkage plot (section 7). Not in the platform. Compare the observed and the mean panels of the area map, or compare the rr of an iid fit and a bym2 fit.
  • The 8-fold cross-validation (section 8). The platform holds out one block of 7 districts. To do more folds, fit the spec again with other values of split.seed.
  • Restricted spatial regression (section 9). Not in the platform. The notebook also does not recommend it.

Next steps:

  • Do "Try it yourself" item 3 of the notebook: put more prior weight on rho near 0, for example rho_alpha: 1 and rho_beta: 3. Do the data still move rho up?
  • Compare BYM2 with a GP on the district centres. See the E07 tutorial for a GP on a grid.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the ladder recipe.

docs.title: E19 protein signalling graphical model
docs.text:
This tutorial does the work of the pymc-challenges notebook E19_graphical_models.py in the web app. You use the model sci.graphical_model@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project biology. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the spec.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads two files from its data/ directory.
  • About 15 minutes. The fit takes about 1 minute of sandbox time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Sachs et al. (2005) measured the phosphorylation of 11 proteins and lipids in thousands of single T cells: Raf, Mek, PLCγ, PIP2, PIP3, Erk, Akt, PKA, PKC, p38 and Jnk. The notebook uses only the 853 cells with the plain CD3/CD28 stimulus. These cells got no inhibitor or activator, so they come from one system.

The notebook asks these questions:

  1. Which pairs of molecules are directly linked? Two molecules can have a correlation because one acts on the other, or because both follow a third molecule. A direct link is a partial correlation that is not zero: the correlation that stays when all the other molecules are held constant. (Notebook sections 2 and 3.)
  2. How sure are you of each link? A posterior partial correlation is continuous. Thus an edge needs a threshold. The notebook uses |partial correlation| > 0.1, and the edge probability is P(|ρ| > 0.1 | data). (Section 3.)
  3. When does a sparse prior help? With 100 cells instead of 853, the dense model is not sure of most pairs. (Sections 4 and 5.)
  4. How many of the 20 edges of the literature network do the data show? (Section 7.)

The notebook ends with these decisions:

  • With 853 cells, six edges are certain, and all six are in the consensus network. Two more pairs (p38–Jnk and PLC–PIP3) have a probability above 0.5. About 12 of the 20 consensus edges do not show as linear partial correlations in unperturbed cells.
  • With many cells, the dense model and the sparse model give the same graph. With few cells, the sparse (horseshoe) model gives a better decision. It declares few edges, and a larger experiment confirms almost all of them.
  • Do not pool the nine conditions of the experiment. Each inhibitor changes the system.
  • An undirected graph does not give the direction of a link. That is the subject of E20.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The partial correlation of each pair, with mean, sd and draws (Fields, output pcor) Section 2, the partial correlation matrix, and section 3, the posterior of ρ The edge probability P(|ρ| > 0.1) of each pair (Fields, output edge_prob) Section 3, the edge probabilities The graph of the links, next to the consensus network (net.graph) Section 7, "The graphs" The learned values edges, undecided_pairs and pcor_sd_mean The counts in sections 3 and 4 The neighbourhood model with the AND, OR or ρ rule (kind: neighbourhood) Section 5, model B A fit on 100 cells (a spec with a split) Section 4, the small experiment New simulated cells (Score, mode Simulate) Section 3, the posterior predictive check

See Differences from the notebook for the parts that the port leaves out.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads sachs2005.txt and sachs2005_consensus.txt. It keeps the 853 cells with only the CD3/CD28 stimulus. It reads the 20 directed edges of the consensus file as an undirected network. Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e19 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out sachs_cd3cd28.nc --spec sachs_cd3cd28.yaml

The command writes:

wrote sachs_cd3cd28.nc (variables level, consensus on cell=853, protein=11, protein_=11)
upload it as dataset biology/sachs_cd3cd28 and fit sci.graphical_model
wrote the suggested spec to sachs_cd3cd28.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning cell 853 integer, policy new_levels, strategy pooled The cells. The cells are exchangeable, so you can score new cells protein 11 categorical, policy fixed The molecules, raf to jnk protein_ 11 categorical, policy fixed The molecules again: the second molecule of a pair level cell, protein float64, target, units log_intensity The fluorescence intensity of the molecule in the cell, as log(x + 10) consensus protein, protein_ int64, constant The consensus network of Sachs et al.: 1 is an edge. It has 20 edges

The dataset has no missing values. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes 300 cells of 6 variables (g1 to g6) from a Gaussian graphical model with 4 known edges. The true network is in consensus. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the Sachs cells.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e19 --synthetic --out protein_network.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type sachs_cd3cd28 in Name. Type a description, for example "Flow cytometry of 853 T cells with the CD3/CD28 stimulus (Sachs et al. 2005)".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select sachs_cd3cd28.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Optional: click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows level on cell and protein, and consensus on protein and protein_.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, level has the role target, and consensus has the role constant.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Network.

  3. The network shows consensus, the graph of the 11 proteins from the literature, as a matrix and as a node-link graph.

  4. Correlations uses the 11 proteins as columns and the 853 cells as rows. Compare the strong correlations with the edges of the network.
  5. Group comparison and the time sections are in Not for this data. The cells are not groups, and the data has no time dim.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select sachs_cd3cd28. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type graphical in the search field. Under Models, select sci.graphical_model. The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name sachs-cd3cd28-ggm from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: sachs-cd3cd28-ggm, project: biology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest
  bind:
    dims: {var: protein, var_: protein_}
    vars: {value: level, reference: consensus}
  split: {kind: leave_group_out, dim: cell, n: 170, seed: 2005}
model:
  use: sci.graphical_model@^1
  settings: {kind: dense, threshold: 0.1, lkj_eta: 2.0, reference: true}
  fit:
    mode: evaluate_then_refit
    seed: 2005
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    engine: nutpie
    keep: {log_likelihood: true}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, crps, coverage_90, elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, net.graph, sci.field_map]

The model calls the variables var and var_, the target value and the known network reference. The bind block connects them to the names in the dataset. The results come back with the names of the dataset: protein, protein_ and level.

The split holds out 170 random cells (20%). evaluate_then_refit fits on the other 683 cells and scores the held-out cells. Then it fits again on all 853 cells, as the notebook does. The suggested spec of the export (sachs_cd3cd28.yaml) is the same spec without core.posterior_forest in the plots.

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind dense One multivariate normal over the 11 molecules, with an LKJ prior on the correlations. This is model A of the notebook. It also predicts and simulates new cells threshold 0.1 An edge is a pair with |partial correlation| > 0.1. A partial correlation of 0.1 explains 1% of the remaining variance. This is the δ of the notebook lkj_eta 2.0 The LKJ shape. A value above 1 prefers weaker correlations. The notebook uses 2 reference true The dataset has a known network (consensus). The fit keeps it, and net.graph draws it below the learned edges standardise true (default) The model centres and scales each molecule with the fit data. Partial correlations do not change with the scale sd_rate, mean_sd 1, 1 (default) The Exponential rate of the sd prior and the sd of the mean prior, on the standardised scale log_likelihood auto (default) joint for dense: the fit keeps log p(x) for each cell for elpd_loo expected_neighbours, slab_alpha, slab_beta, edge_rule 2, 2, 2, and (default) Only for kind: neighbourhood (section 6.6)

Settings that do not agree

Validate does a check of each setting by itself. It does not compare two settings, and it does not compare a setting with the split. Two examples show valid but stop the run:

  • kind: neighbourhood with log_likelihood: joint stops with SETTINGS_INVALID.
  • kind: neighbourhood with a split stops with MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED, because the neighbourhood model cannot score held-out cells.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://biology/sachs-cd3cd28-ggm@v1. Click it.

The run does two fits: one on the 683 training cells for the metrics of the held-out cells, and one on all 853 cells. On a laptop, the two fits with nutpie took about 40 seconds.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer, or the plot Sampler convergence on the Plots tab. In this fit, all 583 parameters look converged: the largest R-hat is 1.004, the smallest bulk effective sample size is about 2,700, and there are no divergent transitions. The notebook reports the same values.

The diagnostics also show one warning, PARETO_K_HIGH: one cell has a high Pareto k in elpd_loo. This cell is far from the other cells. The notebook finds the same problem: the measured values have long right tails, and the model is Gaussian.

The plot Posterior forest shows the raw parameters of the model: the standardised means mu and the elements of the Cholesky factor chol. These numbers are not easy to read. Use Fields for the partial correlations.

docs.title: 6.2 The partial correlations and the edge probabilities
docs.text:
Open Fields in the Model Explorer. The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Each grid has the 11 molecules as rows (protein) and as columns (protein_).

  1. In Output, select pcor. The cells show the partial correlation of each pair. The colour scale is diverging: one colour for positive values and another colour for negative values. The diagonal is 1.
  2. Select Mean in Statistic. Look for the cells far from zero.
  3. Select Std. dev.. In this fit, the sd of a partial correlation is about 0.03 everywhere (pcor_sd_mean is 0.033). With 853 cells, the data fix each value well.
  4. In Output, select edge_prob. Select Mean in Statistic. Each cell now shows the edge probability P(|ρ| > 0.1).
  5. Move the pointer over a cell to read its values.

The plot Field map on the Plots tab shows pcor as two panels (mean and sd).

In this fit, the pairs with the highest edge probabilities are:

Pair Edge probability Mean partial correlation In the consensus Erk–Akt 1.00 +0.85 yes Raf–Mek 1.00 +0.70 yes PKC–p38 1.00 +0.68 yes PIP2–PIP3 1.00 +0.37 yes PKC–Jnk 1.00 −0.28 yes Akt–PKA 1.00 +0.25 yes p38–Jnk 0.86 +0.14 no PLC–PIP3 0.61 +0.11 yes Mek–Jnk 0.33 −0.09 no Raf–Jnk 0.18 +0.07 no Mek–Erk 0.12 +0.06 yes

Read the table as the notebook does:

  • Six pairs are certain, and all six are consensus edges.
  • p38–Jnk is a real partial correlation (0.14) that the consensus does not have. Both molecules depend on PKC, in opposite directions. This masks the link in the marginal correlation.
  • Mek–Erk is the kinase step of the MAPK cascade. Its partial correlation is not zero, but it is smaller than the threshold. Thus its edge probability is only 0.12.

docs.title: 6.3 The graph
docs.text:
The plot Network of pcor (net.graph) has two panels:

  • Graph draws the 11 molecules and the 8 links with |pcor| > 0.1. Thicker lines are stronger links. Blue lines are positive and red lines are negative. Move the pointer to the middle of a link to see the share of draws above the threshold.
  • Matrix shows the mean partial correlation of every pair.

Dotted lines and open squares show the links of reference, that is the consensus network. Compare them with the learned links. Most of the consensus links from PKA and PKC have no learned link. These two kinases are hubs of the literature network. The experiment changed them in the other conditions. In unperturbed cells, their effects are weak or do not show.

Note

The graph uses the posterior mean of pcor, not the edge probability. For the decision, use edge_prob in Fields or the learned value edges.

docs.title: 6.4 The learned values and the held-out cells
docs.text:
The Overview tab shows the learned values of the fit:

Learned value This fit Meaning edges 8 The pairs with an edge probability above 0.5 undecided_pairs 2 The pairs with an edge probability between 0.2 and 0.8 pcor_sd_mean 0.033 The mean posterior sd of a partial correlation

The Metrics card of the Overview tab scores the 170 held-out cells (1,870 values):

Metric This fit rmse 0.524 crps 0.284 coverage_90 0.917 elpd_loo (all 853 cells) −5827.8

The coverage of the 90% intervals is near 0.9. The model gets the spread of each molecule right, but it does not get the shape: the measured values are more peaked and have longer tails than a Gaussian.

docs.title: 6.5 The numbers of the notebook and of this port
docs.text:
Quantity Notebook This port Pairs with P = 1.00 6, all in the consensus 6, the same pairs P(p38–Jnk) 0.86 0.86 P(PLC–PIP3) 0.60 0.61 P(Mek–Erk) 0.12 0.12 Edges with P > 0.5 8, 7 in the consensus 8, 7 in the consensus Undecided pairs (0.2 < P < 0.8) 2 2 Mean posterior sd of ρ 0.033 0.033 Largest R-hat, divergences 1.004, 0 1.004, 0 Average precision against the consensus 0.63 0.634 Neighbourhood model: undecided pairs 1 1 Neighbourhood model: divergences, largest R-hat 2, 1.012 1, 1.012 100 cells, dense: mean sd of ρ 0.094 0.095 100 cells, dense: undecided pairs 43 45

The 100-cell rows use a random set of 100 cells. The notebook and the port use different sets, so these numbers can be slightly different. Your numbers can also be slightly different if the sampler or its version is different.

docs.title: 6.6 Make the decisions
docs.text:
Use these outputs to make the decisions of the notebook:

  1. Which edges. Take the pairs with an edge probability above 0.5 (edges). With 853 cells, the graph has 8 edges: the six certain edges, p38–Jnk and PLC–PIP3.
  2. How sure. Look at undecided_pairs. With 853 cells, only 2 pairs are not sure. The threshold, not the data, decides these two pairs. To see the effect of the threshold, fit again with threshold: 0.05 and threshold: 0.2.

  3. Dense or sparse. Fit the neighbourhood model (model B of the notebook) with this spec. It has no split, because this model cannot score held-out cells:

    apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: sachs-cd3cd28-neighbourhood, project: biology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest
  bind:
    dims: {var: protein, var_: protein_}
    vars: {value: level, reference: consensus}
model:
  use: sci.graphical_model@^1
  settings: {kind: neighbourhood, threshold: 0.1, expected_neighbours: 2.0, edge_rule: and,
             reference: true}
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 2005
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    target_accept: 0.99
    engine: nutpie
    keep: {log_likelihood: true}
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, net.graph, sci.field_map]

    In this fit, the neighbourhood model finds 6 edges, all in the consensus: the six certain edges of the dense model (Akt–PKA has 0.92). p38–Jnk has 0.27 and PLC–PIP3 has 0.13. The sampler had 1 divergent transition and a largest R-hat of 1.012. The notebook reports 2 divergences and the same R-hat. With 853 cells, the two models agree on the strong edges. Do not compare the two elpd_loo values: they are not the same log-likelihood. To compare them, set log_likelihood: conditional on both specs.

  4. The small experiment. Fit the dense model on 100 cells. Change the split and the fit mode of the spec of step 4:

      split: {kind: leave_group_out, dim: cell, n: 753, seed: 2005}

    and mode: train_only. The fit then uses the 100 cells that the split keeps. In this fit, the mean sd of ρ goes from 0.033 to 0.095, and undecided_pairs goes from 2 to 45. The dense prior says "maybe" to almost every pair. This is the case where the notebook prefers the sparse model. 5. The consensus. Do not use the consensus network as the truth. It is a summary of the literature for the whole pathway, with links that show only when the experiment changes the pathway. About 12 of its 20 edges do not show in these cells, with any of the models.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
The fitted version uses all 853 cells. The dense model predicts and simulates cells. A score needs a dataset with the dims cell and protein. Send the dataset that you fitted.

Use the names of the model in Variables

Type the names of the model in Variables (optional): pcor, edge_prob and value. The result uses the names of the dataset: value comes back as level. If you type level, the score stops with REF_UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: 7.1 Predict: the graph and the mean of each molecule
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select sachs_cd3cd28.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 19. Type pcor, edge_prob in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score) is:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/sachs-cd3cd28-ggm@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["pcor", "edge_prob"]
  },
  "seed": 19
}

The result has pcor(protein, protein_) and edge_prob(protein, protein_), with the mean and the 90% interval. The mean of edge_prob is the edge probability of section 6.2. With no Variables, the result also has level(cell, protein): the mean of each molecule.

docs.title: 7.2 Simulate: new cells
docs.text:
simulate gives new cells from the model. Use them for a posterior predictive check, as in section 3 of the notebook.

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select sachs_cd3cd28.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive. Set Draws to 20.
  4. Type value in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/sachs-cd3cd28-ggm@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 20,
    "vars": ["value"]
  },
  "seed": 19
}

The result has level(cell, protein) with 20 draws. Each draw is a new set of 853 cells. Compare the histogram of each molecule with the data. Raf agrees well. PKA, Erk and Akt do not agree: the data are more peaked and have a longer right tail than any draw.

  • Evaluate needs a dataset with the measured values. Set Quantity to Predictive. With Expected, the 90% interval holds only the uncertainty of the mean, and coverage_90 is near 0.05.
  • A score of the neighbourhood model (section 6.6) returns only pcor and edge_prob. Simulate, Evaluate and Predictive stop with MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED.
  • The model has no forecast mode.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws. It fits the model with prior predictive draws. A convergence gate needs the largest R-hat below rhat_max (1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above min_ess (400). Only then does it make the posterior predictive check and run the governance checks sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Then it writes a report with the plots. The prior predictive shows the point of section 3 of the notebook: a mild LKJ prior on the correlations is a prior for a dense graph.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Bayesian workflow audit and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select sachs_cd3cd28 in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.graphical_model@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune. In Settings, type {"kind": "dense", "threshold": 0.1, "lkj_eta": 2.0, "reference": true}. In Bind, type {"dims": {"var": "protein", "var_": "protein_"}, "vars": {"value": "level", "reference": "consensus"}}.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Decisions shows the convergence gate and the value that it read. Outputs shows the plots and the report. The model version link opens the Model Explorer.

Give the recipe the binding

Without Bind, the recipe cannot bind the dims protein and protein_ to the dims var and var_ of the model, and the fit stops.

Note

The checks after the gate refit the model. sensitivity.prior fits it one time for each value in Prior scales (two by default), and recovery.simulated fits it N sims times (20 by default). Thus the audit takes much longer than one fit.

The recipe sci_network_ladder is for the latent-space network model of E21 (sci.network_latent_space). It does not apply to this model. The recipes sci_spatial_ladder, sci_phylo_signal, sci_calibrate_then_design and sci_image_model_check are for other science models.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/biology
mapi datasets upload sachs_cd3cd28.nc --name sachs_cd3cd28
mapi check sachs-cd3cd28-ggm.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit sachs-cd3cd28-ggm.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model sachs-cd3cd28-ggm -s params -s diagnostics

cat > new-cells.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://biology/sachs-cd3cd28-ggm@latest
mode: simulate
data: dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest
output: {kind: predictive, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 20, vars: [value]}
seed: 19
EOF
mapi score new-cells.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o new-cells.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init bayes_workflow_audit --name sachs-audit
mapi workflows apply sachs-audit.yaml -m "E19 audit"
mapi workflows run sachs-audit -i data=dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest \
  -p model=sci.graphical_model@^1 \
  -p 'settings={"kind": "dense", "threshold": 0.1, "lkj_eta": 2.0, "reference": true}' \
  -p 'bind={"dims": {"var": "protein", "var_": "protein_"}, "vars": {"value": "level", "reference": "consensus"}}' \
  --watch

sachs-cd3cd28-ggm.yaml is the spec of step 4. The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/biology")
version = api.datasets.upload("sachs_cd3cd28.nc", dataset="sachs_cd3cd28")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("sachs-cd3cd28-ggm.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "sachs-cd3cd28-ggm")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://biology/sachs-cd3cd28-ggm@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "expected",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "vars": ["pcor", "edge_prob"],
        },
        "seed": 19,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
prob = summary["edge_prob"].sel(stat="mean").to_pandas()
pcor = summary["pcor"].sel(stat="mean").to_pandas()
names = list(prob.index)
for i, a in enumerate(names):
    for b in names[i + 1 :]:
        if prob.loc[a, b] > 0.5:
            print(f"{a}-{b}: P={prob.loc[a, b]:.2f} pcor={pcor.loc[a, b]:+.2f}")

To run the audit recipe:

workflow = api.workflows.create(template="bayes_workflow_audit")
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://biology/sachs_cd3cd28@latest"},
    params={
        "model": "sci.graphical_model@^1",
        "settings": {"kind": "dense", "threshold": 0.1, "lkj_eta": 2.0, "reference": True},
        "bind": {"dims": {"var": "protein", "var_": "protein_"},
                 "vars": {"value": "level", "reference": "consensus"}},
    },
    wait=True,
)

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the dense model A (section 3), the neighbourhood model B with the AND, OR and ρ rules (section 5), and the edge probabilities with a stated threshold. It leaves out these parts:

  • The marginal correlations (section 2). The model gives only the partial correlations. Calculate the marginal correlations from the dataset in Python.
  • The naive horseshoe on the precision matrix (section 4). The notebook shows that this model is broken: most of its prior is not positive definite. The port does not include it.
  • The graphical lasso (section 6). The port has no frequentist reference model.
  • The precision-recall curves and the replicate study (section 7). The web app does not calculate the average precision. Calculate it from edge_prob and consensus in Python. The study on eight sets of 100 cells needs eight datasets or eight splits.
  • The pooled conditions (section 8). The export keeps only the CD3/CD28 cells. To get all 7,466 cells, use from_challenges(path, observational=False) from mapi_plugin_science.ggm_data in Python. Do not fit the model to them: each condition is a different system.
  • The direction of the links. An undirected graph cannot give it. See E20 in the notebooks.
  • The Student-t likelihood and the Cholesky parametrisation ("Try it yourself"). The port has only the Gaussian likelihood.

Next steps:

  • Fit the neighbourhood model with edge_rule: or and edge_rule: rho, and compare the edges.
  • Fit the dense model on 100 cells, then the neighbourhood model on the same 100 cells. Export the 100 cells as a separate dataset for the neighbourhood model, because it takes no split.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the audit recipe.

docs.title: E21 law-firm network latent space
docs.text:
This tutorial does the work of the pymc-challenges notebook E21_network_models.py in the web app. You use the model sci.network_latent_space@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project sociology. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the spec.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads two files from its data/ directory.
  • About 20 minutes. Each fit takes less than one minute of sampler time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
From 1988 to 1991, the sociologist Emmanuel Lazega studied a corporate law firm in New England. The firm had 71 lawyers (36 partners and 35 associates) in three offices: Boston, Hartford and Providence. Each lawyer marked the colleagues that they worked with in the last year. The network has a tie between two lawyers when they worked together. It has 378 ties in 2,485 pairs.

A pair of lawyers is a dyad. A logistic regression with one row for each dyad treats the 2,485 dyads as independent. They are not independent: each lawyer is in 70 dyads. A busy partner increases the tie probability of all 70 pairs. Two coworkers of one lawyer also work together much more often than two random lawyers.

The notebook asks these questions:

  1. Do shared traits explain the ties? Same office, same practice, same status, same gender, same law school and the gap in years with the firm. (Notebook section 2, models a0 and a.)
  2. What does a regression of independent dyads get wrong? (Section 2, model b with a sociality effect for each lawyer.)
  3. Who works with whom, after the traits? A latent space gives each lawyer a position on a hidden map. (Section 3, model c, and the Procrustes alignment.)
  4. Does the model make networks like the real one? (Section 5, the posterior predictive checks of the whole graph.)
  5. Which model predicts the ties best? (Section 6, leave-one-dyad-out LOO.)

The notebook ends with this decision. Most of the network comes from homophily on office and practice and from the different activity of each lawyer (sociality). The latent space adds almost nothing to the prediction when the model has the traits and the sociality. Use the sociality model to measure the effects of the traits. Use the latent space to find structure that the traits do not show, and as a check that nothing large is missing.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The effect of each shared trait, sigma_s and sigma_z (Parameters, core.posterior_forest) Section 2, the table of the homophily effects, and section 3 The tie probability of each pair, with mean, sd and draws (Fields, sci.field_map) Section 3, the tie probabilities of model c The network on the latent map, coloured by office, with the observed ties (net.graph) Section 3, the latent map Convergence on the aligned positions (Diagnostics, core.convergence) Section 3, the r_hat before and after Procrustes elpd_loo of each kind (Metrics, and the recipe sci_network_ladder) Section 6, the LOO table Simulated networks and their statistics (Score, mode Simulate, graph_stat) Section 5, the table of the graph statistics

See Differences from the notebook for the parts that the port leaves out. The block models of section 4 are one of them.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads lazega_cowork.txt (the 71 × 71 table of ties) and lazega_attributes.txt (the traits of each lawyer). It makes the six pair covariates of the notebook. Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e21 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out lazega_coworkers.nc --spec lazega_coworkers.yaml

The command writes:

wrote lazega_coworkers.nc (variables cowork, homophily, office on lawyer=71, lawyer_=71, covariate=6)
upload it as dataset sociology/lazega_coworkers and fit sci.network_latent_space
wrote the suggested spec to lazega_coworkers.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning lawyer 71 integer, policy fixed The lawyers, 1 to 71. Lawyers 1 to 36 are partners lawyer_ 71 integer, policy fixed The second lawyer of a pair, with the same labels covariate 6 categorical, policy fixed same_office, same_practice, same_status, same_gender, same_school, years_gap cowork lawyer, lawyer_ float64, target, missing values allowed 1 when the two lawyers worked together, else 0. The table is symmetric, and the diagonal is 0 homophily lawyer, lawyer_, covariate float64, covariate 1 when the two lawyers share the trait, else 0. years_gap is the gap in years with the firm ÷ 10 office lawyer int64, constant The office: 1 Boston (48 lawyers), 2 Hartford (19), 3 Providence (4)

The dataset has no missing ties. The degree (the number of coworkers) of a lawyer is from 0 to 28. Lawyer 8 has no tie. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes a network that the model's own process simulates: 30 nodes in three offices, with three covariates (same_office, same_practice and years_gap) and known parameters. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the law firm.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e21 --synthetic --out coworkers_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type lazega_coworkers in Name. Type a description, for example "Coworker ties of the 71 lawyers of the Lazega law firm".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select lazega_coworkers.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Optional: click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows cowork on lawyer and lawyer_, homophily on three dims, and office on lawyer.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, cowork has the role target, homophily has the role covariate and office has the role constant.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Network.

  3. The first entry shows cowork, the ties between the 71 lawyers. The matrix puts similar lawyers next to each other. The node-link graph gives each office a colour.

  4. The table of homophily gives the fraction of ties in the same office, and the fraction that you expect by chance. A much larger fraction shows that the office explains many ties.
  5. The second entry shows homophily: one matrix for each of the 6 covariates (same_office, same_practice and the other covariates).
  6. Group comparison and the time sections are in Not for this data.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select lazega_coworkers. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type network in the search field. Under Models, select Who works with whom in a network (sci.network_latent_space@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name lazega-coworkers-latent-space from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: lazega-coworkers-latent-space, project: sociology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest
  bind:
    dims: {node: lawyer, node_: lawyer_, cov: covariate}
    vars: {tie: cowork, dyad_cov: homophily, node_group: office}
model:
  use: sci.network_latent_space@^1
  settings: {kind: latent_space, covariates: true, node_groups: true, latent_dims: 2}
  fit: {mode: train_only, seed: 1991, tune: 2000, draws: 1000, chains: 4,
        target_accept: 0.95, engine: nutpie}
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, net.graph, sci.field_map]

The model calls the nodes node and node_, the covariate dim cov, the target tie, the pair covariates dyad_cov and the group code node_group. The bind block connects them to the names in the dataset.

The spec has no split. The fit uses all 2,485 dyads, as the notebook does in sections 2 to 5. elpd_loo is leave-one-dyad-out: the model keeps the log-likelihood of each dyad. The suggested spec of the export (lazega_coworkers.yaml) is the same spec with tune: 1000 and without target_accept.

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind latent_space The log odds of a tie add the pair covariates, a sociality effect for each lawyer (s_i + s_j) and minus the distance between the two positions on the hidden map. This is model c of the notebook. sociality is model b, and covariates is model a covariates true Use the six shared traits in homophily. With false, the model has no traits. kind: covariates with covariates: false is the Erdős-Rényi graph (model a0). kind: latent_space with covariates: false is model c0 node_groups true The dataset has office. The plots colour the lawyers by office latent_dims 2 (default) The dimensions of the hidden map. The notebook uses 2 alpha_mu, alpha_sigma -2, 2 (default) The normal prior of the intercept. It puts the density between about 1% and 50% beta_sigma 1 (default) The prior sd of each trait effect. A shared trait can multiply the odds by up to about 7, or divide them by 7 sociality_scale 1 (default) The half-normal scale of sigma_s, the sd of the sociality effects latent_scale 2 (default) The half-normal scale of sigma_z, the spread of the positions on the map procrustes_iters 10 (default) The passes of the Procrustes alignment after the fit

The fit block uses tune: 2000 and target_accept: 0.95. The scale sigma_z of the hidden map mixes slowly when the model has the covariates. The notebook also reports this. More warm-up steps and smaller steps make the fit more stable. They do not remove the problem.

Why the positions converge

The distances do not change when the map turns, flips or moves. Thus the raw positions z_raw of the sampler do not converge, but each distance converges. After the fit, the model turns each draw onto one reference map (Procrustes analysis). The posterior keeps only the aligned position. The convergence check then uses only quantities that the data identify.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://sociology/lazega-coworkers-latent-space@v1. Click it.

In our test, the fit took about 40 s with nutpie. After the fit, the run aligns the positions, calculates the tie probability of each pair for each draw, the plots and the explorer views.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer, or the plot Sampler convergence on the Plots tab. In our fit, 3 of the 2,000 checked parameters do not pass: sigma_z, alpha and one coordinate of one position. The largest R-hat is 1.015 (sigma_z), and the bulk ESS of sigma_z is about 140. There are no divergent transitions. The trait effects have R-hat below 1.003 and an ESS of more than 1,800.

This agrees with the notebook. sigma_z is wide and mixes slowly when the traits are in the model, because what is left for the map is a weak signal. Trust the trait effects and the tie probabilities. Do not report sigma_z to two digits.

Use more draws if the warning is larger

If R-hat of sigma_z is more than 1.05, set draws: 2000 and fit again. The sampler is random, so a second fit can show a larger warning than ours. With tune: 1000, one of our fits had R-hat 1.08 and 4 divergent transitions.

docs.title: 6.2 Do shared traits explain the ties?
docs.text:
Open Parameters in the Model Explorer, or the plot Posterior forest on the Plots tab. Each trait has one row beta[<trait>]. A positive value makes a tie more probable. In our fit, the posterior means and the 94% HDIs are:

Effect Mean 94% HDI beta[same_office] 2.55 2.22 to 2.89 beta[same_practice] 2.08 1.82 to 2.39 beta[same_status] -0.60 -0.92 to -0.30 beta[same_gender] 0.39 0.10 to 0.73 beta[same_school] 0.33 0.08 to 0.58 beta[years_gap] 0.21 -0.01 to 0.42 sigma_s 0.90 sigma_z 0.92

Read the table as the notebook does:

  • Two lawyers in the same office have about e^2.5 ≈ 13 times the odds of a tie. The same practice multiplies the odds by about 8.
  • Two partners, or two associates, work together less often than a partner and an associate. The firm works in teams of partners and associates.
  • sigma_s ≈ 0.9: a lawyer one sd above the average has about e^0.9 ≈ 2.5 times the odds of a tie with anyone.

The rows sociality[<lawyer>] give the activity of each lawyer after the traits. In our fit, lawyer 15 has the highest sociality (2.1) and lawyer 8, who has no tie, has the lowest (-1.9). Lawyer 22 has the most ties (28), but a lower sociality (1.3), because the traits explain part of these ties.

docs.title: 6.3 The tie probability of each pair
docs.text:
Open Fields in the Model Explorer. The model has 1 output on a grid: tie_prob, the probability of a tie between two lawyers. The rows are lawyer and the columns are lawyer_. The diagonal is 0.

  1. Select Mean in Statistic. A bright cell is a pair that probably works together.
  2. Select Std. dev. to see where you are not sure of the probability.
  3. Select Draws and click Play the draws to see possible tables that agree with the data.
  4. Move the pointer over a cell to read its values. For example, the pair of lawyers 15 and 28 has a mean of about 0.66, and the pair of lawyers 1 and 8 has 0.02.
