The lawyers are in the order of their numbers, so partners (1 to 36) are at the top and the left. Blocks of bright cells show the offices and the practices. The plot Field map of tie_prob on the Plots tab shows the same output as two panels (mean and sd).

docs.title: 6.4 The latent map
docs.text:
Open the plot Network of tie_prob (net.graph) on the Plots tab.

  • The node positions are the posterior mean of position, the aligned map.
  • The colour of a node is its office.
  • A solid line is a pair with a mean tie_prob above 0.5. In our fit, 190 pairs pass. Thicker lines are more probable ties. Point at the middle of a line to see the share of the draws above 0.5.
  • Dotted lines show the observed ties (378), for comparison.
  • The matrix panel shows each pair. Lawyers that link to each other are next to each other.

In this model, the map shows only what the traits do not explain. Thus the offices and the practices are mixed on the map: the centres of the six groups (office × practice) are all within 0.4 of the middle. The direction of the map has no meaning: it is the direction of the Procrustes reference.

To see what the map finds without the traits (notebook model c0), fit the spec again with covariates: false. Then the plot shows these features, as in the notebook:

  • The four groups of Boston and Hartford (litigation and corporate in each office) are in four different areas of the map.
  • The 3 Providence corporate lawyers are near the Boston corporate lawyers.
  • sigma_z is about 2.3, not 0.9.

The model c0 was told nothing about the offices, but it finds them. Most of what the map finds alone is office and practice.

docs.title: 6.5 What a regression of independent dyads gets wrong
docs.text:
Fit the spec two more times to get models a and b of the notebook:

  1. In Build, open the spec lazega-coworkers-latent-space.
  2. Change kind: latent_space to kind: sociality.
  3. Click Validate, then Save revision, then Fit.
  4. Do steps 2 and 3 again with kind: covariates.

Each fit makes a new version of the model. Compare the trait effects in Parameters:

Effect covariates (model a) sociality (model b) beta[same_office] 1.61 (89%: 1.39 to 1.84) 2.44 (89%: 2.14 to 2.74) beta[same_practice] 1.59 (89%: 1.38 to 1.81) 2.01 (89%: 1.76 to 2.26) beta[same_status] -0.50 -0.54

The intervals of the office effect do not overlap. Model a is wrong with confidence, in two ways:

  • Attenuation. A logistic model without the sociality effects moves the effects toward zero. The busy partners, who work with everyone, make the contrast between the offices smaller.
  • Pseudo-replication. Model a thinks that it has 2,485 independent observations. Its intervals are too narrow.

docs.title: 6.6 Which model predicts the ties best?
docs.text:
The Metrics card of the Overview tab shows elpd_loo of each version. A larger value is better. The recipe of step 8 makes the same comparison in one run.

Model Notebook This port a0, Erdős-Rényi (kind: covariates, covariates: false) -1060.5 -1060.5 a, covariates (kind: covariates) -894.2 -894.3 b, sociality (kind: sociality) -763.4 -763.7 c0, latent space without covariates (kind: latent_space, covariates: false) -795.7 -796.2 c, latent space (kind: latent_space) -761.6 -761.0

The fit of c0 shows the warning PARETO_K_HIGH: for 7 dyads, the LOO estimate is not reliable. The notebook also finds such dyads for c0.

The difference between c and b is about 2.7, and its standard error is about 2.6. (We calculated the standard error with ArviZ az.compare on the two fits. The web app does not show it.) A difference of about one standard error is not a real difference: the two models are equal. Both models are far better than model a, which has no sociality.

docs.title: 6.7 The numbers of the notebook and of this port
docs.text:
Quantity (model c) Notebook This port beta[same_office] 2.54 2.55 beta[same_practice] 2.08 2.08 beta[same_status] -0.59 -0.60 beta[same_gender] 0.38 0.39 beta[same_school] 0.33 0.33 beta[years_gap] 0.21 0.21 sigma_s 0.90 0.90 sigma_z 0.88 0.92 (sd 0.29) elpd_loo -761.6 -761.0

Your numbers can be slightly different if the sampler or its version is different. sigma_z changes most from one fit to the next.

docs.title: 6.8 Make the decision
docs.text:
Use these outputs to make the decisions of the notebook:

  1. Do not use a regression of independent dyads. Compare the trait effects of covariates and sociality (section 6.5). If they are different, the sociality is necessary.
  2. Choose the model for the trait effects. Compare elpd_loo (section 6.6). If the latent space is better by less than two standard errors, use the simpler sociality model to report the effects. For the law firm, the two models give the same effects to two digits.
  3. Use the latent space to find structure. Fit latent_space with covariates: false and look at the map in Network of tie_prob. If the map shows groups that you know (the offices, the practices), the traits that you have capture the structure. A group that no trait explains is a reason to look for a new trait.
  4. Do a check of the whole graph. Simulate networks (step 7.2) and compare their statistics with the real network. A statistic far outside the simulations shows what the model does not make.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text: A score needs a dataset with the dims lawyer and lawyer_, and homophily for each pair. Send the dataset that you fitted. The node set is fixed: a lawyer that the fit did not see stops the score with UNSEEN_LEVELS.

docs.title: 7.1 Predict: the tie probabilities and the degrees
docs.text:
1. On the model version page of lazega-coworkers-latent-space, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select lazega_coworkers.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 21. Type tie_prob, degree, sociality in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score) is:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://sociology/lazega-coworkers-latent-space@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["tie_prob", "degree", "sociality"]
  },
  "seed": 21
}

The result has tie_prob(lawyer, lawyer_), degree(lawyer) (the expected number of coworkers) and sociality(lawyer). In our fit, half of the sum of the expected degrees is 378.5. The network has 378 ties. Lawyer 22 has the largest expected degree (26.3).

To score a part of the firm, send a dataset with fewer lawyers. degree then counts only the ties inside that part.

docs.title: 7.2 Simulate: networks for a check of the whole graph
docs.text:
1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select lazega_coworkers.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive. Set Draws to 500.
  4. Type graph_stat, degree in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://sociology/lazega-coworkers-latent-space@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 500,
    "vars": ["graph_stat", "degree"]
  },
  "seed": 21
}

Each draw is one simulated network of the 71 lawyers. graph_stat(statistic) gives nine statistics of each network. Compare them with the real network:

Statistic Real network Simulated, mean Simulated, 90% HDI density 0.152 0.152 0.138 to 0.165 sd_degree 5.74 5.93 5.25 to 6.66 max_degree 28 29.4 24 to 34 isolates 1 0.32 0 to 1 triangles 493 485 364 to 608 transitivity 0.307 0.294 0.261 to 0.325 esp0 12 23.5 12 to 33 mean_geodesic 2.10 2.11 2.04 to 2.19 unreachable 0.028 0.009 0 to 0.028

The web app does not calculate the statistics of the real network. The values in the second column are from the notebook's functions.

  • The model makes the spread of the degrees and the transitivity of the real network.
  • esp0 is the number of ties whose two lawyers have no coworker in common. The real network has 12. In our simulations, 97% of the networks have 12 or more. As in the notebook, the real collaboration is more closed than the model makes.
  • The real network has one isolate (lawyer 8). The simulations have fewer.

Send all the lawyers for graph_stat

Send a dataset with all 71 lawyers in lawyer and lawyer_, and use Simulate or Predictive. Otherwise the score stops with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. A statistic of the whole graph needs the whole graph.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8.1 The network ladder
docs.text:
The recipe sci_network_ladder ("Network ties: which model?") does sections 2, 3, 5 and 6 of the notebook in one run:

  1. It fits the three kinds covariates, sociality and latent_space on the same dyads.
  2. It ranks them by elpd_loo (node compare) and calculates their stacking weights (node weights).
  3. It keeps the model with the best elpd_loo (node best).
  4. It shows alpha and the trait effects of that model (node effects).
  5. It draws the network with net.graph (node graph).
  6. It simulates networks from that model (node simulate) and plots the spread of their density and transitivity with core.ridge (node ppc).
  7. It writes a report.

The defaults of the recipe fit the dataset of the e21 export. You do not change the binding.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Network ties: which model? and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select lazega_coworkers in Dataset.
  4. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set Engine to nutpie. Set Tune to 2000 and Target accept to 0.95, as in step 4.
  5. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs has the comparison table, the stacking weights, the effects, the network plot, the plot of the simulated statistics and the report.

What to look for:

  • The comparison table ranks latent_space first, sociality second and covariates last.
  • The stacking weights put most of the weight on latent_space. In our fits with ArviZ, the weights are about 0.91, 0.08 and 0.01.
  • best selects latent_space, because it has the largest elpd_loo.

The best rung is not always the model to report

select.best uses only the value of elpd_loo. It does not use the standard error of the difference. For the law firm, the difference between latent_space and sociality is about one standard error (section 6.6). Read the table before you report the effects of best. The notebook reports the sociality model.

Note

The recipe fits the model three times and simulates 500 networks. With nutpie, the run takes a few minutes. With the default engine pymc, it takes longer.

docs.title: 8.2 Other recipes
docs.text:
• bayes_workflow_audit ("Bayesian workflow audit") does the checks of a Bayesian workflow on one model. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.network_latent_space@^1 in Model. In Fine-tune, type {"kind": "sociality", "node_groups": true} in Settings and the bind of step 4 as JSON in Bind. The recovery check simulates each graph from the posterior predictive of the model, so each tie is 0 or 1. It fits the model many times, so it takes longer.
  • sci_spatial_ladder, sci_phylo_signal, sci_calibrate_then_design and sci_image_model_check are for other science models. They do not apply to this model.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/sociology
mapi datasets upload lazega_coworkers.nc --name lazega_coworkers
mapi check lazega-coworkers-latent-space.yaml --remote @   # the server's static validation
mapi fit lazega-coworkers-latent-space.yaml --remote @     # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model lazega-coworkers-latent-space -s params -s diagnostics

cat > simulate-networks.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://sociology/lazega-coworkers-latent-space@latest
mode: simulate
data: dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest
output: {kind: predictive, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 500, vars: [graph_stat, degree]}
seed: 21
EOF
mapi score simulate-networks.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 \
  -o simulate-networks.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_network_ladder --name coworker-ladder   # writes coworker-ladder.yaml
mapi workflows apply coworker-ladder.yaml
mapi workflows run coworker-ladder \
  -i data=dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest \
  -p engine=nutpie -p tune=2000 -p target_accept=0.95 --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs coworker-ladder -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare    # the kinds, best first
mapi workflows node "$RUN" effects    # alpha and beta[...] of the best kind
mapi workflows output "$RUN" simulate scores --out graph_stats.zarr.zip

lazega-coworkers-latent-space.yaml is the spec of step 4. The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/sociology")
version = api.datasets.upload("lazega_coworkers.nc", dataset="lazega_coworkers")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("lazega-coworkers-latent-space.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "lazega-coworkers-latent-space")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://sociology/lazega-coworkers-latent-space@latest",
        "mode": "simulate",
        "data": "dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "predictive",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "draws": 500,
            "vars": ["graph_stat"],
        },
        "seed": 21,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["graph_stat"].sel(stat="mean").to_series())

workflow = api.workflows.create(template="sci_network_ladder")
ladder = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://sociology/lazega_coworkers@latest"},
    params={"engine": "nutpie", "tune": 2000, "target_accept": 0.95},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in ladder.nodes}
print(nodes["best"].result["reason_plain"])
print(nodes["effects"].result["params"]["beta[same_office]"])

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the models a0, a, b, c and c0 of sections 2 and 3 and the Procrustes alignment. It also keeps the latent map, the graph checks of section 5 and the leave-one-dyad-out LOO of section 6. It leaves out these parts:

  • The block models (section 4). The port has no stochastic block model and no mixed-membership block model. Thus it does not give the probability that two lawyers are in the same block.
  • The held-out split with AUC (section 6). The port has no AUC metric and no ROC curve. A mask_block split over [node, node_] holds out random cells, and a dyad is out of the fit when one of its two cells is out. The metrics of such a split count the diagonal cells, so use elpd_loo to compare the kinds.
  • The figures of the raw positions (section 3). The port aligns the positions after each fit. It does not show the turn of the map within a chain, or the r_hat of the raw positions.
  • The details of the latent map. net.graph shows the mean positions coloured by office. It does not draw a 50% ellipse for each lawyer or a marker for the practice. Calculate them from the draws of position.
  • The full histograms (section 5). graph_stat gives esp0 and mean_geodesic, not the full distributions of the shared partners and of the geodesics.
  • The statistics of the real network. The web app does not calculate them. Use graph_stats from mapi_plugin_science.network on cowork in Python.
  • Directed ties ("Try it yourself", friendship). The model accepts only a symmetric table.

Next steps:

  • Fit latent_space with covariates: false and compare its map with the offices and the practices.
  • Fit latent_dims: 3 and compare elpd_loo.
  • Read the workflow cookbook to change the network ladder.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.

docs.title: E23 primate phylogenetic regression
docs.text:
This tutorial does the work of the pymc-challenges notebook E23_phylogenetic_regression.py in the web app. You use the model sci.phylo_regression@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project biology. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the spec.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads two files from its data/ directory.
  • About 20 minutes. One fit samples for about 10 seconds on a laptop. The run takes longer because the sandbox must start and load the dataset.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Do primates that live in larger groups have larger brains for their body size? This is the "social brain" hypothesis. The usual test is a regression across species: log brain volume on log body mass and log group size.

That test is not correct, because species are not independent data points. Related species share most of their history. If a large brain and a large group came once in a common ancestor, the regression counts that one event once for each descendant species. The notebook puts the shared history into the model. The residuals of two species are correlated by the length of the branches that they share on the phylogeny.

The notebook asks these questions:

  1. Are the species independent? (Notebook sections 3 and 4.)
  2. Does the slope of group size stay clear of zero when the model includes the tree? (Sections 4 to 6.)
  3. Which model of trait evolution agrees best with the data: no tree, Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck? (Sections 5 and 7.)

The notebook ends with these decisions:

  • Do not use the i.i.d. regression. Its slope of group size (0.12) comes from some deep splits of the tree that it counts once for each species.
  • Use Pagel's lambda. It has the best leave-one-out score, and lambda is about 0.95.
  • The data do not show a clear effect of group size. With the tree, the slope is about 0.03 and its interval touches zero.
  • Brownian motion and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck agree with the data equally well. Report the Brownian rate, not the half-life of the pull to an optimum.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The tree and the brain volume of each species, observed and predicted from its relatives (sci.phylogeny) Section 2, the tree next to the traits The slopes, sigma and lam (Parameters, core.posterior_forest) Sections 3, 4 and 6, the summaries and the slope plot elpd_loo from the leave-one-out density of each species given the others (Metrics card) Section 7, the conditional LOO The four kinds fitted and compared in one run (recipe sci_phylo_signal) Sections 3 to 7 A prediction of the brain volume of 35 species without a value, from their relatives (Score) Section 9 (a different gap, see section 10)

See Differences from the notebook for the parts that the port leaves out.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads the trait table primates301.csv and the tree primates301_tree.rda. The tree is an R object (ape::phylo). The command reads it without R. It keeps the 186 species that have a body mass and a group size. It prunes the tree to these species. Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e23 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out primates301.nc --spec primates301.yaml

The command writes:

wrote primates301.nc (variables parent, branch_length, is_tip, tip_label, brain, body, group_size on node=452, species=186)
upload it as dataset biology/primates301 and fit sci.phylo_regression
wrote the suggested spec to primates301.yaml

The file holds one dataset with two dims. The traits are on species. The tree is on node:

Name Dims Type Meaning species 186 categorical, policy fixed The species, for example Allenopithecus_nigroviridis. Each label is a tip label of the tree node 452 integer, policy fixed Each node of the tree: 186 tips and 266 internal nodes brain species float64, target, unit cc, missing values allowed The brain volume. 151 species have a value. 35 species have no value body species float64, covariate, unit g The body mass group_size species float64, covariate The mean size of the social group parent node int64, constant The position of the parent node on node. The root has -1 branch_length node float64, constant, unit Myr The length of the branch above the node, in millions of years is_tip node bool, constant True for a tip (a species) tip_label node str, constant The species label of each tip. Internal nodes have an empty label

The 151 species with a brain volume are the complete cases of the notebook (sections 3 to 8). The tree is ultrametric: each tip is 73.0 million years from the root. The pruned tree keeps the nodes with one child, so the shared branch lengths do not change. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes 40 species on a random tree, with traits from the model's own process and known parameters. 4 species have no brain volume. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the primates.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e23 --synthetic --out primates_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type primates301 in Name. Type a description, for example "Brain, body mass and group size of 186 primates, with the 10kTrees phylogeny".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select primates301.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Optional: click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows three variables on species and four variables on node.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, brain has the role target, and the four tree variables have the role constant. Missingness shows the 35 species without a brain volume. The model accepts them. It does not use them in the likelihood, and it predicts their brain volume from their relatives.

The tree is part of the same plain dataset, on the dim node. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Tree.

  3. The tree has 452 nodes and 186 tips. The strips next to the tips show brain, body and group_size for each species. The explorer matches the tips to the species by label.

  4. The table of the phylogenetic signal gives Moran's I of each trait on the tree. A small p-value shows that near species have similar traits. This is the question of step 6.2.
  5. Correlations uses the three traits of the 186 species. The variables of the tree (parent, branch_length, is_tip and tip_label) are geometry. They are not in the statistics.
  6. The section Tree shows the tree in the data. It is not the same as a tree dataset (HDF5 groups).

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select primates301. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type phylo in the search field. Under Models, select Traits of related species (sci.phylo_regression@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name primate-social-brain from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: primate-social-brain, project: biology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://biology/primates301@latest
  bind:
    vars: {trait: brain}
model:
  use: sci.phylo_regression@^1
  settings: {kind: lambda, predictors: [body, group_size]}
  fit: {mode: train_only, seed: 2017, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, engine: nutpie}
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.phylogeny]

The model calls its target trait. The bind block connects it to brain. The predictors, the tree variables and the dims have the same names in the model and in the dataset.

The spec has no split. The notebook compares the models with leave-one-out, and the model calculates the leave-one-out density of each species itself. Thus mode: train_only fits once on all species. The suggested spec of the export (primates301.yaml) is the same spec without mode: train_only. Without it, Validate shows a warning, because the default mode evaluate_then_refit needs a split.

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind lambda Pagel's lambda: the residual is a tree part plus a part for each species. iid ignores the tree, brownian uses only the tree, and ou is Ornstein-Uhlenbeck on the distance through the tree predictors [body, group_size] The variables on species that explain the brain volume. These are the names in the dataset log_target, log_predictors true, true (default) The model uses log brain, log body mass and log group size, as the notebook does standardise true (default) The model centres and scales each variable on the 151 species with a brain volume. A slope is then in sd of log brain for each sd of the predictor, as in the notebook intercept_sd, slope_sd 1, 0.5 (default) The normal priors of the notebook sigma_rate 1 (default) The exponential prior of sigma of the notebook lambda_alpha, lambda_beta 1, 1 (default) A flat Beta prior on lam ou_parameterisation rate (default) Only for ou: the prior is on the Brownian rate eta2 rho, the fix of notebook section 5 rate_sd, rho_sd, eta2_sd 1, 5, 5 (default) Only for ou: the half-normal priors of the notebook jitter 1e-6 (default) Only for ou: a small value on the diagonal of the covariance

The fit block has the sampler settings of the notebook: nutpie, 4 chains of 1000 draws and the seed 2017.

The other three kinds

To compare the kinds as the notebook does, save three more specs. Change kind and the name, for example kind: iid with the name primate-brain-iid. For kind: ou, also add target_accept: 0.95 to the fit block, as the notebook does. The recipe of step 8 fits all four kinds in one run.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://biology/primate-social-brain@v1. Click it.

After the sampler, the run calculates two items for each draw. These are the prediction of each species from its relatives and the leave-one-out density of each species with a brain volume. Then it makes the plots and the explorer views.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer. Use the sections Parameters and Diagnostics. The model has no output on a grid and no time dim, so Fields and the time sections do not apply to it.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text: Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer, or the plot Sampler convergence on the Plots tab. In this fit, the largest R-hat is 1.003, the smallest bulk ESS is 1,849, the smallest tail ESS is 2,347, and there are no divergences. The fit is good.

docs.title: 6.2 Are the species independent?
docs.text:
Parameters (or the plot Posterior forest) shows intercept, slope for body and group_size, sigma and lam. In this fit:

Parameter Mean sd slope[body] 0.767 0.031 slope[group_size] 0.027 0.020 lam 0.954 0.018 sigma 0.276 0.022 intercept -0.116 0.119

lam near 1 shows that the residual of brain size is almost all phylogenetic. It is not 1, so a small part of each species is its own. If the species were independent, lam would be near 0. The interval of slope[group_size] includes zero.

The intercept is now the expected log brain size at the root of the tree, 73 million years ago. Its sd is about 7 times the sd of the iid fit, because a small number of deep lineages give it.

docs.title: 6.3 The tree next to the traits
docs.text:
Open the plot Phylogeny with tip estimates (sci.phylogeny) on the Plots tab.

  • The left panel is the tree. The x axis is the distance from the root in millions of years. The colour of each tip is the predicted brain volume.
  • The right panel shows, for each species, the prediction from its relatives (mean and 90% interval) and the observed value (an open circle).
  • The plot has 186 tips, so it does not show the labels. Move the pointer over a tip to read the name of the species.

Look for these features, which the notebook also shows:

  • Brain size comes in blocks of related species: the small lemurs, mouse lemurs and marmosets, and the large apes and baboons.
  • The 35 species without a brain volume have a prediction but no circle. Their predictions follow their relatives.
  • For a fitted species, the prediction leaves that species out. Thus a circle far from its interval is a species that its relatives do not predict well.

docs.title: 6.4 Which model agrees best with the data?
docs.text:
The Metrics card of the Overview tab shows elpd_loo. In this fit, it is 129.9 (se 8.7, p_loo 4.5). A larger value is better.

The model calculates elpd_loo from the density of each species given all the other species (notebook section 7, "Right"). It does not use the marginal density of each species, which puts the models in the opposite order. Fit the other three kinds (see the note in step 4) and compare their elpd_loo. These are the results of the four kinds with the spec of step 4:

kind elpd_loo (se) slope[group_size] slope[body] Notes iid 14.9 (8.9) 0.123 ± 0.023 0.893 ± 0.023 brownian 91.3 (24.1) -0.013 ± 0.020 0.701 ± 0.037 2 species with a Pareto k above 0.7 lambda 129.9 (8.7) 0.027 ± 0.020 0.767 ± 0.031 lam 0.954 ou 90.9 (22.6) -0.008 ± 0.021 0.738 ± 0.042 rate 0.184, 2 species with a Pareto k above 0.7

docs.title: 6.5 The numbers of the notebook and of this port
docs.text:
Quantity Notebook This port lambda: slope[body] 0.766 0.767 lambda: slope[group_size] 0.026 0.027 lambda: lam 0.954 (89% interval 0.92 to 0.98) 0.954 ± 0.018 lambda: sigma 0.277 0.276 lambda: intercept -0.121 -0.116 iid: slope[group_size] 0.123 0.123 brownian: slope[group_size] -0.013 -0.013 ou: rate 0.185 0.184 elpd_loo: lambda 130 129.9 elpd_loo: brownian, ou about 90 91.3, 90.9 elpd_loo: iid last, more than 100 below lambda 14.9

Your numbers can be slightly different if the sampler or its version is different.

docs.title: 6.6 Make the decisions
docs.text:
Use these outputs to make the decisions of the notebook:

  1. Are the species independent? No. lam is 0.954, and elpd_loo of iid is about 115 below lambda. Do not use the iid slope of 0.12.
  2. Which covariance? Keep lambda. It has the best elpd_loo by about 39. brownian and ou are almost equal. Their large p_loo (about 13) and the two species with a high Pareto k come from sister species that predict each other almost exactly. The species part of lambda (1 - lam, about 0.05) stops this overconfidence.
  3. Does the social-brain slope survive? No. In each tree model, slope[group_size] is within 0.03 of zero, and its interval includes zero. The 90% HDI of the lambda slope is -0.007 to 0.060 (step 7.1).
  4. Brownian motion or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck? You cannot tell them apart. Report the Brownian rate rate of the ou fit (0.184), not rho or the half-life.
  5. Do the intervals always become wider? No. Compare the sds of the iid and lambda fits. The sd of the intercept is about 7 times larger. The sd of slope[body] is about 35% larger. The sd of slope[group_size] becomes about 13% smaller, because close relatives give contrasts that are almost independent.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text: The fitted version keeps the tree, the predictors and the observed brain volumes. A score needs a dataset with the dim species and the predictors body and group_size. Send the dataset that you fitted. A score request names the outputs with the names of the model: trait and slope. The result uses the names of your dataset, so trait comes back as brain.

docs.title: 7.1 Predict: each species from its relatives
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select primates301.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 2017. Type trait, slope in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score) is:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/primate-social-brain@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://biology/primates301@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["trait", "slope"]
  },
  "seed": 2017
}

The result has brain(species) and slope(predictor):

  • slope[group_size] has the mean 0.027 and the 90% HDI -0.007 to 0.060. slope[body] has 0.767 and 0.712 to 0.816.
  • For a species with a brain volume, brain is the leave-one-out prediction from all other species. The expected value is the conditional median in cc.
  • For the 35 species without a brain volume, brain is the prediction from all fitted species. For example, Allocebus trichotis gets 2.3 cc and Macaca thibetana gets 110.1 cc.

Set Quantity to Predictive to add the conditional noise. Then the 90% intervals hold the observed brain volume of 137 of the 151 species (91%). The notebook pair of section 7 is a good example. Cercocebus torquatus has 106.0 cc, but its relatives predict 88.8 cc (75.0 to 102.8). Its subspecies C. t. atys has 94.7 cc and gets 111.1 cc (93.7 to 128.1). The subspecies is the heavier of the two but has the smaller brain.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model cannot forecast, so a request without a dataset has no forecast horizon, and the server refuses it. A note under Values to score gives this reason.

docs.title: 7.2 Simulate: brain volumes without the relatives
docs.text:
simulate draws new brain volumes for the species from the fitted parameters and the tree. It does not use the observed brain volumes.

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select primates301.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive. Set Draws to 20.
  4. Type trait in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/primate-social-brain@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://biology/primates301@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 20,
    "vars": ["trait"]
  },
  "seed": 2017
}

Each draw is one possible set of brain volumes of the 186 species, correlated by the tree. The intervals are much wider than the predictions of step 7.1. For example, Cercocebus torquatus gets 27.8 to 101.5 cc. Use the draws to make a predictive check of your own, for example the correlation of the residuals of each species and its closest relative (notebook section 3).

  • Evaluate needs a dataset with brain volumes. It compares them with the predictions from the relatives.
  • To change the predictors of a fitted species, upload a dataset with the new body or group_size values. The prediction then moves by the change in the regression mean of the species.
  • A species that the fit did not see stops the score with UNSEEN_LEVELS. The dim species is fixed, because each species must be a tip of the fitted tree.
  • The model has no forecast mode.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_phylo_signal does sections 3 to 7 of the notebook in one run. It fits sci.phylo_regression four times (iid, brownian, lambda and ou) and ranks the fits by elpd_loo. It gives the stacking weights and keeps the best fit. Then it reads the slope of one predictor (focus) and tests if its HDI excludes zero. Only if it does, the recipe does a predictive check of the winner. The report has the tables and the plot of the tree.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Trait regression across species, with and without the tree and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select primates301 in Dataset.
  4. Optional: open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). The defaults are correct for this dataset: Predictors is ["body", "group_size"], Focus is group_size, Hdi prob is 0.94, and each fit has 4 chains of 1000 draws and the seed 2017.
  5. Click Run this recipe.

The recipe binds the target brain to trait automatically, because the dataset has one target. The tree variables have the names of the model, so you do not give bind.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. A local run with the defaults took 3.3 minutes on a laptop and gave these results:

Node Result iid, brownian, lambda, ou elpd_loo 15.0, 90.5, 129.9 and 91.2 weights lambda 1.00. The other fits get no weight best "Pagel's lambda has the best elpd_loo (130) of 4 candidate(s)." slope slope[group_size] 0.027, 94% range -0.010 to 0.066, p_positive 0.91 clear The else arm: the range of the slope includes zero. ppc does not run

Decisions shows the branch clear and its message: "The range of the slope includes zero. The data do not show a clear effect of the predictor when the model includes the tree." This is the decision of the notebook. Outputs shows the comparison, the weights, the slopes, the plot of the tree and the report. The model version link opens the Model Explorer of the winner.

Note

The recipe fits the model four times. The ou fit is the slowest. The fits use the default engine of the model (pymc) and the default target_accept, not nutpie and 0.95. Thus the numbers are slightly different from those of step 6.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit also applies to this model. It adds a prior predictive check, a convergence gate and the governance checks sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Type sci.phylo_regression@^1 in Model. In Fine-tune, type {"kind": "lambda", "predictors": ["body", "group_size"]} in Settings and {} in Prior predictive: this model keeps no prior draws, so the prior plot of the audit cannot render. The recipes sci_spatial_ladder, sci_network_ladder, sci_calibrate_then_design and sci_image_model_check are for other science models.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/biology
mapi datasets upload primates301.nc --name primates301
mapi check primate-social-brain.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit primate-social-brain.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model primate-social-brain -s params -s diagnostics

cat > relatives.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://biology/primate-social-brain@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://biology/primates301@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [trait, slope]}
seed: 2017
EOF
mapi score relatives.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o relatives.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_phylo_signal --name primate-brains   # writes primate-brains.yaml
mapi workflows apply primate-brains.yaml -m "E23 phylogenetic signal"
mapi workflows run primate-brains -i data=dataset://biology/primates301@latest \
  -p 'predictors=["body","group_size"]' -p focus=group_size --watch
RUN=$(mapi --json workflows runs primate-brains -n 1 | jq -r '.[0].run_id')
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare   # the four fits, the best elpd_loo first
mapi workflows node "$RUN" slope     # the slopes of the winner and the focus value

primate-social-brain.yaml is the spec of step 4. The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/biology")
version = api.datasets.upload("primates301.nc", dataset="primates301")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("primate-social-brain.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "primate-social-brain")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://biology/primate-social-brain@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://biology/primates301@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "expected",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "vars": ["trait", "slope"],
        },
        "seed": 2017,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["slope"].to_pandas())  # mean and 90% HDI of each slope
print(summary["brain"].sel(species="Allocebus_trichotis").values)

To run the recipe, write primate-brains.yaml with mapi workflows init sci_phylo_signal. Then save it and start it:

from pathlib import Path

workflow, revision = api.workflows.upsert(Path("primate-brains.yaml"))
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://biology/primates301@latest"},
    params={"predictors": ["body", "group_size"], "focus": "group_size"},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["compare"].result["ranking"])  # ['lambda', 'ou', 'brownian', 'iid']
focus = nodes["slope"].result["focus"]
print(focus["mean"], focus["hdi_low"], focus["hdi_high"], focus["p_positive"])
print(nodes["clear"].result["arm"])  # "else": the range of the slope includes zero

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the four regressions of sections 3 to 6 (iid, brownian, lambda and ou with the rate parameterisation) and the conditional leave-one-out of section 7. It leaves out these parts:

  • The R reader and the Newick parser (section 1). The export command does this work. In Python, mapi_plugin_science.phylo_data.read_tree reads an R file or a Newick file, and mapi_plugin_science.phylo.to_newick writes a tree as Newick.
  • The check of the nearest relative (sections 3 and 7). The web app has no plot for the correlation of the residuals of each species and its closest relative. Calculate it from the draws of a simulate score (step 7.2).
  • The ridge of the ou posterior (section 5). Fit kind: ou with ou_parameterisation: variance to see it. The web app has no pair plot of eta2 and rho on the log scale. The default rate removes the ridge.
  • The two wrong LOO calculations (section 7). The port stores only the correct conditional density. The difference of elpd_loo for each species is not in the web app.
  • Whitening and the sparse tree precision (section 8). The model uses a dense covariance for each draw. This is fast for 151 species, but slow for some thousand species.
  • The imputation of group size on the tree (section 9). A predictor must have no missing values. Thus the dataset has the 186 species with a body mass and a group size. The 31 species of the notebook with a brain volume but no group size are not in it. The port predicts the other gap: the brain volume of the 35 species without one.
  • The tree in tree order next to the traits (section 2). The plot sci.phylogeny shows the tree and the predicted brain volume. It does not show the three traits side by side.

Next steps:

  • Fit kind: ou with ou_parameterisation: variance and compare the ESS of rho with the default parameterisation.
  • Try the exercises of the notebook ("Try it yourself") in Python with mapi_plugin_science.phylo, for example a tree that is not ultrametric.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the recipe, for example to add a fifth kind or a different focus.

docs.title: E31 Indian buffet process on handwritten digits
docs.text:
This tutorial does the PyMC part of the pymc-challenges notebook E31_indian_buffet_process.py in the web app. You use the model sci.ibp_features@1. You do not write PyMC code. The model finds a small set of parts (features) that many digit images share. It also completes the bottom half of digits from writers that it did not see.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project vision. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads two files from its data/ directory.
  • About 30 minutes. On a laptop, the fit took 11 minutes with the pymc engine.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A handwritten 9 has a closed loop at the top and a stroke down the right side. A 4 also has the stroke down the right side. The Indian buffet process (IBP) is a prior for this type of data: each image owns a set of binary features, and many images share each feature. The prior does not fix the number of features or how the images share them.

The notebook uses the UCI "optdigits" digits. Each digit is 8 × 8 pixels of ink counts from 0 to 16. The notebook removes the two blank border columns (8 × 6 pixels) and scales the ink to 0 to 1. It uses 300 training digits by 30 writers and 200 test digits by 13 other writers. The model is linear and Gaussian: each image is the average image plus the images of the features that it owns, plus noise with sd sigma_X.

The notebook asks three questions:

  1. How many features do the digits need, and what sets that number? (Notebook parts 4 and 5.)
  2. Which features are stable, and which change from chain to chain? (Notebook parts 5 and 6.)
  3. Do the features complete a half-seen digit better than a Gaussian model? (Notebook part 8.)

The notebook ends in this decision: choose the resolution yourself and say why. Report what the chains agree on, not one chain. The noise level sigma_X, not the IBP mass alpha, sets the number of features. The notebook fixes sigma_X = 0.25: one pixel of pen movement in the 32 × 32 original changes up to 4 of the 16 counts. The class templates (for example "a 0", "a 6") are stable. The shared strokes change from chain to chain. With K = 8 features, the truncation is too small (the last feature probability is 0.30, not near 0). The features give the best point completion of the bottom halves (RMSE 0.26 to 0.28), but not the best predictive density.

What you will get, and the notebook part that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The dataset vision/optdigits_e31: 500 digits, with the bottom half of the 200 test digits hidden by a mask Part 1: the data The posterior of alpha, the feature probabilities and the feature images (Parameters) Part 7: the same model in PyMC, K = 8 The convergence warnings and the truncation check (Diagnostics) Part 7: chains that do not agree, and the last stick pi_8 The feature images and the completed digits (Fields) Part 6 (the feature images) and part 8 (the completion) The real digits next to replicated digits, and the residual maps (Plots) Part 8: the posterior predictive check The held-out score of the test bottom halves (learned.heldout) Part 8: held-out writers, IBP (PyMC, K = 8) owns and feature_prob (Score) Part 7: Z recovered after the sampler, and the features that each class owns elpd_loo for each digit Not in the notebook. Use it to compare noise_sd, kind and n_features

The port does not do the collapsed Gibbs sampler (parts 3 to 6), the split-merge moves or the PPCA baselines. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads optdigits_train.csv and optdigits_test.csv and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. It prepares the digits as the notebook does:

  • It draws 30 training digits of each class, then 20 test digits of each class, from numpy.random.default_rng(2005). Thus you get the same 500 digits as the notebook.
  • It removes the two border columns and divides the counts by 16.
  • It hides the bottom 4 rows of each test digit with the mask visible. The pixel values stay in the file, so the fit can score its completion of the hidden pixels.

Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e31 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out optdigits_e31.nc --spec optdigits_e31.yaml

The command writes:

wrote optdigits_e31.nc (variables pixels, visible on digit=500, row=8, col=6)
upload it as dataset vision/optdigits_e31 and fit sci.ibp_features
wrote the suggested spec to optdigits_e31.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning digit 500 categorical, fixed train-000 to train-299, then test-000 to test-199 row, col 8, 6 integer, fixed The pixels. Row 0 is the top row pixels digit, row, col float64, ink, target The ink of each pixel, from 0 (blank) to 1 (full). No value is missing visible digit, row, col bool, mask False for the bottom 4 rows of each test digit (4,800 pixels)

The coordinates label(digit) (the class, 50 digits of each class) and writers(digit) (train or test) keep the class and the file. The model does not use them. They help you read the results. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes 60 simulated 8 × 6 images from the model's own forward process. The images have three known stroke features with probabilities 0.6, 0.45 and 0.3, and noise with sd 0.15. All pixels are visible. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real digits. For the simulated images, use the settings of IBP_SPEC_YAML in mapi_plugin_science.ibp_data (n_features: 4, noise_sd: 0.2).

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e31 --synthetic --out ibp_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type optdigits_e31 in Name. Type a description, for example "UCI optdigits, 8 × 6 pixels, 300 training and 200 test digits, bottom halves of the test digits hidden".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select optdigits_e31.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows pixels and visible on digit, row and col.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, pixels has the role target and visible the role mask. Missingness shows no missing values. The hidden pixels are not missing: the mask hides them.

The file is one flat dataset, so the tree path (HDF5 groups and nodes) does not apply here.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows pixels, the 8 × 6 images of the digits. The frame slider goes from digit to digit. The viewer shows 24 of the 500 digits. The mask visible shows as a layer.

  4. Below the viewer, the mean image of each class (the coord label) shows the typical shape of each digit from 0 to 9.
  5. The histogram shows the values of all pixels.
  6. The time sections and Group comparison are in Not for this data. The digits are not time and not groups.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select optdigits_e31. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type parts in the search field. Under Models, select Shared parts of small images (sci.ibp_features@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name optdigits-ibp from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: optdigits-ibp
  project: vision
data:
  dataset: dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest
  bind:
    dims: {y: row, x: col}
    vars: {ink: pixels, shown: visible}
model:
  use: sci.ibp_features@^1
  settings:
    n_features: 8
    kind: fixed_noise
    noise_sd: 0.25
    shown_mask: true
    start: digits
    score_draws: 200
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 2005
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    keep:
      log_likelihood: true
      posterior_predictive: {thin: 100}
evaluate:
  metrics: [elpd_loo]
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - sci.field_map
    - sci.ppc_image_grid
    - sci.image_residuals

The spec is the suggested spec of the export (optdigits_e31.yaml) with three changes. It shows the defaults kind, start and score_draws, and it adds the plot sci.image_residuals.

The binding. The model names its inputs ink(digit, y, x) and shown(digit, y, x). The dataset uses pixels, visible, row and col. data.bind maps the names of the model to the names of the dataset. Outputs keep the dataset names (row and col).

This table tells what each setting means for this question:

Setting Value Meaning for this question n_features 8 The truncation K: the largest number of features. The model sums over the 2^K = 256 patterns of each image. Each extra feature doubles the time, so the limit is 10 kind fixed_noise Keep the pixel noise at noise_sd, as the notebook does. free_noise learns it. The notebook shows that a free noise falls to 0.10 and the number of features grows to 90 noise_sd 0.25 The pixel noise sigma_X, in ink units. It is the resolution: a difference smaller than one pixel of pen movement is noise, not a feature. A smaller value makes more features useful shown_mask true Read shown and hide the pixels where it is false. The fit does not see the bottom halves of the test digits, and it scores its completion of them start digits Start each chain, with no jitter, at features equal to half of 8 random digits, with nu = 0.8. With default, some chains go to a trap where all features are off (notebook part 7) score_draws 200 The posterior draws that each score uses, and that the held-out score uses. The notebook uses 200 alpha_shape, alpha_rate 1, 1 (defaults) The Gamma(1, 1) prior of the IBP mass alpha, as in the notebook feature_scale_sd 1 (default) The HalfNormal scale of sigma_A, the size of the feature images truncation_warn 0.05 (default) The warning TRUNCATION_BINDS shows when the mean of the last feature probability is more than this value
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all of the digits. Without it, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation"). The mask, not a split, makes the holdout of this question.
  • tune: 1000, draws: 1000 and chains: 4 are the values of the notebook.
  • keep.log_likelihood: true keeps the log-likelihood of each digit. Then elpd_loo is available, and you can compare variants of the model (step 6.5).
  • keep.posterior_predictive: {thin: 100} keeps 40 replicated sets of the 500 digits for sci.ppc_image_grid and sci.image_residuals.

Do not forget shown_mask: true

If you bind shown but leave out shown_mask: true, the spec is still valid. But the model then ignores the mask and fits the full test digits. The bottom halves are then not held out, and the fit does not give learned.heldout. If you set shown_mask: true and do not bind shown, the validator shows the error SCHEMA_INVALID: "the model needs variable 'shown', but the pipeline does not make it".

The plots

The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. The model declares core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.field_map, sci.ppc_image_grid and sci.image_residuals. The spec keeps all five. In the Insert panel, the Plots section adds a plot for you. sci.field_map draws the feature images (the posterior variable features), one feature for each position of the slider.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the steps of the fit. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://vision/optdigits-ibp@v1. Click it.

The sampler takes most of the time: about 10 minutes with the pymc engine. Then the progress shows "pointwise log-likelihood": the model calculates the log-likelihood of each digit for each draw. The last message is "posterior ready". After the fit, the run calculates the plots and the explorer views. You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

A faster engine

Add engine: nutpie to the fit block if your platform has nutpie. The notebook used nutpie, and its K = 8 fit took less than one minute. The digits start works with all engines.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

Expect these results:

Code Value Message RHAT 2.62 "The independent sampler runs do not agree about 'logpi'. Its estimates are not reliable at this time." ESS_BULK 5 "There is too little independent information about 'logpi' (about 5 effective draws). The averages are not stable." ESS_TAIL 11 The same message for the intervals DIVERGENCES 26 "The sampler had problems in 26 of 4000 steps. The results can be biased." TRUNCATION_BINDS 0.20 "The model uses all the features it has. More features would possibly describe the images better." PARETO_K_HIGH 15 "Some data points have a strong effect on the model, so the leave-one-out score is only approximate."

These warnings are the result of the notebook, not a fault of the fit. The posterior of the feature images has many modes, as in a mixture model. Each chain finds a different set of features, so the feature probabilities logpi do not agree between the chains. The notebook found R-hat values from 1.15 to 1.9 and a bulk ESS from 6 to 17 for the same quantities. The quantities that do not depend on the labels of the features agree: alpha has an R-hat of 1.00 and an ESS of more than 2000. More draws do not correct this. Do not report one feature probability as a result.

The divergences are in one chain (26 of its 1,000 draws). The notebook had none. Look at core.convergence in Plots. Its caption says that 394 of 402 parameters have not converged, for example features[0, 2, 3] and logpi[1].

docs.title: 6.2 What did the model learn?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The posterior has these variables:

Variable Meaning alpha The IBP mass. A larger value gives more features nu (feature) The sticks. pi_k = nu_1 × … × nu_k logpi (feature) The log of the feature probabilities pi_k sigma_A The scale of the feature images features (feature, row, col) The feature images A: the change of ink that each feature adds to the average image

The posterior means, with the notebook values:

Parameter This fit Notebook Meaning alpha 3.49 ± 1.17 4.19 The IBP mass sigma_A 0.186 0.16 The size of the feature images logpi −0.87 to −1.59 −0.69 to −1.15 The log feature probabilities, feature 1 to feature 8 pi_8, by chain 0.19 to 0.22 0.30 to 0.33 The last feature probability: the truncation check

The chains of this fit found different modes from the chains of the notebook. Thus the feature probabilities are lower. Both fits fail the truncation check by a large amount: a ninth feature would be owned by about one digit in five.

docs.title: 6.3 The images (Fields)
docs.text:
Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Select the output in Output:

  • features is the image of each feature, in a diverging scale. Red pixels get more ink than the average digit, blue pixels get less ink. The slider feature selects the feature. Select Statistic Mean. A feature that is a class template looks like a digit minus the average digit. For example, the 0 template has red pixels on a ring and blue pixels at the centre.
  • ink_hat is the expected image of each digit, in a grey scale. Where the fit saw a pixel, it is the denoised image. Where the fit did not see a pixel, it is the completion. The slider digit selects the digit. The details table shows 24 of the 500 digits, evenly spaced. Select a test digit, for example test-000, and look at the bottom half. Std. dev. is larger in the hidden bottom half than in the top half.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one pixel.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence Large R-hat values for logpi, nu and features, and R-hat near 1 for alpha (step 6.1) core.posterior_forest The intervals of alpha, sigma_A and logpi. The intervals of logpi are wide because the chains do not agree sci.field_map The feature images (mean, sd, mean ÷ sd, 5% and 95%). A feature with a large sd in all its pixels is a feature that changes from chain to chain sci.ppc_image_grid The real digit next to 5 replicated digits, on one colour scale. Use the slider to go through the digits sci.image_residuals The real digit, the mean of the 40 replicated digits, the residual and the normalised residual

In this fit, the caption of sci.image_residuals says: "The normalised residuals have an sd of 0.82 and 3% are outside ±2." A perfect model gives 1 and 5%. The model noise of 0.25 is too large for most pixels. This is the misfit that the notebook finds in part 8: the real ink has many exact zeros and some full pixels, and the Gaussian noise makes smooth values, some of them negative. In sci.ppc_image_grid, the replicated digits have fewer blank pixels than the real digit. The model describes the structure at a resolution that you chose. It is not a generative model of ink.

docs.title: 6.4 Which digits own which features?
docs.text:
owns(digit, feature) is the probability that each digit owns each feature. Get it with a score (step 7). Then average it over the digits of each class (the coordinate label). In this fit:

Feature Owned by most digits of Also owned by 4 0 (100%) 9 (21%) 3 1 (96%) 4 (64%) 7 6 (93%) 4 (66%) 5 7 (88%) 3 (45%) 1 5 (88%) 6 (52%), 2 (51%) 6 9 (87%), 3 (75%) 5 (41%) 2 2 (81%) 1 (56%), 9 (43%) 0 7 (79%) 3 (54%), 5 (53%)

owns averages over the draws of all chains. A feature that has the same image in all chains gives clear values near 0 or 1. Feature 4 (the 0 template) is in all digits 0 and in almost no other digit, as in the notebook. Features with values between 0.3 and 0.6 for many classes are broad corrections, or features that change from chain to chain. The notebook says the same: with only 8 features, each feature must do more work, and it is shared across classes.

docs.title: 6.5 Make the decision
docs.text:
The notebook makes four statements. This is how to make each one from the outputs:

  1. Choose the resolution. noise_sd is a setting that you choose, not a result. To see its effect, save a revision with noise_sd: 0.35 and one with noise_sd: 0.15. Fit both. A smaller value keeps more features in use: the last pi_k gets larger. Do not compare noise_sd values with elpd_loo alone: a smaller noise always explains the training digits better (notebook part 4).
  2. K = 8 is too small. TRUNCATION_BINDS shows pi_last = 0.20, much more than 0.05. The notebook finds 16 to 21 features at the same noise with its Gibbs sampler. Each extra feature doubles the time of this model, so n_features: 10 is the limit. Thus this model is correct only when a small number of features is sufficient.
  3. Report what the chains agree on. alpha, sigma_A, the completions and elpd_loo agree between the chains. The feature probabilities and most shared features do not. Use the class templates (for example feature 4 for the 0s), not one shared stroke.
  4. The completion. learned.heldout on the Overview tab gives the score of the 200 hidden bottom halves: an RMSE of 0.284 and a log predictive density of −0.70 nats for each digit. The notebook gives 0.28 for this model, and 0.275 to 0.31 for the Gaussian baselines. Thus the features give a good point completion. The notebook also shows that a full-covariance Gaussian gives a better predictive density, by about 4 nats for each digit.

To compare variants of the model, use elpd_loo (the metric of this fit is −615.3, se 124.8, with p_loo 749.9). Select two model versions in Models and click Compare. Because 15 digits have a high Pareto k, the leave-one-out values are approximate.

docs.title: 6.6 The numbers of the notebook and of this port
docs.text:
Quantity This fit Notebook Held-out RMSE of the bottom halves 0.284 0.283 Held-out log density for each digit −0.70 −0.3 alpha 3.49 4.19 Last stick pi_8 (mean for each chain) 0.19 to 0.22 0.30 to 0.33 Largest R-hat of logpi 2.6 1.9 Divergences 26 0 Fit time 10.5 min (pymc) less than 1 min (nutpie)

The log density is different because the two fits use different data. The notebook fits the 300 training digits only. This spec also fits the top halves of the 200 test digits. A separate fit on the 300 training digits only, as in the notebook, gives 0.283 and −0.34 nats. The RMSE agrees.

docs.title: 7.1 Which digits own which features
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Then select optdigits_e31, the dataset of the fit.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 31. Type feature_prob, owns in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each output. In this fit, feature_prob is 0.42, 0.37, 0.29, 0.25, 0.23, 0.23, 0.22 and 0.20.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://vision/optdigits-ibp@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["feature_prob", "owns"]
  },
  "seed": 31
}

docs.title: 7.2 The completion of one test digit
docs.text:
The Score page has no field to select digits. To get only some digits, send the request from the CLI, the Python client or Schema and Try it of an endpoint, with a select block:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://vision/optdigits-ibp@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest",
  "select": {"digit": ["test-000", "test-001"]},
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["ink_hat", "owns"]
  },
  "seed": 31
}

ink_hat has the dims digit, row and col. Rows 4 to 7 are the completion. The two digits are 0s. In this fit, both own feature 4 (the 0 template) with a probability of 1.00. The completion of test-000 closes the loop of the 0: rows 4 to 7 have ink in columns 1 and 4, and the bottom row has ink in columns 2 and 3. The mean sd of the hidden pixels is 0.044, and of the seen pixels 0.033.

To get completed digits with noise, set "kind": "predictive" and "draws": 20. Each draw then has a pattern of features and pixel noise with sd noise_sd.

  • A score uses the pixels that the fit stored, never the target values in the score data. Thus a hidden pixel cannot get into its own prediction.
  • digit is fixed. A score can use only the digits of the fit. If you select a digit that the fit did not see, the score fails with UNSEEN_LEVELS. To complete a new digit, add it to the dataset with its unseen pixels hidden by visible, and fit again.
  • The model has no simulate mode. Use predict with "kind": "predictive".

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_image_model_check (Image model check) is for models that predict an image. It fits the model, makes the residual maps and the image grid, does a posterior predictive check and writes a report.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Image model check and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select optdigits_e31 in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.ibp_features@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set these values:
    • Settings: {"n_features": 8, "noise_sd": 0.25, "shown_mask": true}.
    • Bind: {"dims": {"y": "row", "x": "col"}, "vars": {"ink": "pixels", "shown": "visible"}}. Without the binding, the fit does not find ink.
    • Draws 1000, Tune 1000 and Seed 2005.
    • Var: ink_hat. Frame: digit. The model has two outputs on a grid, and the check is for the digits.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs shows the parameter table, the two plots, the coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges and the report.

A short run of the recipe (draws 300, tune 300) gave these results:

  • Predictions against the data: 63% of the pixels are in their 50% range, and 94.6% in their 90% range. The check fails (ok is false): the ranges are too wide for the many blank pixels. This is the misfit of step 6.3.
  • Residual maps: the normalised residuals have an sd of 3.81. The recipe reads the expected images (source: predictions), with no pixel noise, so the normalised residuals are too large. For this model, use sci.image_residuals of the fit (step 6.3). It reads the replicated digits with their noise.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does all the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws: a convergence gate, the posterior predictive check, sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Run it in the same way with the model sci.ibp_features@^1, the same Settings and Bind, and Prior predictive set to {}. For this model, the gate stops the audit: the R-hat of logpi (2.6) is more than Rhat max (1.01). Decisions shows "R-hat is too large or the effective sample size is too small, so the chains do not agree." That is the correct result for a posterior with many modes (step 6.1). Do not increase Rhat max to pass the gate.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/vision
mapi datasets upload optdigits_e31.nc --name optdigits_e31
mapi check optdigits-ibp.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit optdigits-ibp.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model optdigits-ibp -s params -s diagnostics

cat > digits-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://vision/optdigits-ibp@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest
select: {digit: [test-000, test-001]}
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [ink_hat, owns]}
seed: 31
EOF
mapi score digits-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o digits.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_image_model_check --name digits-check
mapi workflows apply digits-check.yaml -m "E31 image check"
mapi workflows run digits-check -i data=dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest \
  -p model=sci.ibp_features@^1 -p var=ink_hat -p frame=digit \
  -p 'settings={"n_features": 8, "noise_sd": 0.25, "shown_mask": true}' \
  -p 'bind={"dims": {"y": "row", "x": "col"}, "vars": {"ink": "pixels", "shown": "visible"}}' \
  -p seed=2005 --watch

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/vision")
version = api.datasets.upload("optdigits_e31.nc", dataset="optdigits_e31")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("optdigits-ibp.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "optdigits-ibp")
mv = api.models.version(model.id, model.latest_version)
print(mv.ref, mv.metrics)

result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    mv.version,
    {
        "model": mv.ref,
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://vision/optdigits_e31@latest",
        "select": {"digit": ["test-000", "test-001"]},
        "output": {"summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"], "vars": ["ink_hat", "owns"]},
        "seed": 31,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["owns"].sel(stat="mean").round(2).values)  # (digit, feature)
print(summary["ink_hat"].sel(stat="mean", digit="test-000").round(2).values)  # (row, col)

The CLI and the client send the same spec and the same score request as the web app.

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the PyMC model of notebook part 7 (truncated stick-breaking, Z summed out over 2^K patterns, the digits start) and the held-out completion of part 8. It leaves out these parts:

  • The IBP prior simulations (part 2). The customers-and-dishes simulation, the Poisson law of K+ and the comparison of the finite beta-Bernoulli model are not in the port.
  • The collapsed Gibbs sampler (parts 3 to 6). The port has only the NUTS model with Z summed out. Thus it has no unbounded number of features, no brute-force test of the sampler and no runs with free sigma_X and free alpha at 90 features. kind: free_noise learns the noise, but with at most 10 features.
  • The split-merge moves (part 5). The notebook shows that random split-merge moves are never accepted.
  • The label-free summaries (part 6). The port does not give the shared-feature matrix E[Z Zᵀ] or the match of features across draws. owns gives the probability that each digit owns each feature, averaged over all chains.
  • The timings of K (part 7). The port stops at n_features: 10.
  • The baselines (part 8). The port does not fit PPCA or a full-covariance Gaussian. Thus you cannot make the density comparison of the notebook in the platform.
  • The data of the fit. The notebook fits the 300 training digits. The export also puts the top halves of the 200 test digits into the fit (step 6.6).

Next steps:

  • Fit the spec again with start: default and look for FEATURES_COLLAPSED. This is the "no features at all" trap of notebook part 7.
  • Fit with n_features: 10. The fit takes about four times as long. Look at the last pi_k in TRUNCATION_BINDS.
  • Give each pixel its own noise (notebook "Try it yourself", item 1). The model does not do this, so it needs a custom model.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.

docs.title: E50: a scratch assay as a reaction-diffusion PDE
docs.text:
A sheet of PC-3 prostate cancer cells has a wound scratched through it. The cells move in from the two sides and divide, and the wound closes in about two days. How fast do the cells move, and how fast do they divide? This tutorial answers that question with the model sci.fisher_kpp@1 in the web app. It uses the same real data as part one of the pymc-challenges notebook E50_reaction_diffusion_signaling.py.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and an account that can upload datasets and fit models.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges, with its data/ directory.
  • About 30 minutes. Each fit takes some minutes.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
The notebook fits the Fisher-KPP equation to cell counts:

du/dt = a(t) (D d²u/dx² + lam u (1 - u))

  • u(x, t) is the cell density as a part of the carrying capacity K.
  • D (µm²/h) is the diffusivity: how fast the cells move at random.
  • lam (1/h) is the growth rate: how fast the cells divide when they have space.
  • a(t) = tanh(beta t) is a start-up delay. The cells move and divide slowly immediately after the scratch. a(t) = 1 when there is no delay.
  • The count in each 50 µm column is Poisson with the mean K u(x, t).

The model solves the PDE in the model graph. Each column is a finite volume, the edges have zero flux and time moves in explicit Euler steps. The front of the wound moves at the wave speed 2 sqrt(D lam).

The notebook ends in two decisions:

  1. Keep the start-up delay. The model with the delay fits much better (PSIS-LOO), and the model without it gives a diffusivity that is about four times too small.
  2. Report the wave speed first. The data identify the wave speed better than D. lam trades off against the capacity K and the delay beta, so it is a model parameter, not a direct measurement of the cell cycle.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:
