In the web app Notebook The dataset biology/scratch_assay_pc3: cells(hours, position), 5 × 38 counts Section 1, the scratch assay sci.fisher_kpp@1. The model does the method of lines and the stability check Section 2, Fisher-KPP by the method of lines Two fits (delay: true and delay: false) and Compare Section 3, two models: with and without a start-up delay The Parameters section, the posterior forest, wave_speed and the Fields section (the kymograph) Section 4, what the data identify, and the invasion wave A forecast past 48 h on the Score page Section 4, the wound as it closes, hour by hour

Sections 5 to 8 (morphogen gradient, FRAP, positional information) are not in the platform. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads scratch_assay_pc3.csv from pymc-challenges. It writes a NetCDF dataset that has the raw schema of the model. Run it from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e50 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out scratch_assay_pc3.nc --spec scratch_assay_pc3.yaml

The command prints this output:

wrote scratch_assay_pc3.nc (variables cells on hours=5, position=38)
upload it as dataset biology/scratch_assay_pc3 and fit sci.fisher_kpp
wrote the suggested spec to scratch_assay_pc3.yaml

The dataset has two dims and one variable:

Name Kind Values hours dim, integer, policy extend 0, 12, 24, 36, 48 position dim, float, policy fixed 25, 75, …, 1875 (the centres of 38 columns of 50 µm) cells(hours, position) variable, int64, role target, units cells 0 to 127 cells in each column

No copy of pymc-challenges?

Use --synthetic in place of --challenges. The command then writes a scratch assay that the model itself simulates, with known parameters (D = 1500, lam = 0.06, K = 120, no delay). That dataset has 16 columns of 100 µm and the times 0, 8, 16, 24 and 32 h:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e50 --synthetic --out assay.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, click Datasets.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. In Name, type scratch_assay_pc3. Then click Create dataset.
  4. In the upload panel, click Choose files and select scratch_assay_pc3.nc.
  5. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file: the dims hours (5) and position (38) and the variable cells.
  6. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest reads the raw schema from the file (the mapi_schema attribute). Thus cells gets the role target and you do not map the columns. When the ingest is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. Click Copy reference to copy dataset://<project>/scratch_assay_pc3@latest.

The dataset is one plain array. It is not a tree, and you do not need the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Profiles and spectra.

  3. The profile shows cells along position, with one line for each of the 5 times in hours. Use the picker to show one time. The table gives the peak of each line.

  4. Look at how the cells fill the scratch from line to line. The Fisher-KPP model describes this movement.
  5. Over time shows hours as a sequence. The time patterns are in Not for this data: hours is an ordered sequence, not time.
  6. Data quality does not give the warning SHORT_HISTORY.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, click Build. Click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel. Open the Datasets section and click scratch_assay_pc3. The toast Dataset set shows.
  4. In the search box, type fisher. Under Models, click sci.fisher_kpp. The toast Model set shows.
  5. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. Then click Validate.
  6. When the status shows valid, click Save spec.

This is the full spec. It starts from the spec that the export command wrote and adds the priors of the notebook:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp, project: biology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://biology/scratch_assay_pc3@latest
  bind:
    dims: {t: hours, x: position}
    vars: {count: cells}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: t, last: 1}
model:
  use: sci.fisher_kpp@^1
  settings:
    steps_per_hour: 10
    delay: true
    max_extension: 4
    diffusivity_median: 1000
    growth_median: 0.05
    capacity_mu: 122
    capacity_sigma: 15
  fit:
    mode: evaluate_then_refit
    seed: 50
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    engine: nutpie
    keep: {log_likelihood: true}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mae, coverage_90, elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.profile_bands, sci.field_map]

Keep the log-likelihood

Keep keep: {log_likelihood: true} in the spec. Without it, the fit does not calculate elpd_loo, and the metrics show "the model did not store a log_likelihood group". You need elpd_loo to compare the two models.

Use the name of your project

Change biology in metadata.project and in data.dataset to the name of your project. If you do not, the spec does not validate: the platform reads datasets only from the project that you work in. The Insert panel writes the correct data.dataset for you.

The bind block connects the names in the dataset to the names of the model. The model calls time t, position x and the counts count. The split keeps the last time (48 h) back. The fit with evaluate_then_refit first fits on 0 to 36 h and scores the 48 h counts. Then it fits again on all the data.

Setting Value What it means for this question steps_per_hour 10 Euler steps of 0.1 h, as in the notebook (480 steps for 48 h). With 50 µm columns, the steps are stable for D up to 12,500 µm²/h delay true Multiply the movement and the growth by tanh(beta t). This is the notebook's second model. Set false for the first model max_extension 4 A forecast can go 4 periods (4 × 12 h) after the last fitted time, that is to 96 h diffusivity_median 1000 The prior median of D (µm²/h). With diffusivity_log_sd 1, the prior covers about 100 to 10,000 µm²/h growth_median 0.05 The prior median of lam (1/h): doubling times from about 5 hours to some days capacity_mu, capacity_sigma 122, 15 The prior of the capacity K. A full column has about 122 cells. The model estimates K, it does not fix it delay_rate_median 0.1 (default) The prior median of beta (1/h). The start-up time is about 1/beta initial_floor 0.1 (default) The smallest initial count. An empty column can then fill cfl_quantile 0.99 (default) The model makes sure that the Euler steps are stable at this quantile of the prior of D

The first time (0 h) is the initial condition. The PDE starts from the counts at that time, and the likelihood does not use them. Each later time minus the first time must be a whole number of Euler steps.

When the steps are not stable

If the Euler steps are not stable at the cfl_quantile of the prior of D, Validate does not find the problem. The fit then stops with SETTINGS_INVALID. The message gives the smallest steps_per_hour that is stable.

For the notebook's first model, save a second spec. Use the same YAML with name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay and delay: false.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. On the spec page, click Fit. The button is available when the spec is saved and valid.
  2. The run page opens. The badge shows Live while the page gets events.
  3. Look at the Progress card. The fit goes through the evaluation fit (0 to 36 h), the score of the 48 h counts and the refit on all the data. Then the run renders the plots.
  4. Look at the Events card. It shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics and the warnings. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  5. When the run is done, click Inspect model://…@v1.

Do the same steps for the spec without the delay.

Faster fits

Each fit runs the 480 Euler steps for each gradient. On a laptop with nutpie, the full fit (the evaluation fit and the refit) took about 2.5 minutes with the delay and about 1 minute without it. For a quick first look, set tune: 300 and draws: 300.

docs.title: Model Explorer
docs.text:
On the model version page, click Explore. These sections are the most important for this question:

  • Overview (At a glance): the holdout metrics on the 48 h counts (rmse, mae, coverage_90) and the About card of the model.
  • Parameters: D, lam, K, beta and wave_speed, with their intervals, R-hat and ESS.
  • Diagnostics: the convergence of the sampler.
  • Fields: the page says "The model has 1 output on a grid." The output is density(hours, position), the expected cells in each column. Time is on the rows and position is on the columns, so the map is a kymograph. The wound is the dark band in the middle. It becomes narrow from the bottom (0 h) to the top (48 h). Use the Statistic buttons:
    • Mean shows the expected density.
    • Std. dev. shows where the model is not sure. It is largest at the edges of the wound.
    • Draws shows single posterior draws. Click Play the draws to see them one after the other.

Move the pointer over the map to read the value of a cell.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
On the model version page, open the Plots tab. The left list has one entry for each plot of the spec:

Plot What to look for Sampler convergence (core.convergence) R-hat near 1.00 and a large ESS for D, lam, K and beta Posterior forest (core.posterior_forest) The rows of D, lam, K, beta and wave_speed. Relative to its value, the interval of wave_speed is narrower than the interval of D. The plot also shows rows of mu, the expected count of each cell Profiles with bands (sci.profile_bands) The title is "Profiles of mu". Each line is the median count across the wound at one time, with 50% and 90% bands and the actual counts. Use the slider to show one time. With the delay, the bands follow the 12 h and 24 h profiles. Without the delay, they do not Field map (sci.field_map) The title is "Field map of mu". It shows the mean and the sd of the expected count for each time and column: the same kymograph as the Fields section

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
Make the notebook's two decisions with these outputs:

  1. Delay or no delay. Click Compare on the model version page. Select the two versions (with and without the delay), then click Compare. Look at elpd_loo (larger is better) and at the holdout metrics. Then compare D in the two posterior forests. The model with the delay has an elpd_loo that is about 110 larger, many times the standard errors (11 and 24). Its D is about four and a half times the D of the model without the delay. Thus keep the delay, and do not use the D of the model without it. Its interval is narrow, but it is wrong.
  2. What to report. In Parameters, compare the relative widths (sd ÷ mean) of D, lam and wave_speed. Report the wave speed with its interval. Report D and lam with the note that lam, K and beta trade off.

docs.title: Numbers: the notebook and the platform
docs.text:
We fitted both specs on the real data with nutpie (seed 50, 4 chains of 1000 draws). The table shows the posterior means of the refit on all five times. The 90% intervals are in brackets. The notebook gives most values in its text, so they are approximate.

Quantity Notebook Platform, with delay Platform, no delay D (µm²/h) about 1,260 (with delay), about 280 (no delay) 1,274 [986, 1,632] 284 [212, 377] lam (1/h) doubling time ln 2 / lam about 5 h 0.147 [0.124, 0.177], doubling time 4.8 h 0.103 [0.095, 0.109] K (cells for each column) about 114 113.4 [110.2, 116.8] 108.5 [106.1, 111.0] beta (1/h) 0.03 to 0.06 0.043 [0.033, 0.054], start-up time 1/beta 23 h — wave_speed (µm/h) about 27 27.3 [23.1, 33.1] 10.7 [9.6, 12.0] Correlation of log D and log lam 0.41 0.35 — Correlation of lam and K −0.46 −0.47 — Correlation of lam and beta −0.81 −0.81 — elpd_loo (152 counts) delay better by many standard errors −536.4 (se 11.0) −646.4 (se 23.9) Holdout at 48 h: rmse, mae, coverage_90 not calculated 9.2, 8.3, 1.00 12.6, 10.4, 0.79

The two fits had no diagnostic warnings. With the delay, the largest R-hat is 1.004, the smallest bulk ESS is 783 and there are no divergences. The Diagnostics section shows these values. The correlations are not in the Model Explorer. To get them, download the bundle and use the posterior draws.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
The notebook replays the assay between the observations. The platform continues the PDE past the last fitted time. It starts from the initial profile that it keeps with the model version.

  1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. Under What do you want to do?, select Forecast.
  3. Under How far ahead?, type 2 in Periods. One period is 12 h, so the forecast is at 60 h and 72 h. The model accepts at most 4 periods (max_extension).
  4. Under Values to score, select No new data.
  5. Click Forecast.

The Results region shows density at 60 h and 72 h and wave_speed. At 60 h, the centre columns have about 111 cells. At 72 h, all columns are at the capacity, about 113 cells. Thus the model says that the wound closes between 60 h and 72 h. The request that the page sends is:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/scratch-assay-pc3-kpp@latest",
  "mode": "forecast",
  "horizon": {"dim": "t", "periods": 2},
  "output": {"kind": "expected", "summary": ["mean", "q5", "q95"]}
}

For Poisson draws of new counts in place of the expected density, set "output": {"kind": "predictive"}. The model also does predict (in-sample, all five times) and evaluate (a dataset with new counts). It does not do simulate or counterfactual.

Try it on an endpoint

If you promote the version to an endpoint, open Integrations, then the endpoint, then the Schema and Try it tab. Paste the same request there, without the model field, and click Score.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does the checks of a Bayesian workflow for any model in one run. It fits the model with prior predictive draws and plots them. A convergence gate needs the largest R-hat below rhat_max (1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above min_ess (400). Only then does it do a posterior predictive check, a prior sensitivity check and a recovery check on simulated data. It writes a report with the plots.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Bayesian workflow audit and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select scratch_assay_pc3 in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.fisher_kpp@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune. In Settings, type the settings of step 4 as JSON: {"steps_per_hour": 10, "delay": true, "max_extension": 4, "diffusivity_median": 1000, "growth_median": 0.05, "capacity_mu": 122, "capacity_sigma": 15}. In Bind, type {"dims": {"t": "hours", "x": "position"}, "vars": {"count": "cells"}}.
  6. Click Run this recipe. The run monitor shows the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events.

In Decisions, see if the convergence gate passed. In Outputs, open the report.

Note

Without Bind, the recipe cannot find the dims t and x of the model, and the fit stops. Without Settings, the fit uses the default settings of the model, not the settings of step 4. sci.fisher_kpp is not an image model, so sci_image_model_check does not apply to it.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
# get the data and the suggested spec
uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e50 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out scratch_assay_pc3.nc --spec scratch_assay_pc3.yaml

# save the full spec of step 4 as scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml, then make the copy
# without the delay
sed -e 's/name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp,/name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay,/' \
    -e 's/delay: true/delay: false/' \
    scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml > scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay.yaml

# upload, check and fit the two specs on the platform
mapi datasets upload scratch_assay_pc3.nc --name scratch_assay_pc3
mapi check scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml --remote @
mapi fit scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml --remote @
mapi fit scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay.yaml --remote @

# a forecast to 72 h
cat > forecast.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://biology/scratch-assay-pc3-kpp@latest
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: t, periods: 2}
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, q5, q95]}
EOF
mapi score forecast.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o forecast.zarr.zip

# the Model Explorer and the comparison
mapi explore model model://biology/scratch-assay-pc3-kpp@v1 -s params -s fields
mapi explore compare model://biology/scratch-assay-pc3-kpp@v1 \
    model://biology/scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay@v1

# the recipe
mapi workflows init bayes_workflow_audit --name kpp-audit
mapi workflows apply kpp-audit.yaml
mapi workflows run kpp-audit -i data=dataset://biology/scratch_assay_pc3@latest \
    -p model=sci.fisher_kpp@^1 \
    -p 'settings={"steps_per_hour": 10, "delay": true, "max_extension": 4, "diffusivity_median": 1000, "growth_median": 0.05, "capacity_mu": 122, "capacity_sigma": 15}' \
    -p 'bind={"dims": {"t": "hours", "x": "position"}, "vars": {"count": "cells"}}' --watch

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()  # MAPI_URL, the `mapi login` sign-in (or MAPI_TOKEN) and MAPI_PROJECT

version = api.datasets.upload("scratch_assay_pc3.nc", dataset="scratch_assay_pc3")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

# the full spec of step 4, and the same spec without the delay
with open("scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
no_delay = spec_yaml.replace(
    "name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp,", "name: scratch-assay-pc3-kpp-no-delay,"
).replace("delay: true", "delay: false")
for text in (spec_yaml, no_delay):
    check = api.specs.validate(text)
    print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
    revision = api.specs.upsert(text)
    run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
    run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "scratch-assay-pc3-kpp")
mv = api.models.version(model.id, model.latest_version)
print(mv.ref, mv.metrics)

result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    mv.version,
    {
        "model": mv.ref,
        "mode": "forecast",
        "horizon": {"dim": "t", "periods": 2},
        "output": {"kind": "expected", "summary": ["mean", "q5", "q95"]},
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["wave_speed"].values)
print(summary["density"].sel(stat="mean").round(0).values)  # (hours, position)

scratch-assay-pc3-kpp.yaml is the full spec of step 4: the spec that the export command writes, with the priors of the notebook. The CLI and the client then send the same two specs and the same score request as the web app.

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
• Part two is not in the platform. The notebook's sections 5 to 8 use simulated morphogen images and FRAP data. They have the exact eigenbasis solution of a linear PDE, the decay length sqrt(D/k) and the positional information of a cell. No sci.* model does this yet.
  • The holdout. The notebook fits all five times. The spec keeps the 48 h counts back for the holdout metrics, then fits again on all the data. The parameters of the refit are comparable with the notebook.
  • The model comparison. The notebook compares the two models with az.compare on 152 pointwise terms (4 times × 38 columns). It also counts the Pareto k values above 0.7. The platform gives elpd_loo for each version on the same 152 terms, and Compare shows the versions side by side. It does not give elpd_diff and its standard error.
  • The correlations and the posterior predictive plots. The notebook plots D against lam and lam against K. The platform gives the marginal intervals. Add core.pair to outputs.plots to see the pairs.
  • The animation. The notebook draws the density each hour from 200 posterior draws. The platform gives the density at the observation times (Fields) and at forecast times (Score). Between the observation times, it gives no values.
  • The sampler. The spec uses nutpie. The notebook uses pm.sample. The numbers agree to within the Monte Carlo error.

Next steps:

  • Do the notebook's "Try it yourself" exercise 1 in part: change the priors (for example capacity_sigma) and compare the versions. See which conclusions about D and lam stay.
  • Read the reference of the model: sci.fisher_kpp.
  • Read Model Explorer and Workflows.

docs.title: E51 thermal gradient plate design
docs.text:
This tutorial does the calibration and the heater design check of the pymc-challenges notebook E51_heat_equation_design.py in the web app. You use the model sci.heat_plate@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project engineering. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the spec.
  • The modeling-api repository with its Python environment (uv). The notebook simulates its data, so you do not need a copy of pymc-challenges.
  • About 20 minutes. The fit takes about one minute of sandbox time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A gradient plate holds a surface at a temperature gradient, not at one temperature. Biologists use it to test seeds or bacteria at many temperatures at the same time. The notebook designs a 40 × 20 cm metal plate in a 20 °C room. Its working area must go from 30 °C at the left to 70 °C at the right, with the same temperature across its width. The working area starts 5 cm from the left and right edges and 3 cm from the long edges.

Heat spreads through the plate and goes out through its faces and edges. The 2-D steady heat equation gives the temperature of each point. But the properties of the plate are not known exactly. Thus the notebook first does a calibration experiment, then designs the heaters for all the plates that agree with the calibration.

The notebook asks these questions:

  1. What do three test runs with twelve thermocouples tell you about the plate? (Notebook section 2.) The unknowns are the conductivity k, the face loss h, the edge loss h_edge and the heater efficiency eta.
  2. Where do you put six heaters, and how much power does each heater get? (Notebook section 3.)
  3. How much do insulation and sensors with feedback help? (Notebook sections 4 to 6.)

The decision of section 3 is this: use the greedy heater layout, not six heaters spaced evenly along the long edges. Over the posterior, the greedy layout is 1.4 °C RMS from the target in the working area. The even layout is 2.0 °C RMS. Both layouts run 2 to 4 °C too warm at the cold end, because no heater can remove heat there.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The posterior of k, h, h_edge, eta, sigma and spread_length (Parameters, core.posterior_forest, core.pair) Section 2, the table of the calibration and the correlations The temperature field of each calibration run, with mean, sd and draws (Fields, sci.field_map) Section 1, the field of one 10 W heater The residual of each thermocouple (sci.image_residuals) Section 2, the fit to the readings The predicted field of two heater layouts, with a 90% range for each cell (Score) Section 3, the comparison of the greedy layout with the even layout A recipe that calibrates, tests the calibration on a run that the fit did not see, and then predicts a layout (sci_calibrate_then_design) Sections 2 and 3 in one run

The platform does not search for the best heater layout. You give the layouts, and the model predicts them. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The notebook simulates its calibration experiment. The export command makes the same experiment again with the notebook's random generator and seed. Thus the readings are the same as the notebook's T_cal. Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e51 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out heat_plate_e51.nc --spec heat_plate_e51.yaml

The command ignores --challenges for this case, because E51 has no data file. The command writes:

wrote heat_plate_e51.nc (variables heater_w, reading_c on run=3, y_cm=12, x_cm=24)
upload it as dataset engineering/heat_plate_e51 and fit sci.heat_plate
wrote the suggested spec to heat_plate_e51.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning run 3 categorical, cal1, cal2 and cal3 One calibration run with one test heater y_cm, x_cm 12, 24 float, cm The centres of the square cells. The step is 1.667 cm heater_w run, y_cm, x_cm float64, W, covariate The power of the test heater: 10 W in one cell, 0 W in the other cells reading_c run, y_cm, x_cm float64, °C, target The thermocouple reading. Only 12 cells of each run have a value (36 readings in total). The other cells have no value (NaN)

The test heaters are at (5.8, 10.8) cm in cal1, (20.8, 5.8) cm in cal2 and (32.5, 14.2) cm in cal3. The twelve thermocouples are in the same cells in each run. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

The names of the dataset and of the model

The dataset uses the names y_cm, x_cm, heater_w and reading_c. The model uses the names y, x, heater_power and temperature. The data.bind block of the spec in step 4 connects them.

The simulated data of the model

--synthetic writes a smaller experiment on a 12 × 6 grid with the same true plate. Use it to try the steps quickly. The numbers in this tutorial are for the notebook's 24 × 12 grid.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e51 --synthetic --out heat_plate_small.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type heat_plate_e51 in Name. Type a description, for example "Calibration of the gradient plate: three 10 W test runs, twelve thermocouples".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select heat_plate_e51.nc.
  6. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows heater_w and reading_c on run, y_cm and x_cm.

7. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional). 8. Click Upload and ingest.

When the ingest run is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, reading_c has the role target and heater_w the role covariate. Missingness shows that most cells of reading_c have no value. This is correct: a cell without a thermocouple has no measured value, and the model uses only the 36 readings.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows reading_c and heater_w on the plate, 12 × 24 cells. The frame slider goes from run to run (3 runs).

  4. Compare the hot cells of reading_c with the heaters of heater_w in each run.
  5. Group comparison compares the 3 runs. The rows and the columns of the plate are not groups.
  6. The time sections are in Not for this data.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select heat_plate_e51. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type heat in the search field. Under Models, select Temperature of a heated plate (sci.heat_plate@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name heat-plate-e51 from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: heat-plate-e51
  project: engineering
data:
  dataset: dataset://engineering/heat_plate_e51@latest
  bind:
    dims: {run: run, y: y_cm, x: x_cm}
    vars: {heater_power: heater_w, temperature: reading_c}
model:
  use: sci.heat_plate@^1
  settings:
    thickness_mm: 5.0
    room_temperature: 20.0
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 51
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    engine: nutpie
    target_accept: 0.9
    keep: {log_likelihood: true}
evaluate:
  metrics: [elpd_loo]
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - core.pair
    - sci.field_map
    - sci.image_residuals

The settings of the plate come from challenges_settings(). The other settings keep their defaults, which are the priors of the notebook. This table tells what each setting means for the gradient plate:

Setting Value Meaning for this question thickness_mm 5 The thickness of the plate. The conduction term is k × thickness, so an error here moves k room_temperature 20 The temperature of the plate without heat. The model calculates the rise above this value use_insulation false (default) The calibration plate has no insulation. Set it to true only if the dataset has insulation(y, x) insulated_back_loss 0.1 (default) The back-face loss under insulation, as a part of the bare loss. It has no effect here k_median, k_log_sd 50, 0.5 (default) The prior of the conductivity in W/m/K: brass or aluminium alloys h_median, h_log_sd 10, 0.5 (default) The prior of the face loss in W/m²/K: natural convection and radiation h_edge_median, h_edge_log_sd 10, 0.7 (default) The prior of the edge loss. The data say little about it, so this prior has a large effect (step 6.2) eta_alpha, eta_beta 40, 4 (default) The Beta prior of the heater efficiency: most of the power goes into the plate sigma_scale 0.5 (default) The half-normal scale of the thermocouple noise in °C
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all three runs. Three runs leave no run for a hold-out in the spec. Without this line, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation"). The recipe in step 8 holds out one run.
  • The fit uses the sampler settings of the notebook: 4 chains of 1000 draws after 1000 tuning steps, target_accept 0.9 and the seed 51.
  • keep: {log_likelihood: true} keeps one log-likelihood value for each reading. Thus elpd_loo is available.

Type the bind block

Type the data.bind block. If you do not, the validator shows the errors "the model needs dim 'y', but the pipeline does not make it" and "the model needs variable 'heater_power', but the pipeline does not make it".

The plots

The model declares the five plots of outputs.plots. The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. The Plots section of the Insert panel adds a plot for you.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the NUTS progress. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://engineering/heat-plate-e51@v1. Click it.

The fit samples five numbers: k, h, h_edge, eta and sigma. For each draw, the model solves the heat equation of the 288 cells for each run. The model does this in the model graph, with gradients. The fit took 45 s in our test.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text:
On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

Open Overview to see the scorecard. The check "Few missing values" passes. The cells without a thermocouple have no measured value, but sci.heat_plate declares these NaN as part of the design of the data (structural_missing). Thus the check does not count them. The expert message names reading_c.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

  • R-hat is near 1.005. The bulk ESS is near 450 and the tail ESS is near 480. The ESS is low for 4000 draws, because k, h and eta are strongly correlated (step 6.2).
  • Expect no divergences. The notebook had 2 divergences with the PyMC sampler.
  • The Overview shows elpd_loo near 8.1. It has one term for each of the 36 readings. Use it to compare this spec with a spec that has different priors on the same data.

Open Plots on the model version page and select sci.image_residuals ("Residuals of field"). It has a slider for run. For each run it shows:

  • the readings (only the 12 cells with a thermocouple),
  • the mean field of the model,
  • the residual (reading − mean),
  • the normalised residual and its histogram against N(0, 1).

The residuals are less than about 0.4 °C. That is the size of two sd of the thermocouple noise (0.2 °C). The histogram has only 36 values, so do not expect a smooth curve.

docs.title: 6.2 What does the calibration tell you about the plate?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). These are the values that you can expect:

Parameter Notebook (mean ± sd, 89% interval) This fit (mean ± sd, 89% interval) True value k (W/m/K) 59.3 ± 2.8 (54.4 to 63.2) 59.1 ± 2.8 (54.2 to 63.1) 60 h (W/m²/K) 9.07 ± 0.44 (8.32 to 9.68) 9.04 ± 0.44 (8.23 to 9.66) 9 h_edge (W/m²/K) 6.8 ± 3.5 (2.4 to 13.3) 6.8 ± 3.5 (2.4 to 13.0) 15 eta 0.912 ± 0.042 (0.839 to 0.967) 0.908 ± 0.041 (0.836 to 0.966) 0.93 sigma (°C) 0.189 ± 0.023 0.189 ± 0.025 0.2 spread_length (cm) 12.9 (true plate) 12.8 ± 0.13 12.9

The Parameters view can show a different interval (for example an HDI). The means and the sd are the values to compare.

  • k, h and eta are known to about 5% and their intervals contain the true values.
  • They are strongly correlated. Open core.pair on the Plots tab. The pairs k–h, k–eta and h–eta lie on narrow diagonal lines. The run stores the correlations in the model version: 0.91, 0.96 and 0.95, the same as the notebook. A thermocouple measures a rise in temperature. The rise depends on ratios such as eta / k and eta / h. Thus a less efficient heater on a plate that conducts and loses less heat gives almost the same readings.
  • spread_length is very precise (± 1%), although k and h are not. It is sqrt(k δ / 2h), and the data fix the ratio k / h. It tells you how far the heat of a heater goes before the faces lose it: about 13 cm.
  • h_edge is almost not learned. Few thermocouples are near an edge. Its posterior is mostly the prior, and its 89% interval misses the true value of 15. This is the warning of the notebook: a weak parameter with a prior in the wrong place gives a range that looks correct but is wrong. The design must be robust to the edge loss, or a second experiment must put thermocouples near the edges.

docs.title: 6.3 The temperature fields
docs.text:
Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 1 output on a grid."

  • The slider run selects cal1, cal2 or cal3.
  • Mean shows the steady field of the run. Each test heater makes a hot spot of about 42 to 45 °C. The plate is near 20 °C at about 15 cm from the heater.
  • Std. dev. is largest at the heater and near the edges. The data fix the field less well there.
  • Draws and Play the draws show possible fields that agree with the readings.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one cell.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence R-hat near 1 and the trace of the five parameters core.posterior_forest Narrow intervals for k, h and eta. A wide interval for h_edge core.pair The diagonal ridges of k, h and eta sci.field_map The mean and the sd of the field for each run sci.image_residuals The residuals of the 36 readings (step 6.1)

docs.title: 6.4 Which heater layout?
docs.text:
The field is linear in the heater power. Thus the calibration predicts the field of any heater layout on the same plate. Step 7 scores two layouts of the notebook:

  • even_edges: six heaters spaced evenly along the two long edges.
  • greedy: the six heaters that the notebook's greedy search selects. Most of the power goes to the hot end.

Both layouts use the powers of the notebook (about 52 W in total). With the score result, you can calculate the RMS error of each layout against the target, over the working area and over the posterior draws (step 9). These are the results:

Layout Notebook RMS error, median (90th percentile) This model, median (90th percentile) even_edges 2.00 °C (2.02 °C) 2.00 °C (2.02 °C) greedy 1.43 °C (1.45 °C) 1.43 °C (1.46 °C)

In the left column of the working area, both layouts are about 3 °C warmer than the target. The largest error of the mean field is 5.0 °C for even_edges and 4.1 °C for greedy.

The decision. Use the greedy layout. Its error is about 30% smaller than that of the even layout, in almost all the plates that agree with the calibration. The range of the RMS error is narrow (1.43 to 1.46 °C). Thus the remaining error comes from the layout, not from the uncertainty about the plate. To make the cold end correct, add a cooler at the left edge. Another heater cannot help there.

docs.title: 7.1 Make a dataset of the layouts
docs.text:
The score needs a dataset with the heater power of each new layout on the same grid. Save this script as make_layouts.py in the folder of heat_plate_e51.nc. Then run it with uv run python make_layouts.py from that folder.

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
from mapi_plugin_science.export import write_export
from mapi_plugin_science.heat_plate_data import HEAT_SCHEMA

plate = xr.open_dataset("heat_plate_e51.nc")
x, y = plate["x_cm"].values, plate["y_cm"].values
layouts = {  # (x in cm, y in cm, power in W) of each heater
    "even_edges": [(14.2, 0.8, 1.7), (25.8, 0.8, 10.3), (34.2, 0.8, 14.0),
                   (14.2, 19.2, 1.7), (25.8, 19.2, 10.3), (34.2, 19.2, 14.0)],
    "greedy": [(29.2, 2.5, 9.8), (29.2, 17.5, 9.2), (35.8, 9.2, 6.6),
               (19.2, 19.2, 6.1), (19.2, 2.5, 5.7), (39.2, 10.8, 14.0)],
}
power = np.zeros((len(layouts), y.size, x.size))
for r, heaters in enumerate(layouts.values()):
    for hx, hy, watts in heaters:
        power[r, np.abs(y - hy).argmin(), np.abs(x - hx).argmin()] = watts
layout = xr.Dataset(
    {"heater_w": (("run", "y_cm", "x_cm"), power, {"units": "W"})},
    coords={"run": list(layouts), "y_cm": y, "x_cm": x},
)
schema = HEAT_SCHEMA.model_copy(update={"vars": {"heater_w": HEAT_SCHEMA.vars["heater_w"]}})
write_export(layout, "heater_layouts.nc", schema=schema)

Upload heater_layouts.nc as the dataset heater_layouts, as in step 3. The new runs need only heater_w. They have no measured temperatures.

docs.title: 7.2 Predict the layouts
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset.
  4. In Dataset, select dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest.
  5. Open Advanced. Type field in Variables (optional). Set Seed (optional) to 51. To calculate the RMS error over the draws (step 9), set Draws to 200.
  6. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each cell for the runs even_edges and greedy. The 90% interval of a cell in the working area is about 0.6 °C wide. The result can show the information note UNSEEN_LEVELS: the two runs are new levels of run. This is correct.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model has no forecast horizon, so the server refuses a request without a dataset ("the score request has no data"). A note under Values to score gives this reason. The dataset heat_plate_e51 gives the predictions of the calibration runs.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://engineering/heat-plate-e51@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "inputs_stage": "raw",
  "data": "dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 200,
    "units": "original",
    "names": "dataset",
    "vars": ["field"]
  },
  "seed": 51
}
  • "kind": "expected" gives the steady field without thermocouple noise. Use it to compare layouts.
  • "mode": "simulate" gives simulated thermocouple readings in all cells: the field plus noise with sd sigma. Use it to plan a test of the built plate.
  • spread_length is also an output. Add it to vars to get it.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same request.

docs.title: 8.1 Calibrate, then test a heater layout
docs.text:
The recipe sci_calibrate_then_design ("Calibrate a heated plate, then test a heater layout") does sections 2 and 3 of the notebook in one run:

  1. It holds out one calibration run and fits the other runs.
  2. It scores the run that the fit did not see, then fits all the runs again.
  3. It shows the parameters and the residual maps.
  4. A decision: is the RMSE on the hold-out run at most Max error (0.5 °C), and is R-hat at most Max rhat (1.01)?
  5. If yes, it predicts the field of the new layouts and draws it with sci.field_map.
  6. It writes a report.

The recipe page sends only one dataset. Thus first run it on the calibration data:

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Calibrate a heated plate, then test a heater layout and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select heat_plate_e51 in Dataset.

  4. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). In Bind, type:

    {"dims": {"run": "run", "y": "y_cm", "x": "x_cm"},
 "vars": {"heater_power": "heater_w", "temperature": "reading_c"}}

  5. Click Run this recipe.

Without a layout, the design step predicts the three calibration runs. To predict the layouts of step 7, run the workflow again with a second dataset:

  1. Open Workflows and the workflow that the recipe made.
  2. Click Run workflow. The dialog "Run revision 1" opens.
  3. In Data for data, select heat_plate_e51. In Data for layout (optional), select heater_layouts.
  4. In Parameters, type the same JSON in Bind.
  5. Click Start run.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. These are the results with the defaults (seed 51):

  • The split holds out cal1. The RMSE on cal1 is 0.12 °C, and all its readings are in the 90% range (coverage_90 1.0).
  • The parameters are the same as in step 6.2: k 59.2 ± 2.8, h 9.05 ± 0.44, h_edge 6.9 ± 3.7 and R-hat below 1.003.
  • Decisions shows "Is the calibration good enough?" with the arm then: "The calibration predicted the run that it did not see within the error limit, and the sampler converged."
  • Outputs has the field map of even_edges and greedy, and the report.

Note

The recipe fits the model two times (evaluate_then_refit). With the defaults, it takes about ten minutes.

docs.title: 8.2 Other recipes
docs.text:
• bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws. Type sci.heat_plate@^1 in Model. In Fine-tune, type the settings of step 4 as JSON in Settings and the same Bind. The prior draws of this model are on the sensors, and the observed data is on the grid. Thus the prior plot of the audit fails, and the audit continues without it. The recovery check refits the model N sims times (20 by default), so it takes much longer than one fit.
  • sci_image_model_check compares the predicted images with the observed image. It runs on this model, but the plate has readings in only 12 of 288 cells. Thus its residual maps are almost empty. Use sci.image_residuals of step 6.1.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/engineering

# get the data and the suggested spec
uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e51 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out heat_plate_e51.nc --spec heat_plate_e51.yaml
uv run python make_layouts.py   # the script of step 7.1

# upload, check and fit on the platform
mapi datasets upload heat_plate_e51.nc --name heat_plate_e51
mapi datasets upload heater_layouts.nc --name heater_layouts
mapi check heat-plate-e51.yaml --remote @
mapi fit heat-plate-e51.yaml --remote @
mapi explore model model://engineering/heat-plate-e51@v1 -s params -s diagnostics -s fields

# predict the two layouts
cat > layouts-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://engineering/heat-plate-e51@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 200, vars: [field]}
seed: 51
EOF
mapi score layouts-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o layouts.zarr.zip

# the recipe
mapi workflows init sci_calibrate_then_design --name heat-plate-design
mapi workflows apply heat-plate-design.yaml -m "E51 calibration and design"
mapi workflows run heat-plate-design \
  -i data=dataset://engineering/heat_plate_e51@latest \
  -i layout=dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest \
  -p bind='{"dims": {"run": "run", "y": "y_cm", "x": "x_cm"}, "vars": {"heater_power": "heater_w", "temperature": "reading_c"}}' \
  --watch

heat-plate-e51.yaml is the spec of step 4. The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

import numpy as np
from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/engineering")
for path, name in [("heat_plate_e51.nc", "heat_plate_e51"),
                   ("heater_layouts.nc", "heater_layouts")]:
    version = api.datasets.upload(path, dataset=name)
    print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("heat-plate-e51.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "heat-plate-e51")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://engineering/heat-plate-e51@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest",
        "output": {"kind": "expected", "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
                   "draws": 200, "vars": ["field"]},
        "seed": 51,
    },
)
field = result.tree["draws"]["field"]  # (sample, run, y_cm, x_cm), needs the `xarray` extra
x, y = field["x_cm"], field["y_cm"]
work = (x >= 5) & (x <= 35) & (y >= 3) & (y <= 17)
target = 30 + 40 * (x - 5) / 30
rms = np.sqrt(((field - target) ** 2).where(work).mean(["y_cm", "x_cm"]))
print(rms.median("sample").round(2).values)           # about [2.00, 1.43]
print(rms.quantile(0.9, "sample").round(2).values)    # about [2.02, 1.46]

bind = {"dims": {"run": "run", "y": "y_cm", "x": "x_cm"},
        "vars": {"heater_power": "heater_w", "temperature": "reading_c"}}
wf = api.workflows.create(template="sci_calibrate_then_design")
wrun = api.workflows.run(
    wf.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://engineering/heat_plate_e51@latest",
            "layout": "dataset://engineering/heater_layouts@latest"},
    params={"bind": bind},
    wait=True,
)
print(wrun.status, wrun.decisions)

The CLI and the client send the same spec and the same score request as the web app.

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the physics, the priors and the calibration of notebook section 2. It also gives the predicted fields that section 3 compares. It leaves out these parts:

  • The search for the heater layout (section 3). The notebook tries the 144 candidate cells in the frame and adds heaters one at a time. This is a greedy search with constrained least squares over 60 posterior draws. The platform does not search. You give the layouts, and the model predicts them. This tutorial uses the sites and the powers that the notebook found.
  • The comparison with the plug-in design. The notebook also designs against the posterior mean only and gets the same layout. To do this check, score the layout with the mean values of the parameters in your own code.
  • Insulation (section 4). The model has use_insulation and insulated_back_loss. Thus it can predict a layout with insulation strips, but it does not select the strips. The notebook's disturbances (a room that drifts, air currents and heaters that age) are not in the model.
  • Sensors and feedback (section 5). The controller, the Bayesian estimate of the disturbances and the greedy placement of the sensors are not in the platform.
  • The time to warm up (section 6). The model is steady state. It has no heat capacity, so it does not give the 74 minutes that the notebook calculates.
  • The true plate. The notebook compares its designs on the true plate. The platform knows only the posterior. Use heat_plate_data.HEAT_TRUTH and heat_plate.steady_rise() in Python to do the same.

Next steps:

  • Add thermocouples near the edges to the calibration and fit again. Does h_edge become correct? (Notebook "Try it yourself", items 1 and 2.)
  • Score a layout with insulation: add a bool insulation(y_cm, x_cm) to the dataset and set use_insulation: true.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the recipe.

docs.title: E58 STORM localisation microscopy
docs.text:
This tutorial does the main part of the pymc-challenges notebook E58_storm_localization_microscopy.py in the web app. You use the model sci.storm_localisation@1. You do not write PyMC code. The model reads the raw camera frames, finds the isolated spots and gives the position of each molecule with an error bar in nm.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project microscopy. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads one file from its data/ directory.
  • About 20 minutes. On a laptop, the fit of 200 spots took less than 2 minutes with nutpie.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A light microscope cannot separate two points that are closer than about 250 nm. This is the diffraction limit. A single fluorescent molecule shows as a blob of about that width: the point spread function (PSF). Single-molecule localisation microscopy (STORM, PALM and dSTORM) uses molecules that blink. In each camera frame, only a small number of molecules are bright, and they are far apart. The centre of an isolated blob is much more precise than its width. The positions of all the blinks make a super-resolved image.

The notebook uses 2,000 raw frames of a dSTORM recording of the synaptic protein Unc-13 at a Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Dannhäuser et al. 2022). Each frame is a 40 × 40 pixel crop with 127 nm pixels and an exposure of 10 ms. The camera is an EMCCD. The notebook asks these questions:

  1. What does the camera do to the photons? (Notebook section 1: the photon-transfer curve.)
  2. Where is each molecule, and how sure are we? (Notebook sections 2 and 3.)
  3. How precise can a position be? (Notebook section 4: the Cramér-Rao bound.)
  4. Is a blob one molecule or more? (Notebook sections 5 and 6.)
  5. How do we make an image from uncertain points? (Notebook section 7.)
  6. How many molecules made a cluster of blinks? (Notebook section 8.)

The notebook ends in this decision for the real recording: keep each localisation with an error bar of less than 30 nm, and draw each one as a Gaussian with its own error bar. On the real frames, a model with a Gaussian PSF on a flat background adds faint emitters around bright spots. The evidence for the number of emitters is only as good as the forward model. Thus the notebook does not trust the emitter counts of bright blobs. The notebook keeps 4,506 of 8,342 localisations, with a median error bar of 9.5 nm and a median of about 2,300 photons. One isolated spot (blob 12 in frame 5) has a position error of about 7 nm.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The dataset microscopy/dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm: the raw frames in ADU Section 1: the raw frames The camera calibration as two settings (offset_adu, scale_adu) Section 1: the photon-transfer curve The posterior of the position, photons, background and PSF sd of 200 isolated spots (Parameters) Section 3: one spot in PyMC, here for 200 spots in one model The positions with 90% error ellipses over the super-resolved image (Plots, sci.point_pattern) Section 7: the render with each error bar The data, the fit and the residuals of each spot (Plots, sci.image_residuals) Section 3: the residuals of one spot The positions in nm with a 90% interval for each spot (Score) Section 3: the position in nm A comparison of a flat and a sloped background by elpd_loo "Try it yourself", item 1

The port does not do sections 4, 5, 6 and 8. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm_roi.npz and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. It does these steps:

  • It keeps the 2,000 frames of 40 × 40 pixels as integers in ADU (the camera units).
  • It numbers the frames, rows and columns from 0, as the notebook does.
  • It calculates the camera calibration from the photon-transfer curve of the full 200 × 200 field, as notebook section 1 does. The file keeps the result in its attributes.

Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e58 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out unc13_dstorm.nc --spec unc13_dstorm.yaml

The command writes:

wrote unc13_dstorm.nc (variables frames on frame=2000, row=40, col=40)
upload it as dataset microscopy/dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm and fit sci.storm_localisation
wrote the suggested spec to unc13_dstorm.yaml

The file holds one dataset of about 13 MB:

Name Dims Type Meaning frame 2000 integer, fixed The camera frames, 0 to 1999 row, col 40, 40 integer, fixed The camera pixels of the crop, 0 to 39 frames frame, row, col int32, ADU, target The raw camera counts. The values are from 783 to 40,176

The attributes of the file keep the constants of the recording:

Attribute Value Meaning pixel_nm 127 The size of one camera pixel in the sample (nm) offset_adu 457.04 The camera offset (ADU) from the photon-transfer curve scale_adu 13.86 ADU for each effective count. This is twice the EM gain of 6.93 ADU for each photon exposure_s 0.01 The exposure of one frame (s) first_frame, roi_row, roi_col 3000, 25, 50 The position of the crop in the full recording

The attribute mapi_schema gives the variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes a movie that the model's own forward model simulates: 60 frames of 24 × 24 pixels with known blinks, on the camera of the real recording (offset 457 ADU, gain 6.9). Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real frames. For the simulated movie, use the settings of STORM_SPEC_YAML in mapi_plugin_science.storm_data.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e58 --synthetic --out storm_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm in Name. Type a description, for example "Raw dSTORM frames of Unc-13 at a Drosophila synapse, 2,000 frames of 40 × 40 pixels".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select unc13_dstorm.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows frames on frame, row and col.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, frames has the role target and the units ADU. The three dims are integer and fixed. Missingness shows no missing values. The model needs each pixel of each frame.

The file is a plain dataset, not a tree. Do not open "Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)".

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows frames, the camera images of 40 × 40 pixels. The frame slider shows 24 of the 2,000 frames.

  4. The line below the image covers all 2,000 frames: the mean, the minimum and the maximum of each frame. A peak of the maximum is a frame with a bright spot (a molecule that blinks).
  5. The histogram shows the values of all pixels. Most pixels show only the background.
  6. The time sections are in Not for this data. The frame number is a list of images, not a time dim of the schema.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type storm in the search field. Under Models, select Molecule positions in STORM images (sci.storm_localisation@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name unc13-dstorm-localisation from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: unc13-dstorm-localisation
  project: microscopy
data:
  dataset: dataset://microscopy/dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm@latest
model:
  use: sci.storm_localisation@^1
  settings:
    pixel_nm: 127.0
    offset_adu: 457.04184713091655
    scale_adu: 13.861648333299126
    kind: flat
    max_spots: 200
    threshold_sd: 5
    smooth_px: 1
    patch_px: 11
    photons_median: 1500
    psf_sd_px: 1.0
    position_sd_px: 2
    score_draws: 40
    ppc_draws: 20
    render_px_nm: 16
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 58
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    engine: nutpie
    keep:
      log_likelihood: true
evaluate:
  metrics: [elpd_loo, rmse, mae, coverage_90]
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - sci.point_pattern
    - sci.image_residuals
    - sci.field_map

The settings pixel_nm, offset_adu, scale_adu and max_spots come from the suggested spec of the export (unc13_dstorm.yaml). Copy the two camera values with all their digits. With 457.04 and 13.86, the detector finds 4,193 blobs, not the 4,192 of the notebook. The spec adds some defaults so that you can see them. This table tells what each setting means for this recording:

Setting Value Meaning for this question pixel_nm 127.0 The pixel size in the sample. The model gives all positions and the PSF sd in nm offset_adu, scale_adu 457.04, 13.86 The camera calibration of notebook section 1. The model changes ADU to effective counts: (ADU − 457.04) / 13.86. These counts are Poisson with a mean of half the photons. Set the two values together kind flat One background value in each patch, as in the notebook. plane adds a slope in x and y (notebook "Try it yourself", item 1) max_spots 200 The number of isolated spots to fit, evenly spaced in frame order. The notebook fits one spot with NUTS threshold_sd, smooth_px 5, 1 The detector of notebook section 3: smooth each frame with a Gaussian of 1 px and keep the regions above 5 robust noise sds patch_px 11 Each spot gets a patch of 11 × 11 pixels (1.4 µm). The value must be odd photons_median 1500 The prior median of the photons of a spot, as in the notebook. The prior sd on the log scale is 1 (photons_log_sd) psf_sd_px 1.0 The prior median of the PSF sd: one pixel (127 nm), with a log sd of 0.2. A 1.49 NA objective at 670 nm gives about this width position_sd_px 2 The prior sd of the position around the centre of the detected blob (px) score_draws 40 The posterior draws that each score uses, and the draws of the render ppc_draws 20 The predictive patch draws that the fit keeps for sci.image_residuals render_px_nm 16 The pixel size of the super-resolved image render. The render is 318 × 318 pixels
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all of the frames. The model has no split, because the detector needs each frame. Without this line, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation"). The suggested spec of the export does not have this line, so add it.
  • engine: nutpie is the sampler of the notebook. The default engine of the model is pymc. It gives the same posterior, but it is slower.
  • keep.log_likelihood: true keeps the pointwise log likelihood of each patch pixel. The fit then calculates elpd_loo. You need it to compare flat and plane (step 6.5).
  • The fit does not calculate rmse, mae and coverage_90, because there is no holdout. The Evaluate score of step 7.2 uses them.

Settings that the validator does not check

Validate checks the type and the range of each setting. It does not check the rules between settings. For example, offset_adu without scale_adu, or an even patch_px, is valid in the editor. The fit then stops at once with SETTINGS_INVALID, before the detector starts.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the steps of the fit. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://microscopy/unc13-dstorm-localisation@v1. Click it.

The first progress message tells you what the detector found: "200 spots of 4192 blobs selected". The detector finds 4,192 blobs, as in the notebook. 1,503 of them are isolated in their patch and have 13 to 39 pixels. The fit uses 200 of the isolated blobs. Then nutpie samples the 1,000 parameters (5 for each spot) in one model. The last message is "posterior ready".

After the fit, the run calculates the plots and the explorer views. You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

The warning EVALUATION_VIEW_FAILED

After the fit, the run tries to score all 2,000 frames for the plots of the predictions. That score has more than 50 million values, so the model refuses it. The run shows the warning EVALUATION_VIEW_FAILED, and the fit is correct. The four plots of the spec do not need that score. The fit stores the super-resolved image and the patch draws in the model version.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

Expect these results:

Code Value Message RHAT 1.018 "The independent sampler runs do not agree about 'logN'. Its estimates are not reliable at this time." ESS_BULK 426 "There are enough effective draws for stable averages." ESS_TAIL 389 "There is too little independent information about 'logs' (about 389 effective draws). The intervals are not stable." DIVERGENCES 0 "The sampler had no problems with the model." PARETO_K_HIGH 47 "Some data points have a strong effect on the model, so the leave-one-out score is only approximate."

The warnings are for three of the 200 spots: 18, 56 and 66. On the Plots tab, the caption of core.convergence says "16 of 2000 parameters have not converged". It names photons[66], logN[66] and x[66]. Spot 66 is the brightest spot, with about 9,800 photons, and its error bar is 24 nm. A blob this bright is possibly two molecules (notebook section 7). Most of the other spots have a bulk ESS of more than 1,000. If you want fewer warnings, fit with tune: 2000.

The model has its own check, PATCH_MISFIT. It shows when the Pearson χ² for each patch pixel is more than 1.5 at the posterior mean. The flat model does not show it on this recording.

docs.title: 6.2 What did the model learn?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The posterior has these variables, each with one value for each spot:

Variable Meaning x_px, y_px The position in the patch (px). These are the parameters of the notebook table logN, logb, logs The log of the photons, of the background and of the PSF sd (px) x, y The position in the movie (nm): the column or row number times pixel_nm photons The photons that the molecule emitted in the frame background The background at the centre of the patch (photons for each pixel) psf_sd The PSF sd (nm)

The table shows the posterior mean, the sd and the 90% interval of each value. It has 2,000 rows, so it does not show all of them. The summary of the 200 spots:

Quantity This fit Notebook Blobs found by the detector 4,192 4,192 EM gain (ADU for each photon) 6.93 6.9 Median background (photons for each pixel) 115 about 110 Median PSF sd 137 nm 125 nm for blob 12 Median photons of a spot 2,862 about 2,300 (the 4,506 kept localisations) Median error bar of a position 7.5 nm 9.5 nm (the 4,506 kept localisations) Spots with an error bar of less than 30 nm 198 of 200 (99%) 4,506 of 8,342 (54%)

The error bar of a spot is the posterior sd of x and y (the root mean square of the two). The fit uses only isolated blobs of 13 to 39 pixels. These are brighter and cleaner than the localisations of the notebook, which include the faint extra emitters of the count model. Thus the median error bar is smaller, and almost all spots pass the 30 nm filter.

docs.title: 6.3 The plots
docs.text:
On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence R-hat near 1. Some warnings for faint spots (step 6.1) sci.point_pattern Each dot is one spot at its posterior mean, with an ellipse that has the true position with 90% probability. The background is the mean of render. Small ellipses are bright spots. A large ellipse is a spot that you must not trust sci.image_residuals For each spot: the observed patch, the mean of 20 predictive draws, the residual and the normalised residual. The normalised residual must look like noise. A ring or a second peak shows a second molecule or a wrong PSF sci.field_map The mean and the sd of render, the super-resolved image of the 200 spots. The sd is high where the positions are not certain

Use the slider or Play in sci.image_residuals to see each spot. In this fit, the caption says: "The normalised residuals have an sd of 1.07 and 6% are outside ±2." A perfect model gives 1 and 5%. Thus the flat Gaussian model is close for these isolated spots. The caption of sci.point_pattern says: "The median sd of a coordinate is 7.25."

The Fields section

The Model Explorer section Fields shows the grid outputs of a model. For this model, it needs an in-sample score of the full movie, and the model refuses that score (the note in step 5). If Fields shows "The server cannot calculate this view for this data or model.", use the plots sci.field_map and sci.image_residuals. They show the same outputs from the model version.

docs.title: 6.4 The decision
docs.text:
The decision. Keep each localisation with an error bar of less than 30 nm. Draw each one as a Gaussian with its own error bar. Do not use the count of molecules in a bright blob.

To make the decision from these outputs:

  1. Score x and y with their sd (step 7.1). The error bar of a spot is √((sd_x² + sd_y²) / 2).
  2. Remove the spots with an error bar of 30 nm or more. In this fit, two spots go (spots 40 and 54, with 47 nm and 74 nm).
  3. Look at sci.point_pattern. The large ellipses are the spots that the filter removes.
  4. Look at the residuals of the brightest spots in sci.image_residuals. If you see a ring or a slope in the residual, the flat Gaussian model does not describe the spot. Then fit kind: plane (step 6.5) or remove the spot.

The render render is the mean of 40 posterior draws of the positions. Thus a spot with a large error bar spreads over many pixels and is faint. That is the image of notebook section 7.

docs.title: 6.5 One spot as in the notebook, and a sloped background
docs.text:
One spot. To fit the spot of notebook section 3 (blob 12 in frame 5), save a copy of the spec as unc13-one-spot and change two settings:

    max_spots: 1
    amplitude_band: [0.45, 0.55]

amplitude_band keeps the isolated blobs whose amplitude is between the 45% and 55% quantiles: a typical spot. The fit takes some seconds. These are the results:

Parameter This fit Notebook x_px 4.460 ± 0.053 4.461 ± 0.056 y_px 4.399 ± 0.052 4.399 ± 0.053 sd of x, y 6.8 nm, 6.7 nm 7.1 nm, 6.7 nm photons 2,161 2,157 background 112 112 psf_sd 125 nm 125 nm

R-hat is 1.002 and there are no divergences.

A sloped background. Fit the spec again with kind: plane and compare the two versions by elpd_loo (Compare on the model version page). Both versions use the same 200 patches. On this recording, the plane model does not converge with the default gradient_sd (R-hat 1.76) and it shows PATCH_MISFIT. Its elpd_loo is lower (−94,436 against −85,943). Keep kind: flat for these isolated spots.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
A score uses only the spots that the fit found. It cannot find spots in new frames. Each score also makes frames_hat, the camera image of each scored frame. For all 2,000 frames, frames_hat has more than 50 million values, and the model refuses the score with PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE. Thus you score a short part of the movie.

Make a dataset with the first 100 frames. Run this Python script in the directory of the export:

import xarray as xr
from mapi_plugin_science import storm_data
from mapi_plugin_science.export import write_export

ds = xr.load_dataset("unc13_dstorm.nc")
window = ds.isel(frame=slice(0, 100)).copy()
window.attrs.pop("mapi_schema", None)  # write_export adds the schema again
write_export(window, "unc13_dstorm_first100.nc", schema=storm_data.STORM_SCHEMA)

Upload unc13_dstorm_first100.nc as the dataset unc13_dstorm_first100, as in step 3.

docs.title: 7.1 The positions with their error bars
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select unc13_dstorm_first100 in Dataset.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 58. Type x, y, photons, psf_sd in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each output for each of the 200 spots. The frames of the dataset do not change these values. For example, spot 0 is at x = 2,386 nm (90% interval 2,379 to 2,389 nm) with 4,975 photons.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model cannot forecast, so a request without a dataset has no forecast horizon, and the server refuses it. A note under Values to score gives this reason. Do not select the full movie dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm. The model then refuses the score with PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://microscopy/unc13-dstorm-localisation@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://microscopy/unc13_dstorm_first100@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "sd", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["x", "y", "photons", "psf_sd"]
  },
  "seed": 58
}

The sd of x and y gives the error bar of step 6.4. To get the camera image of the fit, type frames_hat in Variables (optional). Set Quantity to Predictive to add Poisson noise to the background and to the patches.

docs.title: 7.2 Evaluate the fit on the frames
docs.text:
1. In What do you want to do?, select Evaluate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select unc13_dstorm_first100.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive and Seed (optional) to 58.
  4. Click Evaluate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://microscopy/unc13-dstorm-localisation@latest",
  "mode": "evaluate",
  "data": "dataset://microscopy/unc13_dstorm_first100@latest",
  "output": {"kind": "predictive"},
  "seed": 58
}

The metrics compare frames_hat with the frames of the dataset. In this fit: rmse 469 ADU, mae 138 ADU and coverage_90 0.81. Spots that the fit did not use are misfit, because the model shows only the background there. Thus the coverage is less than 0.9. Use the metrics to compare two fits of the same frames, not as a measure of one spot.

  • The model has no simulate mode. To make new frames from known blinks, use storm_data.simulate_storm() in Python.
  • If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_image_model_check (Image model check) is for models that predict an image. It fits the model, makes the residual maps and the image grid, does a posterior predictive check and writes a report.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Image model check and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.storm_localisation@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set these values:
    • Settings: the settings of step 4 as JSON, for example {"pixel_nm": 127.0, "offset_adu": 457.04184713091655, "scale_adu": 13.861648333299126, "max_spots": 200}.
    • Draws 1000, Tune 1000 and Seed 58.
    • Var: patch_fit. The image check is for the fitted patches, one image for each spot.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs shows the parameter table, the plots sci.image_residuals and sci.ppc_image_grid of patch_fit, and the report.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does all the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws: prior predictive draws, a convergence gate, the posterior predictive check, sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Run it in the same way with the model sci.storm_localisation@^1. The gate needs the largest R-hat below Rhat max (1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above Min ess (400). The R-hat of logN in step 6 is 1.018, so the default gate stops the audit before the checks. Increase Draws and Tune, or make the gate less strict.

The posterior predictive check of a long movie

If a step of a recipe scores all 2,000 frames, the model refuses it with PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE. Then run the recipe on a shorter movie. A dataset of the first 500 frames is below the limit with score_draws: 40. Make it with the script of step 7 and slice(0, 500).

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/microscopy
mapi datasets upload unc13_dstorm.nc --name dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm
mapi datasets upload unc13_dstorm_first100.nc --name unc13_dstorm_first100
mapi check unc13-dstorm-localisation.yaml --remote @   # the server's static validation
mapi fit unc13-dstorm-localisation.yaml --remote @     # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model unc13-dstorm-localisation -s params -s diagnostics

cat > storm-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://microscopy/unc13-dstorm-localisation@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://microscopy/unc13_dstorm_first100@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, sd, hdi_90], vars: [x, y, photons, psf_sd]}
seed: 58
EOF
mapi score storm-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o storm.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_image_model_check --name storm-check
mapi workflows apply storm-check.yaml -m "E58 image check"
mapi workflows run storm-check \
  -i data=dataset://microscopy/dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm@latest \
  -p model=sci.storm_localisation@^1 -p var=patch_fit \
  -p 'settings={"pixel_nm": 127.0, "offset_adu": 457.04184713091655, "scale_adu": 13.861648333299126, "max_spots": 200}' \
  -p seed=58 --watch

For a local check without the server, export the data as a zarr zip (--out unc13_dstorm.zarr.zip). Then mapi check unc13-dstorm-localisation.yaml --data unc13_dstorm.zarr.zip validates the spec against the schema of the file.

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

import numpy as np
from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/microscopy")
api.datasets.upload("unc13_dstorm.nc", dataset="dannhauser2022_unc13_dstorm")
api.datasets.upload("unc13_dstorm_first100.nc", dataset="unc13_dstorm_first100")

with open("unc13-dstorm-localisation.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "unc13-dstorm-localisation")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://microscopy/unc13-dstorm-localisation@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://microscopy/unc13_dstorm_first100@latest",
        "output": {"summary": ["mean", "sd"], "vars": ["x", "y"]},
        "seed": 58,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
sd_x = summary["x"].sel(stat="sd").values
sd_y = summary["y"].sel(stat="sd").values
error_nm = np.sqrt((sd_x**2 + sd_y**2) / 2)
keep = error_nm < 30  # the quality filter of the notebook
print(f"{keep.sum()} of {keep.size} spots pass, median error {np.median(error_nm):.1f} nm")

api.datasets.upload also takes an xr.Dataset. Thus you can upload the 100-frame window of step 7 without a file: api.datasets.upload(window, dataset="unc13_dstorm_first100").

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the camera model of notebook sections 1 and 2 and the Bayesian localisation of section 3, for many spots at once. It leaves out these parts:

  • The photon-transfer curve of the full field. The recording has no dark frames. The notebook fits the curve on the statistics of the full 200 × 200 field.
