The export does the same and gives the result as offset_adu and scale_adu. If you do not set them, the model fits the curve on the 40 × 40 crop. The crop is over one bright structure, so that calibration is less good.
  • The simulated camera check (section 2). The package tests of the plugin do the same check.
  • The least squares and maximum likelihood fits, and the Cramér-Rao bound (section 4). The model gives only the Bayesian posterior.
  • The emitter count (sections 5 and 6). The model fits one emitter in each patch. It uses only isolated blobs of 13 to 39 pixels. It does not do the Laplace evidence, the SMC check or the comparison with a simple threshold at two densities.
  • The Laplace fit of all spots (section 7). The notebook localises all 8,342 spots with a Laplace approximation. The model samples up to max_spots (at most 5,000) isolated spots with NUTS.
  • The Fourier ring correlation (section 7). The platform does not calculate it.
  • The count of molecules from their blinks (section 8). The platform does not have the negative-binomial blink model.

Next steps:

  • Fit the spec again with max_spots: 1000 and compare the share of spots with an error bar of less than 30 nm.
  • Fit the simulated movie of step 2 (--synthetic). In Python, storm_data.simulate_storm() returns the same movie and its true blinks, so you can measure the error of each position.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.

docs.title: E60 traction force microscopy
docs.text:
This tutorial does the real-data part of the pymc-challenges notebook E60_traction_force_microscopy.py in the web app. You use the model sci.traction_force@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project biophysics. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads one file from its data/ directory.
  • Some time for the fit. The model estimates three minutes of sandbox time. On a busy laptop, our fit took 45 minutes.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A cell on a soft gel pulls on the gel surface. Beads in the gel move. Traction force microscopy (TFM) calculates the forces of the cell from the bead movement. This is an inverse problem: many force maps agree with the measured movement. Thus each TFM method adds an assumption. In a Bayesian model, that assumption is the prior.

The notebook asks two questions about a colony of 7 cells on a 49 kPa gel (pyTFM example data, Bauer et al. 2021):

  1. Which prior on the traction field do the data support? (Notebook section 7.)
  2. How hard does the colony pull, with an honest range? The notebook reports the strain energy (fJ) and the contractility (µN), and compares them with pyTFM. (Notebook section 8.)

The decision at the end of the notebook is this: use the Matérn prior, and report the strain energy and the contractility with a range that includes the uncertainty of the gel stiffness. The range from the displacement noise alone is less than 1%. A 15% error in Young's modulus moves the forces by about −21% to +25%.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The posterior of the noise sd and of the three Matérn hyperparameters (Parameters) Section 7, the ML-II fits and the full-Bayes fit of section 8 The NOISE_SPECTRUM_MISMATCH diagnostic (Diagnostics) Section 7, the right panel of the spectrum plot Traction maps with mean, sd and draws (Fields, sci.vector_field) Section 8, the map of the posterior mean and the map of mean ÷ sd strain_energy and contractility with a 90% range (Score) Section 8, the table of numbers A second fit with young_cv: 0.15 Section 8, the row "Matérn posterior, E ± 15%"

Notebook sections 1 to 6 use a simulated cell with known forces. The port does not repeat them. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads pytfm_colony_ko04.npz and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. Run it from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e60 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out pytfm_colony.nc --spec pytfm_colony.yaml

The command writes:

wrote pytfm_colony.nc (variables displacement, force_mask on component=2, row=189, col=193)
upload it as dataset biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04 and fit sci.traction_force
wrote the suggested spec to pytfm_colony.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning component 2 categorical, x and y The direction of the displacement row, col 189, 193 integer The PIV grid. y goes along row, x along col displacement component, row, col float64, µm, target The PIV displacement of the gel surface force_mask row, col bool, mask The region that pyTFM sums the forces over (7,218 pixels)

The attributes of the file keep the gel constants: grid_um 2.117, young_pa 49000, poisson 0.49, thickness_um 300 and piv_window_um 20. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes simulated data from the model's own prior: a 32 × 32 grid with a known traction field. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real colony.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e60 --synthetic --out tfm_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type pytfm_colony_ko04 in Name. Type a description, for example "PIV displacement under a colony of 7 cells, 49 kPa gel".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select pytfm_colony.nc.
  6. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows displacement on component, row and col, and force_mask on row and col.
  7. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  8. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, displacement has the role target and force_mask the role mask. Missingness must show no missing values: the model needs a value at each pixel.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows displacement as a vector field: the colour shows the magnitude, and the arrows show the direction. The grid has 189 × 193 cells. The viewer shows the mean of blocks of cells (95 × 97).

  4. The mask force_mask (the colony) shows as a layer.
  5. The histogram of each component (x and y) is below the viewer.
  6. Most other sections are in Not for this data. The data is one field, without time and without groups.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select pytfm_colony_ko04. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type traction in the search field. Under Models, select Cell forces from gel movement (sci.traction_force@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: pytfm-colony-traction
  project: biophysics
data:
  dataset: dataset://biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04@latest
model:
  use: sci.traction_force@^1
  settings:
    grid_um: 2.117341064232256
    young_pa: 49000.0
    poisson: 0.49
    young_cv: 0.0
    prior: matern
    noise_um: 0.003
    traction_pa: 1000.0
    lengthscale_um: 20.0
    field_draws: 200
    force_mask: true
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 60
    tune: 1000
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - sci.vector_field

The settings come from challenges_settings() (the --spec file of the export has the same values). This table tells what each one means for the colony:

Setting Value Meaning for this question grid_um 2.117 The PIV step in µm (20 µm windows that move by 2.1 µm). It sets the wavenumbers young_pa 49000 Young's modulus of the gel. The tractions scale exactly with it poisson 0.49 The Poisson ratio of the gel (almost incompressible) young_cv 0 The relative error of young_pa. 0 gives the notebook row "E known". Step 6.4 uses 0.15 prior matern The prior spectrum of the tractions. Section 7 of the notebook selects it. white is Tikhonov and smooth is a squared exponential noise_um 0.003 The prior median of the noise sd: 3 nm. The notebook found 3.4 nm traction_pa 1000 The prior median of the traction scale in Pa lengthscale_um 20 The prior median of the Matérn length scale, near the PIV window. The notebook found 23 µm field_draws 200 The number of traction fields that each score draws. The notebook also uses 200 force_mask true Sum the strain energy and the contractility inside force_mask only, as pyTFM does
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all of the data. The model needs the full raster, so it has no split. Without this line, the validator shows the note SPLIT_INVALID ("there is no holdout for the evaluation").
  • The spec has no evaluate block. Without a split, the fit skips the metrics rmse and mae ("no data.split is declared").
  • The model has no pointwise log likelihood, so elpd_loo is not available.

The plots

The model declares core.convergence, core.posterior_forest and sci.vector_field. The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots, so the spec names them. The Plots section of the Insert panel adds a plot for you.

Do not add sci.field_map. For the traction field, that recipe needs the settings y and x, and the fit skips it with the warning PLOT_SKIPPED. The Fields section of the Model Explorer shows the same maps.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the NUTS progress. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://biophysics/pytfm-colony-traction@v1. Click it.

The fit samples only 4 numbers (noise_sd, traction_sd, lengthscale and smoothness). The model integrates the traction field out, with one closed-form likelihood for each of the 72,952 Fourier modes. Each gradient uses all modes, so the fit takes some minutes. After the fit, the run calculates the plots and the explorer views. For these it draws 200 traction fields.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

  • R-hat and ESS are for the 4 hyperparameters. Our fit had a largest R-hat of 1.003, a smallest bulk ESS of 1,205 and no divergent transitions.
  • Expect the warning NOISE_SPECTRUM_MISMATCH. The plain message is "The noise in the displacements is not the same at all scales. The ranges of the tractions are possibly too narrow."

The warning is correct, and the notebook finds the same problem. Neighbour PIV vectors come from windows that overlap by 90%. Thus their errors are correlated, and the finest Fourier modes have much less power than white noise gives. The diagnostic compares the two in the finest quarter of the modes. A value below 0.5 starts the warning. Our fit gave 0.33. The consequence: the ranges with E known are too narrow. Use them only to compare priors, not as the error bar of the colony.

Fit vs actual compares displacement_hat with the PIV field. The fit is almost exact. A small residual is not a sign of a good model here, because many force maps give the same displacement.

docs.title: 6.2 Which prior do the data support?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned").

Parameter Mean 89% interval Notebook (ML-II) noise_sd (µm) 0.00335 0.00331 to 0.00339 3.4 nm traction_sd (Pa) 1,799 1,495 to 2,191 not given lengthscale (µm) 23.8 18.9 to 30.0 23 smoothness (α) 0.937 0.920 to 0.955 0.94

The intervals are the 5.5% and 94.5% quantiles of the 4,000 draws, as in the notebook. The Model Explorer shows the interval that you select in Explore with options.

The notebook finds the Matérn spectrum with ML-II: ℓ = 23 µm, α = 0.94 and 3.4 nm of noise. Its log marginal likelihood is 2,157 above the squared exponential and 14,104 above the white prior. The platform does not show the marginal likelihood (see section 10). To compare the priors, fit the spec again with prior: white and prior: smooth, and compare:

  • noise_sd. With the white prior, the notebook finds that the noise goes to zero, that is no regularisation. The noise_um prior of the spec keeps the noise sd above zero. A noise sd much smaller than 3 nm tells you that the prior explains the noise as force.
  • The NOISE_SPECTRUM_MISMATCH value on Diagnostics.
  • The strain energy (step 6.4). It moves with the prior by more than its range.

docs.title: 6.3 The traction maps
docs.text:
Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Select traction in Output.

  • Statistic Mean shows the posterior mean of the traction length. Select Show the arrows to see the direction. The colony pulls at its edge, with the largest tractions (about 1 kPa) at its left, top and lower right edges. The cells at the edges of the image show too.
  • Std. dev. is almost flat. A stationary prior gives the same uncertainty at each pixel. This map does not show where the model is wrong.
  • Mean ÷ sd is the notebook's right panel. Inside the colony, the tractions are many sd from zero.
  • Draws and Play the draws show 200 possible force maps that agree with the data.
  • Artefacts along the image edges come from the periodic FFT. They are outside the force mask.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one pixel.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence R-hat near 1 and a high ESS for the 4 hyperparameters core.posterior_forest Narrow intervals. With 72,952 modes, the data fix the hyperparameters well sci.vector_field The heatmap of the traction length with arrows of the mean vector, and its sd. Compare it with the pyTFM map in notebook section 8

docs.title: 6.4 How hard does the colony pull?
docs.text:
The strain energy and the contractility are outputs of a score. Do step 7 to get them. These are the results:

Output Our fit: mean, 89% interval Notebook: Matérn posterior, E known, 89% pyTFM strain_energy (fJ) 271.3, 270.9 to 271.6 271.0 to 271.6 246 (252 with the notebook formula) contractility (µN) 2.173, 2.168 to 2.179 2.167 to 2.180 2.13

The contractility agrees with pyTFM to within 2%. The strain energy is about 8% higher than pyTFM. pyTFM smooths its tractions with a Gaussian filter, and a smoother field has less energy. The web app shows hdi_90, so its interval is a little wider than the 89% interval here.

Then do the stiffness part of the decision:

  1. Open the spec in Build.
  2. Change young_cv: 0.0 to young_cv: 0.15.
  3. Click Save revision, then Fit.
  4. Score the new version as in step 7.

young_cv gives each posterior draw a lognormal draw of Young's modulus. The displacements carry no information about it, so its posterior is its prior. Each draw scales its traction field, its strain energy and its contractility.

Output Our fit: mean, 89% interval Notebook: E ± 15%, 89% strain_energy (fJ) 271.0, 211.4 to 340.8 213 to 338 contractility (µN) 2.171, 1.689 to 2.733 1.71 to 2.70 young_pa (Pa, in Parameters) 49,379, 38,331 to 62,518 (the prior)

The hyperparameters do not change: the same seed gives the same draws, and only the scale of each field changes.

The decision. The data support the Matérn prior. With the stiffness known, the ranges are less than 1% wide. With a 15% stiffness error, they are about 100 to 200 times wider. Thus report the second set of ranges for the colony. In a real study, the gel stiffness causes most of the uncertainty, then the selection of the prior, and last the displacement noise.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
Each score draws new traction fields from the posterior. A score needs a dataset, but the model does not use its values: the field is the posterior for the fitted data. The dataset only selects the pixels. Send the dataset that you fitted.

  1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select pytfm_colony_ko04.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 60. Type strain_energy, contractility in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each output.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model cannot forecast, so a request without a dataset has no forecast horizon, and the server refuses it. A note under Values to score gives this reason.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biophysics/pytfm-colony-traction@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["strain_energy", "contractility"]
  },
  "seed": 60
}
  • To get the map of one area, add "select": {"row": [90, 91, 92], "col": [100, 101]} and "vars": ["traction"].
  • "kind": "predictive" adds white noise with sd noise_sd to displacement_hat. It does not change traction.
  • The model has no simulate mode. To make new data from known forces, use traction_data.simulate_traction() in Python.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same request.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws. It fits the model with prior predictive draws. A convergence gate needs the largest R-hat below rhat_max (1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above min_ess (400). Only then does it make the posterior predictive check and run the governance checks sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Then it writes a report with the plots.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Bayesian workflow audit and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select pytfm_colony_ko04 in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.traction_force@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune. In Settings, type the settings of step 4 as JSON: {"grid_um": 2.117341064232256, "young_pa": 49000.0, "poisson": 0.49, "young_cv": 0.0, "prior": "matern", "noise_um": 0.003, "traction_pa": 1000.0, "lengthscale_um": 20.0, "field_draws": 200, "force_mask": true}. If you do not, the model uses young_pa: 10000, and the forces are 4.9 times too small. Set N sims to 5 (see the note below).
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Decisions shows the convergence gate and the value that it read. Outputs shows the plots and the report. The model version link opens the Model Explorer.

The audit takes a long time on the full colony

The checks after the gate refit the model. sensitivity.prior fits it one time for each value in Prior scales (two by default), and recovery.simulated fits it N sims times (20 by default). One fit of the full colony takes from 3 minutes to more than 40 minutes, as a function of the load of the machine. Thus decrease N sims before you start the audit.

The image recipe sci_image_model_check is for models with images of a scalar field. It does not apply to this model.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython

Save the spec of step 4 as pytfm-colony-traction.yaml.

mapi use <tenant>/biophysics
mapi datasets upload pytfm_colony.nc --name pytfm_colony_ko04
mapi check pytfm-colony-traction.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit pytfm-colony-traction.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model pytfm-colony-traction -s params -s diagnostics

cat > traction-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://biophysics/pytfm-colony-traction@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [strain_energy, contractility]}
seed: 60
EOF
mapi score traction-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o traction.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init bayes_workflow_audit --name traction-audit
mapi workflows apply traction-audit.yaml -m "E60 audit"
mapi workflows run traction-audit -i data=dataset://biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04@latest \
  -p model=sci.traction_force@^1 -p n_sims=5 \
  -p 'settings={"grid_um": 2.117341064232256, "young_pa": 49000.0, "poisson": 0.49, "young_cv": 0.0, "prior": "matern", "noise_um": 0.003, "traction_pa": 1000.0, "lengthscale_um": 20.0, "field_draws": 200, "force_mask": true}' \
  --watch

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

The file pytfm-colony-traction.yaml holds the spec of step 4.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/biophysics")
version = api.datasets.upload("pytfm_colony.nc", dataset="pytfm_colony_ko04")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("pytfm-colony-traction.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "pytfm-colony-traction")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://biophysics/pytfm-colony-traction@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://biophysics/pytfm_colony_ko04@latest",
        "output": {"summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"], "vars": ["strain_energy", "contractility"]},
        "seed": 60,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["strain_energy"].values, summary["contractility"].values)

To compare with pyTFM's own map and numbers, load them with mapi_plugin_science.traction_data.challenges_reference("<path>/data").

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the physics and the model of notebook sections 7 and 8. It leaves out these parts:

  • The simulated cell (sections 1 to 6). The --synthetic data come from the model's own Matérn prior. They are not the notebook's cell with 16 focal adhesions.
  • The L-curve and the discrepancy principle (section 3). The platform fits the hyperparameters with NUTS and does not offer a scan of λ.
  • The marginal likelihood as a number. The notebook compares the priors by log marginal likelihood. The platform does not show it, and elpd_loo is not valid for this model. Compare the priors with the noise sd, the diagnostic and the strain energy (step 6.2).
  • The radial power spectrum plot (section 7). The diagnostic NOISE_SPECTRUM_MISMATCH keeps one number from it: the power ratio in the finest modes.
  • The footprint and horseshoe priors (section 6). The model has only stationary priors. The forces are not limited to the cells, and sharp adhesions become smooth.
  • A finite gel thickness. The model uses an infinite half-space, as the notebook does. pyTFM uses a finite thickness. The difference is only in the longest wavelengths.
  • A model of the correlated PIV noise. The noise is white, so the ranges with E known are too narrow (notebook "Try it yourself", item 2).
  • pyTFM's map. The web app does not show pyTFM's tractions. Use challenges_reference() in Python.

Next steps:

  • Fit the two wild-type and two knock-out colonies of the pyTFM example data. Compare their contractility with one shared young_cv (notebook "Try it yourself", item 1).
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the audit recipe.

docs.title: E61 Turing patterns
docs.text:
This tutorial does part A of the pymc-challenges notebook E61_turing_patterns_kinetic_proofreading.py in the web app. You use the model sci.turing_pattern@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project biology. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • The modeling-api repository. Part A of the notebook has no data file: the notebook makes its images with a simulation. The export command does the same simulation, so you do not need a copy of pymc-challenges.
  • About 20 minutes. The fit takes about 5 minutes of sandbox time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Two chemicals that react and diffuse at different rates can change a uniform tissue into spots or stripes. This is a Turing pattern. The notebook uses the Schnakenberg system: an activator u and a substrate v, with the supply rates a and b, the diffusion ratio d and the reaction scale γ (g in the platform).

The notebook asks what images can tell you about these rates:

  1. A settled pattern gives one length: its wavelength. Many sets of rates give the same wavelength. (Notebook section 3.)
  2. Four early images, taken while the pattern starts to grow, have an exact likelihood. Do they identify all the rates? (Notebook section 4.)
  3. Do the rates satisfy the Turing conditions, and how large is the region of supply rates that makes a pattern? (Notebook section 5, the Schnakenberg part.)

The decision at the end of part A is this: a steady state gives a length scale, and the approach to it gives the rates. To measure the kinetics, record the start of the pattern (or disturb a settled pattern and record its recovery). Do not fit the settled pattern. With four early images, the 89% intervals of d and γ are about ±12% and ±9%, and they contain the true values.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The posterior of s, rho, d, g, s0, sigma, a and b (Parameters) Section 4, the mode-growth fit and its table The dispersion relation growth(wavenumber) with bands (Plots, sci.profile_bands) Section 4, the left panel ("Dispersion relation"), blue band wavelength and max_growth of the mode that grows fastest Section 4, the printed "fastest growth rate 90%" line p_turing, the probability that the Turing conditions hold Section 5, the Turing conditions for the fitted system The map turing_space(b_supply, a_supply) (Fields) Section 5, the left panel ("Turing space in (a, b)") The observed images next to predicted images (Plots, sci.ppc_image_grid, sci.image_residuals) Not in the notebook. A check of the linear likelihood New patterns from the nonlinear solver (Score, Simulate) Section 2, the spectral solver

Notebook part B (kinetic proofreading) and the Nodal/Lefty calculation of section 5 are not in the port. See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command does the simulation of notebook section 4 and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. Run it from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e61 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out e61_turing.nc --spec e61_turing.yaml

The command writes:

wrote e61_turing.nc (variables activator on t=4, y=128, x=128)
upload it as dataset biology/e61_turing_early_images and fit sci.turing_pattern
wrote the suggested spec to e61_turing.yaml

The case reads no file, so --challenges is optional. Without it, the command writes the same file.

The simulation is the notebook's simulation:

  • A 128 × 128 periodic square of side 100. The activator diffuses at a rate of 1 in these units.
  • The truth: a = 0.1, b = 0.9 (thus s = 1 and rho = 0.1), d = 20 and g = 1.
  • The uniform state plus white noise of sd 0.001 (seed 1). The spectral solver uses a step of 0.005.
  • Images at t = 4, 8, 12 and 16, with white camera noise of sd 0.0005 (seed 613).

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning t 4 float, extend The time since the start: 4, 8, 12 and 16 y, x 128, 128 integer, fixed The pixel rows and columns activator t, y, x float64, target The activator concentration in each pixel

The images are near the uniform state 1. Their sd is 0.0006 at t = 4 and 0.006 at t = 16. The largest deviation from the mean is 2.3%, so the linear likelihood is correct. The attributes of the file keep the truth (truth_s, truth_rho, truth_d, truth_g), box_length 100 and camera_noise_sd 0.0005. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

A smaller dataset

--synthetic writes a 32 × 32 version of the same simulation (seed 0). A fit on it is much faster. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the 128 × 128 images.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e61 --synthetic --out turing_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type e61_turing_early_images in Name. Type a description, for example "Four early images of a Schnakenberg pattern, 128 × 128, t = 4 to 16".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select e61_turing.nc.
  6. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows activator on t, y and x.
  7. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  8. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, activator has the role target. Missingness must show no missing values. The model needs a value in each pixel of a square raster.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows activator, images of 128 × 128 cells. The frame slider goes through the 4 times of t. Look at the pattern of spots in each frame.

  4. Over time shows one series: the mean of all cells at each time. The explorer does not make a series for each cell.
  5. The time patterns are in Not for this data: t is an ordered sequence, not time.
  6. Data quality does not give the warning SHORT_HISTORY.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select e61_turing_early_images. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type turing in the search field. Under Models, select Turing patterns from early images (sci.turing_pattern@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name e61-turing-mode-growth from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: e61-turing-mode-growth
  project: biology
data:
  dataset: dataset://biology/e61_turing_early_images@latest
model:
  use: sci.turing_pattern@^1
  settings:
    box_length: 100.0
    k2_max: 1.5
    max_extension: 2
    d_median: 10.0
    d_log_sd: 1.0
    initial_noise_median: 0.001
    camera_noise_median: 0.001
    field_draws: 40
    simulate_draws: 4
    settle_time: 300.0
    precondition: true
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 61
    tune: 1500
    draws: 1000
    chains: 4
    target_accept: 0.95
    engine: pymc
    keep:
      log_likelihood: true
evaluate:
  metrics: [elpd_loo]
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - sci.field_map
    - sci.ppc_image_grid
    - sci.profile_bands
    - sci.image_residuals

The settings are the defaults of the model and the values of the notebook. The --spec file of the export has the short form of the same spec. This table tells what each setting means for the question:

Setting Value Meaning for this question box_length 100 The side of the square, in the length unit of the model. It sets the wavenumbers of the Fourier modes. Use the side of your images in units of sqrt(D_u / k) k2_max 1.5 Use only the modes with k² less than 1.5. Faster modes decay below the camera noise before the first image. 581 modes in 138 groups remain max_extension 2 A prediction can go to 2 image times after t = 16, that is t = 20 and 24. The linear theory is correct only while the pattern is small d_median, d_log_sd 10, 1 The prior of the diffusion ratio: LogNormal(log 10, 1), as in the notebook initial_noise_median, camera_noise_median 0.001, 0.001 The prior medians of s0 and sigma (log-normal, log sd 1.5) field_draws 40 The posterior draws that each score uses for pattern, growth and turing_space simulate_draws 4 The nonlinear runs for each simulate score. Each run is a full PDE solution settle_time 300 The time of the settled pattern in simulate. The notebook also uses 300 precondition true Find the mode first, then let NUTS sample near it with a Laplace preconditioner. The model does not change
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all four images. The model needs all the images, so the spec has no split. Without this line, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("there is no holdout for the evaluation").
  • tune: 1500 and target_accept: 0.95 are the sampler settings of the notebook.
  • keep.log_likelihood: true keeps the log-likelihood of each Fourier mode. The modes are independent, so elpd_loo over the modes is valid.

The plots

The model declares core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.field_map, sci.ppc_image_grid and sci.profile_bands. The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. Thus the spec names them, and it adds sci.image_residuals. The Plots section of the Insert panel adds a plot for you.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows "finding the mode" first, then the NUTS progress. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://biology/e61-turing-mode-growth@v1. Click it.

The fit samples 6 numbers. The model calculates the FFT of the images once. Then it groups the modes by their integer k², so each gradient needs only 2 × 2 algebra for each of the 138 groups. Before NUTS starts, the model finds the posterior mode from 4 starts. After the fit, the run calculates the plots and the explorer views from 40 posterior draws.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

Expect four warnings: RHAT (largest R-hat 1.016), ESS_BULK (smallest bulk ESS 166), ESS_TAIL (152) and DIVERGENCES (5). The slow parameters are rho and g. The notebook also found that this posterior is curved, not only correlated. Its fit had 0 divergences and a bulk ESS above 500. The posterior means and intervals agree with the notebook (step 6.5). Thus the warnings tell you to get more draws, not that the model is wrong. To get a larger ESS, set draws: 2000 and fit again.

The diagnostic NONLINEAR_REGIME must not show. It shows when the images are more than 10% from their mean. These images are at most 2.3% from their mean.

docs.title: 6.2 What the early images identify
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The table has s, rho, d, g, s0, sigma, and the derived a, b, wavelength, max_growth and p_turing.

  • d is 20.9, with a 90% interval from 17.8 to 24.8. The truth is 20.
  • g is 0.99 (0.91 to 1.07). The truth is 1.
  • b is 0.94 (0.84 to 1.03) and a is 0.096 (0.060 to 0.130). The truth is 0.9 and 0.1. a is the parameter with the widest relative interval, as in the notebook.
  • s0 and sigma are at their true values, 0.001 and 0.0005.

On the model version page, open Plots and select Profiles with bands. The title is "Profiles of growth". The line is the median growth rate of each wavenumber, with 50% and 90% bands. This is the blue band of the notebook's left panel:

  • Near the peak, the band is very narrow. The largest growth rate is 0.262 to 0.264 (truth 0.263), at the wavenumber 0.485.
  • At small wavenumbers, the band is wide (at k = 0, from −0.20 to −0.08). These modes decay below the camera noise in the first images, so the data say little about them.

docs.title: 6.3 Is it Turing?
docs.text:
• p_turing is 1 in every draw. Thus the posterior probability that the Turing conditions hold is 1.00. At s = 1 and rho = 0.1, the smallest diffusion ratio for a pattern is about 8.6. All draws of d are far above it.
  • wavelength is 12.95 in almost all draws. This is 2π / 0.485. The model finds the peak on a grid of 600 values of k², so the interval of wavelength has almost no width.

Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Select turing_space in Output.

  • Statistic Mean shows P(Turing) for each pair of supply rates. a_supply is on the horizontal axis and b_supply on the vertical axis. The region where the mean is near 1 is the Turing wedge of the notebook's left panel in section 5, for the posterior d (about 21).
  • The point a = 0.1, b = 0.9 of the simulation is inside the wedge.
  • Std. dev. is larger than 0 only along the edge of the wedge. There, the uncertainty of d moves the edge.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one cell.

docs.title: 6.4 Do the predicted images look like the data?
docs.text:
The notebook does not do this check. It is a good check of the linear likelihood.

In Fields, select pattern in Output. Use the slider t to show each image time. Mean shows the activator field given the fitted images. Draws and Play the draws show possible fields.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for Sampler convergence (core.convergence) R-hat and ESS of the 6 parameters. rho and g have the lowest ESS Posterior forest (core.posterior_forest) The intervals of step 6.2. a and rho have the widest relative intervals Field map (sci.field_map) The title is "Field map of pattern". The mean and the sd of pattern for each time. Use the slider to show a different t Predictive image grid (sci.ppc_image_grid) The title is "Predictive images of pattern". The observed image is the first panel, then 5 predicted images on one colour scale. The observed image must look like one more draw Profiles with bands (sci.profile_bands) The dispersion relation of step 6.2 Image residuals (sci.image_residuals) The title is "Residuals of pattern". The normalised residuals must look like noise, with an sd near 1 and about 5% outside ±2. Here the sd is 1.02

The predicted images have the same sd as the data at each time (0.0006 at t = 4 and 0.006 at t = 16).

docs.title: 6.5 The decision and the numbers
docs.text:
Make the notebook's decision with these outputs:

  1. Look at the intervals of d, g, a and b in Parameters. All four contain the truth, and d and g are known to about ±12% and ±9%. Thus four early images identify the kinetics.
  2. Look at the dispersion relation. The data fix the peak and the band of unstable wavenumbers. A settled pattern gives only the position of the peak (notebook section 3).
  3. Thus, to measure the rates of a reaction-diffusion system, record the start of the pattern while it is small. Use the NONLINEAR_REGIME diagnostic to make sure that the images are early enough.

We fitted the spec above on the exported images (seed 61, 4 chains of 1000 draws). The table gives the 89% intervals, as the notebook does:

Quantity Truth Notebook Platform d 20 17.7 to 25.2 17.8 to 24.7 (mean 20.9) g (γ) 1 0.90 to 1.08 0.91 to 1.07 (mean 0.99) b 0.9 0.84 to 1.04 0.85 to 1.03 (mean 0.94) a 0.1 0.054 to 0.133 0.060 to 0.129 (mean 0.096) s0 0.001 at the true value 0.00092 to 0.00101 sigma 0.0005 at the true value 0.00049 to 0.00051 Largest growth rate, 90% 0.263 0.262 to 0.264 0.262 to 0.264 Its wavenumber 0.485 the truth 0.485 (wavelength 12.95) P(Turing conditions hold) 1 not given 1.00 elpd_loo (581 modes) not given 28,473.5 Sampler 0 divergences, R-hat up to 1.013, bulk ESS above 500, 93 s 5 divergences, R-hat up to 1.016, bulk ESS 166, about 5 minutes

Your numbers can be a little different if your sandbox has a different version of PyMC.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text:
The scores ignore the values of any dataset that you send. The predictions are given the fitted images.

Predict the summaries:

  1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Then select e61_turing_early_images, the dataset of the fit.
  4. Open Advanced. Type p_turing, wavelength, growth in Variables (optional). Set Seed (optional) to 61.
  5. Click Predict.

The Results region shows p_turing (mean 1.0), wavelength (12.94, hdi_90 12.95 to 12.95) and the dispersion relation growth with its hdi_90 for each wavenumber.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://biology/e61-turing-mode-growth@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://biology/e61_turing_early_images@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 0,
    "units": "original",
    "names": "dataset",
    "vars": ["p_turing", "wavelength", "growth"]
  },
  "seed": 61
}

Simulate new patterns:

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Then select e61_turing_early_images, the dataset of the fit.
  3. In Advanced, type settled, p_turing, wavelength in Variables (optional).
  4. Click Simulate.

The model takes 4 posterior draws (simulate_draws). For each draw, it grows a new pattern from new random noise with the nonlinear spectral solver to t = 300. settled is the pattern at t = 300: spots, with values from about 0.2 to 3.2. The 4 runs took about 30 s in our sandbox. The request is the same as above, with "mode": "simulate" and "vars": ["settled", "p_turing", "wavelength"]. The output pattern of a simulate score is a new pattern at the times of the dataset, with camera noise.

  • "kind": "predictive" adds camera noise with sd sigma to pattern in predict.
  • To predict later images, send a dataset with new t values, for example 20 and 24. The model accepts at most 2 times after t = 16 (max_extension). Its predictions are correct only while the pattern is small.
  • forecast and counterfactual give MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED.

Try it on an endpoint

If you promote the version to an endpoint, open Integrations, then the endpoint, then the Schema and Try it tab. Paste the same request there, without the model field, and click Score.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_image_model_check (Image model check) is for models that predict an image. It fits the model, makes a table of the parameters with R-hat and ESS, renders the residual maps (sci.image_residuals) and the predictive image grid (sci.ppc_image_grid), does a predictive check, and writes a report.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Image model check and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select e61_turing_early_images in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.turing_pattern@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). In Settings, type {"box_length": 100, "k2_max": 1.5}. Set Tune to 1500 and Seed to 61. Type t in Frame.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs shows the two plots and the report. The model version link opens the Model Explorer. The predictive check compares the sd of the observed images with the sd of the predicted images. If it fails, the workflow continues.

Note

The dataset names are the names of the model (t, y, x and activator). Thus you do not need Bind. If your images have other names, give them in Bind, for example {"dims": {"t": "minutes"}, "vars": {"activator": "intensity"}}.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) also applies to this model. It adds a prior predictive check, a convergence gate, a prior sensitivity check and a recovery check on simulated data. The gate needs the largest R-hat below Rhat max (default 1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above Min ess (default 400). In step 6.1, R-hat is 1.016 and the bulk ESS is 166, so the default gate stops the audit. In Fine-tune, increase Draws and Tune, or set Rhat max to 1.02 and Min ess to 150. The checks after the gate fit the model again: two times for the prior sensitivity check and N sims times (20 by default) for the recovery check.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
# get the data and the suggested spec
uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e61 \
    --out e61_turing.nc --spec e61_turing.yaml

# upload, check and fit on the platform (e61-turing-mode-growth.yaml is the spec of step 4)
mapi use <tenant>/biology
mapi datasets upload e61_turing.nc --name e61_turing_early_images
mapi check e61-turing-mode-growth.yaml --remote @
mapi fit e61-turing-mode-growth.yaml --remote @
mapi explore model e61-turing-mode-growth -s params -s diagnostics -s fields

# the summaries of step 7
cat > turing-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://biology/e61-turing-mode-growth@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://biology/e61_turing_early_images@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [p_turing, wavelength, growth]}
seed: 61
EOF
mapi score turing-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o turing.zarr.zip

# the recipe
mapi workflows init sci_image_model_check --name turing-check
mapi workflows apply turing-check.yaml
mapi workflows run turing-check \
    -i data=dataset://biology/e61_turing_early_images@latest \
    -p model=sci.turing_pattern@^1 \
    -p settings='{"box_length": 100, "k2_max": 1.5}' \
    -p tune=1500 -p seed=61 -p frame=t --watch

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client()  # MAPI_URL, the `mapi login` sign-in (or MAPI_TOKEN) and MAPI_PROJECT

version = api.datasets.upload("e61_turing.nc", dataset="e61_turing_early_images")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("e61-turing-mode-growth.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])

revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "e61-turing-mode-growth")
mv = api.models.version(model.id, model.latest_version)
print(mv.ref, mv.metrics)

result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    mv.version,
    {
        "model": mv.ref,
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://biology/e61_turing_early_images@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "expected",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "vars": ["p_turing", "wavelength", "growth"],
        },
        "seed": 61,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["p_turing"].values, summary["wavelength"].values)
print(summary["growth"].sel(stat="mean").max().values)  # the largest growth rate

To compare with the notebook, load its printed estimates with mapi_plugin_science.turing_data.challenges_reference().

The CLI and the client send the same spec and the same score request as the web app.

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the kinetics, the priors and the exact mode-growth likelihood of notebook section 4. It leaves out these parts:

  • The settled-pattern posterior (section 3). The notebook calibrates the wavelength of settled patterns against the linear theory and uses importance sampling from the prior. The platform does not fit a settled pattern. simulate gives settled patterns, but the platform does not measure their wavelength. The grey bands and clouds of the section 4 figure are not in the platform.
  • The pair plots of section 4. The Model Explorer does not show draws of two parameters against each other. Download the bundle and use the posterior draws, or add core.pair to outputs.plots.
  • Nodal and Lefty (section 5). The probability that the measured Nodal/Lefty diffusion ratios exceed the critical ratio is a different model. It is not in the port.
  • The fraction of Turing space against d (section 5, middle panel). The platform gives the map turing_space for the posterior d only.
  • Part B, kinetic proofreading (sections 6 to 10). Not in the port.
  • The sampler. The platform finds the mode first and samples with a Laplace preconditioner. The notebook samples the parameters directly. To do the same, set precondition: false. Then you need a long warm-up, for example tune: 1500.

Next steps:

  • Do "Try it yourself" item 2 of the notebook: fit only two images, or add an image at t = 30. At t = 30 the pattern is large. Look for the NONLINEAR_REGIME diagnostic and for normalised residuals with an sd far from 1.
  • Fit your own time-lapse images. Measure box_length in units of sqrt(D_u / k), or fit several values and compare elpd_loo.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the image recipe.

docs.title: E77 how languages name colours
docs.text:
This tutorial does the work of the pymc-challenges notebook E77_colour_naming.py in the web app. You use the model sci.colour_naming@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project linguistics. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the spec.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads four files from its data/ directory.
  • About 15 minutes. The fit takes about four minutes of sandbox time.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
The World Color Survey (WCS) asked the speakers of 110 unwritten languages to name 330 colour chips. Each speaker named each chip once. This tutorial uses Nafaanra, a language of Ghana with 29 speakers in the survey. Nafaanra has a small system of four major terms: F (finge, white and the palest chips), W (wɔɔ, dark, green, blue and purple), N (nyie, red, orange, yellow and brown) and B (bubuo, some pale purples).

The notebook asks these questions of the naming of one language:

  1. Where are the boundaries between the colour terms, and how sure are you of them? (Notebook parts A, B and D.)
  2. Do the speakers agree? 55% of the speakers call a chip N. Is this chip on a fuzzy boundary that all speakers share? Or is it near a sharp boundary that each speaker puts in a different place? (Part C.)
  3. How many categories does the language really have? (Part E, the effective number of categories.)
  4. How well can you predict a new speaker? (Part G, the held-out speakers.)

The notebook ends with these decisions:

  • Use a model in CIELAB colour space, not on the printed grid. A grid model must know that hue is a circle.
  • Use the hierarchical model (speaker effects) to describe the speakers. The pooled model gets each chip right, but it fails a check for each speaker.
  • Keep two uncertainties apart. New speakers vary much along the boundaries. The language itself is known to about one chip.
  • A focus (the best example that speakers mark) is not the chip that most speakers agree on.

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The share of the speakers who give each term to each chip, on the palette, with mean, sd and draws (Fields, sci.field_map) Part D, the disc charts of each term Each chip in the colour of its most probable term, next to the observed naming (sci.swatches) Parts A and B, the raw naming map and the "poster" maps The between-speaker sds sd and the weights W (Parameters, core.posterior_forest) Part C, the sds of the speaker effects The scores of the 9 held-out speakers (log_score, accuracy, accuracy_lift, brier) Part G, the log score of new speakers The effective number of categories of one speaker and of the language (Score) Part E, the effective categories Simulated new speakers (Score, mode Simulate) Part D, the animation of new speakers

See Differences from the notebook for the parts that the port leaves out.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads wcs_naming.npz, wcs_terms.csv, wcs_chips.csv and wcs_languages.csv. It keeps the 29 speakers of Nafaanra (WCS language 77). A term is major if at least a third of the speakers used it. Each major term keeps its WCS abbreviation, and all other terms become other. Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e77 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out wcs_nafaanra.nc --spec wcs_nafaanra.yaml

The command writes:

wrote wcs_nafaanra.nc (variables response, cie_l, cie_a, cie_b, wcs_row, wcs_col on speaker=29, chip=330)
upload it as dataset linguistics/wcs_nafaanra and fit sci.colour_naming
wrote the suggested spec to wcs_nafaanra.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning speaker 29 categorical, policy new_levels, strategy hyperprior The speakers, s01 to s29 chip 330 integer, policy fixed The WCS chip number grid chip text coordinate The name of the chip on the palette, for example E29 response speaker, chip str, target, missing values allowed The term that the speaker gave to the chip. An empty value is no answer cie_l, cie_a, cie_b chip float64, covariate The CIELAB colour of the chip wcs_row, wcs_col chip int64, covariate The place of the chip on the palette. Rows A to J are 0 to 9. Column 0 holds the greys, and columns 1 to 40 are the hues

The dataset holds 9,570 answers: W 5,082, N 2,757, F 1,550 and B 173. Only 8 cells have no answer. All terms of Nafaanra are major, so the dataset has no other term. 16 of the 29 speakers never use B. The other 13 use it for 1 to 24 chips. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns. The attribute glosses gives the word for each abbreviation.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes naming that the model's own process simulates: 12 speakers, a small palette of 38 chips and three terms (light, dark and warm), with known parameters. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for Nafaanra. With --synthetic, the --spec file holds out 2 random speakers, because the simulated data does not have the 9 speakers of the notebook.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e77 --synthetic --out colour_naming.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type wcs_nafaanra in Name. Type a description, for example "Colour naming of the 29 Nafaanra speakers of the World Color Survey".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select wcs_nafaanra.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Optional: click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows response on speaker and chip, and five variables on chip.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, response has the role target and the type str. Missingness shows the 8 cells without an answer. The model accepts them: a missing answer leaves the likelihood.

The file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Points.

  3. The chart shows the 330 chips on the grid of the survey (wcs_col and wcs_row). Each chip has its colour from cie_l, cie_a and cie_b.

  4. Set the colour to the most frequent term to see the four terms of Nafaanra on the chart.
  5. Set the colour to the agreement. Low agreement shows the boundaries between the terms, where the 29 speakers do not give the same answer.
  6. wcs_row and wcs_col are positions. Correlations does not use them.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select wcs_nafaanra. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type colour in the search field. Under Models, select How people name colours (sci.colour_naming@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name nafaanra-colour-naming from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: nafaanra-colour-naming, project: linguistics}
data:
  dataset: dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest
  bind:
    vars: {naming: response, lab_l: cie_l, lab_a: cie_a, lab_b: cie_b,
           grid_row: wcs_row, grid_col: wcs_col}
  split: {kind: leave_group_out, dim: speaker,
          groups: [s03, s04, s07, s13, s18, s19, s22, s25, s27]}
model:
  use: sci.colour_naming@^1
  settings: {kind: hierarchical, features: cielab, new_speakers: 20}
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, seed: 77, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4,
        engine: nutpie}
evaluate: {metrics: [log_score, accuracy, accuracy_lift, brier, elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.swatches, sci.field_map]

The model calls the target naming and the chip variables lab_l, lab_a, lab_b, grid_row and grid_col. The bind block connects them to the names in the dataset. The dims speaker and chip have the same names in the model and in the dataset.

The split holds out the same 9 speakers as the notebook. evaluate_then_refit fits on the other 20 speakers and scores the 9 held-out speakers as new speakers. Then it fits again on all 29 speakers. The suggested spec of the export (wcs_nafaanra.yaml) is the same spec without new_speakers: 20, which is the default.

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind hierarchical Each speaker gets an intercept and linear weights (on L, a and b) of their own, around those of the language. A speaker can use a term more or less, and move its boundaries. pooled gives all speakers the same naming features cielab The logit of each term is a quadratic surface in CIELAB colour space. grid_line and grid_circle use the row and the hue column of the palette (notebook part B) new_speakers 20 In each draw, the fit simulates 20 new speakers to calculate the share of the speakers who give each term to each chip. The notebook also uses 20 w_sd 3 (default) The prior sd of the zero-sum weights. The notebook uses the same scale after its prior predictive check sd_scale 1 (default) The half-normal scale of the sds between the speakers n_random 4 (default) The speaker effects are on the first 4 features: the intercept, L, a and b hue_columns the largest grid_col (default) Only for grid_circle: the number of hue columns around the circle. The WCS has 40 score_draws 200 (default) The number of posterior draws that one score uses

Settings that do not agree

Validate does a check of each setting by itself. It does not compare two settings. For example, features: grid_line with n_random: 9 shows valid, but the run stops with SETTINGS_INVALID because grid_line has only 7 features.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://linguistics/nafaanra-colour-naming@v1. Click it.

The run does two fits: one on the 20 training speakers for the metrics of the held-out speakers, and one on all 29 speakers. On a laptop with nutpie, the two fits took 232 seconds. After the fits, the run calculates the language-level shares for each draw, the plots and the explorer views.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text: Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer, or the plot Sampler convergence on the Plots tab. In the fit for this tutorial, there were no divergences. The largest R-hat was 1.02 and the smallest bulk ESS was 278 (of 4,000 draws). Both values are for the weights W. The sds sd mix well (R-hat 1.01 or less, bulk ESS 730 or more). The scorecard shows warnings for R-hat, for the bulk ESS and for 17 chips with a high Pareto k in elpd_loo. If you need a stricter result, increase tune and draws to 2000.

docs.title: 6.2 Do the speakers agree?
docs.text:
Posterior forest shows the weights W and the sds sd between the speakers. The sds are on the logit scale of the standardised features. In this fit, the means of sd are:

Feature W N F B Intercept (1) 0.25 0.36 0.47 2.64 L 0.56 0.09 0.22 0.45 a 0.54 0.54 0.13 1.13 b 0.36 0.29 0.10 0.20

Read the table as the notebook does:

  • The intercept sds of F, N and W are small. The speakers use these three terms at similar rates.
  • The intercept sd of B is large. Some speakers use B for a patch of chips, and others never use it.
  • The larger linear sds (W on L and a, N on a) show that the speakers put the light/dark and the warm/cool boundaries in different places.

The pooled model cannot show this. It says that each speaker names a boundary chip with the same probabilities.

docs.title: 6.3 Where are the boundaries? The maps
docs.text:
Open Fields in the Model Explorer. The model has 1 output on a grid: p_term, the share of the speakers of the language who give each term to each chip. The rows are the 10 rows of the palette (A at the top), and the columns are the 41 columns (the greys in column 0).

  1. Move the slider term to select a term: W, N, F or B.
  2. Select Mean in Statistic. A bright cell is a chip that most speakers give this term.
  3. Select Std. dev. to see where you are not sure of the share. The sd is large along the boundaries.
  4. Select Draws and click Play the draws to see possible maps that agree with the data.
  5. Move the pointer over a cell to read its values.

The cells of row A and row J, except column 0, have no chip. They are empty. The plot Field map on the Plots tab shows the same output as panels (mean and sd) with a slider.

Look for these features, which the notebook also finds:

  • F covers white and row B. Its boundary under row B is sharp.
  • W covers the dark greys, black and almost all greens, blues and purples.
  • N covers the reds, oranges, pinks, browns and yellows. The N/W boundary runs along a diagonal from the dark browns to the yellow-greens, and through the purples near columns 34 to 37. It is wide: a band of several chips, not a line.
  • B is small everywhere. Its most probable chip is D35, a pale purple. Only 11% of new speakers (90% range 3% to 21%) give it B.

docs.title: 6.4 The posterised map
docs.text:
The plot Colour swatches (sci.swatches, title "Colours of mode_term_rgb") paints each chip on the palette in the display colour of its most probable term. The display colour of a term is the average colour of the chips where the term is most probable.

  • The first panel shows the observed naming: each chip in the colour of the term that most speakers gave it.
  • The mean panel shows the average over the draws.
  • The draw panels show possible maps of the language. Where they differ, the majority term of the chip is not sure.

In this fit, the draw panels differ only on a small number of chips. On 27 of the 330 chips, less than 95% of the draws give the same majority term. Look for these chips along the boundaries of section 6.3.

docs.title: 6.5 The held-out speakers
docs.text:
The metrics are in the Metrics card of the Overview tab. They score the 2,970 answers of the 9 held-out speakers. The model did not see these speakers, so it predicts them as new speakers.

Metric Value Meaning log_score −0.403 The mean log probability of the answer that the speaker gave, in nats for each answer. Higher is better accuracy 0.882 The share of the answers that are the most probable term accuracy_lift 0.341 The accuracy minus the accuracy of the most frequent term (W) brier 0.195 The mean squared error of the probabilities. Lower is better elpd_loo −3,959 (se 197) Leave one chip out, on the fit of all 29 speakers. 17 chips have a high Pareto k

Compare elpd_loo only between fits with the same speakers and the same fit.mode. The value of a fit on 20 speakers is not on the same scale as the value of a fit on 29 speakers.

docs.title: 6.6 The numbers of the notebook and of this port
docs.text:
Quantity Notebook This port Intercept sd between the speakers: W, N, F 0.25 to 0.47 0.25, 0.36, 0.47 Intercept sd between the speakers: B About 2.6 2.64 Held-out log_score, pooled, CIELAB −0.392 −0.392 Held-out log_score, grid with hue as a line, minus CIELAB −0.034 −0.034 Held-out log_score, grid with hue as a circle, minus CIELAB −0.004 −0.004 Held-out log_score, pooled and hierarchical −0.389 and −0.398 (part G, 150 chips for each speaker) −0.392 and −0.403 (all 330 chips) Effective categories of one speaker About 2 1.92 (90% range 1.86 to 1.98) Effective categories of the language Lower than for one speaker 1.84 (90% range 1.77 to 1.90) Chips where a new speaker gives the top term with probability below 0.7 71 71 Chips with a majority term that is not sure (less than 0.95) 26 27 Safest chip of B D35, 11% (4% to 21%) D35, 11% (3% to 21%) Safest chips of W and N G23 (0.99) and E4 G23 (0.99) and E4 (0.98)

The last four rows come from the draws of p_term. Fields shows the same values for each chip. The held-out scores of the pooled and grid fits come from three fits of the spec with kind: pooled, one for each value of features.

Your numbers can be slightly different if the sampler or its version is different.

docs.title: 6.7 Make the decisions
docs.text:
Use these outputs to make the decisions of the notebook:

  1. CIELAB or the grid. Fit the spec again with kind: pooled and each value of features. Compare log_score of the held-out speakers. In the fits for this tutorial, cielab scores −0.392 nats for each answer, the grid with hue as a line −0.426, and the grid with hue as a circle −0.396. Hue as a line costs about 100 nats over the 2,970 held-out answers. Keep cielab. It knows that hue is a circle, and its distances are about perceptual.
  2. Pooled or hierarchical. Look at the sds of section 6.2. A large intercept sd (B) or large linear sds (W, N) show that the speakers do not name the same way. Use the hierarchical model to describe the speakers. For the share of all speakers on one chip, the pooled model is as good and slightly better on log_score.
  3. Two uncertainties. For the variation between the speakers, use the predictions for new speakers (step 7, mode Simulate). For the uncertainty about the language, use the Std. dev. of p_term in Fields, and the draw panels of Colour swatches. In this fit, a new speaker gives the most probable term with a probability below 0.7 on 71 chips. But the majority term of the language is not sure on only 27 chips.
  4. How many categories. Use k_eff_speaker and k_eff_language (step 7). A language with k equally used, sharp categories scores k. Nafaanra has 4 major terms, but it acts like 2 sharp categories.
  5. Best example or safest chip. The model gives the chip that most speakers agree on. It does not give the focus. The dataset has no foci, so make this comparison in the notebook.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text: The fitted version uses all 29 speakers. A score needs a dataset that has the dims speaker and chip. Send the dataset that you fitted.

docs.title: 7.1 Predict: the speakers and the effective categories
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select wcs_nafaanra.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 77. Type p_name, k_eff_speaker, k_eff_language in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score) is:

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://linguistics/nafaanra-colour-naming@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["p_name", "k_eff_speaker", "k_eff_language"]
  },
  "seed": 77
}

The result has p_name(speaker, chip, term): the probability that each of the 29 speakers gives each term to each chip. Each fitted speaker keeps their own effects. The outputs k_eff_speaker and k_eff_language are the same for each speaker, because they describe the language. In this fit, k_eff_speaker is 1.92 (about 1.87 to 1.98) and k_eff_language is 1.83 (about 1.77 to 1.90). The value for the language is lower because the speakers do not agree on all chips.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model cannot forecast, so a request without a dataset has no forecast horizon, and the server refuses it. A note under Values to score gives this reason.

docs.title: 7.2 Simulate: new speakers
docs.text:
simulate gives each speaker of the dataset new speaker effects. Thus the result is 29 new Nafaanra speakers, as in the animation of the notebook.

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Select wcs_nafaanra.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive. Set Draws to 20.
  4. Type p_name in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://linguistics/nafaanra-colour-naming@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 20,
    "vars": ["p_name"]
  },
  "seed": 77
}

With Predictive, each draw holds one sampled term for each speaker and chip (a one-hot vector over the terms). Thus each draw is one complete naming of the palette by a new speaker. In this score, 37% of the simulated speakers never use B, and one simulated speaker uses B for 142 chips. In the data, 16 of the 29 speakers (55%) never use B, and no speaker uses it for more than 24 chips. The numbers of chips for each term also vary more between the simulated speakers (sd 12.5 for W) than between the real speakers (sd 8.9). The notebook finds the same weakness: a shift of one shared shape does not describe a term that only some speakers have.

  • To score a speaker that the fit did not see, upload a dataset with a new speaker label (for example new01) and the same chips. Predict then gives that speaker new effects in each draw. The mean over the draws is the prediction for a new speaker.
  • Evaluate needs a dataset with answers. It scores them with log_score, accuracy, accuracy_lift and brier.
  • A dataset with a chip that the fit did not see stops the score with UNSEEN_LEVELS.
  • The model has no forecast mode.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws. It fits the model with prior predictive draws and plots them. A convergence gate needs the largest R-hat below Rhat max (1.01) and the smallest bulk ESS at or above Min ess (400). Only then does it make the posterior predictive check and run the governance checks sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Then it writes a report with the plots.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Bayesian workflow audit and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select wcs_nafaanra in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.colour_naming@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune. In Settings, type {"kind": "hierarchical", "features": "cielab", "new_speakers": 20}. In Bind, type {"vars": {"naming": "response", "lab_l": "cie_l", "lab_a": "cie_a", "lab_b": "cie_b", "grid_row": "wcs_row", "grid_col": "wcs_col"}}.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Decisions shows the convergence gate and the value that it read. Outputs shows the plots and the report. The model version link opens the Model Explorer.

Give the recipe the binding

Without Bind, the recipe binds only the target response to naming. It cannot bind the five chip variables, because they all have the role covariate, and the fit stops.

The default gate can stop this audit

In the fit of this tutorial, the largest R-hat was 1.019 and the smallest bulk ESS was 278. Thus the default gate (R-hat below 1.01, bulk ESS 400 or more) takes the else arm, and the recipe skips the checks after the gate. Increase Tune and Draws to 2000 in Fine-tune, then run the recipe again.

Note

The checks after the gate refit the model. sensitivity.prior fits it one time for each value in Prior scales (two by default), and recovery.simulated fits it N sims times (20 by default). Thus the recipe takes many times as long as one fit.

The recipes sci_spatial_ladder, sci_network_ladder, sci_phylo_signal, sci_calibrate_then_design and sci_image_model_check are for other science models. They do not apply to this model.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/linguistics
mapi datasets upload wcs_nafaanra.nc --name wcs_nafaanra
mapi check nafaanra-colour-naming.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit nafaanra-colour-naming.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model nafaanra-colour-naming -s params -s diagnostics

cat > new-speakers.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://linguistics/nafaanra-colour-naming@latest
mode: simulate
data: dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest
output: {kind: predictive, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 20, vars: [p_name]}
seed: 77
EOF
mapi score new-speakers.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o new-speakers.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init bayes_workflow_audit --name nafaanra-audit
mapi workflows apply nafaanra-audit.yaml -m "E77 audit"
mapi workflows run nafaanra-audit -i data=dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest \
  -p model=sci.colour_naming@^1 \
  -p 'settings={"kind": "hierarchical", "features": "cielab", "new_speakers": 20}' \
  -p 'bind={"vars": {"naming": "response", "lab_l": "cie_l", "lab_a": "cie_a", "lab_b": "cie_b", "grid_row": "wcs_row", "grid_col": "wcs_col"}}' --watch

nafaanra-colour-naming.yaml is the spec of step 4. The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/linguistics")
version = api.datasets.upload("wcs_nafaanra.nc", dataset="wcs_nafaanra")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("nafaanra-colour-naming.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
check = api.specs.validate(spec_yaml)
print("valid" if check.valid else [(i.code, i.pointer) for i in check.issues])
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "nafaanra-colour-naming")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://linguistics/nafaanra-colour-naming@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest",
        "output": {
            "kind": "expected",
            "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
            "vars": ["k_eff_speaker", "k_eff_language"],
        },
        "seed": 77,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["k_eff_speaker"].sel(stat="mean").values)
print(summary["k_eff_language"].sel(stat="mean").values)

To run the audit recipe:

workflow = api.workflows.create(template="bayes_workflow_audit")
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
