    inputs={"data": "dataset://linguistics/wcs_nafaanra@latest"},
    params={
        "model": "sci.colour_naming@^1",
        "settings": {
            "kind": "hierarchical",
            "features": "cielab",
            "new_speakers": 20
        },
        "bind": {
            "vars": {
                "naming": "response",
                "lab_l": "cie_l",
                "lab_a": "cie_a",
                "lab_b": "cie_b",
                "grid_row": "wcs_row",
                "grid_col": "wcs_col"
            }
        }
    },
    wait=True,
)

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the naming model of parts B and C (pooled and hierarchical, CIELAB and the two grid feature sets) and the held-out speakers of part G. It leaves out these parts:

  • The other languages (parts E and F). The model fits one language. To compare languages, export each language with from_challenges(path, language=<WCS number>) in Python, and fit one spec for each. The web app does not calculate the similarity of two partitions (NMI) or the hue-rotation null.
  • The clusters of centroids and foci across 110 languages (part F). The notebook uses a Bayesian bootstrap over the speakers, not this model.
  • The foci. The dataset has no best examples. Thus the port cannot compare the safest chip with the focus of each term.
  • The per-speaker predictive check and the lineup (part C and part D). The web app has no plot for them. Calculate them from the draws of a simulate score (step 7.2): for each term, count the chips of each simulated speaker, and compare the sd over the speakers with the data.
  • The prior predictive check of part B. The default w_sd: 3 is the scale that the notebook chose after that check.
  • The glyph maps, the boundary widths and the disc charts of part D. Fields and Colour swatches show the same quantities in a different form.
  • The adaptive choice of the next chip (part G). The port does not update one speaker from some answers, and it does not calculate the expected information gain.

Next steps:

  • Fit the pooled model and the three feature sets, and compare them with elpd_loo and the held-out metrics.
  • Fit a language with more terms, for example one of the five languages of part E.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Workflows to change the audit recipe.

docs.title: E79 CMB sky behind the LMC mask
docs.text:
This tutorial does the main part of the pymc-challenges notebook E79_cmb_field_level.py in the web app. You use the model sci.cmb_field@1. You do not write NumPy or PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project astronomy. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads two files from its data/ directory.
  • About 30 minutes. On a laptop, the fit took about 2 minutes.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the oldest light in the universe. Its temperature changes by about 100 µK from one part of the sky to another. These spots are a Gaussian random field. The power spectrum gives the strength of the spots at each angular scale (multipole ℓ ≈ 180° / angle).

The notebook uses a 16 × 16 degree patch of the Planck 2018 SMICA map. The patch is around the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The dust and the gas of the LMC are brighter than the CMB, so the Planck mask removes a hole of about 4 degrees. The mask also removes some small holes around bright radio sources. In total, 16.5% of the pixels have no data.

The notebook makes each pixel of the sky a parameter (field-level inference). It samples the sky together with the power spectrum in 26 bins (bandpowers). It asks two questions:

  1. What does the CMB look like behind the LMC, and how sure are we of each pixel? (Notebook part F.)
  2. Does the visible part of the patch agree with the Planck spectrum? (Notebook parts F and H.)

The notebook ends in this result: the LMC patch agrees with the Planck spectrum. The amplitude of the patch is within 1.4% of Planck (log amplitude −0.014 ± 0.023), and the tilt is −0.009 ± 0.030. Behind the LMC, the posterior mean is not a plausible sky. It is too smooth. Each posterior draw is a plausible sky, and each draw fills the hole differently. Thus show the draws and the sd map, not one "true" sky behind the mask.

What you will get, and the notebook part that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The dataset astronomy/planck_smica_lmc: the map with the mask, a noise map, the Planck spectrum and the pixel window Part A: the data, the mask and the noise from the half-mission maps A fit with the Wandelt-Eriksen Gibbs sampler (Runs) Part E: the Gibbs sampler The posterior of the 26 bandpowers, the amplitude and the tilt (Parameters, sci.power_spectrum) Part F, "Bandpowers", and part H, the amplitude-and-tilt model Sky maps with mean, sd and draws (Fields) Part F: the posterior sky, the sd map and the animation The observed map next to posterior skies (sci.ppc_image_grid) Part F: the posterior mean map and four posterior skies log_amplitude, tilt and bandpower_ratio with a 90% range (Score) Part H: amplitude and tilt on the real patch Skies of new patches with the same spectrum (Score, mode Simulate) Part B: "Is the real sky just a random draw?"

The port does not do parts C (the naive spectrum estimate), D (PyMC and HMC) and G (the coverage on simulated skies). See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads planck_smica_patches.npz and planck_theory_tt.txt. It writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. It prepares the map as the notebook does:

  • It averages the 3.75 arcmin pixels to 7.5 arcmin pixels: 128 × 128 pixels.
  • A pixel is usable only if all of its samples are inside the Planck common mask. The other pixels get NaN.
  • The noise sd of each pixel is the local rms of the half-mission half-difference map, smoothed over 1 degree.
  • The reference spectrum is the Planck 2018 best-fit TT spectrum, with the HEALPix pixel window of the source map.

Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e79 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out planck_smica_lmc.nc --spec planck_smica_lmc.yaml

The command writes:

wrote planck_smica_lmc.nc (variables temperature, noise_sd, reference_dl, pixel_window on row=128, col=128, multipole=4097)
upload it as dataset astronomy/planck_smica_lmc and fit sci.cmb_field
wrote the suggested spec to planck_smica_lmc.yaml

The file holds one dataset (about 370 KB):

Name Dims Type Meaning row, col 128, 128 integer, fixed The pixels of the patch. Row 0 is the bottom row multipole 4097 integer, fixed, 0 to 4096 The multipole ℓ of the spectrum temperature row, col float64, µK, target The SMICA temperature. NaN in 2,703 masked pixels (16.5%) noise_sd row, col float64, µK, weight The noise sd of each pixel: 1.5 µK to 3.4 µK reference_dl multipole float64, µK², constant The Planck best-fit spectrum D_ℓ = ℓ(ℓ+1)C_ℓ/2π pixel_window multipole float64, constant The HEALPix pixel window (Nside 2048)

The attributes of the file keep the constants of the map: pixel_arcmin 7.5, beam_fwhm_arcmin 5.0, pixel_subsamples 8, patch lmc and centre_lb_deg (280, −35). The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes a simulated patch from the model's own prior: a 32 × 32 map with a hole, a test spectrum and a known amplitude (1.15) and tilt (−0.1). Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real patch. For the simulated patch, use the settings of CMB_SPEC_YAML in mapi_plugin_science.cmb_data. With --synthetic, the --spec file has the bandpower bins of that spec (bin_edges), because the simulated patch is too small for the first default bin.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e79 --synthetic --out cmb_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type planck_smica_lmc in Name. Type a description, for example "Planck 2018 SMICA patch around the LMC, with the common mask and a noise map".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select planck_smica_lmc.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows temperature and noise_sd on row and col, and reference_dl and pixel_window on multipole.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, temperature has the role target, noise_sd the role weight, and reference_dl and pixel_window the role constant. Missingness shows 2,703 missing values in temperature. These are the masked pixels. The model does not fill them before the fit: a masked pixel has no data term.

Note

The file has no groups, so the upload makes a flat dataset. Do not open "Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)".

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows temperature and noise_sd on a grid of 128 × 128 pixels. temperature has values on the two sides of zero, thus its colour map has two colours.

  4. Click Profiles and spectra. The profiles show reference_dl and pixel_window along multipole (4,097 values). The x axis is logarithmic.
  5. The time sections are in Not for this data.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select planck_smica_lmc. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type cmb in the search field. Under Models, select Sky map behind a mask (CMB) (sci.cmb_field@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name planck-smica-lmc from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: planck-smica-lmc
  project: astronomy
data:
  dataset: dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest
model:
  use: sci.cmb_field@^1
  settings:
    pixel_arcmin: 7.5
    beam_fwhm_arcmin: 5.0
    pixel_subsamples: 8
    pixel_window: true
    projection: gnomonic
    border: 8
    field_draws: 40
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    engine: gibbs
    seed: 79
    tune: 16
    draws: 64
    chains: 4
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - sci.power_spectrum
    - sci.field_map
    - sci.image_residuals
    - sci.ppc_image_grid

The settings come from the suggested spec of the export (planck_smica_lmc.yaml). This table tells what each setting means for this patch:

Setting Value Meaning for this question pixel_arcmin 7.5 The side of a map pixel in arcmin. With 128 pixels, the patch is 16 degrees wide beam_fwhm_arcmin 5.0 The SMICA beam: a Gaussian with a FWHM of 5 arcmin. The model compares the data with the sky as Planck sees it, after the beam pixel_subsamples 8 Each 7.5 arcmin pixel is the mean of 8 × 8 point samples (a box window) pixel_window true Use the variable pixel_window: the HEALPix pixels of the source map also smooth the sky projection gnomonic Correct the multipoles for the mean stretch of the tangent-plane projection (about 1%). flat turns the correction off border 8 8 pixels (1 degree) without data on each side. The sky is periodic on a 144 × 144 torus, but the real patch is not periodic. Without the border, the seam makes false small-scale power field_draws 40 The number of sky maps that each score draws. The notebook animation also uses 40 skies

These settings keep their defaults, which are the values of the notebook:

  • bin_edges: the 26 bins of the notebook, from ℓ = 0 to ℓ = 2100.
  • ell_dense: 300: the dense preconditioner of CG for the 681 modes below ℓ = 300.
  • cg_tol: 1e-5: the stop rule of CG. A looser stop rule makes the large-scale bins too low (notebook part G).
  • rescale: true: the non-centred rescaling move. It helps in the bins where the noise is larger than the sky.
  • tilt_pivot: 500 and tilt_max_ell: 1450: the pivot of the tilt, and the three top bins that the amplitude-and-tilt summary leaves out (notebook part H).

Notes about the other blocks:

  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all of the pixels. The suggested spec of the export has evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mae, coverage_90]} and no split. With that spec, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation"). Remove the evaluate block and add mode: train_only.
  • tune: 16 and draws: 64 give 4 chains of 80 Gibbs iterations, as in the notebook. The first 16 iterations of each chain are burn-in.
  • engine: gibbs is the only engine of this model. The model has no NUTS.
  • The model has no pointwise log likelihood (loo_valid is false), because all of the pixels share one latent sky. Thus elpd_loo is not available. Compare two fits by their bandpowers, amplitude and tilt.

The plots

The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. The spec keeps all five plots that the model declares. sci.field_map, sci.image_residuals and sci.ppc_image_grid use the in-sample sky maps that the run makes after the fit. In the Insert panel, the Plots section adds a plot for you.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows "Gibbs iteration N of 80". The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://astronomy/planck-smica-lmc@v1. Click it.

All four chains run together. Each Gibbs iteration has three steps:

  1. A constrained realisation: a draw of the full sky (20,736 pixels on the torus) for the current bandpowers. Preconditioned conjugate gradients (CG) solve one linear system. In our fit, CG took about 370 iterations for each solve.
  2. A draw of each bandpower from its inverse-gamma distribution, given the sky.
  3. The rescaling move for each bin. It is almost always rejected in the large-scale bins and accepted about half of the time in the top bins. The notebook found the same.

After the fit, the run calculates the in-sample sky maps, the plots and the explorer views. You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

With 4 chains of 64 kept draws, expect these results:

Code Value Message RHAT 1.10 (error) "The independent sampler runs do not agree about 'q'. Its estimates are not reliable at this time." ESS_BULK 42 "There is too little independent information about 'q' (about 42 effective draws). The averages are not stable." ESS_TAIL 59 The same message for the intervals

These values agree with the notebook. The notebook reports "r_hat is at most 1.11 and bulk ESS runs from 28 to about 200 out of 256 draws - enough for bandpowers". The worst bins are in the middle of the spectrum (ℓ ≈ 600 and ℓ ≈ 1400). The amplitude and the tilt converge better: R-hat 1.01 and a bulk ESS of about 250.

If the diagnostic CG_NOT_CONVERGED shows, a CG solve stopped at cg_max_iter. Then the large-scale bandpowers can be too low. Increase cg_max_iter or ell_dense.

A longer fit

The RHAT error comes from the short chains of the notebook, not from a wrong model. Set tune: 40 and draws: 240 and fit again. On a laptop, this fit took about 4 minutes. It gave R-hat 1.04 (a warning) and a bulk ESS of 100. The amplitude and the tilt changed by less than 0.2 posterior sd.

On the model version page, the Plots tab has core.convergence. Its caption names the parameters that did not converge. The caption uses the limits 1.01 and 400 effective draws, so with 256 draws it lists all 80 values of q, bandpower and bandpower_ratio.

docs.title: 6.2 What did the model learn?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The posterior has these variables:

Variable Meaning q (bin) The log ratio of the bandpower to the Planck reference in each of the 26 bins bandpower (bin) The bandpower D_ℓ of each bin in µK² bandpower_ratio (bin) exp(q): the bandpower divided by the reference log_amplitude The log amplitude of the bandpowers relative to Planck tilt The tilt of the bandpowers relative to Planck, at ℓ = 500

The bin dim has the coords ell (the centre of the bin), ell_low and ell_high.

The main results, with the notebook values:

Quantity This fit Notebook Meaning log_amplitude −0.018 ± 0.022 −0.014 ± 0.023 The patch is within 2% of the Planck amplitude tilt 0.001 ± 0.030 −0.009 ± 0.030 No tilt relative to Planck bandpower_ratio at ℓ ≈ 80 1.39 ± 0.33 40% high, 25% uncertainty The largest departure. A 16-degree patch has few large-scale modes (cosmic variance) bandpower_ratio at ℓ ≈ 1950 1.17 ± 0.12 18% high The top bin Masked fraction 16.5% 16.5% (masked_fraction in the learned values) The LMC hole and the small holes

The amplitude and the tilt are the exact Gaussian posterior of the notebook's part H model, q_b = log A + tilt · log(ℓ_b / 500), with the bins below ℓ = 1450. The fit gives one draw of them for each Gibbs draw. The learned values also keep log_amplitude_mean, log_amplitude_sd, tilt_mean and tilt_sd.

On the model version page, open Plots and select sci.power_spectrum. Its caption says "The line is the median of bandpower in each bin of ell, from 256 draws of posterior. The shaded bands are the 50% and 90% intervals." The line must follow the acoustic peaks of the Planck spectrum, with wide bands at small ℓ and narrow bands at large ℓ. The plot does not draw the Planck reference. To compare with Planck, read bandpower_ratio in Parameters or score it (step 7.1). Each bin must be near 1.

docs.title: 6.3 The sky behind the LMC (Fields)
docs.text:
Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Select the output in Output:

  • sky is the sky as Planck sees it (after the beam), on row and col, in diverging colours. The view uses 40 posterior draws.
  • temperature_hat is the same map. It adds noise only in a predictive score, so here it is equal to sky.

Select sky and do these steps:

  1. Select Statistic Mean. Outside the mask, the map is the SMICA map. In the LMC hole, the mean continues the spots that cross the edge of the hole for a fraction of a degree. Then it fades to a smooth, almost flat level. The mean is the best single guess, but it is not a plausible sky.
  2. Select Std. dev. The sd is near the noise level (about 2.5 µK) where there are data. In the LMC hole, it rises to about 90 µK in the middle. That is almost the prior sd of a pixel: the data tell nothing there. The small holes around the radio sources are between, at about 37 µK.
  3. Select Draws and click Play the draws. This is the animation of the notebook. The pixels that stand still are known. The pixels that flicker are not known. Each draw fills the hole with spots of the correct size and contrast, and each draw is different.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one pixel.

The fit also keeps the derived group sky_moments: the mean and the sd of each pixel over all 256 kept Gibbs draws. The Fields view uses the 40 draws of the in-sample score, so its sd is a little noisier. In our fit, the mean sd over the LMC hole was 80 µK, with a maximum of 108 µK.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence R-hat and ESS of the bins (step 6.1) sci.power_spectrum The bandpowers with their 50% and 90% bands (step 6.2) sci.field_map The mean and the sd of sky. The sd map shows the LMC hole as a large bright area and the small holes as dots sci.image_residuals The observed temperature, the mean of sky, the residual and the normalised residual sci.ppc_image_grid The observed map next to 5 posterior skies on one colour scale. The observed map has an empty hole. Each sky fills the hole differently

The residual plot of this model

In our fit, the caption of sci.image_residuals says: "The normalised residuals have an sd of 0.28 and 0% are outside ±2 … Here the residuals are too small: the uncertainty is too large." For this model, that is not a sign of a bad fit. On this map, the sky is stronger than the noise at almost all the scales of the grid. Thus each sky draw follows the data closely, and the residual is small (about 0.7 µK). The sd of the draws is about the noise level (2.5 µK). The residual plot cannot separate the noise from the sky here. The notebook does the calibration check with simulated skies (part G), not with the residuals.

docs.title: 6.4 The decision
docs.text:
The decision. The visible part of the patch agrees with the Planck spectrum. Report the amplitude and the tilt with their posterior sd: −0.018 ± 0.022 and 0.001 ± 0.030 in this fit. Both are within one sd of zero. No bin is more than about 1.7 sd from Planck (in q).

For the sky behind the LMC, show the posterior draws and the sd map, not the mean alone. The mean is too smooth inside the hole. The draws are plausible skies, but no draw is "the" answer. The sd map shows where the data stop: inside the hole, the map knows almost nothing 1 to 2 degrees from the nearest data.

Remember that one 16-degree patch is 0.6% of the sky. The error bars are large. A systematic error of 1% to 2% (for example the projection correction) is small here, but it would be many sds on the full sky. Do step 10, "Next steps", to measure one of these systematic errors.

docs.title: 7. Score the model
docs.text: Each score draws new sky maps from the posterior. A score needs a dataset. Send the dataset that you fitted. The model uses its grid and its noise map.

docs.title: 7.1 The amplitude, the tilt and the bandpowers
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset.
  4. Type or select dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest in Dataset.
  5. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 79. Type log_amplitude, tilt, bandpower_ratio in Variables (optional).
  6. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each output.

No new data

The page does not show No new data for this model. The model cannot forecast, so a request without a dataset has no forecast horizon, and the server refuses it. A note under Values to score gives this reason.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://astronomy/planck-smica-lmc@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["log_amplitude", "tilt", "bandpower_ratio"]
  },
  "seed": 79
}

In our fit, the result was log_amplitude −0.018 (90% interval −0.055 to 0.005) and tilt 0.003 (−0.034 to 0.057). A score uses field_draws (40) posterior draws, not all 256. Thus its numbers are a little different from the Parameters section.

  • To get the sky maps, type sky in Variables (optional). Each draw is a constrained realisation, so the result is the mean and the 90% interval of each pixel.
  • To get a part of the map, add "select": {"row": [60, 61, 62], "col": [60, 61, 62]}.
  • "kind": "predictive" adds white noise with noise_sd to temperature_hat. It does not change sky.

docs.title: 7.2 Simulate new patches
docs.text:
simulate makes skies of a new patch with the spectrum of each posterior draw, plus noise. The data do not constrain these skies. The notebook asks the same question in part B: does the real sky look like a random draw with this spectrum?

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset, with the same dataset.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive.
  4. Type temperature_hat in Variables (optional). Set Draws to 8.
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://astronomy/planck-smica-lmc@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "sd"],
    "draws": 8,
    "vars": ["temperature_hat"]
  },
  "seed": 79
}

The result has 8 simulated maps of 128 × 128 pixels. The sd over the maps is about 96 µK in each pixel, the same as the rms of the real map (96 µK). A simulated map has no hole and no LMC. Compare it with the real map outside the mask. It must have spots of the same size and contrast.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_image_model_check (Image model check) is for models that predict an image. It fits the model, makes the residual maps and the image grid, does a posterior predictive check and writes a report.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Image model check and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select planck_smica_lmc in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.cmb_field@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set these values:
    • Settings: the settings of step 4 as JSON: {"pixel_arcmin": 7.5, "beam_fwhm_arcmin": 5.0, "pixel_subsamples": 8, "pixel_window": true, "projection": "gnomonic", "border": 8, "field_draws": 40}.
    • Draws 64, Tune 16, Chains 4 and Seed 79.
    • Var: sky.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

Set draws and tune

Set Draws and Tune before you run the recipe. The defaults are 1000 and 1000. For this model, that is 2,000 Gibbs iterations, about 25 times as long as the fit of step 5.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs shows the parameter table, the two plots, the coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges and the report. For this model, expect a coverage near 100% and the same note as in step 6.3. The sky draws follow the data closely, so the in-sample check cannot find a problem with the noise model.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does all the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws: a convergence gate, the posterior predictive check, sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Run it in the same way with the model sci.cmb_field@^1 and these changes:

  • Set Prior predictive to {}. This model does not sample its priors.
  • Set Draws 240 and Tune 40. Set Rhat max to 1.1 and Min ess to 50. With the defaults (1.01 and 400), the gate stops the audit for this model, because the Gibbs chains are short (step 6.1).
  • Set N sims to 5 for a first run.

Note

The checks of bayes_workflow_audit that fit the model again (sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated) each take as long as one fit or longer. With 5 simulated datasets, expect the audit to take half an hour or more.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/astronomy
mapi datasets upload planck_smica_lmc.nc --name planck_smica_lmc
mapi check planck-smica-lmc.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit planck-smica-lmc.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model planck-smica-lmc -s params -s diagnostics -s fields

cat > cmb-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://astronomy/planck-smica-lmc@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [log_amplitude, tilt, bandpower_ratio]}
seed: 79
EOF
mapi score cmb-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o cmb.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_image_model_check --name cmb-check
mapi workflows apply cmb-check.yaml -m "E79 image check"
mapi workflows run cmb-check -i data=dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest \
  -p model=sci.cmb_field@^1 -p var=sky -p draws=64 -p tune=16 -p seed=79 \
  -p 'settings={"pixel_window": true, "projection": "gnomonic", "border": 8}' \
  --watch

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/astronomy")
version = api.datasets.upload("planck_smica_lmc.nc", dataset="planck_smica_lmc")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("planck-smica-lmc.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "planck-smica-lmc")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://astronomy/planck-smica-lmc@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://astronomy/planck_smica_lmc@latest",
        "output": {"summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"], "vars": ["log_amplitude", "tilt"]},
        "seed": 79,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["log_amplitude"].values, summary["tilt"].values)

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the data of part A, the Gibbs sampler of part E, the posterior sky and the bandpowers of part F and the amplitude and tilt of part H. It leaves out these parts:

  • The Gaussian random field lessons (part B). The port has no plots of the Hartley modes or of the phases. simulate gives skies with the posterior spectrum instead.
  • The naive spectrum estimate (part C). The platform has no masked-map estimate to compare with. The notebook shows that such an estimate is biased at high ℓ.
  • The PyMC model with NUTS (part D). The centred and non-centred models, and the failure of HMC on a masked map, are not in the port. The model always uses the Gibbs sampler.
  • The coverage on simulated skies (part G). The notebook fits 8 simulated skies with a known, non-Planck spectrum and finds that 83% of the truths are in the 90% intervals. The platform does not do this check for you. The recovery.simulated check of bayes_workflow_audit (step 8) is the nearest replacement.
  • The amplitude-and-tilt model in PyMC (part H). The port calculates the same posterior exactly, inside the fit, as log_amplitude and tilt. It does not refit it on the 8 simulated skies.
  • The comparison with the SMICA inpainted map (part F). The dataset does not have the inpainted map. In the notebook, the inpainted map is within one posterior sd of the mean in 67% of the hole pixels. With cmb_data.challenges_reference() in Python, our fit gave 66%.
  • The Planck full-sky bandpowers and the theory curve in the plots. sci.power_spectrum shows the bandpowers of the patch only.
  • The north patch. The export reads only the LMC patch. In Python, cmb_data.from_challenges(path, patch="north") reads the other patch.

Next steps:

  • Fit the spec again with projection: flat and compare log_amplitude. The notebook finds a change of 1.4% (about 0.6 sd). This is the systematic error of step 6.4.
  • Fit the north patch. Make the dataset in Python with patch="north". It has almost no mask and about two times the noise.
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Model Explorer for more about the Fields section.

docs.title: E80 gravitational lens pixel by pixel (also the tree/HDF5 path)
docs.text:
This tutorial does the main part of the pymc-challenges notebook E80_strong_lensing.py in the web app. You use the model sci.strong_lens@1. You do not write PyMC or JAX code. The tutorial also shows the tree path: the same image as a NetCDF file with HDF5 groups, with the PSF in its own node.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and a project that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the project astronomy. If your project has a different name, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export command reads one file from its data/ directory.
  • About 40 minutes. On a laptop, the fit took 13 minutes: 3 minutes to find the mode and 10 minutes to sample.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A massive galaxy bends the light of a more distant galaxy. When the two galaxies are almost on one line, the distant galaxy becomes a ring around the near galaxy: an Einstein ring. The radius of the ring gives the mass inside the ring, dark matter included.

The notebook uses a Hubble Space Telescope image of the lens SDSS J1627-0053 (ACS, filter F814W). The lens galaxy is at redshift 0.2076 and the ring galaxy is at redshift 0.5241. The notebook predicts each of the 6,561 pixels of an 81 × 81 cutout. The prediction has the light of the lens galaxy, the lensed source galaxy, the blur of the telescope (the PSF) and the noise. The notebook asks three questions:

  1. How much mass is inside the ring, and how sure are we? (Notebook parts C and F.)
  2. What does the source galaxy look like without the lens? (Notebook part D.)
  3. What can an image not tell us? (Notebook part E.)

The notebook ends in this decision: report the Einstein radius and the mass inside it, with an error from the model choices, not from the posterior alone. The posterior gives θ_E = 1.2231 ± 0.0012 arcsec and M(<θ_E) = 2.258 ± 0.004 × 10¹¹ solar masses. That range is 0.1% to 0.2%. A different source model moves θ_E by two posterior sds, and the published models (1.21 and 1.23 arcsec) are 17 sds apart. Thus the true error is about 1% to 2%. The image alone does not give the slope of the mass profile or the size of the source: the mass-sheet degeneracy changes them and keeps the image the same.

What you will get, and the notebook part that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The dataset astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w: the image, a noise map and a PSF from the stars Part A: the noise in each pixel and the PSF The posterior of the 23 lens, light and source parameters and the noise scale (Parameters) Part C: the posterior with NUTS The predicted image and the source without the lens (Fields) Part C, the posterior predictive check, and part D, the source with its uncertainty The residual maps and the predicted images next to the real image (Plots) Part C: the residual panels einstein_radius and einstein_mass with a 90% range (Score) Part F: the mass in the ring Simulated images with noise (Score, mode Simulate) Part B: the prior predictive check, here from the posterior The derived group critical_curves Part F: the critical curves and caustics of 60 draws

The port does not do parts D (pixelated source) and E (mass-sheet degeneracy). See Differences from the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text:
The export command reads slacs_j1627_f814w.npz and writes a NetCDF file that the platform can read. It prepares the image as the notebook does:

  • It cuts the 81 × 81 pixels (4.05 arcsec) around the lens.
  • It measures the sky noise in an empty patch of the image.
  • It makes the noise map from the sky noise and the photon counts. weight is 1 / noise².
  • It makes the PSF from the median of the stars that are not near saturation (31 × 31).

Run the command from the root of the modeling-api repository:

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e80 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out slacs_j1627.nc --spec slacs_j1627.yaml

The command writes:

wrote slacs_j1627.nc (variables image, weight, psf on row=81, col=81, psf_row=31, psf_col=31)
upload it as dataset astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w and fit sci.strong_lens
wrote the suggested spec to slacs_j1627.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning row, col 81, 81 integer, fixed The pixels of the cutout. Row 0 is the bottom row psf_row, psf_col 31, 31 integer, fixed, −15 to 15 The pixels of the PSF kernel image row, col float64, electron/s, target The HST image weight row, col float64, s²/electron², weight The inverse variance of each pixel psf psf_row, psf_col float64, constant The PSF. Its sum is 1

The attributes of the file keep the constants of the image: pixel_scale 0.05 arcsec, noise_correlation 0.229, sky_sd 0.0059 electron/s, exptime 2224 s, z_lens 0.2076 and z_source 0.5241. The attribute mapi_schema gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes a simulated lens from the model's own forward model: a 24 × 24 image with 0.1 arcsec pixels, a Gaussian PSF and a known Einstein radius of 0.7 arcsec. Use it to try the steps. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real image. For the simulated lens, use the settings of LENS_SPEC_YAML in mapi_plugin_science.lens_data.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e80 --synthetic --out lens_synthetic.nc

docs.title: 2.1 Optional: the same data as a tree (HDF5 groups)
docs.text:
An instrument often writes the image and the PSF in different groups of one HDF5 file. The platform reads such a file as a tree dataset. Each group becomes a node. sci.strong_lens reads a tree: it takes the image from one node and the PSF from the node /psf.

To make the tree file from the export, run this Python script in the same directory:

import xarray as xr
from mapi_plugin_science import lens_data
from mapi_plugin_science.export import write_export

ds = xr.load_dataset("slacs_j1627.nc")
ds.attrs.pop("mapi_schema", None)  # the tree file gets its own tree schema
tree = lens_data.to_tree(ds)  # /image: image and weight; /psf: psf
write_export(tree, "slacs_j1627_tree.nc", schema=lens_data.LENS_TREE_SCHEMA)

The file slacs_j1627_tree.nc is NetCDF-4, that is HDF5 with one group for each node:

Node Variables Dims / none (the attributes only) none /image image (target), weight (weight) row 81, col 81 /psf psf (constant) psf_row 31, psf_col 31

Steps 3 and 4 show the plain dataset first and then the changes for the tree. The fit and the results are the same.

docs.title: 3. Upload the dataset
docs.text:
1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type slacs_j1627_f814w in Name. Type a description, for example "HST F814W image of the lens SDSS J1627-0053, with a noise map and a PSF".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select slacs_j1627.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows image and weight on row and col, and psf on psf_row and psf_col.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, image has the role target, weight the role weight and psf the role constant. Missingness shows no missing values.

docs.title: 3.1 The tree file
docs.text:
To upload the tree file, do the same steps with these changes:

  1. Type slacs_j1627_tree in Name.
  2. Select slacs_j1627_tree.nc. The format is also netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  3. Click Preview structure. The panel shows the groups /image and /psf with their arrays. A file with groups becomes a tree of nodes.
  4. Do not open "Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)". The groups of the file become the nodes below /.
  5. Click Upload and ingest.

The version page of a tree dataset shows the tabs Nodes, Missingness and About. Nodes shows /, /image and /psf. Click Explore this node to see one node in the Data Explorer.

A raw HDF5 file

An HDF5 file from an instrument (written with h5py) has arrays but no dim names. Select the format raw HDF5 (map the arrays) and click Upload and list the arrays. In Variables, give each array a name, a node and its dims: image and weight in node /image on row, col, psf in node /psf on psf_row, psf_col. Set the roles target, weight and constant. Refer to Tree datasets for the mapping file.

docs.title: 3.2 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Images and fields.

  3. The viewer shows image and weight (81 × 81 pixels) and psf (31 × 31 pixels). Look for the arc of the lensed galaxy around the lens.

  4. The statistics of each image give the fraction of saturated pixels.
  5. Correlations compares image and weight pixel by pixel.
  6. For the tree file, click Explore this node. The node /image has the two images of 81 × 81 pixels. The node /psf has the image of 31 × 31 pixels. The explorer finds the sections of each node separately.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4. Build the spec
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select slacs_j1627_f814w. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type lens in the search field. Under Models, select Gravitational lens from an image (sci.strong_lens@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name slacs-j1627-lens from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata:
  name: slacs-j1627-lens
  project: astronomy
data:
  dataset: dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest
model:
  use: sci.strong_lens@^1
  settings:
    pixel_scale: 0.05
    subsample: 2
    lens_light_components: 2
    external_shear: true
    noise_correlation: 0.2
    fit_noise_scale: true
    theta_e_median: 1.0
    theta_e_log_sd: 0.5
    n_starts: 5
    source_grid: 30
    source_half_width: 0.45
    curve_draws: 100
    z_lens: 0.2076
    z_source: 0.5241
  fit:
    mode: train_only
    seed: 80
    tune: 400
    draws: 600
    chains: 4
    target_accept: 0.9
outputs:
  plots:
    - core.convergence
    - core.posterior_forest
    - sci.image_residuals
    - sci.ppc_image_grid

The settings come from the suggested spec of the export (slacs_j1627.yaml). The spec adds some defaults so that you can see them. This table tells what each setting means for this image:

Setting Value Meaning for this question pixel_scale 0.05 The pixel size of the drizzled ACS image in arcsec. All angles (θ_E, the radii) are in arcsec subsample 2 The model traces 2 × 2 rays through each pixel. The ring is thin, so one ray for each pixel is too coarse lens_light_components 2 Two Sérsic profiles for the light of the lens galaxy, as in the notebook. The second one is a broad halo external_shear true Add the tidal pull of the galaxies near the lens. The notebook finds a shear of about 0.026 noise_correlation 0.2 Drizzle correlates the noise of neighbour pixels. The file attribute gives 0.23. With 0, the posterior sds are about 1.4 times too small (notebook "Failure 2") fit_noise_scale true Multiply the noise map by a free factor. The notebook finds 0.885: the noise map is too large by 13% theta_e_median, theta_e_log_sd 1.0, 0.5 The log-normal prior of θ_E: 1 arcsec, times or divided by about 1.6 n_starts 5 The starts of the search for the mode. Lens posteriors have wrong modes (notebook part C) source_grid, source_half_width 30, 0.45 The grid of the source output: 30 × 30 pixels over ±0.45 arcsec around the source curve_draws 100 The posterior draws that get a critical curve and a caustic z_lens, z_source 0.2076, 0.5241 The SLACS redshifts. With them, the model gives einstein_mass (flat ΛCDM, h0 70, omega_m 0.3)
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on all of the pixels. Without it, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation").
  • target_accept: 0.9 is the value of the notebook. At 0.8 the notebook got some divergences.
  • The spec has no evaluate block. Metrics need a holdout (data.split), and this fit uses all of the pixels. The recipe of step 8 measures the in-sample coverage.
  • The model has no pointwise log likelihood (loo_valid is false), so elpd_loo is not available.

The plots

The fit makes only the plots in outputs.plots. The model declares core.convergence, core.posterior_forest and sci.field_map. The spec keeps the first two and adds the two image checks sci.image_residuals and sci.ppc_image_grid. In the Insert panel, the Plots section adds a plot for you.

Do not add sci.field_map. The fit draws that plot from the first posterior variable with two dims, e_light, and not from the image. To see the predicted image as a map, use the Fields section of the Model Explorer (step 6.3).

docs.title: 4.1 The spec for the tree dataset
docs.text:
For the tree dataset, change the data block and add one setting:

data:
  dataset: dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_tree@latest
  nodes:
    image: {path: /image}
model:
  use: sci.strong_lens@^1
  settings:
    psf_source: tree
    # ... the other settings as above
  • data.nodes selects the node /image. The pipeline reads image and weight from it. In the Insert panel, the section Tree nodes adds a node. The toast "Node added" shows.
  • psf_source: tree tells the model to read the PSF from the node /psf. The flat input then does not need psf.
  • If you do not set psf_source: tree, the validator shows three SCHEMA_INVALID errors, for example "the model needs variable 'psf', but the pipeline does not make it". Another solution is to also select the node /psf in data.nodes.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the steps of the fit. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://astronomy/slacs-j1627-lens@v1. Click it.

The fit has four stages. The progress messages tell you the stage:

  1. "finding the mode in stages". The model fits the lens light first, with the ring masked. It reads the Einstein radius off the ring in the image without the lens light. Then it starts the full model from n_starts source positions and keeps the best. The notebook does the same staged start in part C, because starts from random prior draws end in wrong modes.
  2. "sampling the posterior". NUTS samples near the mode. A Laplace approximation at the mode removes the strong correlations before the warm-up. That is the job of nutpie's low-rank mass matrix in the notebook.
  3. "drawing the light amplitudes". The four brightness amplitudes are linear, so the fit integrates them out. After the fit, each draw gets its amplitudes from their exact conditional distribution.
  4. "tracing the critical curves". The model calculates the critical curve and the caustic of curve_draws draws.

After the fit, the run calculates the plots and the explorer views. You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer.

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer (group "Can you trust it?").

Expect these results:

Code Value Message RHAT 1.009 "The independent sampler runs agree with each other." ESS_BULK 352 "There is too little independent information about 'n_light' (about 352 effective draws). The averages are not stable." ESS_TAIL 309 The same message for the intervals DIVERGENCES 6 "The sampler had problems in 6 of 2400 steps. The results can be biased."

These warnings agree with the notebook. The notebook had one divergence in 2,400 draws and an ESS of "several hundred" for the index of the second light profile, n_light[2]. That profile is at the lower limit of its index (0.5, a Gaussian). It is a broad halo of the lens light, and its parameters are not of interest. The parameters of the lens have a high ESS. If you want fewer warnings, fit with tune: 1000 and draws: 1000.

On the model version page, the Plots tab has core.convergence. Its caption names the parameters that did not converge: n_light[2] and e_light[1, e1].

docs.title: 6.2 What did the model learn?
docs.text:
Open Parameters (group "What it learned"). The posterior has these variables:

Variable Meaning theta_E The Einstein radius in arcsec e_mass (e1, e2) The ellipticity of the mass xy_mass (x, y) The centre of the mass in arcsec, from the centre of the cutout shear (e1, e2) The external shear xy_light, R_light, n_light, e_light The centre, the half-light radii, the Sérsic indices and the ellipticities of the lens light R_src, n_src, e_src, xy_src The half-light radius, the Sérsic index, the ellipticity and the position of the source noise_scale The factor on the noise map amplitude The brightness of each light component and of the sky

The posterior mean and sd of the main parameters, with the notebook values:

Parameter This fit Notebook Meaning theta_E 1.2230 ± 0.0011 1.2231 ± 0.0012 The Einstein radius (arcsec) e_mass e1 −0.087 ± 0.004 −0.087 The mass is flat: axis ratio q ≈ 0.84 shear e1, e2 −0.026, 0.005 about 0.026 in total A small external shear xy_mass (−0.002, −0.006) within 0.01 of the light The mass centre is on the light centre, less than a fifth of a pixel away R_src 0.138 ± 0.004 0.14 The half-light radius of the source (arcsec) n_src 0.87 ± 0.04 0.87 The Sérsic index of the source: almost an exponential disc xy_src y −0.155 0.15 south The source is 0.15 arcsec south of the lens centre n_light[2] 0.52 ± 0.01 0.5 (at the limit) The second light profile is a broad halo noise_scale 0.884 ± 0.008 0.885 The noise map is too large by 13%

The model does not force the mass centre onto the light centre, but the data put it there. The Laplace approximation at the mode gives an sd of 0.00114 arcsec for theta_E. NUTS gives almost the same value. The fit stores it in the learned values as laplace_sd_theta_E.

docs.title: 6.3 The images (Fields)
docs.text:
Open Fields (group "What it learned"). The text says "The model has 2 outputs on a grid." Select the output in Output:

  • model_image is the predicted image on row and col, in a grey scale. Select Statistic Mean. It must look like the HST image: the lens galaxy at the centre and the ring around it. Std. dev. is small everywhere. Draws and Play the draws show that the draws are almost the same.
  • source is the source galaxy without the lens, on the source-plane grid (source_row, source_col). This is the notebook's "unlensed galaxy". Mean shows a small, smooth galaxy. Mean ÷ sd shows where its shape is certain.

Move the pointer over the map to read the values of one pixel.

On the model version page, open Plots:

Plot What to look for core.convergence R-hat near 1. A low ESS only for the second light profile (step 6.1) core.posterior_forest Very narrow intervals for theta_E, xy_mass and e_mass. Wider intervals for the source and the second light profile sci.image_residuals The real image, the mean prediction, the residual and the normalised residual. The normalised residual must look like noise with sd near 1, with no ring structure. A wrong lens leaves a pattern along the ring sci.ppc_image_grid The real image next to predicted images with noise, on one colour scale. You must not see which image is the real one

In this fit, the caption of sci.image_residuals says: "The normalised residuals have an sd of 1.07 and 7% are outside ±2." A perfect model gives 1 and 5%. Thus the model is close, but it leaves a small structure. Look at the residual panel for structure along the ring. In this fit, about 88% of the pixels are in their 90% predictive range.

docs.title: 6.4 How much mass is in the ring?
docs.text:
einstein_radius and einstein_mass are outputs of a score. Do step 7 to get them. These are the results:

Output Mean 90% interval Notebook einstein_radius (arcsec) 1.2230 1.2212 to 1.2249 1.2231 ± 0.0012 einstein_mass (solar masses) 2.259 × 10¹¹ 2.252 to 2.265 × 10¹¹ 2.258 ± 0.004 × 10¹¹

The published values are 1.23 arcsec (Bolton et al. 2008, with a 2% error) and 1.21 arcsec, 2.22 × 10¹¹ solar masses (Koopmans et al. 2006). The fit is between the two. The two published values are 0.02 arcsec apart. That is about 17 posterior sds. Thus the posterior range is not the real error of θ_E.

The decision. Report θ_E and the mass inside it. These two numbers are robust: the mass-sheet degeneracy does not change them. Do not report the posterior range alone. Use an error of about 2% from the model choices, as the SLACS papers do. Do not use this fit for the slope of the mass profile or the true size of the source. One image cannot give them.

docs.title: 7.1 The Einstein radius and the mass
docs.text:
1. On the model version page, click Score.
  2. In What do you want to do?, select Predict.
  3. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Then select slacs_j1627_f814w, the dataset of the fit.
  4. Open Advanced. Set Seed (optional) to 80. Type einstein_radius, einstein_mass in Variables (optional).
  5. Click Predict.

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval (hdi_90) of each output.

This is the request that the page sends (POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{v}:score):

{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://astronomy/slacs-j1627-lens@latest",
  "mode": "predict",
  "data": "dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "expected",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "vars": ["einstein_radius", "einstein_mass"]
  },
  "seed": 80
}

docs.title: 7.2 Simulated images
docs.text:
simulate makes new images from the posterior: each draw gives an image with correlated noise, at the noise level of the fit.

  1. In What do you want to do?, select Simulate.
  2. In Values to score, select Use a dataset. Then select slacs_j1627_f814w, the dataset of the fit.
  3. Open Advanced. Set Quantity to Predictive.
  4. Type model_image in Variables (optional). Set Draws to 20.
  5. Click Simulate.
{
  "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
  "kind": "ScoreRequest",
  "model": "model://astronomy/slacs-j1627-lens@latest",
  "mode": "simulate",
  "data": "dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest",
  "output": {
    "kind": "predictive",
    "summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"],
    "draws": 20,
    "vars": ["model_image"]
  },
  "seed": 80
}

The Results card shows the mean and the 90% interval of each pixel, and the result has 20 simulated images. The mean is the predicted image. In this fit, the sd of the simulated images is about 0.011 electron/s for each pixel: the noise of the image plus the small spread of the posterior. Compare one simulated image with the real image. It must look like a second exposure of the same lens.

  • To get a part of the image, add "select": {"row": [40, 41, 42], "col": [40, 41, 42]}.
  • "kind": "predictive" in a predict request also adds the noise.
  • The score always uses the PSF that the fit stored. The tree dataset is not necessary to score.

If you promote the version to an endpoint, Integrations → the endpoint → Schema and Try it sends the same requests.

docs.title: 8. Run a workflow recipe
docs.text:
The recipe sci_image_model_check (Image model check) is for models that predict an image. It fits the model, makes the residual maps and the image grid, does a posterior predictive check and writes a report.

  1. Set the header to Guided and open Recipes. In Expert mode, open Workflows and then the Templates tab.
  2. Find the card Image model check and click Run on my data.
  3. In 1. Your data, select slacs_j1627_f814w in Dataset.
  4. In 2. What the recipe needs to know, type sci.strong_lens@^1 in Model.
  5. Open Fine-tune (optional: the defaults are correct for most data). Set these values:
    • Settings: the settings of step 4 as JSON, for example {"pixel_scale": 0.05, "subsample": 2, "lens_light_components": 2, "noise_correlation": 0.2, "z_lens": 0.2076, "z_source": 0.5241}.
    • Draws 600, Tune 400 and Seed 80.
    • Var: model_image. The model has two outputs on a grid, and the check is for the image.
  6. Click Run this recipe.

The monitor of the run has the tabs Graph, Steps, Decisions, Outputs and Events. Outputs shows the parameter table, the two plots, the coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges and the report.

The recipe bayes_workflow_audit (Bayesian workflow audit) does all the checks of a Bayesian workflow on any model with draws: a convergence gate, the posterior predictive check, sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated. Run it in the same way with the model sci.strong_lens@^1. Set Prior predictive to {}, because this model does not sample its priors. The gate needs the smallest bulk ESS at or above Min ess (400). In step 6, the bulk ESS of n_light is 352, so the default gate can stop the audit. Increase Draws, or set Min ess to 300.

Note

The checks of bayes_workflow_audit that fit the model again (sensitivity.prior and recovery.simulated) each take as long as one fit. With 20 simulated datasets, the audit of the lens takes some hours. Set N sims to 5 for a first run.

docs.title: 9. The same with the CLI and the Python client
docs.text:
CLIPython 
mapi use <tenant>/astronomy
mapi datasets upload slacs_j1627.nc --name slacs_j1627_f814w
mapi check slacs-j1627-lens.yaml --remote @     # the server's static validation
mapi fit slacs-j1627-lens.yaml --remote @       # create or revise the spec, fit, follow
mapi explore model slacs-j1627-lens -s params -s diagnostics

cat > lens-score.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: model://astronomy/slacs-j1627-lens@latest
mode: predict
data: dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], vars: [einstein_radius, einstein_mass]}
seed: 80
EOF
mapi score lens-score.yaml --remote @ --model <model id> --version 1 -o lens.zarr.zip

mapi workflows init sci_image_model_check --name lens-check
mapi workflows apply lens-check.yaml -m "E80 image check"
mapi workflows run lens-check -i data=dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest \
  -p model=sci.strong_lens@^1 -p var=model_image \
  -p 'settings={"pixel_scale": 0.05, "subsample": 2, "lens_light_components": 2, "noise_correlation": 0.2, "z_lens": 0.2076, "z_source": 0.5241}' \
  -p draws=600 -p tune=400 -p seed=80 --watch

The tree file uploads in the same way: mapi datasets upload slacs_j1627_tree.nc --name slacs_j1627_tree. The ingest makes one node for each group. A local mapi check spec.yaml --data <file>.tree.zip reads the tree schema of a tree dataset.

The CLI has no models command. Take the model id from the run (mapi runs get <run>) or from Models in the web app.

from mapi_client import Client

api = Client(project="<tenant>/astronomy")
version = api.datasets.upload("slacs_j1627.nc", dataset="slacs_j1627_f814w")
print(version.ref, version.status.value)

with open("slacs-j1627-lens.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    spec_yaml = fh.read()
revision = api.specs.upsert(spec_yaml)
run = api.runs.fit(revision.spec_id, revision.revision)
run = api.runs.wait(run.id, raise_on_failure=True)

model = next(m for m in api.models.list() if m.name == "slacs-j1627-lens")
result = api.models.score(
    model.id,
    model.latest_version,
    {
        "model": "model://astronomy/slacs-j1627-lens@latest",
        "mode": "predict",
        "data": "dataset://astronomy/slacs_j1627_f814w@latest",
        "output": {"summary": ["mean", "hdi_90"], "vars": ["einstein_radius", "einstein_mass"]},
        "seed": 80,
    },
)
summary = result.tree["summary"]  # an xr.DataTree (needs the `xarray` extra)
print(summary["einstein_radius"].values, summary["einstein_mass"].values)

api.datasets.upload also takes an xr.DataTree. Thus you can upload the tree of step 2.1 without a file: api.datasets.upload(tree, dataset="slacs_j1627_tree").

docs.title: 10. Differences from the notebook
docs.text:
The port keeps the forward model and the posterior of notebook part C, and the mass of part F. It leaves out these parts:

  • The tests of the deflection with automatic differentiation (part B). The package tests of the plugin do the same checks.
  • The prior predictive check (part B). The model does not sample its priors. simulate gives images from the posterior instead.
  • The failures (part C). You can do "Failure 2" again: fit with noise_correlation: 0 and compare the sd of theta_E. "Failure 1" (no PSF) needs a dataset with a 1 × 1 PSF.
  • The full whitening of the drizzle noise. The notebook whitens the noise in Fourier space with the measured correlation. The model uses one lag-one correlation along the rows and the columns.
  • The pixelated source and the Bayesian evidence (part D). The source output is the parametric Sérsic source of each draw on a grid, not a free pixel source. Thus the model does not give the second value θ_E = 1.2253 arcsec of the notebook.
  • The mass-sheet degeneracy (part E). The platform does not show it. The decision of step 6.4 keeps its result: use θ_E and the mass inside it, not the slope.
  • The velocity dispersion (part F). The model does not give σ_SIE (273 km/s in the notebook).
  • The plots of the critical curves and the caustics. The fit stores them in the derived group critical_curves, but no plot recipe draws them yet.

Next steps:

  • Fit the spec again with external_shear: false and compare the shape of the mass with the published shear-free models (axis ratio 0.91 to 0.92).
  • Fit another SLACS lens. Make the same three variables (image, weight, psf) from its MAST image (notebook "Try it yourself", item 2).
  • Read the model reference for the other science models.
  • Read Tree datasets for more about nodes, HDF5 and files with several nodes.

docs.title: E81 wind directions and animal activity (circular)
docs.text:
This tutorial does the work of the pymc-challenges notebook E81_circular_data.py in the web app. You use the model sci.circular_regression@1. You do not write PyMC code.

You need:

  • The platform (start it with make dev) and two projects that you can upload datasets to. This tutorial uses the projects meteorology (the wind) and ecology (the camera traps). If your projects have different names, change the project part of each dataset:// and model:// reference, and metadata.project in the specs.
  • A local copy of pymc-challenges. The export commands read one file each from its data/ directory.
  • About 20 minutes. The two fits of the main path take about one minute of sandbox time together.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Some measurements are angles. A wind blows from a direction between 0 and 360 degrees, and 359 degrees is next to 1 degree. An animal walks past a camera at a time of day, and 23:59 is next to 00:01. An arithmetic mean or a normal likelihood on these values can give a wrong answer with high confidence. The notebook uses two real datasets:

  • Wind at Santa Barbara airport (ASOS station KSBA, 2021 to 2023). At night, cool air flows down from the mountains to the sea. In the afternoon, the sea breeze blows inland. Thus the direction turns through half of the compass each day, and the turn changes with the season.
  • Camera traps on Barro Colorado Island, Panama (Rowcliffe et al. 2014). The ocelot hunts at night. The data give the time of day of 16,282 photographs of the ocelot and five animals that it can hunt.

The notebook asks these questions:

  1. How does the wind direction change with the hour and the season, and how sure are you? (Notebook parts B and D.)
  2. Which model of the direction predicts better on a year that it did not see? The models are one von Mises direction for each hour and season, a projected normal and a mixture of two wind regimes. (Part D, LOO and the held-out year 2023.)
  3. When is the ocelot active, and how much does its day overlap with the day of each prey animal? (Part E, the log-Fourier density, the overlap and the activity level.)

The notebook ends with these decisions:

  • Use the von Mises in its natural parameters (the canonical link). It has one mode, and it has no seam at ±180 degrees. Do not use a uniform prior on an angle.
  • For the wind, a mixture of two regimes predicts much better than one direction for each hour. The single von Mises puts mass between the two lobes of the evening rose, where the wind seldom blows.
  • Report the overlap of two activity curves with its posterior range. The ocelot overlaps least with the agouti (0.30) and most with the brocket, the spiny rat and the paca (0.66 to 0.75).

What you will get, and the notebook section that each item replaces:

In the web app Notebook The rose of the observed directions with the range of the model in each sector (sci.rose) Part D, the circular posterior predictive check The density of the direction in each block of three hours, with mean, sd and draws (Fields, sci.field_map) Part B, the rose diagrams by hour, and part D, the model roses The mean direction and the mean resultant length of each block of three hours (Score) Part D, the clock of wind arrows elpd_loo of the 12,023 reports of 2021 and 2022 (Metrics) Part D, "Which model predicts better?" The circular holdout metrics of 2023 (Score, mode Evaluate) Part D, the held-out year The activity density of each species (Fields, sci.profile_bands) Part E, the log-Fourier density The overlap of each pair of species, and the activity level of each species (Fields and Score) Part E, the overlap and the activity level

See Differences from the notebook for the parts that the port leaves out.

docs.title: 2. Get the data
docs.text: The two datasets have different cases in the export command: e81 for the wind and e81b for the camera traps. Run the commands from the root of the modeling-api repository.

docs.title: 2.1 The wind
docs.text:
The export reads asos_ksba_2021_2023.csv.gz. It removes the calm reports, because a calm wind has no direction. It uses Pacific standard time (UTC − 8) all year, so that the sea breeze follows the sun and not the clock.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e81 \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out ksba_wind_2021_2023.nc --spec ksba_wind_2021_2023.yaml

The command writes:

wrote ksba_wind_2021_2023.nc (variables wind_from, hour_lst, day_of_year, year on report=18049)
upload it as dataset meteorology/ksba_wind_2021_2023 and fit sci.circular_regression
wrote the suggested spec to ksba_wind_2021_2023.yaml

The file holds one dataset:

Name Dims Type Meaning report 18,049 integer, policy extend The reports in time order. The 6,026 reports of 2023 are the last ones wind_from report float64, target, deg The direction that the wind blows from, clockwise from true north. ASOS gives it in steps of 10 degrees hour_lst report float64, covariate, h Hours since midnight, local standard time day_of_year report float64, covariate, d Days since 1 January, with the fraction of the day year report int64, constant The year of the report: 6,096 reports in 2021, 5,919 in 2022 and 6,026 in 2023

docs.title: 2.2 The camera traps
docs.text:
The export reads bci_camera_trap_times.csv. It keeps the ocelot and the five prey species of the notebook, and it changes the time of each photograph to hours since midnight.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e81b \
    --challenges <path to pymc-challenges>/data \
    --out bci_camera_traps.nc --spec bci_camera_traps.yaml

The command writes:

wrote bci_camera_traps.nc (variables clock_time, species_idx on record=16282, species=6)
upload it as dataset ecology/bci_camera_traps and fit sci.circular_regression
wrote the suggested spec to bci_camera_traps.yaml
Name Dims Type Meaning record 16,282 integer, policy extend One photograph species 6 categorical, policy fixed ocelot, agouti, paca, rat, brocket and peccary clock_time record float64, target, h The time of day of the photograph, 0 to 24 hours species_idx record int64, index of species The species of the photograph

The attribute mapi_schema of each file gives each variable its role, so you do not map columns.

No pymc-challenges copy?

--synthetic writes data that the model itself simulates, with known parameters. The wind file has 480 reports of one year (2021). The camera-trap file has 700 records of three groups (owl, lark and drifter). Use them to try the steps. Remove the split line from the wind spec of step 4, because the synthetic file has no year 2023. The numbers in this tutorial are for the real data.

uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e81 --synthetic --out wind.nc
uv run python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e81b --synthetic --out activity.nc

docs.title: 3. Upload the datasets
docs.text:
Do these steps in the project meteorology for the wind file. Then do them again in the project ecology for the camera-trap file.

  1. Open Datasets in the sidebar.
  2. Click New dataset.
  3. Type ksba_wind_2021_2023 in Name. Type a description, for example "Hourly wind directions at Santa Barbara airport, 2021 to 2023, without calms".
  4. Click Create dataset. The upload panel opens.
  5. Click Choose files and select ksba_wind_2021_2023.nc.
  6. Make sure that the format is netCDF (or HDF5 written by xarray).
  7. Optional: click Preview structure. The panel shows Structure of the file. Make sure that it shows four variables on report.
  8. Optional: type a message in Version message (optional).
  9. Click Upload and ingest.

For the camera traps, use the name bci_camera_traps and the file bci_camera_traps.nc. Structure of the file shows clock_time and species_idx on record, and the coordinate species.

The ingest run reads the file in the sandbox. When it is done, the version page shows the tabs Schema, Coordinates, Missingness, Preview and About. On Schema, wind_from has the role target and the units deg. clock_time has the role target and the units h.

Each file is one plain dataset. You do not need the tree fields ("Put this file in a node of a tree (optional)") or the HDF5 path.

docs.title: 3.1 Explore the data
docs.text:
Look at the data before you build the spec.

  1. On the version page, click Explore this version. The Data Explorer opens. The sections under Pictures of the data come first.

  2. Click Directions and times of day.

  3. For the wind, the roses show wind_from (bins of 10°, north at the top, clockwise), hour_lst (24 bins) and day_of_year. There is one rose for each year.

  4. The heat map of hour_lst and wind_from shows the sea breeze: in the afternoon, the wind comes from the sea.
  5. For the camera traps, there is one rose of clock_time for each of the 6 species. Compare the roses: some species are active at night, and other species in the day.
  6. The Rayleigh test tells if the values have a preferred direction or time.
  7. Over time and the time patterns are in Not for this data. report and record are lists of observations, not time.

Refer to Scientific data.

docs.title: 4.1 The wind
docs.text:
1. Open Build and click New spec. The editor opens with the geo MMM template.
  2. Set the Editor view to YAML.
  3. Open the Insert panel on the right.
  4. Open the Datasets section and select ksba_wind_2021_2023. The toast "Dataset set" shows.
  5. Type circular in the search field. Under Models, select Directions and times of day (sci.circular_regression@^1). The toast "Model set" shows.
  6. Select all the text in the editor and paste the full spec below. The template has other blocks (a pipeline, a split and the MMM plots), so the spec must replace all of it.
  7. Click Validate. The status shows valid.
  8. Click Save spec. The spec gets its name ksba-wind-direction from metadata.name.

This is the full spec:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: ksba-wind-direction, project: meteorology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://meteorology/ksba_wind_2021_2023@latest
  bind:
    dims: {obs: report}
    vars: {direction: wind_from, hour: hour_lst, day: day_of_year}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: obs, last: 6026}
model:
  use: sci.circular_regression@^1
  settings: {kind: von_mises, units: degrees, daily_harmonics: 3, annual_harmonics: 2,
             interaction_harmonics: 2}
  fit: {mode: train_only, seed: 81, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, engine: nutpie,
        keep: {log_likelihood: true, posterior_predictive: {thin: 20}}}
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
outputs:
  plots: [core.convergence, core.posterior_forest, sci.rose, sci.profile_bands, sci.field_map]

The model calls its row dim obs, the target direction, and the covariates hour and day. The bind block connects them to the names in the dataset.

The split and the fit mode do the same as the notebook:

  • split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: obs, last: 6026} keeps the last 6,026 reports (all of 2023) out of the fit.
  • fit.mode: train_only fits on the 12,023 reports of 2021 and 2022, and it does not fit again on all reports. Thus the model version is the model of the notebook, and you can score 2023 in step 7.
  • keep.log_likelihood: true keeps the log density of each report, for elpd_loo.
  • keep.posterior_predictive: {thin: 20} keeps simulated directions from 200 draws, for the rose of sci.rose.

The suggested spec of the export (ksba_wind_2021_2023.yaml) is the same spec without sci.profile_bands in the plots.

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind von_mises One von Mises direction for each report. The hour and the day of the year move its natural parameters η = F B (the canonical link). The mean direction is atan2(η₂, η₁) and the concentration is |η|. regime_mixture is the mixture of two regimes (section 6.5) units degrees The direction is in degrees. A turn is 360. Use hours for a time of day and radians for radians daily_harmonics 3 The cosine and the sine of 1, 2 and 3 cycles each day. Midnight is next to 00:01 annual_harmonics 2 The cosine and the sine of 1 and 2 cycles each year. 31 December is next to 1 January interaction_harmonics 2 The first two daily harmonics times the first annual harmonic. The daily turn of the wind can change with the season. With 3, 2 and 2, the model has 19 features, the same as the notebook intercept_sd, coef_sd 2, 1 (default) The prior sds of the intercepts and of the other coefficients, as in the notebook frames 8 (default) The density output has one row for each block of 24 / 8 = 3 hours, as the rose diagrams of the notebook angle_points 72 (default) The density output has 72 angles, one each 5 degrees rows_per_frame 200 (default) The density of a block is the mean of the densities of up to 200 fit reports in that block score_draws 400 (default) The number of posterior draws that one score uses

Settings that do not agree

Validate does a check of each setting by itself. It does not compare two settings. For example, interaction_harmonics: 4 with daily_harmonics: 3 shows valid, but the run stops with SETTINGS_INVALID.

docs.title: 4.2 The camera traps
docs.text:
Make a second spec in the project ecology. Do the steps of section 4.1 with the dataset bci_camera_traps and the name bci-ocelot-activity:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: bci-ocelot-activity, project: ecology}
data:
  dataset: dataset://ecology/bci_camera_traps@latest
  bind:
    dims: {obs: record}
    vars: {direction: clock_time, species_idx: species_idx}
model:
  use: sci.circular_regression@^1
  settings: {kind: activity, units: hours, group_dim: species, harmonics: 16, tau_sd: 2.0,
             grid_points: 256}
  fit: {mode: train_only, seed: 81, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, engine: nutpie,
        keep: {log_likelihood: true}}
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
outputs: {plots: [core.convergence, sci.field_map, sci.profile_bands]}

The settings for this question:

Setting Value What it means here kind activity One log-Fourier density for each species: log f(θ) = Σ aₖ cos kθ + bₖ sin kθ − log Z. It has no components, so no labels can change places units hours The angle is a time of day. A turn is 24 hours group_dim species The dim of the groups. The index variable is species_idx harmonics 16 The number of Fourier terms K, as in the notebook tau_sd 2.0 The prior is aₖ, bₖ ~ N(0, (τ/k)²) with τ ~ HalfNormal(2) for each species. Higher harmonics shrink more. This prior sets how smooth each curve is grid_points 256 The number of angles in the sum that gives Z angle_points 72 (default) The density output has 72 times of day, one each 20 minutes

fit.mode: train_only fits on all records. The spec has no split. Without this line, the validator shows the warning SPLIT_INVALID ("There is no holdout for the evaluation"). The suggested spec of the export (bci_camera_traps.yaml) does not have this line, so add it.

engine: nutpie is the sampler of the notebook. The default engine of the model is pymc.

docs.title: 5. Fit and watch the run
docs.text:
1. Click Fit. The app opens the run page.
  2. The badge shows Live while the run sends events.
  3. The Progress card shows the progress of the sampler. The Events card shows the stages of the run and, at the end, the diagnostics. The Logs card stays empty when the model writes no output.
  4. When the run is done, the Result card shows Inspect model://meteorology/ksba-wind-direction@v1. Click it.

On a laptop with nutpie, the wind fit took 45 seconds and the camera-trap fit took 21 seconds. After the sampler, the run calculates the pointwise log densities, the simulated directions, the density field, the plots and the explorer views.

You can also find the run under Runs. Filter it with the kind fit.

docs.title: 6. Read the result
docs.text: On the model version page, the tabs are Overview, Diagnostics, Plots, Data tree, Preprocessing and Provenance. Click Explore to open the Model Explorer. Sections that do not apply to this model are under "Does not apply".

docs.title: 6.1 Can you trust the fit?
docs.text:
Open Diagnostics in the Model Explorer, or the plot Sampler convergence on the Plots tab. In the wind fit for this tutorial, there were no divergences. The largest R-hat was 1.003 and the smallest bulk ESS was 6,416 (of 4,000 draws). The caption says "All 614 parameters look converged". This count includes the cells of the density field.

In the camera-trap fit, there were no divergences. The largest R-hat was 1.010 and the smallest bulk ESS was 578. Both values are for the standardised coefficients za and zb.
